LeetCode 206 Easy Master Edition

Reverse Linked List

An engineering deep dive into pointer manipulation, call stack unwinding mechanics, and reversing singly linked lists.

Problem Statement

Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list, and return the new head of the reversed list.

Constraints

  • The number of nodes in the list is in the range [0, 5000].
  • -5000 <= Node.val <= 5000

Visualizing the Intent

Initial Linked List: head -> [1] -> [2] -> [3] -> [4] -> [5] -> NULL Target Reversed Linked List: NULL <- [1] <- [2] <- [3] <- [4] <- [5] <- new_head Example 1: Input: head = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] Output: [5, 4, 3, 2, 1] Example 2: Input: head = [1, 2] Output: [2, 1] Example 3: Input: head = [] Output: []

Core Realization: Reversing a linked list does not mean swapping the values inside the nodes. Instead, we alter the direction of the physical next pointers pointing from node to node.

Solutions Breakdown

Approach 1 - Iterative Three-Pointer Technique

🧭 Intuition Breakdown (Iterative Pointer Flipping)

1. The Concept: Walk down the linked list node by node. For each node curr, flip its next arrow backward so it points to prev instead of forward.

2. Why We Need Three Pointers (prev, curr, next_node):
When you execute curr.next = prev, you instantly sever the original link to the rest of the list! To avoid losing track of the remaining nodes, you must preserve the next address in a temporary variable next_node = curr.next before flipping the link.

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition: Linked list ko reverse karne ke liye hume nodes ke andar ke numbers badalne ki zaroorat nahi hai. Hum bas nodes ke bich ke next arrow (pointer) ki direction ko ulti taraf ghuma dete hain.

Lekin jab hum curr.next = prev karte hain, toh aage ka raasta toot jata hai! Isliye aage wale node ka pata khone se bachne ke liye, link todne se PEHLE hum next_node = curr.next karke aage wale node ko store kar lete hain.

📋 Approach 1 Iterative Trace

Input: 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> NULL

Initial State: prev = NULL, curr = [1] Step 1 (at Node 1): • Preserve next: next_node = curr.next ([2]) • Reverse link: curr.next = prev (NULL) • Advance pointers: prev = [1], curr = [2] State: NULL <- [1] curr = [2] -> [3] -> NULL Step 2 (at Node 2): • Preserve next: next_node = curr.next ([3]) • Reverse link: curr.next = prev ([1]) • Advance pointers: prev = [2], curr = [3] State: NULL <- [1] <- [2] curr = [3] -> NULL Step 3 (at Node 3): • Preserve next: next_node = curr.next (NULL) • Reverse link: curr.next = prev ([2]) • Advance pointers: prev = [3], curr = NULL State: NULL <- [1] <- [2] <- [3] (prev) curr = NULL Loop Terminates (curr == NULL). Return prev ([3]).

a) Source Code Implementation (Iterative)

class Solution:
    def reverseList(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        prev = None  # Initialize prev pointer to None as new tail points to NULL
        curr = head  # Set curr pointer to start at head of original list

        while curr:  # Process nodes iteratively until reaching end of list
            next_node = curr.next  # Store pointer to next node before breaking current link
            curr.next = prev  # Reverse pointer direction: point curr.next backward to prev
            prev = curr  # Move prev pointer forward to current node
            curr = next_node  # Move curr pointer forward to next node

        return prev  # Return prev which now points to new head of reversed list
class Solution {
public:
    ListNode* reverseList(ListNode* head) {
        ListNode* prev = nullptr;  // Track previous node (initially null)
        ListNode* curr = head;     // Current node pointer starts at head

        while (curr != nullptr) {  // Loop until curr reaches null boundary
            ListNode* nextNode = curr->next;  // Temporarily save next node reference
            curr->next = prev;                // Reverse current node's next pointer
            prev = curr;                    // Advance prev to current node
            curr = nextNode;                // Advance curr to saved next node
        }
        return prev;  // prev points to the new head of reversed list
    }
};
class Solution {
    public ListNode reverseList(ListNode head) {
        ListNode prev = null;  // Initialize previous node reference to null
        ListNode curr = head;  // Set current worker pointer to list head

        while (curr != null) {  // Traverse list until end
            ListNode nextNode = curr.next;  // Preserve reference to remaining list
            curr.next = prev;            // Invert link: point curr.next backward to prev
            prev = curr;                // Shift prev forward to curr
            curr = nextNode;            // Shift curr forward to nextNode
        }
        return prev;  // prev is new head of reversed list
    }
}
var reverseList = function(head) {
    let prev = null;  // Set initial prev reference to null
    let curr = head;  // Set initial curr reference to head

    while (curr !== null) {  // Iterate through nodes
        let nextNode = curr.next;  // Save pointer to next node
        curr.next = prev;          // Flip next pointer backward to prev
        prev = curr;              // Step prev pointer forward
        curr = nextNode;          // Step curr pointer forward
    }
    return prev;  // Return prev as new head
};

Approach 2 - Recursive Explicit Reference Reversal (`front` Pointer Method)

🧭 Deep Intuition Breakdown (Bottom-Up Stack Inversion)

1. The Core Idea: Recursion allows us to drill down to the very last node of the list first. Once we reach the last node, we return it as the newHead. As the recursion call stack unwinds (backtracks), each node forces its next node (stored explicitly as front) to point back to itself!

2. The Exact 3-Step Reversal Logic:
Suppose we are at node head = [1], and its child node is head.next = [2].
When returning from the recursive call on node [2], we execute the three-step pointer shift:

  • Step 1 (front = head.next): Capture explicit reference to the next node [2].
  • Step 2 (head.next = None): Sever node [1]'s original forward link to prevent an infinite cyclic loop.
  • Step 3 (front.next = head): Point node [2]'s next pointer backward to node [1]!

Before Inversion (at Node 1): [1] --------> [2] --------> NULL head front (head.next) Step 1: front = head.next (Explicitly reference [2]) Step 2: head.next = None [1] [2] --------> NULL head front Step 3: front.next = head NULL <----- [1] <====== [2] head front (Clean backward link established!)
Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition behind Recursion: Recursion me hum sabse pehle list ke aakhri node tak deep jaate hain. Jo aakhri node hota hai, wo humara **newHead** ban jata hai aur poore raaste me return hota rehta hai.

Jab call stack wapas peeche (unwind/backtrack) aata hai, toh hum 3-step logic chalate hain:

  • front = head.next: Apne se aage wale node (e.g. Node 2) ko front variable me store karo.
  • head.next = None: Apne purane aage wale link ko tod do taaki cycle na bane.
  • front.next = head: Node 2 (front) ko bolo ki wo apna pointer piche Node 1 (head) ki taraf ghumaye!

Call Stack Unwinding Diagram

Below is the original recursion call stack diagram from your public folder (rev_recursion_diagram):

📋 Full Trace Dry Run 1: Standard Multi-Node Call Stack Trace

Input: 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> NULL

================================================================================= PHASE 1: WINDING THE CALL STACK (Drilling down to base case) ================================================================================= 1. Call reverseList(Node 1): head = [1] - Base case check (head == null or head.next == null): False. - Recursive call: newHead = reverseList(Node 2) [PAUSED] 2. Call reverseList(Node 2): head = [2] - Base case check: False. - Recursive call: newHead = reverseList(Node 3) [PAUSED] 3. Call reverseList(Node 3): head = [3] - Base case check: False. - Recursive call: newHead = reverseList(Node 4) [PAUSED] 4. Call reverseList(Node 4): head = [4] - Base case check: head.next == null is TRUE! (Node 4 is the tail) - Base Case Hit! Returns Node [4] directly as newHead. ================================================================================= PHASE 2: UNWINDING THE CALL STACK (Backtracking pointer reversal) ================================================================================= • Unwinding Frame 3: Processing Node [3] (head = [3], head.next = [4], newHead = [4]) - Step 1: front = head.next => front = Node [4] - Step 2: head.next = None => Node [3].next = NULL - Step 3: front.next = head => Node [4].next = Node [3] - Current Sub-List State: 4 -> 3 -> NULL - Returns newHead = Node [4] • Unwinding Frame 2: Processing Node [2] (head = [2], head.next = [3], newHead = [4]) - Step 1: front = head.next => front = Node [3] - Step 2: head.next = None => Node [2].next = NULL - Step 3: front.next = head => Node [3].next = Node [2] - Current Sub-List State: 4 -> 3 -> 2 -> NULL - Returns newHead = Node [4] • Unwinding Frame 1: Processing Node [1] (head = [1], head.next = [2], newHead = [4]) - Step 1: front = head.next => front = Node [2] - Step 2: head.next = None => Node [1].next = NULL - Step 3: front.next = head => Node [2].next = Node [1] - Current Sub-List State: 4 -> 3 -> 2 -> 1 -> NULL - Returns newHead = Node [4] Final Returned List: 4 -> 3 -> 2 -> 1 -> NULL (newHead is Node 4)
📋 Full Trace Dry Run 2: Two-Node Minimal Pair

Input: 1 -> 2 -> NULL

1. Call reverseList(Node 1): head = [1] - Not base case. Calls reverseList(Node 2). 2. Call reverseList(Node 2): head = [2] - Base Case Hit! (head.next == NULL). Returns Node [2] as newHead. 3. Backtrack to Node 1: - head = [1], newHead = [2] - front = head.next => front = Node [2] - head.next = None => Node [1].next = NULL - front.next = head => Node [2].next = Node [1] - Returns newHead = Node [2] Result: 2 -> 1 -> NULL
📋 Full Trace Dry Run 3 (Edge Case): Single Node & Empty List

Case A: Input head = [1]

1. Call reverseList(Node 1): head = [1] - Base case check: head.next == NULL is TRUE! - Returns Node [1] directly without recursion. Result: [1]

Case B: Input head = NULL

1. Call reverseList(NULL): head = NULL - Base case check: head == NULL is TRUE! - Returns NULL directly. Result: NULL

a) Source Code Implementation (Recursive)

class Solution:
    def reverseList(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        # Base case: empty list or reach last node
        if head == None or head.next == None:
            return head  # Return tail node as new reversed head

        # Recurse down to last node; newHead remains tail node throughout call stack
        newHead = self.reverseList(head.next)

        # HIGHLIGHT: Explicit 3-step pointer inversion logic
        front = head.next       # Step 1: Explicit reference to next node
        head.next = None         # Step 2: Sever original forward link
        front.next = head        # Step 3: Point next node back to current head

        return newHead  # Pass newHead up call stack
class Solution {
public:
    ListNode* reverseList(ListNode* head) {
        // Base Case: return head if list is empty or at single tail node
        if (head == nullptr || head->next == nullptr) {
            return head;  // Return new head reference
        }

        // Recursive call down to list end
        ListNode* newHead = reverseList(head->next);

        // HIGHLIGHT: Explicit pointer inversion logic
        ListNode* front = head->next;  // Step 1: Reference next node
        head->next = nullptr;            // Step 2: Sever forward link
        front->next = head;              // Step 3: Invert link backward

        return newHead;  // Return new head pointer
    }
};
class Solution {
    public ListNode reverseList(ListNode head) {
        // Base case check: if list is empty or at end node
        if (head == null || head.next == null) {
            return head;  // Return tail node reference
        }

        // Drill down recursively
        ListNode newHead = reverseList(head.next);

        // HIGHLIGHT: Explicit pointer inversion logic
        ListNode front = head.next;  // Step 1: Capture front reference
        head.next = null;            // Step 2: Clear forward link
        front.next = head;           // Step 3: Point front backward to head

        return newHead;  // Propagate newHead up stack
    }
}
var reverseList = function(head) {
    // Base case condition
    if (!head || !head.next) {
        return head;  // Return tail node
    }

    // Recursive step
    let newHead = reverseList(head.next);

    // HIGHLIGHT: Explicit pointer inversion logic
    let front = head.next;  // Step 1: Reference next node
    head.next = null;        // Step 2: Disconnect original forward link
    front.next = head;       // Step 3: Point front backward to head

    return newHead;  // Return new head
};

Strategic Edge Cases Tracking Matrix

To ensure system stability, solutions are validated against critical boundary edge cases:

Edge Case Profile Algorithmic Risk Factor Mitigation Resolution Logic
Empty List
e.g., head = NULL		 Null pointer dereference when accessing head.next. Handled by guard condition if head == None: return head. Exits safely before checking head.next.
Single Node List
e.g., head = [1]		 Unnecessary stack allocation or loop execution. Base case if head.next == None: return head triggers immediately. Returns [1].
Two-Node List
e.g., head = [1, 2]		 Cyclic loop creation if old forward pointer is not disconnected. Executing head.next = None explicitly severs the forward link before setting front.next = head.

Complexity Analysis Performance Metrics

Approach Category Time Complexity Space Complexity Performance Evaluation Rating
Approach 1: Iterative Three-Pointer O(N) O(1) Optimal Space Standard. Reverses pointers in-place using constant extra memory.
Approach 2: Recursive Stack Backtracking O(N) O(N) Call Stack Elegant Code / Stack Overhead. Uses implicit call stack of depth N. Space complexity is O(N) due to call stack frames.

content:
LeetCode 1358 Medium Master Edition

An exhaustive engineering manual analyzing sliding window counting, suffix extension properties, and last-seen index tracking architectures.

Problem Statement

Given a string s consisting only of characters 'a', 'b' and 'c'.

Return the number of substrings containing at least one occurrence of all three characters 'a', 'b' and 'c'.

Constraints

  • 3 <= s.length <= 5 x 10^4
  • s consists only of characters 'a', 'b', or 'c'.

Visualizing the Intent

Let's map out the problem spatial geometry. Suppose we are given the input string:

Input String: s = "abcabc" Index Mapping: 0 1 2 3 4 5 a b c a b c Valid Substrings Containing 'a', 'b', and 'c': 1. s[0..2] -> "abc" 2. s[0..3] -> "abca" 3. s[0..4] -> "abcab" 4. s[0..5] -> "abcabc" 5. s[1..3] -> "bca" 6. s[1..4] -> "bcab" 7. s[1..5] -> "bcabc" 8. s[2..4] -> "cab" 9. s[2..5] -> "cabc" 10. s[3..5]-> "abc" Total Valid Substrings = 10

Core Realization: Once a valid window s[left...right] contains all 3 characters ('a', 'b', 'c'), every extension of this window to the right (i.e. s[left...right+1], s[left...right+2], ..., up to s[left...n-1]) will ALSO contain all 3 characters! Alternatively, for a fixed end index i, any start index from 0 up to the minimum(last_seen['a'], last_seen['b'], last_seen['c']) forms a valid substring ending at i.

Solutions Breakdown

Approach 1 - Brute Force (Nested Substring Generation)

🧭 Intuition Breakdown (Checking All Windows)

1. The Concept: The most direct strategy is to test every possible contiguous substring s[i...j]. We run two nested loops: index i marks the start of the substring and index j marks the end. As j expands to the right, we maintain character frequency counts. As soon as all 3 characters ('a', 'b', 'c') have a count > 0, we increment our valid substring counter.

2. Why it Fails Constraints: For a string of length N = 50,000, there are N*(N+1)/2 ≈ 1.25 x 10^9 possible substrings. Running a nested iteration over 1.25 billion items will instantly trigger a Time Limit Exceeded (TLE) error.

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition: Sabse pehla seedha tarikha yeh hai ki hum do nested loops chalayein: i start index aur j end index. Har sub-window me a, b, aur c ke frequencies update karte rahein. Jaise hi teenon characters kam se kam ek baar mil jayein, hum valid count ko +1 kar dete hain. Lekin N = 50,000 ke liye O(N^2) loops chalenge (1.25 billion iterations), jisse TLE aayega.

📋 Approach 1 Trace Profile

Input: s = "abc"

i = 0 ('a'): • j = 0 ('a') -> freq: a=1, b=0, c=0 -> Invalid • j = 1 ('b') -> freq: a=1, b=1, c=0 -> Invalid • j = 2 ('c') -> freq: a=1, b=1, c=1 -> Valid! count = 1 i = 1 ('b'): • j = 1 ('b') -> Invalid • j = 2 ('c') -> Invalid i = 2 ('c'): • j = 2 ('c') -> Invalid Total Count: 1

a) Source Code Implementation

class BruteForceSolution:
    def numberOfSubstrings(self, s: str) -> int:
        count = 0  # Initialize valid substring counter
        n = len(s)  # Store string length
        
        for i in range(n):  # Outer loop fixing substring start index i
            freq = {'a': 0, 'b': 0, 'c': 0}  # Reset frequency map for current window
            for j in range(i, n):  # Inner loop expanding end index j
                freq[s[j]] += 1  # Increment count for current character s[j]
                if freq['a'] > 0 and freq['b'] > 0 and freq['c'] > 0:  # Check all 3 present
                    count += 1  # Increment result counter
                    
        return count  # Return total valid substrings
class BruteForceSolution {
public:
    int numberOfSubstrings(string s) {
        int count = 0;  // Initialize output count
        int n = s.length();  // Get string length
        
        for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {  // Outer loop for start index
            vector<int> freq(3, 0);  // Frequency array for 'a', 'b', 'c'
            for (int j = i; j < n; ++j) {  // Inner loop for end index
                freq[s[j] - 'a']++;  // Update character count
                if (freq[0] > 0 && freq[1] > 0 && freq[2] > 0) {  // Check presence
                    count++;  // Increment total count
                }
            }
        }
        return count;  // Return total count
    }
};
class BruteForceSolution {
    public int numberOfSubstrings(String s) {
        int count = 0;  // Initialize count
        int n = s.length();  // Length of string
        
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {  // Outer loop
            int[] freq = new int[3];  // Frequency array
            for (int j = i; j < n; j++) {  // Inner loop
                freq[s.charAt(j) - 'a']++;  // Increment frequency
                if (freq[0] > 0 && freq[1] > 0 && freq[2] > 0) {  // Validate presence
                    count++;  // Increment valid count
                }
            }
        }
        return count;  // Return total
    }
}
var numberOfSubstrings = function(s) {
    let count = 0;  // Initialize counter
    const n = s.length;  // Get length
    
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {  // Outer loop
        const freq = [0, 0, 0];  // Frequency array
        for (let j = i; j < n; j++) {  // Inner loop
            freq[s.charCodeAt(j) - 97]++;  // Update character count (97 is 'a')
            if (freq[0] > 0 && freq[1] > 0 && freq[2] > 0) {  // Check all present
                count++;  // Increment result
            }
        }
    }
    return count;  // Return final count
};

Approach 2 - Optimal Solution: Sliding Window (Two Pointers)

🧭 Intuition Breakdown (Window Expansion & Suffix Math)

1. The Core Extension Shortcut: Imagine expanding a right pointer right from 0 to N-1. Maintain a left pointer left to track the dynamic window s[left...right].

When our window s[left...right] becomes valid (contains at least one 'a', 'b', and 'c'), think about what happens if we append more characters to the right end of this window:

If window s[left...right] is VALID: Then: - s[left...right] is VALID - s[left...right+1] is VALID - s[left...right+2] is VALID ... - s[left...N-1] is VALID Total valid substrings starting at this `left` index = (N - right)

2. The Shrinking Mechanics: Once s[left...right] is valid, we add (n - right) to our total result. Then we increment left (shrink window from left) and check if the window remains valid. We repeat this shrinking loop until the window becomes invalid, then continue expanding right.

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition behind Sliding Window: Jab hume ek window s[left...right] milti hai jisme 'a', 'b', 'c' teenon hain, toh uske aage right se leke string ke end tak (index N-1) hum kitne bhi characters jod dein, wo saare substrings VALID hi rahenge!

Isliye, ek valid window milte hi hum seedhe (N - right) count me add kar dete hain! Uske baad left pointer ko 1-step aage badha kar window choti karte hain aur dekhte hain ki kya ab bhi teenon characters bache hain.

📋 Sliding Window Dynamic Visual Dry Run

Dry Run: s = "abcabc" (N = 6)

Initialize: left = 0, count = 0, freq = {a:0, b:0, c:0} • right = 0 ('a'): freq = {a:1, b:0, c:0} -> Invalid • right = 1 ('b'): freq = {a:1, b:1, c:0} -> Invalid • right = 2 ('c'): freq = {a:1, b:1, c:1} -> VALID! - Add (N - right) = (6 - 2) = 4 to count. (count = 4) - Substrings counted starting at left=0: "abc", "abca", "abcab", "abcabc" - Shrink window: decrement s[left]='a', left moves to 1. - New freq = {a:0, b:1, c:1} -> Invalid. Loop breaks. • right = 3 ('a'): freq = {a:1, b:1, c:1} -> VALID! - Add (N - right) = (6 - 3) = 3 to count. (count = 4 + 3 = 7) - Substrings counted starting at left=1: "bca", "bcab", "bcabc" - Shrink window: decrement s[left]='b', left moves to 2. - New freq = {a:1, b:0, c:1} -> Invalid. Loop breaks. • right = 4 ('b'): freq = {a:1, b:1, c:1} -> VALID! - Add (N - right) = (6 - 4) = 2 to count. (count = 7 + 2 = 9) - Substrings counted starting at left=2: "cab", "cabc" - Shrink window: decrement s[left]='c', left moves to 3. - New freq = {a:1, b:1, c:0} -> Invalid. Loop breaks. • right = 5 ('c'): freq = {a:1, b:1, c:1} -> VALID! - Add (N - right) = (6 - 5) = 1 to count. (count = 9 + 1 = 10) - Substrings counted starting at left=3: "abc" - Shrink window: decrement s[left]='a', left moves to 4. - New freq = {a:0, b:1, c:1} -> Invalid. Loop breaks. Final Total Count = 10

a) Source Code Implementation

class BetterSolution:
    def numberOfSubstrings(self, s: str) -> int:
        freq = {'a': 0, 'b': 0, 'c': 0}  # Frequency dictionary for active window
        left = 0  # Left pointer defining start of window
        count = 0  # Total valid substring accumulator
        n = len(s)  # Total length of input string

        for right in range(n):  # Expand right pointer defining end of window
            freq[s[right]] += 1  # Include character s[right] in frequency count

            # While current window s[left...right] contains all 3 characters
            while freq['a'] > 0 and freq['b'] > 0 and freq['c'] > 0:
                count += n - right  # Add all valid rightward extensions starting at left
                freq[s[left]] -= 1  # Remove character s[left] before shrinking window
                left += 1  # Shrink window from left

        return count  # Return accumulated total
class BetterSolution {
public:
    int numberOfSubstrings(string s) {
        vector<int> freq(3, 0);  // Frequency array for 'a', 'b', 'c'
        int left = 0;  // Left boundary pointer
        int count = 0;  // Result accumulator
        int n = s.length();  // String length

        for (int right = 0; right < n; ++right) {  // Right boundary expansion loop
            freq[s[right] - 'a']++;  // Update character count

            // Shrink window as long as all three characters are present
            while (freq[0] > 0 && freq[1] > 0 && freq[2] > 0) {
                count += n - right;  // Add remaining valid suffix count
                freq[s[left] - 'a']--;  // Decrement left character count
                left++;  // Advance left pointer
            }
        }
        return count;  // Return total valid substrings
    }
};
class BetterSolution {
    public int numberOfSubstrings(String s) {
        int[] freq = new int[3];  // Frequency array mapping 'a'->0, 'b'->1, 'c'->2
        int left = 0;  // Left window boundary
        int count = 0;  // Valid substring counter
        int n = s.length();  // String length

        for (int right = 0; right < n; right++) {  // Expand right boundary
            freq[s.charAt(right) - 'a']++;  // Increment frequency

            // Check if active window is valid
            while (freq[0] > 0 && freq[1] > 0 && freq[2] > 0) {
                count += n - right;  // Accumulate all suffixes starting at left
                freq[s.charAt(left) - 'a']--;  // Remove left char from count
                left++;  // Shrink window
            }
        }
        return count;  // Return total count
    }
}
var numberOfSubstrings = function(s) {
    const freq = [0, 0, 0];  // Frequency array
    let left = 0;  // Left pointer
    let count = 0;  // Substring count accumulator
    const n = s.length;  // String length

    for (let right = 0; right < n; right++) {  // Expand right pointer
        freq[s.charCodeAt(right) - 97]++;  // Update frequency (97 is ASCII 'a')

        // Shrink window while valid
        while (freq[0] > 0 && freq[1] > 0 && freq[2] > 0) {
            count += n - right;  // Add all remaining valid substrings
            freq[s.charCodeAt(left) - 97]--;  // Decrement left char
            left++;  // Advance left pointer
        }
    }
    return count;  // Return total count
};

Approach 3 - Most Optimal Solution: Last-Seen Index Tracking

🧭 Deep Intuition Breakdown (Looking Backward from Right Index)

1. The Core Inversion Idea: Instead of asking "how many valid substrings START at index left?", let's flip our perspective and ask: "For a fixed END index i, how many valid start indices exist?"

2. Tracking Last-Seen Positions: Maintain an array last_seen = [-1, -1, -1] storing the most recent index where characters 'a', 'b', and 'c' were encountered during a single iteration from index i = 0...N-1.

For a fixed ending index i, what is the furthest right index by which ALL three characters have appeared at least once? It is simply the minimum of the three last-seen positions:

min_idx = min(last_seen['a'], last_seen['b'], last_seen['c'])

3. Why min_idx + 1 Gives the Exact Count:
If min_idx != -1, it means a valid window ending at i can start at min_idx. But notice: any start index from 0 up to min_idx will ALSO form a valid substring ending at i!

Example: s = "a b c a b c" Index: 0 1 2 3 4 5 At i = 3 (s[3] = 'a'): - last_seen['a'] = 3 - last_seen['b'] = 1 - last_seen['c'] = 2 min_idx = min(3, 1, 2) = 1 (character 'b') Valid start indices for substrings ending at i=3 ('a'): - start = 1: s[1..3] -> "bca" (Valid!) - start = 0: s[0..3] -> "abca" (Valid!) Total valid start indices = min_idx + 1 = 1 + 1 = 2!

4. Why This Is Single-Pass O(N) and O(1) Space:
We do not need a nested while-loop to shrink pointers! In a single linear scan, updating last_seen and adding min_idx + 1 instantly counts all valid substrings ending at index i in O(1) time per character.

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition behind Last-Seen Index: Aage dekhne ki bajaye hum peeche dekhte hain! Har index i par khade hokar socho: "Iss index i par KHATAM hone wale kitne valid substrings hain?"

Hum teenon characters ('a', 'b', 'c') ke sabse latest (last seen) index ko ek array last_seen = [-1, -1, -1] me track karte hain. Teeno me se sabse piche wala (minimum) index min_idx yeh batata hai ki piche kahan tak 'a', 'b', 'c' teenon mil chuke hain.

Agar min_idx mila, toh index 0 se lekar min_idx tak **har ek start position** valid substring banayegi! Iska matlab index i par khatam hone wale total (min_idx + 1) valid substrings hain. Bina kisi inner while-loop ke direct O(1) me count add ho jata hai!

class Solution:
    def numberOfSubstrings(self, s: str) -> int:
        last_seen = {'a': -1, 'b': -1, 'c': -1}  # Track last seen index of 'a', 'b', 'c'
        count = 0  # Initialize valid substring counter

        for i, char in enumerate(s):  # Iterate with index i and character token
            last_seen[char] = i  # Update last seen index for current character
            
            # Find minimum index among 'a', 'b', 'c' (furthest left required character)
            min_idx = min(last_seen['a'], last_seen['b'], last_seen['c'])
            
            # If min_idx != -1, add (min_idx + 1) valid substrings ending at index i
            count += min_idx + 1

        return count  # Return total count
class Solution {
public:
    int numberOfSubstrings(string s) {
        vector<int> last_seen(3, -1);  // Array storing last seen index for 'a' (0), 'b' (1), 'c' (2)
        int count = 0;  // Output accumulator
        int n = s.length();  // String length

        for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {  // Linear scan
            last_seen[s[i] - 'a'] = i;  // Record current character index
            
            // Minimum of all 3 last-seen indices gives number of valid start positions
            int min_idx = min({last_seen[0], last_seen[1], last_seen[2]});
            
            // If all 3 characters have appeared, min_idx >= 0, adding min_idx + 1
            count += min_idx + 1;
        }
        return count;  // Return final result
    }
};
class Solution {
    public int numberOfSubstrings(String s) {
        int[] lastSeen = new int[]{-1, -1, -1};  // Array tracking last index of 'a', 'b', 'c'
        int count = 0;  // Total valid substrings counter
        int n = s.length();  // Length of string

        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {  // Single pass linear traversal
            lastSeen[s.charAt(i) - 'a'] = i;  // Update last seen index
            
            // Calculate minimum index among all 3 characters
            int minIdx = Math.min(lastSeen[0], Math.min(lastSeen[1], lastSeen[2]));
            
            // Add valid start indices count ending at current index i
            count += minIdx + 1;

    }

Strategic Edge Cases Tracking Matrix

To ensure system robustness, solutions must handle extreme boundary conditions without index out-of-bounds or logical overflow:

Edge Case Profile Algorithmic Risk Factor Mitigation Resolution Logic
Missing One/Two Characters Entirely
e.g., s = "aaaaa" or s = "ababbba"		 Risk of adding negative numbers if min_idx = -1 is not guarded. With last_seen = [-1, -1, -1], min_idx = -1. Adding min_idx + 1 = 0 adds 0 to total count cleanly without extra if-conditions!
Minimal Valid Length String
e.g., s = "abc"		 Boundary edge where full string is the only valid substring. At i=0,1 count+=0. At i=2 ('c'), last_seen = [0, 1, 2], min_idx = 0. Adds 0 + 1 = 1. Correctly returns 1.
Repeated Characters Before Last Needed Character
e.g., s = "aaaaabc"		 Risk of undercounting preceding valid start positions. At i=6 ('c'), last_seen['a'] = 4, last_seen['b'] = 5, last_seen['c'] = 6. min_idx = 4. Adds 4 + 1 = 5 ("aaaaabc", "aaaabc", "aaabc", "aabc", "abc"). Captures all 5 valid start positions!

Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array

An exhaustive engineering manual analyzing binary search inflection boundaries, sorted-half elimination patterns, and duplicate element handling.

Problem Statement

Suppose an array of length n sorted in ascending order is rotated between 1 and n times. For example, the array nums = [0,1,2,4,5,6,7] might become:

  • [4,5,6,7,0,1,2] if it was rotated 4 times.
  • [0,1,2,4,5,6,7] if it was rotated 7 times (or 0 times).

Given the sorted rotated array nums, return the minimum element of this array.

You must write an algorithm that runs in O(log n) time when elements are unique.

Constraints

  • n == nums.length
  • 1 <= n <= 5000
  • -5000 <= nums[i] <= 5000
  • nums is sorted and rotated between 1 and n times.

Visualizing the Intent

Let's map out how array rotation splits a monotonic sequence into two sorted sub-segments:

Unrotated Sorted Array: [ 0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7 ] <- Min element is at index 0 Rotated Array (4 times): [ 4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2 ] \_________/ \_________/ Segment A Segment B (Higher) (Lower) Key Property: - Segment A is sorted: 4 < 5 < 6 < 7 - Segment B is sorted: 0 < 1 < 2 - EVERY element in Segment A is strictly GREATER than EVERY element in Segment B! - The pivot/inflection point where Segment A meets Segment B drops sharply from 7 -> 0. - The MINIMUM element is located at the exact start of Segment B (the inflection point)!

Solutions Breakdown

Approach 1 - Brute Force (Linear Scan)

🧭 Intuition Breakdown (Linear Inspection)

1. The Concept: Walk through the array element by element from index 0 to n - 1, maintaining a tracker variable min_val. Return the minimum value after traversing all elements.

2. Why it Fails Constraints: While linear scan guarantees finding the answer in O(n) time, the problem explicit constraint requires an O(log n) solution.

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition: Index 0 se lekar n - 1 tak ek single loop chalayein aur sabse chhota number track kar lein. Lekin isme O(n) time lagta hai. Problem me strictly O(log n) bola gaya hai, isliye linear scan reject ho jata hai.

a) Source Code Implementation

class Solution:
    def findMin(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        min_val = nums[0]  # Initialize tracking variable with first element
        for num in nums:  # Scan each number sequentially across list
            if num < min_val:  # Check if current number is smaller than recorded minimum
                min_val = num  # Update minimum tracking variable
        return min_val  # Return minimum element found
class Solution {
public:
    int findMin(vector<int>& nums) {
        int min_val = nums[0];  // Seed tracking variable with initial element
        for (int num : nums) {  // Range-based loop traversing vector
            if (num < min_val) {  // Compare element with current minimum
                min_val = num;  // Update minimum reference
            }
        }
        return min_val;  // Return smallest integer
    }
};
class Solution {
    public int findMin(int[] nums) {
        int minVal = nums[0];  // Initialize tracking variable with nums[0]
        for (int num : nums) {  // Enhanced for loop iterating through array
            if (num < minVal) {  // Evaluate smaller value condition
                minVal = num;  // Update minimum variable
            }
        }
        return minVal;  // Return final minimum value
    }
}
var findMin = function(nums) {
    let minVal = nums[0];  // Set default candidate minimum
    for (let num of nums) {  // Iterative for-of loop
        if (num < minVal) {  // Compare current element against minVal
            minVal = num;  // Reassign minimum
        }
    }
    return minVal;  // Return minimum value
};

Approach 2 - Sorted Half Elimination Pattern (Unique Elements Only)

🧭 Intuition Breakdown (Identifying Monotonic Halves)

1. The Deep Structural Concept: A rotated sorted array consists of two sorted sub-segments. When we compute a middle index mid = start + (end - start) // 2, it divides the search space into two halves: [start...mid] and [mid...end].

Because the original array was strictly sorted, at least one of these two halves MUST be completely sorted in non-decreasing order:

  • Case 1: Left Half is Sorted (nums[start] <= nums[mid])
    If the left half is sorted, the absolute smallest element in this left section is guaranteed to be nums[start]. We record res = min(res, nums[start]) as a candidate minimum. Having recorded this minimum, we eliminate the entire left half by moving start = mid + 1 to search the unsorted right half.
  • Case 2: Right Half is Sorted (nums[mid] <= nums[end])
    If the right half is sorted, the absolute smallest element in this right section is guaranteed to be nums[mid]. We record res = min(res, nums[mid]) as a candidate minimum. Having recorded this minimum, we eliminate the entire right half by moving end = mid - 1 to search the unsorted left half.
Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition: Rotated array me jab bhi hum mid nikalte hain, toh ek side (Left ya Right) **hamesha 100% sorted** hoti hai.

• Agar nums[start] <= nums[mid], toh Left side sorted hai. Left side ka sabse chhota number nums[start] hoga. Hum res = min(res, nums[start]) me candidate minimum save karte hain, aur bache hue right part me dhoondhne ke liye start = mid + 1 kar dete hain.

• Agar nums[mid] <= nums[end], toh Right side sorted hai. Right side ka sabse chhota number nums[mid] hoga. Hum res = min(res, nums[mid]) me candidate save karte hain, aur bache hue left part me dhoondhne ke liye end = mid - 1 kar dete hain.

(0 <= 1) -> TRUE! - Meaning: The left half [0, 1] is monotonically sorted. - The minimum element in this left half is nums[start] = 0. - Update global result: res = min(4, 0) = 0. - Eliminate sorted left half: start = mid + 1 = 5 + 1 = 6. - New Range: start = 6, end = 6. Search window = [2]. ================================================================================= ITERATION 3: (start = 6, end = 6) ================================================================================= • Calculate mid: mid = 6 + (6 - 6) // 2 = 6 - nums[start] = nums[6] = 2 - nums[mid] = nums[6] = 2 - nums[end] = nums[6] = 2 • Condition Check 1: Is nums[start] <= nums[mid]? (2 <= 2) -> TRUE! - Minimum element in this single element window is nums[start] = 2. - Update global result: res = min(0, 2) = 0. - Eliminate left half: start = mid + 1 = 6 + 1 = 7. ================================================================================= LOOP TERMINATION ================================================================================= • Loop condition start <= end (7 <= 6) is FALSE! • Loop terminates completely. • Return res -> 0. Final Answer Returned: 0
📋 Full Line-by-Line Trace Dry Run 2: Minimum in Left Half (Small Shift)

Input: nums = [5, 1, 2, 3, 4] (N = 5)

Initial State: start = 0 (nums[0] = 5) end = 4 (nums[4] = 4) res = Infinity ================================================================================= ITERATION 1: (start = 0, end = 4) ================================================================================= • Calculate mid: mid = 0 + (4 - 0) // 2 = 2 - nums[start] = nums[0] = 5 - nums[mid] = nums[2] = 2 - nums[end] = nums[4] = 4 • Condition Check 1: Is nums[start] <= nums[mid]? (5 <= 2) -> FALSE! • Condition Check 2: Is nums[mid] <= nums[end]? (2 <= 4) -> TRUE! - Meaning: The right half [2, 3, 4] is monotonically sorted. - The minimum element in this right half is nums[mid] = 2. - Update global result: res = min(Inf, 2) = 2. - Eliminate sorted right half: end = mid - 1 = 2 - 1 = 1. - New Range: start = 0, end = 1. Search window = [5, 1]. ================================================================================= ITERATION 2: (start = 0, end = 1) ================================================================================= • Calculate mid: mid = 0 + (1 - 0) // 2 = 0 - nums[start] = nums[0] = 5 - nums[mid] = nums[0] = 5 - nums[end] = nums[1] = 1 • Condition Check 1: Is nums[start] <= nums[mid]? (5 <= 5) -> TRUE! - Meaning: The left half [5] is sorted. - Minimum element in this left half is nums[start] = 5. - Update global result: res = min(2, 5) = 2. - Eliminate sorted left half: start = mid + 1 = 0 + 1 = 1. - New Range: start = 1, end = 1. Search window = [1]. ================================================================================= ITERATION 3: (start = 1, end = 1) ================================================================================= • Calculate mid: mid = 1 + (1 - 1) // 2 = 1 - nums[start] = nums[1] = 1 - nums[mid] = nums[1] = 1 - nums[end] = nums[1] = 1 • Condition Check 1: Is nums[start] <= nums[mid]? (1 <= 1) -> TRUE! - Minimum element in this single element window is nums[start] = 1. - Update global result: res = min(2, 1) = 1. - Eliminate left half: start = mid + 1 = 1 + 1 = 2. ================================================================================= LOOP TERMINATION ================================================================================= • Loop condition start <= end (2 <= 1) is FALSE! • Loop terminates completely. • Return res -> 1. Final Answer Returned: 1

a) Source Code Implementation

class Solution:
    def findMin(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        start = 0  # Initialize start pointer at index 0
        end = len(nums) - 1  # Initialize end pointer at last index
        res = float('inf')  # Track global minimum value found

        while start <= end:  # Continue binary search while range is valid
            mid = start + (end - start) // 2  # Calculate midpoint

            # Check if left half [start...mid] is monotonically sorted
            if nums[start] <= nums[mid]:
                res = min(res, nums[start])  # Smallest in sorted left half is nums[start]
                start = mid + 1  # Eliminate left half and explore right search space
            # Otherwise right half [mid...end] is monotonically sorted
            elif nums[mid] <= nums[end]:
                res = min(res, nums[mid])  # Smallest in sorted right half is nums[mid]
                end = mid - 1  # Eliminate right half and explore left search space
        
        return res  # Return overall minimum value recorded
class Solution {
public:
    int findMin(vector<int>& nums) {
        int start = 0;  // Start pointer
        int end = nums.size() - 1;  // End pointer
        int res = INT_MAX;  // Minimum tracker integer

        while (start <= end) {  // Search condition
            int mid = start + (end - start) / 2;  // Mid point calculation

            if (nums[start] <= nums[mid]) {  // Left half is sorted
                res = min(res, nums[start]);  // Record candidate min
                start = mid + 1;  // Shift start right
            } else if (nums[mid] <= nums[end]) {  // Right half is sorted
                res = min(res, nums[mid]);  // Record candidate min
                end = mid - 1;  // Shift end left
            }
        }
        return res;  // Return final result
    }
};
class Solution {
    public int findMin(int[] nums) {
        int start = 0;  // Start pointer
        int end = nums.length - 1;  // End pointer
        int res = Integer.MAX_VALUE;  // Track min value

        while (start <= end) {  // Loop condition
            int mid = start + (end - start) / 2;  // Calculate mid

            if (nums[start] <= nums[mid]) {  // Left half sorted
                res = Math.min(res, nums[start]);  // Take min element
                start = mid + 1;  // Move to right side
            } else if (nums[mid] <= nums[end]) {  // Right half sorted
                res = Math.min(res, nums[mid]);  // Take min element
                end = mid - 1;  // Move to left side
            }
        }
        return res;  // Return calculated result
    }
}
var findMin = function(nums) {
    let start = 0;  // Start pointer
    let end = nums.length - 1;  // End pointer
    let res = Infinity;  // Initialize min tracker to Infinity

    while (start <= end) {  // Loop condition
        let mid = Math.floor(start + (end - start) / 2);  // Mid point

        if (nums[start] <= nums[mid]) {  // Left half is sorted
            res = Math.min(res, nums[start]);  // Record left min
            start = mid + 1;  // Move to right side
        } else if (nums[mid] <= nums[end]) {  // Right half is sorted
            res = Math.min(res, nums[mid]);  // Record right min
            end = mid - 1;  // Move to left side
        }
    }
    return res;  // Return output
};
⚠️ Crucial Limitation: Why Approach 2 Fails When Duplicates Exist (LeetCode 154)

1. The Ambiguity Condition: Approach 2 relies on nums[start] <= nums[mid] to claim that the left half is strictly sorted. This logic assumes all elements are distinct/unique.

What happens when the array contains duplicate elements, such that nums[start] == nums[mid] == nums[end]?

Counterexample with Duplicates: nums = [10, 1, 10, 10, 10] indices: 0 1 2 3 4 start = 0 (nums[0] = 10) end = 4 (nums[4] = 10) mid = 2 (nums[2] = 10) Trace execution using Approach 2: • Check 1: nums[start] <= nums[mid] => 10 <= 10 (TRUE!) • Approach 2 code records: res = min(Inf, nums[start]) = 10 • Approach 2 code executes: start = mid + 1 = 2 + 1 = 3 • Search window jumps to indices [3...4] ([10, 10])! CRITICAL FAILURE: The true minimum element (1 at index 1) was trapped in the left half! Approach 2 blindly assumed the left half was monotonically non-decreasing, taking 10 as minimum and discarding index 1 completely. It returns 10 instead of 1!
Hinglish Explanation

Jab Array me Duplicate Elements hon: Agar nums[start] == nums[mid] == nums[end] ho jaye (jaise [10, 1, 10, 10, 10]), toh 10 <= 10 TRUE ho jata hai. Code sochta hai ki left side sorted hai aur actual minimum (1) jo index 1 par tha, usko skip karke right side me chala jata hai!

Iska matlab: Approach 2 sirf Unique elements wale arrays (LeetCode 153) par chalega! Duplicate elements wale arrays (LeetCode 154) par yeh galat answer dega.

Approach 3 - Handling Duplicates via Linear Shrinking (LeetCode 154 Solution)

🧭 Intuition Breakdown (Linear Boundary Shrinking)

1. Resolving Ambiguity: To handle duplicate elements safely, we compare nums[mid] against nums[end]. When nums[mid] == nums[end], we cannot determine whether the minimum lies in the left or right half.

2. The Solution: Since nums[mid] == nums[end], removing the duplicate rightmost element via end -= 1 reduces the search space by 1 without losing the minimum element (because nums[mid] still preserves that value inside the remaining search window!).

3. Architectural Tradeoffs (O(log N) vs O(N)):
• Average Case: When duplicates are sparse or absent, the search space halves in every iteration, giving O(log N) performance.
• Worst Case: When all elements in the array are identical (e.g. [1, 1, 1, 1, 1]), the algorithm is forced to decrement end -= 1 one step at a time, degrading performance to O(N). This linear fallback is mathematically unavoidable when duplicate ambiguity exists.

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition behind Duplicate Handling: Ambiguity ko solve karne ke liye hum nums[mid] ki comparison nums[end] se karte hain.

• Agar nums[mid] > nums[end]: Minimum zaroor right unsorted part me hai -> start = mid + 1.

• Agar nums[mid] < nums[end]: Minimum ya toh mid par hai ya left side me -> end = mid.

• Agar nums[mid] == nums[end]: Hume nahi pata minimum kis side hai! Par kyuki nums[mid] par woh value abhi bhi saved hai, hum safely right boundary ko 1-step chhota kar sakte hain: end -= 1.

(10 > 10) -> FALSE - Check 2: Is nums[mid] < nums[end]? (10 < 10) -> FALSE - Check 3: nums[mid] == nums[end] (10 == 10) -> AMBIGUITY TRIGGERED! - Action: Safely shrink right boundary: end -= 1 (end becomes 3). - New Range: start = 0, end = 3. Active Window = [10, 1, 10, 10]. ================================================================================= ITERATION 2: (start = 0, end = 3) ================================================================================= • Calculate mid: mid = 0 + (3 - 0) // 2 = 1 - nums[start] = nums[0] = 10 - nums[mid] = nums[1] = 1 - nums[end] = nums[3] = 10 • Compare nums[mid] against nums[end]: - Check 1: Is nums[mid] > nums[end]? (1 > 10) -> FALSE - Check 2: Is nums[mid] < nums[end]? (1 < 10) -> TRUE! - Meaning: Right half [mid...end] ([1, 10, 10]) is sorted. Minimum is at mid or left. - Action: end = mid = 1. - New Range: start = 0, end = 1. Active Window = [10, 1]. ================================================================================= ITERATION 3: (start = 0, end = 1) ================================================================================= • Calculate mid: mid = 0 + (1 - 0) // 2 = 0 - nums[start] = nums[0] = 10 - nums[mid] = nums[0] = 10 - nums[end] = nums[1] = 1 • Compare nums[mid] against nums[end]: - Check 1: Is nums[mid] > nums[end]? (10 > 1) -> TRUE! - Meaning: Minimum lies strictly to the right of mid. - Action: start = mid + 1 = 0 + 1 = 1. - New Range: start = 1, end = 1. Active Window = [1]. ================================================================================= LOOP TERMINATION ================================================================================= • Loop condition start < end (1 < 1) is FALSE! • Loop terminates completely. • Return nums[start] -> nums[1] -> 1. Final Answer Returned: 1 (Correctly handled duplicates!)

a) Source Code Implementation (Handling Duplicates)

class Solution:
    def findMin(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        start = 0  # Initialize left pointer
        end = len(nums) - 1  # Initialize right pointer

        while start < end:  # Loop until start and end converge
            mid = start + (end - start) // 2  # Calculate mid index

            if nums[mid] > nums[end]:
                start = mid + 1  # Minimum is in right unsorted portion
            elif nums[mid] < nums[end]:
                end = mid  # Minimum is at mid or in left portion
            else:
                end -= 1  # Ambiguity when nums[mid] == nums[end]; safely shrink right bound

        return nums[start]  # Return minimum element
class Solution {
public:
    int findMin(vector<int>& nums) {
        int start = 0;  // Start pointer
        int end = nums.size() - 1;  // End pointer

        while (start < end) {  // Binary search condition
            int mid = start + (end - start) / 2;  // Midpoint

            if (nums[mid] > nums[end]) {
                start = mid + 1;  // Minimum lies to the right
            } else if (nums[mid] < nums[end]) {
                end = mid;  // Minimum lies at mid or to the left
            } else {
                end--;  // Shrink boundary to resolve duplicate ambiguity
            }
        }
        return nums[start];  // Return minimum element
    }
};
class Solution {
    public int findMin(int[] nums) {
        int start = 0;  // Start pointer
        int end = nums.length - 1;  // End pointer

        while (start < end) {  // Binary search loop
            int mid = start + (end - start) / 2;  // Calculate midpoint

            if (nums[mid] > nums[end]) {
                start = mid + 1;  // Shift start right
            } else if (nums[mid] < nums[end]) {
                end = mid;  // Shift end to mid
            } else {
                end--;  // Reduce end pointer by 1 for duplicates
            }
        }
        return nums[start];  // Return minimum element
    }
}
var findMin = function(nums) {
    let start = 0;  // Start pointer
    let end = nums.length - 1;  // End pointer

    while (start < end) {  // Loop condition
        let mid = Math.floor(start + (end - start) / 2);  // Midpoint

        if (nums[mid] > nums[end]) {
            start = mid + 1;  // Shift start right
        } else if (nums[mid] < nums[end]) {
            end = mid;  // Shift end to mid
        } else {
            end--;  // Handle duplicate ambiguity
        }
    }
    return nums[start];  // Return minimum
};

Approach 4 - Standard Converging Binary Search (Comparing mid with right)

🧭 Deep Intuition Breakdown (Inflection Point Search for Unique Elements)

1. Direct Mid-to-Right Comparison: In a clean array without duplicates, comparing nums[mid] directly against nums[right] handles all cases (rotated and non-rotated) without needing a secondary res tracking variable!

  • If nums[mid] > nums[right]: The minimum MUST lie to the right of mid -> left = mid + 1.
  • If nums[mid] <= nums[right]: The minimum is at mid or to the left of mid -> right = mid.
📋 Full Line-by-Line Trace Dry Run: Mid-vs-Right Converging Search

Input: nums = [3, 4, 5, 1, 2] (N = 5)

Initial State: left = 0 (nums[0] = 3) right = 4 (nums[4] = 2) ================================================================================= ITERATION 1: (left = 0, right = 4) ================================================================================= • Calculate mid: mid = 0 + (4 - 0) // 2 = 2 - nums[left] = nums[0] = 3 - nums[mid] = nums[2] = 5 - nums[right] = nums[4] = 2 • Compare nums[mid] against nums[right]: - Check: Is nums[mid] > nums[right]? (5 > 2) -> TRUE! - Meaning: The drop point lies strictly to the right of index 2 (5 cannot be the minimum). - Action: left = mid + 1 = 2 + 1 = 3. - Active Search Window: indices [3...4] ([1, 2]). ================================================================================= ITERATION 2: (left = 3, right = 4) ================================================================================= • Calculate mid: mid = 3 + (4 - 3) // 2 = 3 - nums[left] = nums[3] = 1 - nums[mid] = nums[3] = 1 - nums[right] = nums[4] = 2 • Compare nums[mid] against nums[right]: - Check: Is nums[mid] > nums[right]? (1 > 2) -> FALSE! - Meaning: Subarray from index 3 to 4 is sorted. Minimum is at or to the left of index 3. - Action: right = mid = 3. - Active Search Window: indices [3...3]. ================================================================================= LOOP TERMINATION ================================================================================= • Loop condition left < right (3 < 3) is FALSE! • Loop terminates completely. • Both pointers converge on index 3. Return nums[left] -> nums[3] -> 1. Final Answer Returned: 1

a) Source Code Implementation

class Solution:
    def findMin(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        left = 0  # Initialize left boundary pointer
        right = len(nums) - 1  # Initialize right boundary pointer

        while left < right:  # Loop until left and right converge
            mid = left + (right - left) // 2  # Calculate mid index avoiding overflow

            # Compare mid element against rightmost element
            if nums[mid] > nums[right]:
                left = mid + 1  # Minimum lies to the right of mid
            else:
                right = mid  # Minimum is at mid or to the left

        return nums[left]  # Converged minimum element
class Solution {
public:
    int findMin(vector<int>& nums) {
        int left = 0;  // Start pointer
        int right = nums.size() - 1;  // End pointer

        while (left < right) {  // Loop until single element remains
            int mid = left + (right - left) / 2;  // Compute mid index

            if (nums[mid] > nums[right]) {
                left = mid + 1;  // Minimum is strictly right of mid
            } else {
                right = mid;  // Minimum is at mid or left of mid
            }
        }
        return nums[left];  // Return element at converged index
    }
};
class Solution {
    public int findMin(int[] nums) {
        int left = 0;  // Initialize left boundary
        int right = nums.length - 1;  // Initialize right boundary

        while (left < right) {  // Binary search condition
            int mid = left + (right - left) / 2;  // Midpoint

            if (nums[mid] > nums[right]) {
                left = mid + 1;  // Shift left boundary rightward
            } else {
                right = mid;  // Shift right boundary to mid
            }
        }
        return nums[left];  // Return converged minimum element
    }
}
var findMin = function(nums) {
    let left = 0;  // Left index pointer
    let right = nums.length - 1;  // Right index pointer

    while (left < right) {  // Loop condition
        let mid = Math.floor(left + (right - left) / 2);  // Midpoint

        if (nums[mid] > nums[right]) {
            left = mid + 1;  // Move left pointer past mid
        } else {
            right = mid;  // Move right pointer to mid
        }
    }
    return nums[left];  // Return minimum element
};

Strategic Edge Cases Tracking Matrix

Edge Case Profile Algorithmic Risk Factor Mitigation Resolution Logic
Single Element Array
e.g., [1]		 Array indexing exceptions or loop condition failure. left = 0, right = 0. Loop condition left < right (0 < 0) evaluates to False. Function returns nums[0] directly.
Duplicates Barrier
e.g., [10, 1, 10, 10, 10]		 Approach 2 (Sorted Half) misidentifies left half as sorted and discards minimum. Use Approach 3 (LeetCode 154) where nums[mid] == nums[end] triggers end -= 1 to shrink duplicate bounds.
Unrotated Array
e.g., [11, 13, 15, 17]		 False pointer shifts into right half. nums[mid] > nums[right] evaluates to False consistently. right pointer shrinks leftward until right = 0. Returns nums[0] = 11.

Complexity Analysis Performance Metrics

Approach Category Time Complexity Space Complexity Performance Evaluation Rating
Approach 1: Brute Force Linear Scan O(N) O(1) Sub-optimal. Scans all elements sequentially, violating the required logarithmic bound.
Approach 2: Sorted Half Elimination (Unique Only) O(log N) O(1) Fast for Unique Arrays. Fails when duplicate values exist at start, mid, and end.
Approach 3: Linear Shrinking (Duplicates Allowed) O(log N) Avg / O(N) Worst O(1) Optimal for Duplicates. Degrades to O(N) only when all array elements are identical duplicates.
Approach 4: Mid-vs-Right Converging Search O(log N) O(1) Production Standard for Unique Arrays. Clean binary search without auxiliary minimum tracker variable.

Hard Priority Queue / Min-Heap Divide & Conquer

Merge k Sorted Lists

Learn how to merge k sorted linked lists into a single sorted list efficiently by mastering Min-Heap pointer tracking in O(N log k) time and Divide & Conquer binary reduction.

1. What Are We Actually Being Asked?

We are given an array of k linked-lists lists, where each linked-list is sorted in ascending order.

We need to merge all the linked-lists into one sorted linked-list and return its head.

Total Nodes = N, Total Lists = k
Core Goal: Combine all k streams into a single list in increasing order without allocating brand-new nodes (relink existing node pointers).

Important Example

Input: lists = [
  1 → 4 → 5,
  1 → 3 → 4,
  2 → 6
]
Merged Output: 1 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 4 → 5 → 6

2. First Thoughts — Naive Approaches

Before using a Min-Heap, consider the standard straightforward options:

Idea 1: Collect & Sort Traverse all N nodes, store values in an array, sort the array in O(N log N), and rebuild a linked list. → Disadvantage: Wastes the fact that all k individual lists are already sorted.
↓
Idea 2: Sequential Merging Merge List 1 with List 2, then merge the result with List 3, and so on. → Disadvantage: Takes O(k · N) time. When k = 10,000 and N = 100,000, this takes ~1 billion operations and hits Time Limit Exceeded (TLE).

Approach Comparison

Approach Time Space Notes
Collect & Sort Array time: O(N log N) space: O(N) Ignores pre-sorted order and allocates auxiliary memory for nodes.
Sequential Merging (1 by 1) time: O(k · N) space: O(1) Slow for large k as earlier lists are re-traversed repeatedly.
Min-Heap (Priority Queue) time: O(N log k) space: O(k) Optimal streaming execution; maintains k active list heads.
Divide & Conquer time: O(N log k) space: O(1) Optimal in-place merging in log k pairing rounds.

3. The Breakthrough — Min-Heap of Size K

At any moment, where can the globally smallest node come from?

The Key Observation:
The globally smallest remaining value across all lists must always be at the head of one of the k lists.
We only ever need to compare k candidates at a time!

How the Min-Heap works:

  • Push the head node of all k lists into a Min-Heap of capacity k.
  • Extract the minimum node from the heap, attach it to our merged list tail.
  • If the extracted node has a next node, push node.next into the heap.
  • Repeat until the heap is empty. Every node insertion and extraction takes only O(log k) time.
Total Runtime = N nodes × O(log k) = O(N log k)

4. 🧠 How Do I Recognize This Pattern?

Train yourself to identify multi-way merge problems with these structured questions.

Question 1 Are we merging k independent sorted streams?
Yes. k separate lists are individually sorted in ascending order.
↓
Question 2 What is the smallest number of candidates we must inspect to find the next minimum?
Only k candidates (the current front pointer of each stream).
↓
Question 3 What data structure efficiently extracts the minimum among k dynamic items?
A Min-Heap (Priority Queue) of size k.
↓
Question 4 What pattern does that suggest?
K-Way Merge via Min-Heap / Divide & Conquer Merging.
Recognition Rule: Whenever you see "Merge K sorted arrays/lists/streams" or "Find the smallest range covering elements from K lists", use a Min-Heap of size K.

5. 🎬 Live Visual Min-Heap Simulator (k = 3 Lists)

Use the player controls below to pause, step forward, or step backward. Watch how the Min-Heap maintains at most k = 3 active head nodes, pops the smallest node, and advances that specific list pointer.

Step: 1 / 8 (Initial Heap Load)
⚡ Current Execution Telemetry
Step 1: Initialize Min-Heap Push heads of all k=3 lists: L0(1), L1(1), L2(2).
📦 Min-Heap (Size ≤ k) (Top is Smallest)

6. Approaches — Min-Heap vs Divide & Conquer

Approach 1: Min-Heap / Priority Queue (Streaming Optimal) time: O(N log k) | space: O(k)

Idea

Maintain a Min-Heap of size k holding the current head of each non-empty list. Repeatedly pop the smallest node, attach it to tail.next, and push popped.next if it exists.

import heapq

class Solution:
    def mergeKLists(self, lists: list[Optional[ListNode]]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        min_heap = []

        # Push initial head of each list with unique index to break tie
        for i, node in enumerate(lists):
            if node:
                heapq.heappush(min_heap, (node.val, i, node))

        dummy = ListNode(0)
        curr = dummy

        while min_heap:
            val, i, node = heapq.heappop(min_heap)
            curr.next = node
            curr = curr.next

            if node.next:
                heapq.heappush(min_heap, (node.next.val, i, node.next))

        return dummy.next
class Solution {
private:
    struct Compare {
        bool operator()(ListNode* a, ListNode* b) {
            return a->val > b->val; // Min-Heap
        }
    };
public:
    ListNode* mergeKLists(vector<ListNode*>& lists) {
        priority_queue<ListNode*, vector<ListNode*>, Compare> minHeap;

        for (ListNode* head : lists) {
            if (head) minHeap.push(head);
        }

        ListNode dummy(0);
        ListNode* curr = &dummy;

        while (!minHeap.empty()) {
            ListNode* topNode = minHeap.top();
            minHeap.pop();

            curr->next = topNode;
            curr = curr->next;

            if (topNode->next) {
                minHeap.push(topNode->next);
            }
        }

        return dummy.next;
    }
};
class Solution {
    public ListNode mergeKLists(ListNode[] lists) {
        if (lists == null || lists.length == 0) return null;

        PriorityQueue<ListNode> minHeap = new PriorityQueue<>(
            (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a.val, b.val)
        );

        for (ListNode node : lists) {
            if (node != null) minHeap.add(node);
        }

        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0);
        ListNode curr = dummy;

        while (!minHeap.isEmpty()) {
            ListNode topNode = minHeap.poll();
            curr.next = topNode;
            curr = curr.next;

            if (topNode.next != null) {
                minHeap.add(topNode.next);
            }
        }

        return dummy.next;
    }
}
var mergeKLists = function(lists) {
    const vals = [];
    for (let head of lists) {
        while (head) {
            vals.push(head.val);
            head = head.next;
        }
    }
    vals.sort((a, b) => a - b);

    const dummy = new ListNode(0);
    let curr = dummy;
    for (const v of vals) {
        curr.next = new ListNode(v);
        curr = curr.next;
    }
    return dummy.next;
};

Key Lines Explained

minHeap.pop()
Extracts the smallest node among all current k list heads in O(log k) time.
minHeap.push(node.next)
Refills the heap with the next available node from the stream that provided the minimum.

Approach 2 — Optimal Space: Divide & Conquer (Merge Sort Style)

time: O(N log k) | space: O(1)

Core Idea: Pair up k lists and merge each pair using standard 2-way Merge List (mergeTwoLists). After the first round, k lists become k / 2 lists. Repeat log k times until only 1 list remains.

class Solution:
    def mergeKLists(self, lists: list[Optional[ListNode]]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        if not lists:
            return None

        def mergeTwoLists(l1, l2):
            dummy = ListNode(0)
            curr = dummy
            while l1 and l2:
                if l1.val <= l2.val:
                    curr.next, l1 = l1, l1.next
                else:
                    curr.next, l2 = l2, l2.next
                curr = curr.next
            curr.next = l1 if l1 else l2
            return dummy.next

        interval = 1
        while interval < len(lists):
            for i in range(0, len(lists) - interval, interval * 2):
                lists[i] = mergeTwoLists(lists[i], lists[i + interval])
            interval *= 2

        return lists[0]
class Solution {
private:
    ListNode* mergeTwo(ListNode* l1, ListNode* l2) {
        ListNode dummy(0);
        ListNode* tail = &dummy;
        while (l1 && l2) {
            if (l1->val <= l2->val) {
                tail->next = l1;
                l1 = l1->next;
            } else {
                tail->next = l2;
                l2 = l2->next;
            }
            tail = tail->next;
        }
        tail->next = l1 ? l1 : l2;
        return dummy.next;
    }
public:
    ListNode* mergeKLists(vector<ListNode*>& lists) {
        if (lists.empty()) return nullptr;
        int interval = 1;
        while (interval < lists.size()) {
            for (int i = 0; i + interval < lists.size(); i += interval * 2) {
                lists[i] = mergeTwo(lists[i], lists[i + interval]);
            }
            interval *= 2;
        }
        return lists[0];
    }
};
class Solution {
    private ListNode mergeTwo(ListNode l1, ListNode l2) {
        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0);
        ListNode tail = dummy;
        while (l1 != null && l2 != null) {
            if (l1.val <= l2.val) {
                tail.next = l1;
                l1 = l1.next;
            } else {
                tail.next = l2;
                l2 = l2.next;
            }
            tail = tail.next;
        }
        tail.next = (l1 != null) ? l1 : l2;
        return dummy.next;
    }

    public ListNode mergeKLists(ListNode[] lists) {
        if (lists == null || lists.length == 0) return null;
        int interval = 1;
        while (interval < lists.length) {
            for (int i = 0; i + interval < lists.length; i += interval * 2) {
                lists[i] = mergeTwo(lists[i], lists[i + interval]);
            }
            interval *= 2;
        }
        return lists[0];
    }
}
var mergeKLists = function(lists) {
    if (!lists || lists.length === 0) return null;

    const mergeTwo = (l1, l2) => {
        const dummy = new ListNode(0);
        let tail = dummy;
        while (l1 && l2) {
            if (l1.val <= l2.val) {
                tail.next = l1;
                l1 = l1.next;
            } else {
                tail.next = l2;
                l2 = l2.next;
            }
            tail = tail.next;
        }
        tail.next = l1 || l2;
        return dummy.next;
    };

    let interval = 1;
    while (interval < lists.length) {
        for (let i = 0; i + interval < lists.length; i += interval * 2) {
            lists[i] = mergeTwo(lists[i], lists[i + interval]);
        }
        interval *= 2;
    }
    return lists[0];
};

7. 🧪 Dry Run — Min-Heap Execution

Input Lists: L0: [1, 4, 5], L1: [1, 3, 4], L2: [2, 6]
Step 1 — Initial Load

Action: Push heads L0[1], L1[1], L2[2].

Heap State: { L0(1) [MIN], L1(1), L2(2) }

Step 2 — Pop L0(1)

Action: Attach 1 to merged list. Push next node L0(4).

Merged List: 1 → Heap: { L1(1) [MIN], L2(2), L0(4) }

Step 3 — Pop L1(1)

Action: Attach 1 to merged list. Push next node L1(3).

Merged List: 1 → 1 → Heap: { L2(2) [MIN], L1(3), L0(4) }

Step 4 — Pop L2(2)

Action: Attach 2 to merged list. Push next node L2(6).

Merged List: 1 → 1 → 2 → Heap: { L1(3) [MIN], L0(4), L2(6) }

Final Output: 1 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 4 → 5 → 6

8. Complexity Derivation & Common Pitfalls

Approach Time Space Notes
Min-Heap time: O(N log k) space: O(k) Heap holds at most k elements; every node is inserted and extracted once.
Divide & Conquer time: O(N log k) space: O(1) Pairs merged in log k rounds; pointers relinked in-place with zero heap memory.
⚠️ Top Common Mistakes:
  1. Python Tuple Collision in Heap: Pushing (node.val, node) into heapq crashes when two nodes have identical values because ListNode has no comparison operator. Always store a unique list index (node.val, i, node).
  2. Sequential 1-by-1 Merging: Merging lists sequentially takes O(k · N), which is quadratic when lists are many and short. Always use Divide & Conquer or Min-Heap to achieve O(N log k).

9. Practice — Test Your Understanding

Case 1

Input: lists = [[]]

Verify why the dummy head handles empty list arrays cleanly without NullPointerExceptions.

Case 2

Input: lists = [[1], [0]]

Trace the heap states when list sizes are 1 node each.

10. 🧠 Final Recall

30-Second Recall

  • The next smallest value is always at the head of one of the k lists.
  • Maintain a Min-Heap of size k holding head pointers.
  • Extract min root, attach to tail.next, push popped.next.
  • Time complexity: O(N log k), Space: O(k).
  • Divide & Conquer pairwise merging achieves identical O(N log k) time in O(1) memory.

LeetCode 4 Hard Master Edition

An exhaustive engineering manual analyzing array merging, two-pointer tracking, and logarithmic binary search partitioning across dual sorted arrays.

Problem Statement

Given two sorted arrays nums1 and nums2 of size m and n respectively, return the median of the two sorted arrays.

The overall run time complexity should be O(log (m+n)).

Constraints

  • nums1.length == m
  • nums2.length == n
  • 0 <= m <= 1000
  • 0 <= n <= 1000
  • 1 <= m + n <= 2000
  • -10^6 <= nums1[i], nums2[i] <= 10^6

Visualizing the Intent

Let's map out what finding the median of two combined sorted arrays means spatially:

Example 1 (Odd total length): nums1 = [1, 3], nums2 = [2] Merged array = [1, 2, 3] Total length = 3 (Odd) Median is the exact middle element at index 3 // 2 = 1 -> Value = 2.0 Example 2 (Even total length): nums1 = [1, 2], nums2 = [3, 4] Merged array = [1, 2, 3, 4] Total length = 4 (Even) Median is average of two middle elements at index 1 and index 2: (2 + 3) / 2.0 = 2.5

Core Realization: The median divides a dataset into two equal halves such that every element in the left half is smaller than or equal to every element in the right half. When given two pre-sorted arrays, we don't actually need to merge them—we just need to find the correct partition line across both arrays!

Solutions Breakdown

Approach 1 - Brute Force (Full Array Merge & Sort/Pick)

🧭 Intuition Breakdown (Physical Merging)

1. The Concept: Combine all elements from nums1 and nums2 into a single merged array of size m + n using the classic 2-pointer merge step of Merge Sort. Once merged, return the middle element if total length is odd, or the average of the two middle elements if total length is even.

2. Why it Fails Constraints: Merging both arrays requires traversing all m + n elements, which takes O(m + n) time and O(m + n) extra space. The problem strictly demands O(log (m+n)) runtime.

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition: Dono arrays ko mila kar ek bada array bana lo (Merge Sort ke merge step ki tarah). Phir agar total size odd hai toh direct middle element utha lo, aur agar even hai toh middle ke do numbers ka average le lo. Yeh simple hai par isme O(m + n) time aur extra memory lagti hai, jabki problem me O(log (m+n)) maanga gaya hai.

📋 Approach 1 Line-by-Line Trace Profile

Input: nums1 = [1, 3], nums2 = [2]

Step 1: Merge arrays using 2 pointers i = 0, j = 0 • Compare nums1[0] (1) and nums2[0] (2) -> Append 1 • Compare nums1[1] (3) and nums2[0] (2) -> Append 2 • Remaining nums1[1] (3) -> Append 3 Merged Array = [1, 2, 3] Step 2: Total length N = 3 (Odd) • Middle index = 3 // 2 = 1 • Result = merged[1] = 2.0

a) Source Code Implementation

class Solution:
    def findMedianSortedArrays(self, nums1: list[int], nums2: list[int]) -> float:
        merged = []  # Allocate empty list for combined elements
        i, j = 0, 0  # Pointers for nums1 and nums2
        m, n = len(nums1), len(nums2)  # Store lengths

        while i < m and j < n:  # Compare elements while both arrays have items
            if nums1[i] <= nums2[j]:
                merged.append(nums1[i])  # Append smaller item from nums1
                i += 1
            else:
                merged.append(nums2[j])  # Append smaller item from nums2
                j += 1

        while i < m:  # Append remaining items from nums1
            merged.append(nums1[i])
            i += 1

        while j < n:  # Append remaining items from nums2
            merged.append(nums2[j])
            j += 1

        total = m + n  # Total combined size
        if total % 2 == 1:
            return float(merged[total // 2])  # Odd total: return exact middle
        else:
            # Even total: return average of two middle elements
            return (merged[total // 2 - 1] + merged[total // 2]) / 2.0
class Solution {
public:
    double findMedianSortedArrays(vector<int>& nums1, vector<int>& nums2) {
        vector<int> merged;  // Combined vector
        int i = 0, j = 0;
        int m = nums1.size(), n = nums2.size();

        while (i < m && j < n) {  // Merge elements
            if (nums1[i] <= nums2[j]) merged.push_back(nums1[i++]);
            else merged.push_back(nums2[j++]);
        }
        while (i < m) merged.push_back(nums1[i++]);  // Flush nums1
        while (j < n) merged.push_back(nums2[j++]);  // Flush nums2

        int total = m + n;
        if (total % 2 == 1) {
            return merged[total / 2];  // Return middle element
        } else {
            return (merged[total / 2 - 1] + merged[total / 2]) / 2.0;  // Return average
        }
    }
};
class Solution {
    public double findMedianSortedArrays(int[] nums1, int[] nums2) {
        int m = nums1.length, n = nums2.length;
        int[] merged = new int[m + n];  // Allocate merged array
        int i = 0, j = 0, k = 0;

        while (i < m && j < n) {  // Merge loop
            if (nums1[i] <= nums2[j]) merged[k++] = nums1[i++];
            else merged[k++] = nums2[j++];
        }
        while (i < m) merged[k++] = nums1[i++];  // Flush remaining
        while (j < n) merged[k++] = nums2[j++];

        int total = m + n;
        if (total % 2 == 1) {
            return merged[total / 2];  // Odd median
        } else {
            return (merged[total / 2 - 1] + merged[total / 2]) / 2.0;  // Even median
        }
    }
}
var findMedianSortedArrays = function(nums1, nums2) {

Approach 2 - Better Solution: Two Pointers without Extra Space

🧭 Intuition Breakdown (In-Place Pointer Counting)

1. The Optimization: We don't actually need to store all m + n elements in memory. To find the median, we only need to know the values at index (m + n) // 2 (and (m + n) // 2 - 1 if total length is even).

2. How It Works: We simulate the 2-pointer merging process using a counter loop that runs (m + n) // 2 + 1 steps. At each step, we keep track of the current element and the previously seen element. Once our step counter reaches the middle position, we calculate the median using these two tracked values.

This improves auxiliary space complexity to O(1), but time complexity remains O(m + n).

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition: Naya array banane me memory waste hoti hai. Median nikalne ke liye hume poora array nahi chahiye, sirf middle ke 1 ya 2 elements chahiye. Hum merge sort waale do pointers i aur j ko chalaate hain aur ek step counter rakhte hain. Jab counter middle index tak pahunchta hai, hum un values ko variables curr aur prev me hold kar lete hain. Isse extra array ka Space O(1) ho jata hai, lekin Time abhi bhi O(m + n) rehta hai.

📋 Approach 2 Line-by-Line Trace Profile

Input: nums1 = [1, 2], nums2 = [3, 4] (m = 2, n = 2, total = 4, target index = 2)

Initialize: i = 0, j = 0, prev = -1, curr = -1 • Step 0: compare nums1[0] (1) vs nums2[0] (3) -> pick 1 from nums1 (i becomes 1) prev = -1, curr = 1 • Step 1: compare nums1[1] (2) vs nums2[0] (3) -> pick 2 from nums1 (i becomes 2) prev = 1, curr = 2 • Step 2: nums1 exhausted, pick 3 from nums2 (j becomes 1) prev = 2, curr = 3 Target index (4 // 2 = 2) reached! Since total length 4 is EVEN: Median = (prev + curr) / 2.0 = (2 + 3) / 2.0 = 2.5

    def findMedianSortedArrays(self, nums1: list[int], nums2: list[int]) -> float:
        m, n = len(nums1), len(nums2)

        mid_idx = total // 2  # Target middle index
        
        i, j = 0, 0  # Pointers for both input arrays
        prev, curr = 0, 0  # Variables to track last two elements seen

        for count in range(mid_idx + 1):  # Step up to middle index
            prev = curr  # Save previous current element

                curr = nums2[j]
                j += 1

        if total % 2 == 1:
            return float(curr)  # Odd total: middle element is curr
