Approach 3 - Optimal Solution: Binary Search Partitioning

🧭 Deep Intuition Breakdown (Binary Search on Partitions)

1. Understanding the Target Left Half:
If we merge nums1 (length m) and nums2 (length n), the total left half of the combined array must contain exactly left_half_size = (m + n + 1) // 2 elements.

2. How Partitioning Works:
Instead of searching through elements, we binary search for the number of elements to pick from nums1 (let's call this px, representing partition index in nums1).
Once we pick px elements from nums1, the number of elements picked from nums2 is automatically fixed: py = left_half_size - px!

3. The Four Boundary Check Variables:
A partition divides nums1 and nums2 into left and right halves:

  • x1 = nums1[px - 1]  (Max element in left half of nums1, or -Infinity if px == 0)
  • x2 = nums1[px]      (Min element in right half of nums1, or +Infinity if px == m)
  • y1 = nums2[py - 1]  (Max element in left half of nums2, or -Infinity if py == 0)
  • y2 = nums2[py]      (Min element in right half of nums2, or +Infinity if py == n)

Spatially Visualizing the Partition: nums1: [ ... x1 ] | [ x2 ... ] (px elements on left) nums2: [ ... y1 ] | [ y2 ... ] (py elements on left) ----------------------- LEFT HALF | RIGHT HALF The Partition is VALID if and only if: 1. x1 <= y2 (Largest element on left of nums1 <= Smallest on right of nums2) 2. y1 <= x2 (Largest element on left of nums2 <= Smallest on right of nums1) Why is this condition sufficient? Since nums1 and nums2 are already pre-sorted internally, x1 <= x2 and y1 <= y2 are ALWAYS true. Checking x1 <= y2 and y1 <= x2 guarantees every element in the combined LEFT HALF is <= every element in the combined RIGHT HALF!

4. How to Adjust Binary Search Pointers:
• If x1 > y2: We picked too many elements from nums1! Move leftwards: high = px - 1.
• If y1 > x2: We picked too few elements from nums1! Move rightwards: low = px + 1.
• When valid partition is found: - If total_length is ODD: Median = max(x1, y1) - If total_length is EVEN: Median = (max(x1, y1) + min(x2, y2)) / 2.0

5. Optimization (Binary Search on the Smaller Array):
Always perform binary search on the array with smaller size (ensure m <= n). This guarantees time complexity O(log(min(m, n))) and prevents py from becoming negative!

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition behind Binary Search Partitioning: Combined array ka **Left Half** banane ke liye total (m + n + 1) // 2 elements chahiye. Hum chote array (nums1) par binary search karke yeh tay karte hain ki nums1 me se kitne elements (px) left side me daalein.

Jaise hi px decide hota hai, nums2 me se kitne elements Lene hain (py) wo automatically fixed ho jata hai: py = left_half_size - px.

Ab char boundary variables bante hain: x1, x2 (nums1 ke left/right elements) aur y1, y2 (nums2 ke left/right elements). Valid partition ke liye bas 2 cheezein honi chahiye:

  • x1 <= y2 (nums1 ka left element, nums2 ke right element se chhota hona chahiye)
  • y1 <= x2 (nums2 ka left element, nums1 ke right element se chhota hona chahiye)

Agar x1 > y2, matlab nums1 se jyada elements le liye, toh high = px - 1 karo. Agar y1 > x2, toh low = px + 1 karo. Target milne par direct answer O(log(min(m,n))) me nikal jata hai!

class Solution:
    def findMedianSortedArrays(self, nums1: list[int], nums2: list[int]) -> float:
        # Ensure nums1 is the shorter array to optimize binary search to O(log(min(m, n)))
        if len(nums1) > len(nums2):
            return self.findMedianSortedArrays(nums2, nums1)

        m, n = len(nums1), len(nums2)  # Store lengths
        left_half_size = (m + n + 1) // 2  # Calculate exact total elements needed in left partition

        low, high = 0, m  # Binary search range for partition index in nums1

        while low <= high:
            px = low + (high - low) // 2  # Partition index for nums1
            py = left_half_size - px  # Dependent partition index for nums2

            # Boundary values for nums1 partition
            x1 = nums1[px - 1] if px > 0 else float('-inf')
            x2 = nums1[px] if px < m else float('inf')

            # Boundary values for nums2 partition
            y1 = nums2[py - 1] if py > 0 else float('-inf')
            y2 = nums2[py] if py < n else float('inf')

            # HIGHLIGHT: Check if partition is valid across cross-boundaries
            if x1 <= y2 and y1 <= x2:
                if (m + n) % 2 == 1:
                    return float(max(x1, y1))  # Odd length: max element on left side
                else:
                    # Even length: average of max-left and min-right
                    return (max(x1, y1) + min(x2, y2)) / 2.0

            elif x1 > y2:
                high = px - 1  # Picked too many elements from nums1; move left
            else:
                low = px + 1  # Picked too few elements from nums1; move right

        return 0.0  # Default fallback (unreachable for valid inputs)

Strategic Edge Cases Tracking Matrix

Binary search partitioning involves delicate boundary conditions. Solutions must handle these edge cases without array index out-of-bounds errors:

Edge Case Profile Algorithmic Risk Factor Mitigation Resolution Logic
One Array Entirely Empty
e.g., nums1 = [], nums2 = [1]		 Index px - 1 or py - 1 accessing negative indices. Guarded: Swap ensures nums1 is empty (m = 0). px = 0, so x1 = -Inf and x2 = +Inf. Partition reduces cleanly to picking elements strictly from nums2.
Pick 0 Elements from nums1
e.g., All elements in nums1 belong to the right half.		 Accessing nums1[-1] causing out-of-bounds error. Handled using ternary condition: x1 = nums1[px - 1] if px > 0 else -Infinity.
Pick ALL Elements from nums1
e.g., All elements in nums1 belong to the left half.		 Accessing nums1[m] causing index out-of-bounds. Handled using ternary condition: x2 = nums1[px] if px < m else +Infinity.
Arrays Completely Disjoint in Range
e.g., nums1 = [1, 2], nums2 = [3, 4]		 Binary search boundaries reaching extreme ends low = 0 or high = m. Infinity sentinel values (-Inf, +Inf) ensure the cross-comparison x1 <= y2 and y1 <= x2 holds true at the extreme boundary.

Complexity Analysis Performance Metrics

Approach Category Time Complexity Space Complexity Performance Evaluation Rating
Approach 1: Full Array Merge & Pick O(m + n) O(m + n) Fails Time Bounds. Allocates a full merged array of size (m+n). Linear time execution.
Approach 2: Two-Pointer Counter O(m + n) O(1) Space Optimal / Time Sub-Optimal. Reduces space to O(1), but still iterates linearly up to mid index.
Approach 3: Binary Search Partitioning O(log(min(m, n))) O(1) Production Standard. Performs logarithmic search on the smaller array. Maximum efficiency in time and memory.

Linked List Medium Master Edition

An engineering manual analyzing sublist pointer inversion, boundary reconnection mechanics, and call-stack unwinding algorithms.

Problem Statement

Given the head of a singly linked list and an integer k, reverse the first k nodes of the linked list and return the new head of the modified list.

The remaining (N - k) nodes after the first k elements must maintain their original relative order.

Constraints

  • The number of nodes in the list is N.
  • 1 <= k <= N <= 5000
  • -5000 <= Node.val <= 5000

Visualizing the Intent

Initial Linked List (N = 5, K = 3): head -> [1] -> [2] -> [3] -> [4] -> [5] -> NULL Phase 1: Partition into two segments: Segment A (First K=3 nodes): [1] -> [2] -> [3] Segment B (Remaining nodes): [4] -> [5] -> NULL Phase 2: Invert Segment A in-place: Reversed Segment A: [3] -> [2] -> [1] Phase 3: Connect tail of Segment A ([1]) to head of Segment B ([4]): new_head -> [3] -> [2] -> [1] -------> [4] -> [5] -> NULL Output List: [3, 2, 1, 4, 5]

Core Realization: Reversing the first K elements requires two steps: reversing the pointer directions for the first K nodes, and then attaching the original head (which becomes the tail of the reversed sublist) to the (k+1)-th node.

Solutions Breakdown

Approach 1 - Brute Force (Stack-Based Value Inversion)

🧭 Intuition Breakdown (Auxiliary Memory Buffer)

1. The Concept: If pointer manipulation feels error-prone, we can use a Stack data structure. Since stacks operate on a Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) principle, pushing the first K nodes (or their values) onto a stack and then popping them off naturally reverses their sequence order.

2. How It Works:

  1. Traverse the first K nodes and push their node references into a stack.
  2. The node at the top of the stack is the K-th node, which becomes our new list head!
  3. Pop nodes sequentially from the stack, wiring each popped node's next pointer to the next popped node.
  4. Connect the last popped node (original head) to the remaining un-reversed list starting at the (k+1)-th node.

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition: Sabse aasan tarika yeh hai ki hum pehle K nodes ko ek **Stack** me daal dein. Stack (LIFO - Last In First Out) automatic items ko ulta kar deta hai. Jab hum stack se ek-ek karke nodes nikalenge, toh wo reverse order me milenge. Aakhri popped node ko bache hue (k+1)-th node se connect kar do. Isme O(K) extra space lagta hai stack ke liye.

📋 Approach 1 Line-by-Line Trace Profile

Input: 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5, k = 3

Step 1: Traverse first K=3 nodes & push to Stack • Push Node(1) -> Stack: [Node(1)] • Push Node(2) -> Stack: [Node(1), Node(2)] • Push Node(3) -> Stack: [Node(1), Node(2), Node(3)] • Remaining list cursor pointer points to Node(4). Step 2: Pop top node as new head • Pop Node(3) -> new_head = Node(3), curr = Node(3) Step 3: Pop remaining stack nodes & reconnect • Pop Node(2) -> curr.next = Node(2) -> curr = Node(2) • Pop Node(1) -> curr.next = Node(1) -> curr = Node(1) Step 4: Attach remaining unreversed list • curr.next = remaining cursor (Node(4)) Result List: 3 -> 2 -> 1 -> 4 -> 5 -> NULL

class Solution:
    def reverseK(self, head: Optional[ListNode], k: int) -> Optional[ListNode]:

        stack = []  # Create empty stack buffer to store first k nodes
        curr = head  # Pointer to traverse linked list
        count = 0  # Counter tracking processed nodes

        # Step 1: Push first k nodes onto stack

            stack.append(curr)  # Push node reference to stack
            curr = curr.next  # Move traversal cursor to next node
            count += 1  # Increment counter

        if count < k:
            return head  # If total nodes < k, return original head (optional boundary check)

        # Step 2: Pop top node as new head of modified list
        new_head = stack.pop()  # Extract k-th node as new head
        temp = new_head  # Pointer to reconstruct reversed list

        # Step 3: Pop remaining nodes and re-link
        while stack:
            temp.next = stack.pop()  # Wire next pointer to popped node
            temp = temp.next  # Advance reconstruction pointer

        # Step 4: Attach tail of reversed portion to remaining (k+1)-th node
        temp.next = curr  # Point last popped node to (k+1)-th node

        return new_head  # Return head of transformed list

            curr = curr->next;  // Move cursor to next node

        ListNode* newHead = st.top();  // Top element is new list head
        st.pop();  // Pop top node

        while (!st.empty()) {  // Unwind stack
            temp->next = st.top();  // Wire current next to stack top
            st.pop();  // Pop processed node
            temp = temp->next;  // Move building cursor
        }

        temp->next = curr;  // Connect tail of reversed section to remaining list
        return newHead;  // Return new head
    }
};

Approach 2 - Optimal Solution: In-Place Three-Pointer Iterative Reversal

🧭 Deep Intuition Breakdown (In-Place Pointer Flipping)

1. The Core Strategy: We can reverse the first K nodes in-place without any extra stack memory using three pointers: prev, curr, and next_node.

2. The Boundary Connection Magic:
Before reversing, notice that the original head node is the FIRST node. After reversing the first K pointers, the original head node becomes the LAST node (tail) of the reversed sub-segment!

Before Loop: head points to Node(1) prev = NULL, curr = head (Node 1) Loop runs for K steps reversing arrows: Reversed portion head = prev (Node K) Reversed portion tail = head (Node 1) Remaining unreversed list head = curr (Node K+1) The Critical Connection Step: head.next = curr <-- Connects tail of reversed sublist to (K+1)-th node!

3. Why This Is O(1) Auxiliary Space:
We only modify existing next pointer addresses directly in memory. Zero extra memory allocation is needed.

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition behind In-Place Iterative: Extra memory bachane ke liye hum 3-pointer technique (prev, curr, next_node) se pehle K nodes ke arrows ko ulta kar dete hain.

Sabse important point (Connection Step): Loop khatam hone ke baad:
• prev naye reversed segment ka HEAD ban jata hai.
• Original head ab naye segment ka TAIL ban chuka hai.
• curr bache hue (K+1)-th node par khada hota hai.
Isliye hum bas head.next = curr karte hain taaki reversed portion aage ke bache hue list se jud jaye, aur prev ko return kar dete hain!

class Solution:
    def reverseK(self, head: Optional[ListNode], k: int) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        if not head or k <= 1:

        while curr and count < k:
            next_node = curr.next  # Save reference to next unreversed node
            curr.next = prev  # Flip current node's pointer backward to prev
            prev = curr  # Shift prev pointer forward to curr
            curr = next_node  # Shift curr pointer forward to next_node

        # HIGHLIGHT: Connect tail of reversed sublist (original head) to remaining list (curr)
        head.next = curr

        return prev  # Return prev which now points to new head of reversed portion

Approach 3 - Recursive Pointer Inversion

🧭 Deep Intuition Breakdown (Recursive Sub-problem Reduction)

1. The Core Idea: We can break the problem of reversing first K nodes into a recursive sub-problem: "Reverse the first K-1 nodes starting from head.next, then attach head at the end."

2. The Base Case (k == 1):
When k == 1, reversing 1 element changes nothing! Node 1 is the new head of the reversed portion, and head.next is the start of the un-reversed list. We save head.next in a global/helper reference successor and return head.

3. Call Stack Backtracking:
As recursion unwinds, head.next.next = head flips the pointer of the child node back to head, and head.next = successor wires the tail to the remaining un-reversed list.

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition behind Recursive Approach: Recursion se jab hum k = 1 tak pahunchte hain, toh 1 element ko reverse karne par koi change nahi hota. Us time par head.next ko hum ek variable successor me save kar lete hain (jo bacha hua (k+1)-th node hai).

Jab call stack backtrack karta hai, head.next.next = head se piche wale node ka arrow ulta ho jata hai, aur head.next = successor se har step par tail aage ke list se juda rehta hai.

False. - Recurse: new_head = reverseK(head.next=Node(3), k=1) [PAUSED] 3. Call reverseK(head=Node(3), k=1) - Base case (k==1)? TRUE! - Store remaining list start: successor = head.next -> Node(4) - Return Node(3) directly as new_head. ================================================================================= UNWINDING THE CALL STACK (Backtracking): ================================================================================= • Unwinding Frame 2: head = Node(2), successor = Node(4), new_head = Node(3) - Execute: head.next.next = head => Node(3).next = Node(2) - Execute: head.next = successor => Node(2).next = Node(4) - Sublist State: 3 -> 2 -> 4 -> 5 - Return new_head = Node(3) • Unwinding Frame 1: head = Node(1), successor = Node(4), new_head = Node(3) - Execute: head.next.next = head => Node(2).next = Node(1) - Execute: head.next = successor => Node(1).next = Node(4) - Sublist State: 3 -> 2 -> 1 -> 4 -> 5 - Return new_head = Node(3) FINAL RESULT: 3 -> 2 -> 1 -> 4 -> 5 -> NULL

class Solution:
    successor = None  # Class-level variable tracking (k+1)-th node

    def reverseK(self, head: Optional[ListNode], k: int) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        # Base case: when k == 1, record remaining list and return head
        if k == 1:
            self.successor = head.next  # Store (k+1)-th node
            return head  # Return k-th node as new sublist head

        # Recurse for first k-1 elements starting from head.next
        new_head = self.reverseK(head.next, k - 1)

        # HIGHLIGHT: Invert next pointer of child node back to head

        head.next = self.successor  # Reconnect current head to remaining list

        return new_head  # Return new head up call stack

private:

public:

        if (k == 1) {
            successor = head->next;  // Save remaining unreversed list head
            return head;  // Return current node as sublist head
        }

        ListNode* newHead = reverseK(head->next, k - 1);  // Recursive call

        // HIGHLIGHT: Invert link and reconnect to successor
        head->next->next = head;  // Reverse link
        head->next = successor;   // Reconnect tail to remaining list

            return head;  // Return base head
        }

        ListNode newHead = reverseK(head.next, k - 1);  // Recurse for k-1 nodes

        // HIGHLIGHT: Invert next pointer and attach successor
        head.next.next = head;  // Point child node back to head
        head.next = successor;  // Point current head to remaining list

var reverseK = function(head, k) {
    let successor = null;  // Closure variable tracking (k+1)-th node

    const helper = (node, count) => {

            return node;  // Return base head
        }

        let newHead = helper(node.next, count - 1);  // Recurse

        node.next.next = node;  // Point child to node
        node.next = successor;  // Attach successor

        return newHead;  // Return new head

title: Reverse first K elements of given linked list

content:
LeetCode 23 Hard Master Edition

An engineering manual analyzing global value collection, Min-Heap priority queues, and optimal divide-and-conquer pairwise reduction.

Problem Statement

You are given an array of k linked-lists lists, where each linked-list is sorted in ascending order.

Merge all the linked-lists into one sorted linked-list and return it.

Constraints

  • k == lists.length
  • 0 <= k <= 10^4
  • 0 <= lists[i].length <= 500
  • -10^4 <= lists[i][j] <= 10^4
  • lists[i] is sorted in ascending order.
  • The sum of lists[i].length will not exceed 10^4.

Visualizing the Intent

Let's visualize merging multiple sorted streams into a single unified stream:

Input: lists = [ 1 -> 4 -> 5, 1 -> 3 -> 4, 2 -> 6 ] Merging Progression: - Compare heads of all lists: min(1, 1, 2) = 1 - Attach 1, advance list pointer - Compare heads: min(4, 1, 2) = 1 - Attach 1, advance list pointer - Compare heads: min(4, 3, 2) = 2 - Attach 2, advance list pointer - Compare heads: min(4, 3, 6) = 3 - Attach 3, advance list pointer - Compare heads: min(4, 4, 6) = 4 - Attach 4, advance list pointer - Compare heads: min(5, 4, 6) = 4 - Attach 4, advance list pointer - Compare heads: min(5, 6) = 5 - Attach 5, advance list pointer - Remaining: 6 - Attach 6 Output: 1 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 4 -> 5 -> 6

Core Realization: We have K sorted streams. At any point, the next absolute smallest node across the entire dataset must be one of the current front heads of the active streams.

Solutions Breakdown

Approach 1 - Brute Force (Extract, Sort, & Rebuild)

🧭 Intuition Breakdown (Global Collection)

1. The Concept: If combining multiple sorted lists feels complex, ignore the list structures initially! Traversal over every node across all K lists allows us to collect all raw values into a standard 1D array. We then sort this array using a built-in sorting algorithm (Timsort/Quicksort) and construct a brand-new linked list from the sorted values.

2. Why it Works: It completely bypasses pointer manipulation logic during the sorting phase. However, it requires extra space O(N) to store all node values and time O(N log N) to sort them, where N is the total number of nodes across all K lists.

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition: Saare K lists ke andar jitne bhi numbers hain, unhe ek simple 1D array me daal do. Us array ko regular sort() function se sort kar do, aur phir ek nayi Linked List banakar result return kar do. Yeh tarika simple hai par extra space O(N) leta hai aur sorting me O(N log N) time lagta hai.

📋 Approach 1 Line-by-Line Trace Profile

Input: lists = [[1, 4], [1, 3], [2]]

Step 1: Traverse and collect all values • List 0: values = [1, 4] • List 1: values = [1, 4, 1, 3] • List 2: values = [1, 4, 1, 3, 2] Step 2: Sort the array values • Array before sort: [1, 4, 1, 3, 2] • Array after sort: [1, 1, 2, 3, 4] Step 3: Rebuild linked list from sorted array • Dummy node created -> [dummy] • Val 1 -> dummy -> [1] • Val 1 -> dummy -> [1] -> [1] • Val 2 -> dummy -> [1] -> [1] -> [2] • Val 3 -> dummy -> [1] -> [1] -> [2] -> [3] • Val 4 -> dummy -> [1] -> [1] -> [2] -> [3] -> [4] Result Returned: 1 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4

a) Source Code Implementation

class Solution:
    def mergeKLists(self, lists: list[Optional[ListNode]]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        nodes = []  # Create list to extract all node values
        
        for head in lists:  # Iterate over each linked list head
            curr = head  # Pointer to traverse current linked list
            while curr:  # Walk till end of current list
                nodes.append(curr.val)  # Store node value in python list
                curr = curr.next  # Move to next node

        nodes.sort()  # Sort extracted values ascending in-place
        
        dummy = ListNode(0)  # Create dummy head node for list construction
        curr = dummy  # Pointer to append nodes to dummy list
        
        for val in nodes:  # Iterate through sorted values
            curr.next = ListNode(val)  # Instantiate new node and attach
            curr = curr.next  # Advance current building pointer
            
        return dummy.next  # Return start of newly constructed linked list
class Solution {
public:
    ListNode* mergeKLists(vector<ListNode*>& lists) {
        vector<int> nodes;  // Vector to accumulate all node values
        
        for (ListNode* head : lists) {  // Iterate through vector of list heads
            ListNode* curr = head;  // Temporary pointer for list traversal
            while (curr != nullptr) {  // Traverse until list end
                nodes.push_back(curr->val);  // Store current integer value
                curr = curr->next;  // Advance traversal pointer
            }
        }
        
        std::sort(nodes.begin(), nodes.end());  // Sort vector values in O(N log N)
        
        ListNode* dummy = new ListNode(0);  // Dummy node for output construction
        ListNode* curr = dummy;  // Construction pointer
        
        for (int val : nodes) {  // Loop over sorted values
            curr->next = new ListNode(val);  // Allocate new node
            curr = curr->next;  // Advance construction pointer
        }
        
        return dummy->next;  // Return head of newly built list
    }
};

                curr = curr.next;  // Advance pointer
            }
        }
        
        Collections.sort(nodes);  // Sort ArrayList values
        
        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0);  // Initialize dummy node
        ListNode curr = dummy;  // Worker pointer for list assembly
        
        for (int val : nodes) {  // Iterate through sorted list

            nodes.push(curr.val);  // Push value to array
            curr = curr.next;  // Step forward
        }
    }
    
    nodes.sort((a, b) => a - b);  // Numeric sort ascending
    
    const dummy = new ListNode(0);  // Dummy node anchor
    let curr = dummy;  // Assembly cursor
    
    for (let val of nodes) {  // Loop sorted array
        curr.next = new ListNode(val);  // Create and attach node
        curr = curr.next;  // Move cursor
    }
    
    return dummy.next;  // Return head of result list
};

Approach 2 - Min-Heap / Priority Queue (K-Way Stream Merge)

🧭 Deep Intuition Breakdown (Real-Time Head Comparison)

1. The Core Mechanical Discovery: Imagine you are holding K sorted decks of cards. To build a single combined deck in perfect sorted order, you do not need to look at every card in every deck. You only need to look at the top card of each deck.

Whichever top card is the smallest gets picked first and placed into your new deck. Then, you look at the new top card exposed in that specific deck and repeat the process. Because every individual list is already sorted, the absolute smallest unmerged node across ALL K lists MUST be sitting at one of the current front heads of the active lists!

2. Why a Min-Heap is Required:
If we manually compare all K heads one by one using a simple loop, finding the minimum head takes O(K) time per node. Doing this for N total nodes gives a time complexity of O(N * K).
Instead, we feed the heads into a Min-Heap (Priority Queue). A Min-Heap automatically keeps the smallest element at the top in O(log K) time for insertion and deletion!

How the Min-Heap Controls Execution: 1. Seed the Min-Heap with the head node of each non-empty list in lists. (Heap size <= K) 2. Pop the root node (which is guaranteed to be the global minimum among all active list heads). 3. Append this popped node directly to our merged list! 4. If the popped node has a next node (popped.next != None), push popped.next into the Min-Heap! 5. Repeat steps 2-4 until the Min-Heap becomes completely empty!

3. Why Space Complexity is O(K) and Time Complexity is O(N log K):
• Heap size is strictly bounded by K (at most 1 node per list in heap).
• Pushing and popping from a heap of size K takes O(log K) time.
• We perform this operation for every node in the total dataset (N total nodes).
• Total Time: O(N log K). Total Auxiliary Space: O(K).

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition behind Min-Heap: Socho tumhare paas K cards ke sorted bundles hain. Sabse chhota card chunne ke liye tumhe saare cards dekhne ki zaroorat nahi hai, sirf har bundle ka pehla (top) card dekhna hai.

Har baar sabse chhota node nikalne ke liye hum ek Min-Heap use karte hain. Puraani saari K lists ke heads ko heap me daal do. Min-Heap hamesha sabse chhoti value wale node ko top par rakhta hai O(log K) time me.

Hum heap se minimum node pop karte hain, use result linked list me attach karte hain, aur **usi list ke agle node ko wapas heap me daal dete hain**. Yeh process tab tak chalta hai jab tak heap khali nahi ho jata. Extra memory sirf O(K) lagti hai aur time complexity O(N log K) ho jati hai.

import heapq  # Import python min-heap module

class Solution:
    def mergeKLists(self, lists: list[Optional[ListNode]]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        min_heap = []  # List to maintain binary min-heap structure
        
        # Seed heap with initial head node of each non-empty list
        # Note: Include index i in tuple (node.val, i, node) to break tie-breaker comparisons
        for i, head in enumerate(lists):
            if head:  # Ensure head is non-null
                heapq.heappush(min_heap, (head.val, i, head))  # Push tuple into heap
                
        dummy = ListNode(0)  # Dummy node anchor for resulting merged list
        curr = dummy  # Pointer tracking end of merged list
        
        while min_heap:  # Loop until min-heap is completely empty
            val, i, node = heapq.heappop(min_heap)  # Pop node with absolute minimum value
            curr.next = node  # Link popped node to merged list
            curr = curr.next  # Advance building pointer
            
            if node.next:  # If popped node has a successor in its original list
                heapq.heappush(min_heap, (node.next.val, i, node.next))  # Push next node to heap
                
        return dummy.next  # Return head of merged list
class Solution {
private:
    // Custom comparator for Min-Heap priority queue comparing ListNode values
    struct Compare {
        bool operator()(ListNode* a, ListNode* b) {
            return a->val > b->val;  // Return true if a.val > b.val (Min-Heap structure)
        }
    };

public:
    ListNode* mergeKLists(vector<ListNode*>& lists) {
        priority_queue<ListNode*, vector<ListNode*>, Compare> pq;  // Declare priority_queue
        
        for (ListNode* head : lists) {  // Iterate through all list heads
            if (head != nullptr) {  // Ensure non-null pointer
                pq.push(head);  // Seed priority queue
            }
        }
        
        ListNode* dummy = new ListNode(0);  // Create dummy node
        ListNode* curr = dummy;  // Worker pointer for list assembly
        
        while (!pq.empty()) {  // Loop until priority queue is empty
            ListNode* minNode = pq.top();  // Get minimum element node pointer
            pq.pop();  // Remove top node from queue
            
            curr->next = minNode;  // Link node to merged chain
            curr = curr->next;  // Advance assembly pointer
            
            if (minNode->next != nullptr) {  // Check if next node exists
                pq.push(minNode->next);  // Push next node into priority queue
            }
        }
        
        return dummy->next;  // Return merged list head
    }
};
class Solution {
    public ListNode mergeKLists(ListNode[] lists) {
        if (lists == null || lists.length == 0) return null;  // Guard clause for empty input
        
        // Instantiate PriorityQueue passing lambda comparator sorting by val
        PriorityQueue<ListNode> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a.val - b.val);
        
        for (ListNode head : lists) {  // Seed priority queue
            if (head != null) {  // Filter non-null heads
                pq.add(head);  // Add head to PriorityQueue
            }
        }
        
        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0);  // Dummy anchor node
        ListNode curr = dummy;  // Assembly worker pointer
        
        while (!pq.isEmpty()) {  // Traverse until PriorityQueue is empty
            ListNode minNode = pq.poll();  // Extract minimum value node
            curr.next = minNode;  // Wire node to merged result list
            curr = curr.next;  // Move assembly pointer forward
            
            if (minNode.next != null) {  // If next node in current list exists
                pq.add(minNode.next);  // Add next node to PriorityQueue
            }
        }
        
        return dummy.next;  // Return head of merged list
    }
}
var mergeKLists = function(lists) {
    if (!lists || lists.length === 0) return null;  // Guard clause
    
    // Instantiate MinPriorityQueue from datastructures-js (LeetCode JS PriorityQueue)
    const pq = new MinPriorityQueue({ priority: node => node.val });
    
    for (let head of lists) {  // Seed queue with heads
        if (head !== null) {  // Check non-null
            pq.enqueue(head);  // Enqueue head node
        }
    }
    
    const dummy = new ListNode(0);  // Create dummy node
    let curr = dummy;  // Creation pointer
    
    while (!pq.isEmpty()) {  // Process queue items
        const minNode = pq.dequeue().element;  // Dequeue minimum node
        curr.next = minNode;  // Attach minNode to result chain
        curr = curr.next;  // Move creation pointer
        
        if (minNode.next !== null) {  // If next node exists
            pq.enqueue(minNode.next);  // Enqueue next node into queue
        }
    }
    
    return dummy.next;  // Return merged list head
};

Approach 3 - Optimal Solution: Divide & Conquer (Pairwise Merge)

🧭 Deep Intuition Breakdown (Pairwise Logarithmic Reduction)

1. Why Sequential Merging is Slow:
Suppose we merge lists one by one sequentially (List 0 + List 1, then + List 2, then + List 3...).
• Step 1: Merge L0 (length N/K) and L1 (length N/K) -> takes 2*(N/K) operations.
• Step 2: Merge combined L01 (length 2N/K) and L2 (length N/K) -> takes 3*(N/K) operations.
• Step 3: Merge combined L012 (length 3N/K) and L3 (length N/K) -> takes 4*(N/K) operations.
Summing these operations up to K lists gives (2 + 3 + ... + K) * (N/K) = O(N * K) time! This is too slow.

2. The Divide & Conquer Solution (Tournament Tree Style):
Instead of merging sequentially into a growing master list, we pair up adjacent lists and merge them in parallel!

  • Round 1: Merge K lists in pairs to produce K/2 merged lists. Every node is processed once (O(N) operations across the whole round).
  • Round 2: Merge K/2 lists in pairs to produce K/4 merged lists. (O(N) operations across the whole round).
  • Round 3: Merge K/4 lists in pairs to produce K/8 merged lists. (O(N) operations across the whole round).
Because the number of lists is halved in every single round, there are log2(K) total rounds! Since each round takes O(N) work to merge two-by-two, total time is O(N log K)!

Divide & Conquer Pairwise Reduction Tree (K = 8 lists): Level 0: L0 L1 L2 L3 L4 L5 L6 L7 (8 lists) \ / \ / \ / \ / Level 1: L01 L23 L45 L67 (4 merged lists) \ / \ / Level 2: L0123 L4567 (2 merged lists) \ / Level 3: L01234567 (1 Final Sorted List!) Total Tree Levels = log2(K) Work done per level = O(N) where N is total nodes across all lists. Overall Time Complexity = O(N log K)! Auxiliary Space = O(1) iterative (no Extra Memory or Heap required)!

3. Why Space is O(1) Iterative:
We re-wire existing pointers in-place using a standard 2-list merge helper function (mergeTwoLists). We overwrite the entries in our lists array in-place, taking zero auxiliary heap memory!

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition behind Divide & Conquer: 2 sorted lists ko merge karna Aasan hota hai (O(N) two pointers se). Agar hum ek-ek karke saari lists ko line se merge karenge, toh time O(N * K) ho jayega jo slow hai.

Iska sabse fast tarika yeh hai ki hum Merge Sort ki tarah **pair-wise merge** karein! List 0 ko List 1 se, List 2 ko List 3 se merge karo. Har round me total lists aadhi (K/2) ho jati hain. Total rounds sirf log2(K) lagte hain. Isse total time O(N log K) aata hai aur space O(1) (iterative mode me) rehta hai!

📋 Full Trace Dry Run: Divide & Conquer Pairwise Merge

Input: lists = [L0: [1,4], L1: [1,3], L2: [2,6], L3: [5,7]] (K = 4 lists)

================================================================================= ROUND 1: (K = 4 lists present, pair adjacent lists) ================================================================================= • Pair 1: Merge L0 [1,4] and L1 [1,3] - Standard 2-list merge trace: - Compare 1 and 1 -> attach 1 (L0). Remaining: L0[4], L1[1,3] - Compare 4 and 1 -> attach 1 (L1). Remaining: L0[4], L1[3] - Compare 4 and 3 -> attach 3 (L1). Remaining: L0[4], L1 empty - Attach remaining L0[4] - Result of Pair 1 (L01): 1 -> 1 -> 3 -> 4 • Pair 2: Merge L2 [2,6] and L3 [5,7] - Standard 2-list merge trace: - Compare 2 and 5 -> attach 2 (L2) - Compare 6 and 5 -> attach 5 (L3) - Compare 6 and 7 -> attach 6 (L2) - Attach remaining L3[7] - Result of Pair 2 (L23): 2 -> 5 -> 6 -> 7 Lists remaining after Round 1: [ L01: [1,1,3,4], L23: [2,5,6,7] ] (Count reduced from 4 to 2!) ================================================================================= ROUND 2: (K = 2 lists present, merge final pair) ================================================================================= • Merge L01 [1,1,3,4] and L23 [2,5,6,7]: - Compare 1 and 2 -> attach 1 (L01) - Compare 1 and 2 -> attach 1 (L01) - Compare 3 and 2 -> attach 2 (L23) - Compare 3 and 5 -> attach 3 (L01) - Compare 4 and 5 -> attach 4 (L01) - L01 exhausted! Attach remaining L23 [5,6,7] Result of Final Pair: 1 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 6 -> 7 FINAL CONVERGED LIST: 1 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 6 -> 7

a) Source Code Implementation

class Solution:
    def mergeKLists(self, lists: list[Optional[ListNode]]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        if not lists or len(lists) == 0:
            return None  # Base guard for empty list input

        # Standard helper function to merge 2 sorted linked lists in O(N1 + N2)
        def mergeTwoLists(l1, l2):
            dummy = ListNode(0)  # Create dummy node for head reference
            curr = dummy  # Assembly cursor pointer
            while l1 and l2:  # Compare head values while both lists exist
                if l1.val <= l2.val:
                    curr.next = l1  # Wire l1 node
                    l1 = l1.next  # Step l1 forward
                else:
                    curr.next = l2  # Wire l2 node
                    l2 = l2.next  # Step l2 forward
                curr = curr.next  # Step assembly cursor forward
            curr.next = l1 if l1 else l2  # Attach remaining nodes directly
            return dummy.next  # Return merged list head

        # Divide and conquer iterative reduction
        while len(lists) > 1:  # Loop until single final list remains
            merged_lists = []  # List to store merged pair outputs for current level
            for i in range(0, len(lists), 2):  # Step by 2 to pair adjacent lists
                l1 = lists[i]  # First list of pair
                l2 = lists[i + 1] if (i + 1) < len(lists) else None  # Second list (or None if odd length)
                merged_lists.append(mergeTwoLists(l1, l2))  # Merge pair and append result
            lists = merged_lists  # Replace original list with halved merged list level

        return lists[0]  # Return single final converged merged list
class Solution {
private:
    // Standard 2-list merge helper function
    ListNode* mergeTwoLists(ListNode* l1, ListNode* l2) {
        ListNode* dummy = new ListNode(0);  // Dummy anchor node
        ListNode* curr = dummy;  // Building cursor
        while (l1 != nullptr && l2 != nullptr) {
            if (l1->val <= l2->val) {
                curr->next = l1;  // Wire l1 node
                l1 = l1->next;  // Step l1
            } else {
                curr->next = l2;  // Wire l2 node
                l2 = l2->next;  // Step l2
            }
            curr = curr->next;  // Step cursor
        }
        curr->next = (l1 != nullptr) ? l1 : l2;  // Attach remaining non-null list
        return dummy->next;  // Return head
    }

public:
    ListNode* mergeKLists(vector<ListNode*>& lists) {
        if (lists.empty()) return nullptr;  // Guard clause for empty vector

        int interval = 1;  // Step distance between pairs to merge in-place
        while (interval < lists.size()) {  // Continue until interval exceeds vector size
            for (size_t i = 0; i + interval < lists.size(); i += interval * 2) {
                // Merge pair at index i and i + interval in-place into lists[i]
                lists[i] = mergeTwoLists(lists[i], lists[i + interval]);
            }
            interval *= 2;  // Double step interval for next reduction level
        }
        return lists[0];  // Return final converged head at index 0
    }
};
class Solution {
    // Helper method to merge two sorted lists
    private ListNode mergeTwoLists(ListNode l1, ListNode l2) {

        ListNode curr = dummy;  // Cursor pointer

            if (l1.val <= l2.val) {
                curr.next = l1;  // Attach l1 node
                l1 = l1.next;  // Step l1
            } else {
                curr.next = l2;  // Attach l2 node
                l2 = l2.next;  // Step l2
            }
            curr = curr.next;  // Step cursor
        }
        curr.next = (l1 != null) ? l1 : l2;  // Attach remaining non-null list
        return dummy.next;  // Return merged head
    }

    public ListNode mergeKLists(ListNode[] lists) {
        if (lists == null || lists.length == 0) return null;  // Guard clause

        int interval = 1;  // Pairwise merge stride interval
        while (interval < lists.length) {  // Loop until interval covers full array
            for (int i = 0; i + interval < lists.length; i += interval * 2) {
                // Merge lists[i] and lists[i + interval] in-place
                lists[i] = mergeTwoLists(lists[i], lists[i + interval]);
            }
            interval *= 2;  // Double the pair stride for next level
        }
        return lists[0];  // Final merged list is stored at index 0
    }
}
var mergeKLists = function(lists) {
    if (!lists || lists.length === 0) return null;  // Guard clause

    // Helper to merge 2 sorted lists
    const mergeTwoLists = (l1, l2) => {
        const dummy = new ListNode(0);  // Dummy anchor
        let curr = dummy;  // Creation cursor
        while (l1 !== null && l2 !== null) {
            if (l1.val <= l2.val) {
                curr.next = l1;  // Wire l1
                l1 = l1.next;  // Move l1
            } else {
                curr.next = l2;  // Wire l2
                l2 = l2.next;  // Move l2
            }
            curr = curr.next;  // Advance cursor
        }
        curr.next = l1 !== null ? l1 : l2;  // Append remaining nodes
        return dummy.next;  // Return merged head
    };

    let interval = 1;  // Stride interval
    while (interval < lists.length) {  // Pairwise merge loop
        for (let i = 0; i + interval < lists.length; i += interval * 2) {
            lists[i] = mergeTwoLists(lists[i], lists[i + interval]);  // In-place pair merge
        }
        interval *= 2;  // Double stride interval
    }
    return lists[0];  // Return merged head at index 0
};

To deliver robust engineering systems, solutions must be validated against extreme edge case scenarios:

e.g., lists = []		 Null pointer dereference or index out-of-bounds exceptions when accessing lists[0]. Guarded at function start: if not lists: return None / if (lists.empty()) return nullptr.

e.g., lists = [[], [], []]		 Min-Heap tries to access head.val on null pointers. Seeding loop explicitly validates if (head != null) before inserting into Min-Heap or processing pairs. Returns None safely.

e.g., [[1], [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], [2, 3]]		 Exhausting one list early causing premature termination of merging. In Min-Heap approach, when a popped node has node.next == None, no new node from that row is pushed. Other list nodes in heap continue processing cleanly.

Approach 2: Min-Heap / Priority Queue O(N log K) O(K) Auxiliary Production Standard for Streaming. Extremely fast. Heap memory is bounded strictly by the number of lists K.

content:
LeetCode 160 Easy Master Edition

An engineering manual analyzing address-based hash tracking, length-difference alignment, and elegant two-pointer trajectory synchronization.

Problem Statement

Given the heads of two singly linked-lists headA and headB, return the node at which the two lists intersect. If the two linked lists have no intersection at all, return null.

The test cases are generated such that there are no cycles anywhere in the entire linked structure.

Note that the linked lists must retain their original structure after the function returns.

Constraints

  • The number of nodes of headA is in m.
  • The number of nodes of headB is in n.
  • 1 <= m, n <= 3 * 10^4
  • 1 <= Node.val <= 10^5
  • 0 <= skipA <= m
  • 0 <= skipB <= n
  • intersectVal is 0 if headA and headB do not intersect.
  • intersectVal == listA[skipA] == listB[skipB] if headA and headB intersect.

Visualizing the Intent

Let's map out two lists intersecting at Node 8:

List A: [4] -> [1] \ [8] -> [4] -> [5] -> NULL List B: [5] -> [6] -> [1] / Index Perspective: List A Nodes: 4 -> 1 -> 8 -> 4 -> 5 -> NULL (Length M = 5) List B Nodes: 5 -> 6 -> 1 -> 8 -> 4 -> 5 -> NULL (Length N = 6) Intersection Node: Node with value 8 (Memory Address Match)

Core Realization: Intersection is determined strictly by reference / memory address equality, not by numerical value equality. Once two linked lists intersect, they share all remaining downstream nodes up to the terminal NULL pointer.

Solutions Breakdown

Approach 1 - Brute Force / Naive (HashSet Memory Tracking)

🧭 Intuition Breakdown (Storing Visited Nodes)

1. The Concept: Walk through List A completely and store the memory reference of every single node in a Hash Set. Then, traverse List B node-by-node and check if the current node's memory reference already exists in the Hash Set.

2. Why it Works: The first node in List B that exists inside the Hash Set is guaranteed to be the exact intersection node. If List B finishes without any set matches, no intersection exists.

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition: List A ke saare nodes par visit karke unke memory addresses ko ek HashSet me save kar lo. Phir List B ke nodes ko ek-ek karke HashSet me dhoondo. Jo pehla node HashSet me mil jayega, wahi dono lists ka intersection point hoga. Yeh simple hai par isme O(M) extra space lagti hai.

📋 Approach 1 Line-by-Line Trace Profile

Input: List A = 1 -> 2 -> 3`, `List B = 4 -> 2 -> 3 (Intersect at Node 2)

Step 1: Traverse List A and store references in Set • Visit Node(1) -> set = { Node(1) } • Visit Node(2) -> set = { Node(1), Node(2) } • Visit Node(3) -> set = { Node(1), Node(2), Node(3) } Step 2: Traverse List B and query Set • Check Node(4): Is Node(4) in set? FALSE. • Check Node(2): Is Node(2) in set? TRUE! Match Found at Node(2). Return Node(2).

a) Source Code Implementation

class Solution:
    def getIntersectionNode(self, headA: ListNode, headB: ListNode) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        visited_nodes = set()  # Instantiate hash set to hold memory references
        
        currA = headA  # Pointer for traversing List A
        while currA:  # Traverse List A to completion
            visited_nodes.add(currA)  # Add node reference into set
            currA = currA.next  # Advance to next node

        currB = headB  # Pointer for traversing List B
        while currB:  # Traverse List B to search for intersection
            if currB in visited_nodes:  # Check O(1) set membership for node reference match
                return currB  # First matching reference is the intersection node
            currB = currB.next  # Advance to next node

        return None  # Return None if no intersection is found
class Solution {
public:
    ListNode *getIntersectionNode(ListNode *headA, ListNode *headB) {
        unordered_set<ListNode*> visited_nodes;  // Hash set for storing pointers
        
        ListNode* currA = headA;  // Cursor for List A
        while (currA != nullptr) {
            visited_nodes.insert(currA);  // Insert pointer to set
            currA = currA->next;  // Step forward
        }
        
        ListNode* currB = headB;  // Cursor for List B
        while (currB != nullptr) {
            if (visited_nodes.count(currB)) {  // Check if pointer exists in set
                return currB;  // Found intersection point
            }
            currB = currB->next;  // Step forward
        }
        
        return nullptr;  // No intersection
    }
};
public class Solution {
    public ListNode getIntersectionNode(ListNode headA, ListNode headB) {
        Set<ListNode> visitedNodes = new HashSet<>();  // Create HashSet for object reference tracking
        
        ListNode currA = headA;  // List A traversal pointer
        while (currA != null) {
            visitedNodes.add(currA);  // Add node to set
            currA = currA.next;  // Advance pointer
        }
        
        ListNode currB = headB;  // List B traversal pointer
        while (currB != null) {
            if (visitedNodes.contains(currB)) {  // Lookup reference match
                return currB;  // Return intersection node
            }
            currB = currB.next;  // Advance pointer
        }
        
        return null;  // No intersection found
    }
}
var getIntersectionNode = function(headA, headB) {
    const visitedNodes = new Set();  // Instantiate Set for memory references
    
    let currA = headA;  // Cursor A
    while (currA !== null) {
        visitedNodes.add(currA);  // Store reference
        currA = currA.next;  // Step forward
    }
    
    let currB = headB;  // Cursor B
    while (currB !== null) {
        if (visitedNodes.has(currB)) {  // Match check
            return currB;  // Found intersection
        }
        currB = currB.next;  // Step forward
    }
    
    return null;  // Return null if disjoint
};

Approach 2 - Optimal Solution: Length Difference Alignment

🧭 Intuition Breakdown (Equalizing Traversal Distance)

1. The Core Insight: If two linked lists intersect, the section from the intersection point to the end of the list is 100% identical in length for both lists.

The only reason the two lists might have different overall lengths is because of the un-shared prefix sections before the intersection!

Length Alignment Visual: List A (Len 5): [A1] -> [A2] -> [C1] -> [C2] -> [C3] List B (Len 6): [B1] -> [B2] -> [B3] -> [C1] -> [C2] -> [C3] Difference diff = Len(B) - Len(A) = 6 - 5 = 1 Align pointers by advancing List B's start pointer by 1 step: List A: [A1] -> [A2] -> [C1] -> [C2] -> [C3] ^ (pA) List B: [B1] -> [B2] -> [B3] -> [C1] -> [C2] -> [C3] ^ (pB advanced 1 step) Now both pA and pB are at equal distance from the intersection node! Advance both pointers together -> They meet at [C1]!

2. How It Works:

  1. Calculate total lengths lenA and lenB.
  2. Calculate the difference diff = abs(lenA - lenB).
  3. Advance the pointer of the longer list by diff steps.
  4. Advance both pointers simultaneously step-by-step. The first node where pA == pB is the intersection node!

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition behind Length Alignment: Intersection ke baad ka hissa dono lists ke liye bilkul barabar length ka hota hai. Jo bhi length me fark hota hai, wo sirf shuruat ke un-shared elements ki wajah se hota hai.

Isliye, pehle dono lists ki length (lenA aur lenB) nikal lo. Lambe waale list ke pointer ko unke difference (diff) jitna aage bada do. Ab dono pointers intersection point se barabar ki doori par hain. Dono pointers ko ek saath 1-1 step aage badhao, wo dono **exact intersection node** par milenge!

📋 Approach 2 Line-by-Line Trace Profile

Input: List A = [4, 1, 8, 4, 5] (lenA = 5), List B = [5, 6, 1, 8, 4, 5] (lenB = 6)

Step 1: Compute Lengths • lenA = 5, lenB = 6 • diff = 6 - 5 = 1 Step 2: Advance longer list (List B) by diff = 1 step • pA starts at List A[0] -> Node(4) • pB starts at List B[1] -> Node(6) Step 3: Advance both pointers together until pA == pB • Move 1: pA = Node(1), pB = Node(1) -> Values match but addresses distinct! • Move 2: pA = Node(8), pB = Node(8) -> Memory Address Match! pA == pB is TRUE! Intersection Found at Node(8).

a) Source Code Implementation

class Solution:
    def getIntersectionNode(self, headA: ListNode, headB: ListNode) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        # Helper function to compute linked list length
        def get_length(node):
            length = 0
            while node:
                length += 1
                node = node.next
            return length

        lenA, lenB = get_length(headA), get_length(headB)  # Compute lengths of both lists
        currA, currB = headA, headB  # Set traversal pointers

        # Advance longer list pointer by length difference
        if lenA > lenB:
            for _ in range(lenA - lenB):
                currA = currA.next
        else:
            for _ in range(lenB - lenA):
                currB = currB.next

        # Traverse both lists together until pointers meet
        while currA and currB:
            if currA == currB:  # Reference equality check
                return currA  # Return intersection node
            currA = currA.next
            currB = currB.next

        return None  # Return None if disjoint
class Solution {
private:
    int getLength(ListNode* node) {
        int len = 0;
        while (node != nullptr) {
            len++;
            node = node->next;
        }
        return len;
    }

public:
    ListNode *getIntersectionNode(ListNode *headA, ListNode *headB) {
        int lenA = getLength(headA);
        int lenB = getLength(headB);
        
        ListNode* currA = headA;
        ListNode* currB = headB;

        // Align starting positions
        if (lenA > lenB) {
            for (int i = 0; i < lenA - lenB; ++i) currA = currA->next;
        } else {
            for (int i = 0; i < lenB - lenA; ++i) currB = currB->next;
        }

        // Step simultaneously
        while (currA != nullptr && currB != nullptr) {
            if (currA == currB) return currA;
            currA = currA->next;
            currB = currB->next;
        }

        return nullptr;
    }
};

    const lenB = getLength(headB);
    
    let currA = headA, currB = headB;

    while (currA && currB) {
        if (currA === currB) return currA;
        currA = currA.next;
        currB = currB.next;

    return null;

Approach 3 - Optimal Solution: Two-Pointer Trajectory Synchronization

🧭 Deep Intuition Breakdown (The Swapping Pointer Trick)

1. The Core Mathematical Concept:
Let a be the number of unique nodes in List A before intersection.
Let b be the number of unique nodes in List B before intersection.
Let c be the number of shared common nodes after intersection.

List A Total Traversal Path = a + c List B Total Traversal Path = b + c What happens if Pointer 1 traverses List A, and upon reaching NULL, jumps to start of List B? Path 1 Distance = (a + c) + b What happens if Pointer 2 traverses List B, and upon reaching NULL, jumps to start of List A? Path 2 Distance = (b + c) + a Notice that: (a + c) + b == (b + c) + a !! Total Traversal Distance for BOTH pointers is EXACTLY equal to a + b + c !

2. How Pointer Synchronization Works:

  • Pointer pA starts at headA, pointer pB starts at headB.
  • Move both pointers forward step-by-step.
  • When pA hits NULL, redirect it to headB.
  • When pB hits NULL, redirect it to head headA.
  • After switching paths, both pointers have traveled identical total distances (a + b + c). They are guaranteed to meet at the exact intersection node!
  • If the lists do NOT intersect (c = 0), both pointers will travel a + b steps and hit NULL at the exact same moment (pA == pB == NULL), terminating the loop cleanly!

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition behind Swapping Pointers: Maan lo List A me a nodes pehle hain, List B me b nodes pehle hain, aur c shared common nodes hain.

Pointer 1 pehle List A poori chalega (a + c), phir List B par chala jayega. Pointer 2 pehle List B poori chalega (b + c), phir List A par chala jayega. Dono ka total distance a + b + c bilkul barabar ho jata hai!

Iska matlab, doosri list par switch karne ke baad, dono pointers **exact ek hi time par intersection node par milenge**! Aur agar koi intersection nahi hoga (c = 0), toh dono ek saath NULL par milenge aur loop ruk jayega. Time complexity O(M + N) aur Space O(1) hai!

📋 Full Trace Dry Run 1: Intersecting Lists (Path Synchronization)

Input Lists:
• List A: [4, 1] -> [8, 4, 5] (a = 2, c = 3)
• List B: [5, 6, 1] -> [8, 4, 5] (b = 3, c = 3)

Condition pA == pB is TRUE! Loop terminates. Returned Intersection Node: Node(8)
📋 Full Trace Dry Run 2: Disjoint Lists (No Intersection)

Input Lists:
• List A: [1, 2, 3] -> NULL (Len = 3)
• List B: [4, 5] -> NULL (Len = 2)

Initialization: pA = Node(1), pB = Node(4) • Step 1: pA -> Node(2), pB -> Node(5) • Step 2: pA -> Node(3), pB -> NULL -> Redirect pB = headA (Node 1) • Step 3: pA -> NULL, pB -> Node(2) -> Redirect pA = headB (Node 4) • Step 4: pA -> Node(5), pB -> Node(3) • Step 5: pA -> NULL, pB -> NULL <-- BOTH HIT NULL AT SAME STEP! Condition pA == pB (NULL == NULL) is TRUE! Loop terminates. Returned Intersection Node: NULL

a) Source Code Implementation

class Solution:
    def getIntersectionNode(self, headA: ListNode, headB: ListNode) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        if not headA or not headB:
            return None  # Base guard for empty inputs

        pA = headA  # Initialize pointer pA to headA
        pB = headB  # Initialize pointer pB to headB

            # If pB reaches end of List B, switch to headA; else step to pB.next
            pB = pB.next if pB else headA

        return pA  # Returns matching intersection node or None
class Solution {
public:

        ListNode* pA = headA;  // Pointer A
        ListNode* pB = headB;  // Pointer B

        while (pA != pB) {
            pA = (pA == nullptr) ? headB : pA->next;  // Switch to headB on nullptr
            pB = (pB == nullptr) ? headA : pB->next;  // Switch to headA on nullptr
        }

    }
};

title: Intersection of Two Linked Lists

content:
LeetCode 328 Medium Master Edition

An engineering manual analyzing node index parity grouping, in-place pointer weave mechanics, and linear tail splicing structures.

Problem Statement

Given the head of a singly linked list, group all the nodes with odd indices together followed by the nodes with even indices, and return the reordered list.

The first node is considered odd, the second node is even, and so on.

Note that the relative order inside both the even and odd groups should remain as it was in the input.

You must solve the problem in O(1) extra space complexity and O(n) time complexity.

Constraints

  • The number of nodes in the linked list is in the range [0, 10^4].
  • -10^6 <= Node.val <= 10^6

Visualizing the Intent

Let's map out the problem's index parity grouping on a linked structure:

Initial Linked List: Index: 1 2 3 4 5 Nodes: [1] -> [2] -> [3] -> [4] -> [5] -> NULL Type: Odd Even Odd Even Odd Desired Grouping: Odd Group Nodes: [1] -> [3] -> [5] Even Group Nodes: [2] -> [4] Spliced Output List: odd_head -> [1] -> [3] -> [5] -------> [2] -> [4] -> NULL (even_head) Output: [1, 3, 5, 2, 4]

Core Realization: The term odd and even refers to the 1-based positional index of the node within the chain, NOT the values stored inside the nodes! We must disentangle the list into two parallel streams and stitch the end of the odd stream to the start of the even stream.

Solutions Breakdown

Approach 1 - Brute Force (Extra Memory Array Extraction)

🧭 Intuition Breakdown (Value Array Splitting)

1. The Concept: Traversal across the original linked list allows us to place values into two separate linear arrays: odd_vals for odd positions (1, 3, 5...) and even_vals for even positions (2, 4, 6...).

2. Reconstruction: Combine odd_vals + even_vals into a single list and overwrite the node values in the original linked list in a second pass.

3. Why it Fails Constraints: Although it correctly handles element ordering in O(n) time, using arrays to store all node values requires O(n) auxiliary space, which violates the strict O(1) space constraint of the problem.

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition: Pehle poori linked list me traversal karo. Position 1, 3, 5... wale node values ko odd_vals array me daalo, aur 2, 4, 6... wale nodes ke values ko even_vals array me daalo. Phir dono arrays ko combine karke linked list ke node values ko overwrite kar do. Yeh simple hai par O(N) extra space leta hai, jo allowed nahi hai.

📋 Approach 1 Line-by-Line Trace Profile

Input: [2, 1, 3, 5, 6]

Step 1: Traverse and split values by position index • Pos 1 (val 2) -> odd_vals = [2] • Pos 2 (val 1) -> even_vals = [1] • Pos 3 (val 3) -> odd_vals = [2, 3] • Pos 4 (val 5) -> even_vals = [1, 5] • Pos 5 (val 6) -> odd_vals = [2, 3, 6] Step 2: Combine arrays -> combined = [2, 3, 6, 1, 5] Step 3: Overwrite linked list values with combined list Result: 2 -> 3 -> 6 -> 1 -> 5 -> NULL

a) Source Code Implementation

class Solution:
    def oddEvenList(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        if not head: return None  # Base guard clause for empty input list

        odd_vals, even_vals = [], []  # Declare auxiliary value buffers
        curr = head  # Traversal pointer setup
        idx = 1  # 1-based position index counter

        while curr:
            if idx % 2 != 0:
                odd_vals.append(curr.val)  # Record odd index value
            else:
                even_vals.append(curr.val)  # Record even index value
            curr = curr.next  # Step cursor forward
            idx += 1  # Increment 1-based index

        combined = odd_vals + even_vals  # Merge values sequentially
        curr = head  # Reset traversal pointer to head

        for val in combined:  # Overwrite original list node values
            curr.val = val
            curr = curr.next

        return head  # Return head of modified list
class Solution {
public:
    ListNode* oddEvenList(ListNode* head) {
        if (head == nullptr) return nullptr;  // Guard clause

        vector<int> odd_vals, even_vals;  // Vector buffers for node values
        ListNode* curr = head;  // Traversal cursor
        int idx = 1;  // 1-based index counter

        while (curr != nullptr) {
            if (idx % 2 != 0) odd_vals.push_back(curr->val);  // Collect odd value
            else even_vals.push_back(curr->val);             // Collect even value
            curr = curr->next;  // Advance pointer
            idx++;  // Increment index
        }

        curr = head;  // Reset cursor
        for (int val : odd_vals) {  // Overwrite odd values
            curr->val = val;
            curr = curr->next;
        }
        for (int val : even_vals) {  // Overwrite even values
            curr->val = val;
            curr = curr->next;
        }

        return head;  // Return head pointer
    }
};
class Solution {
    public ListNode oddEvenList(ListNode head) {
        if (head == null) return null;  // Base guard

        List<Integer> oddVals = new ArrayList<>();  // Odd positions list
        List<Integer> evenVals = new ArrayList<>();  // Even positions list
        ListNode curr = head;  // Cursor
        int idx = 1;  // Index counter

        while (curr != null) {
            if (idx % 2 != 0) oddVals.add(curr.val);  // Store odd value
            else evenVals.add(curr.val);             // Store even value
            curr = curr.next;  // Move cursor
            idx++;
        }

        curr = head;  // Reset cursor to head
        for (int val : oddVals) {  // Overwrite odd elements
            curr.val = val;
            curr = curr.next;
        }
        for (int val : evenVals) {  // Overwrite even elements
            curr.val = val;
            curr = curr.next;
        }

        return head;  // Return head
    }
}
var oddEvenList = function(head) {
    if (!head) return null;  // Guard clause

    const oddVals = [], evenVals = [];  // Value storage buffers
    let curr = head;  // Traversal cursor
    let idx = 1;  // Index counter

    while (curr !== null) {
        if (idx % 2 !== 0) oddVals.push(curr.val);  // Collect odd value
        else evenVals.push(curr.val);             // Collect even value
        curr = curr.next;  // Step forward
        idx++;
    }

    const combined = oddVals.concat(evenVals);  // Merge arrays
    curr = head;  // Reset cursor

    for (let val of combined) {  // Overwrite values in-place
        curr.val = val;
        curr = curr.next;
    }

    return head;  // Return head
};

Approach 2 - Optimal Solution: In-Place Two-Pointer Weaving

🧭 Deep Intuition Breakdown (In-Place Pointer Disentanglement)

1. The Core Mechanical Discovery: We do not need extra memory arrays to separate odd and even indices. Notice that in the original linked list, odd nodes always point to even nodes, and even nodes always point to odd nodes!

We can maintain two pointers: odd starting at head (Node 1) and even starting at head.next (Node 2).

2. Preserving the Even Chain Head (even_head):
Before altering any pointers, we save a reference anchor even_head = even. As we process nodes, even will move down the list. We need even_head at the end to attach the tail of the odd chain to the start of the even chain!

Weaving Step Execution: 1. Make current odd node point to the next odd node: odd.next = even.next 2. Advance odd pointer to its new node: odd = odd.next 3. Make current even node point to the next even node: even.next = odd.next 4. Advance even pointer to its new node: even = even.next Loop Termination Condition: While `even` is not NULL and `even.next` is not NULL (handles both even and odd total list lengths). Final Splicing Step: odd.next = even_head <-- Connects tail of odd sublist to head of even sublist!
Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition behind In-Place Weaving: Bina extra memory ke, hum bas existing pointers ko bypass (leapfrog) kara kar do alag sub-lists banate hain.

• odd pointer ko Node 1 par rakho, aur even pointer ko Node 2 par.
• Sub-list B (even list) ke starting node ko ek variable me save kar lo: even_head = even.
• Har step par: odd.next = even.next karke odd ko agle odd node se jodo, aur even.next = odd.next karke even ko agle even node se jodo.
• Loop khatam hote hi, odd chain ke tail node ko odd.next = even_head karke even list ke start se jod do!

📋 Full Line-by-Line Trace Dry Run 1: Odd Length List (N = 5)

Input List: [1] -> [2] -> [3] -> [4] -> [5] -> NULL

================================================================================= INITIALIZATION: ================================================================================= • head = Node(1) • odd = Node(1) • even = Node(2) • even_head = Node(2) [ANCHOR] ================================================================================= ITERATION 1: (even != NULL and even.next != NULL -> Node(2) and Node(3) are valid) ================================================================================= • Step 1: Link odd to next odd node - odd.next = even.next => Node(1).next = Node(3) - odd chain: [1] -> [3] • Step 2: Advance odd pointer - odd = odd.next => odd = Node(3) • Step 3: Link even to next even node - even.next = odd.next => Node(2).next = Node(4) - even chain: [2] -> [4] • Step 4: Advance even pointer - even = even.next => even = Node(4) State after Iteration 1: odd chain: [1] -> [3] -> [4]... (odd is Node(3)) even chain: [2] -> [4] -> [5]... (even is Node(4)) ================================================================================= ITERATION 2: (even = Node(4), even.next = Node(5) -> Valid) ================================================================================= • Step 1: Link odd to next odd node - odd.next = even.next => Node(3).next = Node(5) - odd chain: [1] -> [3] -> [5] • Step 2: Advance odd pointer - odd = odd.next => odd = Node(5) • Step 3: Link even to next even node - even.next = odd.next => Node(4).next = NULL (since Node(5).next is NULL) - even chain: [2] -> [4] -> NULL • Step 4: Advance even pointer - even = even.next => even = NULL ================================================================================= LOOP TERMINATION & RECONNECTION (even == NULL) ================================================================================= • Loop terminates because even is NULL. • Execute Splicing: odd.next = even_head => Node(5).next = Node(2) FINAL RESULT: 1 -> 3 -> 5 -> 2 -> 4 -> NULL
📋 Full Line-by-Line Trace Dry Run 2: Even Length List (N = 4)

Input List: [2] -> [1] -> [3] -> [5] -> NULL

Initialization: odd = Node(2), even = Node(1), even_head = Node(1) Iteration 1: • odd.next = even.next => Node(2).next = Node(3) • odd = odd.next => odd = Node(3) • even.next = odd.next => Node(1).next = Node(5) • even = even.next => even = Node(5) Check Loop Condition: • even is Node(5), but even.next is NULL! • Loop terminates! Execute Splicing: • odd.next = even_head => Node(3).next = Node(1) FINAL RESULT: 2 -> 3 -> 1 -> 5 -> NULL

a) Source Code Implementation

class Solution:
    def oddEvenList(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        # Base case: empty list or single node requires no reordering
        if not head or not head.next:
            return head

        odd = head  # Pointer for odd-indexed sublist starting at node 1
        even = head.next  # Pointer for even-indexed sublist starting at node 2
        even_head = even  # Anchor reference to head of even sublist

        # Traverse while there are even nodes and an adjacent next node to process
        while even and even.next:
            odd.next = even.next  # Connect current odd node to next odd node
            odd = odd.next        # Advance odd pointer to newly attached node
            even.next = odd.next  # Connect current even node to next even node
            even = even.next      # Advance even pointer to newly attached node

        # HIGHLIGHT: Splice tail of odd sublist to head of even sublist
        odd.next = even_head

        return head  # Return original head pointing to reordered list
class Solution {
public:
    ListNode* oddEvenList(ListNode* head) {
        // Base case guard for list with 0 or 1 nodes
        if (head == nullptr || head->next == nullptr) return head;

        ListNode* odd = head;         // Odd sublist pointer
        ListNode* even = head->next;   // Even sublist pointer
        ListNode* evenHead = even;     // Anchor for even sublist start

        while (even != nullptr && even->next != nullptr) {
            odd->next = even->next;   // Bypass even node to link next odd node
            odd = odd->next;         // Step odd pointer
            even->next = odd->next;  // Bypass odd node to link next even node
            even = even->next;       // Step even pointer
        }

        // HIGHLIGHT: Reconnect odd tail to even head anchor
        odd->next = evenHead;

        return head;  // Return list head
    }
};
class Solution {
    public ListNode oddEvenList(ListNode head) {
        // Base case guard for empty or single-node list
        if (head == null || head.next == null) return head;

        ListNode odd = head;          // Odd sublist traversal pointer
        ListNode even = head.next;    // Even sublist traversal pointer
        ListNode evenHead = even;      // Anchor storing head of even sublist

        while (even != null && even.next != null) {
            odd.next = even.next;    // Link current odd to next odd
            odd = odd.next;          // Move odd cursor
            even.next = odd.next;   // Link current even to next even
            even = even.next;        // Move even cursor
        }

        // HIGHLIGHT: Connect tail of odd sublist to head of even sublist
        odd.next = evenHead;

        return head;  // Return head of reordered list
    }
}
var oddEvenList = function(head) {
    // Base case guard
    if (!head || !head.next) return head;

    let odd = head;           // Odd list cursor
    let even = head.next;     // Even list cursor
    let evenHead = even;      // Anchor for even list start

    while (even !== null && even.next !== null) {
        odd.next = even.next;   // Wire odd to next odd
        odd = odd.next;         // Move odd pointer
        even.next = odd.next;  // Wire even to next even
        even = even.next;       // Move even pointer
    }

    // HIGHLIGHT: Attach even sublist to end of odd sublist
    odd.next = evenHead;

    return head;  // Return head
};

Strategic Edge Cases Tracking Matrix

To ensure total production reliability, solutions must handle list structural variants seamlessly:

Edge Case Profile Algorithmic Risk Factor Mitigation Resolution Logic

e.g., head = NULL		 Null-pointer dereference when attempting to access head.next. Guarded at top: if not head: return None. Exits safely.

e.g., [1] or [1, 2]		 Unnecessary loop execution or null pointer exceptions. Guarded by if not head.next: return head and loop condition while even and even.next. Returns original list unchanged safely.
Even Number of Nodes
e.g., [1, 2, 3, 4]		 even pointer lands on Node(4) whose next is NULL. Loop condition even.next != NULL becomes False, terminating loop safely while odd sits on Node(3). Splices Node(3).next = even_head.
Odd Number of Nodes
e.g., [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]		 even pointer becomes NULL at the end of the loop. Loop condition even != NULL becomes False, terminating loop safely while odd sits on Node(5). Splices Node(5).next = even_head.

Approach 2: In-Place Two-Pointer Weaving O(N) O(1) Space Optimal Production Standard. Re-wires node pointers in-place using O(1) auxiliary memory. Maximum runtime and memory performance.
