LeetCode 2130 Medium Master Edition

An engineering manual analyzing two-pointer midpoint isolation, in-place half-reversal techniques, and optimal symmetric linear traversal algorithms.

Problem Statement

In a linked list of size n, where n is even, the i-th node (0-indexed) of the linked list is known as the twin of the (n - 1 - i)-th node, if 0 <= i <= (n / 2) - 1.

  • For example, if n = 4, then node 0 is the twin of node 3, and node 1 is the twin of node 2. These are the only pairs of nodes that are twins for n = 4.

The twin sum is defined as the sum of a node and its twin.

Given the head of a linked list with an even length, return the maximum twin sum of the linked list.

Constraints

  • The number of nodes in the list is an even integer in the range [2, 10^5].
  • 1 <= Node.val <= 10^5

Visualizing the Intent

Let's map out how twin pairing works across a symmetric linked structure:

Initial Linked List (n = 4): Index: 0 1 2 3 Nodes: [5] -> [4] -> [2] -> [1] -> NULL Twin Pair Formations: - Pair 1 (i = 0, n - 1 - 0 = 3): node[0] + node[3] = 5 + 1 = 6 - Pair 2 (i = 1, n - 1 - 1 = 2): node[1] + node[2] = 4 + 2 = 6 Maximum Twin Sum = max(6, 6) = 6 --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Example 2 (n = 6): Nodes: [4] -> [2] -> [2] -> [3] -> [1] -> [7] -> NULL Pairs: - i = 0 & i = 5: 4 + 7 = 11 - i = 1 & i = 4: 2 + 1 = 3 - i = 2 & i = 3: 2 + 3 = 5 Maximum Twin Sum = max(11, 3, 5) = 11

Core Realization: The twin of an index i sits at the mirror position from the tail. Because a singly linked list only allows forward movement, we cannot easily traverse backward from the end unless we either store values in an array/stack or physically reverse the second half of the list in-place.

Solutions Breakdown

Approach 1 - Brute Force / Naive (Array Buffer Extraction)

🧭 Intuition Breakdown (Linear Array Mapping)

1. The Concept: The primary difficulty with a singly linked list is that we cannot index backward from the end. If we convert the linked list into a standard 1D Array/Vector, we gain instant O(1) random access by index.

2. Execution Pipeline:

  1. Traverse the linked list from head to tail, appending every node's value into a dynamic array arr.
  2. Use a two-pointer technique on the array: set left = 0 and right = len(arr) - 1.
  3. Iterate while left < right, calculating arr[left] + arr[right] at each step, and maintain a global maximum tracker.

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition: Linked List me piche se aage aana mushkil hota hai. Isliye sabse pehle poori list ke values ko ek regular Array me copy kar lo. Phir array me do pointers banao: left = 0 aur right = n - 1. Dono pointers se twin values ko add karo, max track karo, aur pointers ko andar ki taraf shift karo (left++, right--). Yeh simple hai par O(N) extra memory leta hai.

📋 Approach 1 Line-by-Line Trace Profile

Input: [5, 4, 2, 1]

Step 1: Convert to Array • arr = [5, 4, 2, 1] Step 2: Two-Pointer Traversal • Initialization: left = 0, right = 3, max_sum = 0 • Iteration 1: - current_sum = arr[0] + arr[3] = 5 + 1 = 6 - max_sum = max(0, 6) = 6 - Move pointers: left = 1, right = 2 • Iteration 2: - current_sum = arr[1] + arr[2] = 4 + 2 = 6 - max_sum = max(6, 6) = 6 - Move pointers: left = 2, right = 1 • Loop ends (left >= right). Result Returned: 6

a) Source Code Implementation

class Solution:
    def pairSum(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> int:
        arr = []  # Dynamic array buffer to collect values
        curr = head  # Pointer for list traversal

        while curr:
            arr.append(curr.val)  # Extract and append current node value
            curr = curr.next  # Move to next node

        left, right = 0, len(arr) - 1  # Initialize two pointers at extremes
        max_twin_sum = 0  # Global maximum tracking variable

        while left < right:
            twin_sum = arr[left] + arr[right]  # Calculate twin sum for current pair
            max_twin_sum = max(max_twin_sum, twin_sum)  # Update global maximum
            left += 1  # Shift left pointer forward
            right -= 1  # Shift right pointer backward

        return max_twin_sum  # Return calculated maximum twin sum
class Solution {
public:
    int pairSum(ListNode* head) {
        vector<int> arr;  // Dynamic vector buffer
        ListNode* curr = head;  // Cursor pointer

        while (curr != nullptr) {
            arr.push_back(curr->val);  // Push value to vector
            curr = curr->next;  // Advance cursor
        }

        int left = 0;
        int right = arr.size() - 1;
        int max_twin_sum = 0;

        while (left < right) {
            int twin_sum = arr[left] + arr[right];  // Add twin pair values
            max_twin_sum = max(max_twin_sum, twin_sum);  // Record max
            left++;
            right--;
        }

        return max_twin_sum;  // Return result
    }
};
class Solution {
    public int pairSum(ListNode head) {
        List<Integer> arr = new ArrayList<>();  // ArrayList buffer
        ListNode curr = head;

        while (curr != null) {
            arr.add(curr.val);  // Collect node value
            curr = curr.next;  // Move forward
        }

        int left = 0;
        int right = arr.size() - 1;
        int maxTwinSum = 0;

        while (left < right) {
            int twinSum = arr.get(left) + arr.get(right);  // Compute sum
            maxTwinSum = Math.max(maxTwinSum, twinSum);  // Update max
            left++;
            right--;
        }

        return maxTwinSum;  // Return final max twin sum
    }
}
var pairSum = function(head) {
    const arr = [];  // Array buffer
    let curr = head;

    while (curr !== null) {
        arr.push(curr.val);  // Push value
        curr = curr.next;
    }

    let left = 0;
    let right = arr.length - 1;
    let maxTwinSum = 0;

    while (left < right) {
        let twinSum = arr[left] + arr[right];  // Compute twin sum
        maxTwinSum = Math.max(maxTwinSum, twinSum);  // Track max
        left++;
        right--;
    }

    return maxTwinSum;  // Return max twin sum
};

Approach 2 - Optimal Solution: Slow/Fast Midpoint Isolation & Second Half In-Place Reversal

🧭 Deep Intuition Breakdown (In-Place Structural Reorientation)

1. The Core Insight: We can achieve O(1) auxiliary space by modifying the linked list in-place! Since the list length is guaranteed to be even, we can split the list into two equal halves, reverse the second half, and then traverse both halves simultaneously from their heads to compute twin sums.

2. The 3-Step Algorithmic Pipeline:

  • Step 1 (Find Midpoint using Slow & Fast Pointers): Advance slow by 1 step and fast by 2 steps. When fast reaches NULL, slow sits exactly at the start of the second half.
  • Step 2 (Reverse Second Half In-Place): Reverse the linked list starting from slow using the classic 3-pointer technique. Let the new head of this reversed second half be prev.
  • Step 3 (Simultaneous Traversal & Twin Sum Matching): Set p1 = head (start of first half) and p2 = prev (start of reversed second half). Walk both pointers together step-by-step, calculating p1.val + p2.val and updating max_twin_sum until p2 becomes NULL!

Phase 1: Find Midpoint (slow/fast) List: [5] -> [4] -> [2] -> [1] -> NULL S,F - S F (at end) Slow reaches [2] (start of second half). Phase 2: Reverse Second Half starting from [2] Original 2nd Half: [2] -> [1] -> NULL Reversed 2nd Half: [1] -> [2] -> NULL (head is `prev` pointing to [1]) Phase 3: Traversal Alignment First Half Head (p1): [5] -> [4] -> ... Second Half Head (p2): [1] -> [2] -> NULL Step 1: p1=[5], p2=[1] -> twin_sum = 5 + 1 = 6 Step 2: p1=[4], p2=[2] -> twin_sum = 4 + 2 = 6 Max Twin Sum = 6! Space = O(1)!
Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition behind In-Place Reversal: Extra space O(N) bachane ke liye hum poori list ko 3 clean steps me process karte hain:

  • Step 1 (Midpoint Dhoondo): slow aur fast pointers chalao (slow = 1 step, fast = 2 steps). Jab fast end par pahunchega, slow second half ke shuruat wale node par hoga.
  • Step 2 (Second Half Ko Reverse Karo): slow se lekar end tak ki aadhi list ko in-place reverse kar do. Reversed list ka naya head prev ban jata hai.
  • Step 3 (Dono Halves Ko Saath Me Traverse Karo): Pointer p1 ko original head par rakho aur p2 ko reversed second half ke head (prev) par. Dono ko 1-1 step aage badhao, har step par p1.val + p2.val add karke max track kar lo! Time O(N) aur Space O(1) hai.
📋 Full Line-by-Line Trace Dry Run 1: Standard 4-Node List

Input List: [5] -> [4] -> [2] -> [1] -> NULL (n = 4)

================================================================================= STEP 1: ISOLATE MIDPOINT USING SLOW & FAST POINTERS ================================================================================= • Initial State: slow = Node(5), fast = Node(5) • Move 1: - slow = slow.next -> Node(4) - fast = fast.next.next -> Node(2) • Move 2: - slow = slow.next -> Node(2) - fast = fast.next.next -> NULL (fast reached end!) • Midpoint Isolated: slow points to Node(2) [Start of Second Half]. ================================================================================= STEP 2: REVERSE SECOND HALF IN-PLACE STARTING FROM Node(2) ================================================================================= • Sublist to reverse: Node(2) -> Node(1) -> NULL • Set prev_node = NULL, curr_node = Node(2) • Iteration 1 (at Node 2): - next_tmp = curr_node.next -> Node(1) - curr_node.next = prev_node -> Node(2).next = NULL - prev_node = Node(2) - curr_node = Node(1) • Iteration 2 (at Node 1): - next_tmp = curr_node.next -> NULL - curr_node.next = prev_node -> Node(1).next = Node(2) - prev_node = Node(1) - curr_node = NULL • Reversal Finished! Head of reversed second half is prev_node = Node(1). Reversed Second Half Chain: Node(1) -> Node(2) -> NULL ================================================================================= STEP 3: SIMULTANEOUS TWIN PAIR SUM CALCULATION ================================================================================= • p1 = head (Node 5), p2 = prev_node (Node 1), max_twin_sum = 0 • Pair 1: - p1 = Node(5), p2 = Node(1) - twin_sum = 5 + 1 = 6 - max_twin_sum = max(0, 6) = 6 - Advance: p1 = Node(4), p2 = Node(2) • Pair 2: - p1 = Node(4), p2 = Node(2) - twin_sum = 4 + 2 = 6 - max_twin_sum = max(6, 6) = 6 - Advance: p1 = Node(2), p2 = NULL • Loop Terminates (p2 == NULL). FINAL RESULT RETURNED: 6
📋 Full Line-by-Line Trace Dry Run 2: Asymmetric Twin Values (N = 6)

Input List: [4] -> [2] -> [2] -> [3] -> [1] -> [7] -> NULL (n = 6)

================================================================================= STEP 1: FIND MIDPOINT ================================================================================= • slow = Node(4), fast = Node(4) • Move 1: slow = Node(2) [index 1], fast = Node(2) [index 2] • Move 2: slow = Node(2) [index 2], fast = Node(1) [index 4] • Move 3: slow = Node(3) [index 3], fast = NULL • Midpoint found: slow = Node(3) [index 3]. ================================================================================= STEP 2: REVERSE SECOND HALF ([3] -> [1] -> [7] -> NULL) ================================================================================= • Reverse process converts [3] -> [1] -> [7] into [7] -> [1] -> [3] -> NULL. • Head of reversed second half: prev_node = Node(7). ================================================================================= STEP 3: COMPUTE TWIN SUMS ================================================================================= • Pair 1: p1 = Node(4), p2 = Node(7) -> sum = 4 + 7 = 11. max_sum = 11 • Pair 2: p1 = Node(2), p2 = Node(1) -> sum = 2 + 1 = 3. max_sum = max(11, 3) = 11 • Pair 3: p1 = Node(2), p2 = Node(3) -> sum = 2 + 3 = 5. max_sum = max(11, 5) = 11 • p2 reaches NULL. Loop ends. FINAL RESULT RETURNED: 11

a) Source Code Implementation

class Solution:
    def pairSum(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> int:
        # Step 1: Find midpoint of linked list using slow and fast pointers
        slow, fast = head, head
        while fast and fast.next:
            slow = slow.next  # Advance slow pointer 1 step
            fast = fast.next.next  # Advance fast pointer 2 steps

        # Step 2: Reverse second half of linked list in-place starting from slow
        prev_node = None
        curr_node = slow
        while curr_node:
            next_tmp = curr_node.next  # Save reference to next unreversed node
            curr_node.next = prev_node  # Invert arrow pointer backward
            prev_node = curr_node  # Shift prev_node forward
            curr_node = next_tmp  # Shift curr_node forward

        # Step 3: Traverse both halves simultaneously and calculate max twin sum
        p1 = head  # Pointer for first half starting at original head
        p2 = prev_node  # Pointer for second half starting at reversed head
        max_twin_sum = 0  # Initialize maximum tracker

        while p2:  # Loop until end of reversed second half
            twin_sum = p1.val + p2.val  # Add twin pair values
            max_twin_sum = max(max_twin_sum, twin_sum)  # Update global maximum
            p1 = p1.next  # Step p1 forward
            p2 = p2.next  # Step p2 forward

        return max_twin_sum  # Return maximum twin sum
class Solution {
public:
    int pairSum(ListNode* head) {
        // Step 1: Find start of second half using slow and fast pointers
        ListNode* slow = head;
        ListNode* fast = head;
        while (fast != nullptr && fast->next != nullptr) {
            slow = slow->next;
            fast = fast->next->next;
        }

        // Step 2: Reverse second half in-place starting at slow
        ListNode* prevNode = nullptr;
        ListNode* currNode = slow;
        while (currNode != nullptr) {
            ListNode* nextTmp = currNode->next;
            currNode->next = prevNode;
            prevNode = currNode;
            currNode = nextTmp;
        }

        // Step 3: Compute twin sums simultaneously
        ListNode* p1 = head;
        ListNode* p2 = prevNode;
        int maxTwinSum = 0;

        while (p2 != nullptr) {
            int twinSum = p1->val + p2->val;
            maxTwinSum = max(maxTwinSum, twinSum);
            p1 = p1->next;
            p2 = p2->next;
        }

        return maxTwinSum;
    }
};
class Solution {
    public int pairSum(ListNode head) {
        // Step 1: Locate midpoint via slow/fast pointers
        ListNode slow = head;
        ListNode fast = head;
        while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
            slow = slow.next;
            fast = fast.next.next;
        }

        // Step 2: Reverse second half starting from slow
        ListNode prevNode = null;
        ListNode currNode = slow;
        while (currNode != null) {
            ListNode nextTmp = currNode.next;
            currNode.next = prevNode;
            prevNode = currNode;
            currNode = nextTmp;
        }

        // Step 3: Compare symmetric twin pairs
        ListNode p1 = head;
        ListNode p2 = prevNode;
        int maxTwinSum = 0;

        while (p2 != null) {
            int twinSum = p1.val + p2.val;
            maxTwinSum = Math.max(maxTwinSum, twinSum);
            p1 = p1.next;
            p2 = p2.next;
        }

        return maxTwinSum;
    }
}
var pairSum = function(head) {
    // Step 1: Slow/Fast pointer midpoint location
    let slow = head;
    let fast = head;
    while (fast !== null && fast.next !== null) {
        slow = slow.next;
        fast = fast.next.next;
    }

    // Step 2: In-place reversal of second half
    let prevNode = null;
    let currNode = slow;
    while (currNode !== null) {
        let nextTmp = currNode.next;
        currNode.next = prevNode;
        prevNode = currNode;
        currNode = nextTmp;
    }

    // Step 3: Compute maximum twin sum
    let p1 = head;
    let p2 = prevNode;
    let maxTwinSum = 0;

    while (p2 !== null) {
        let twinSum = p1.val + p2.val;
        maxTwinSum = Math.max(maxTwinSum, twinSum);
        p1 = p1.next;
        p2 = p2.next;
    }

    return maxTwinSum;
};

Strategic Edge Cases Tracking Matrix

To ensure system robustness, solutions are validated against critical boundary conditions:

Edge Case Profile Algorithmic Risk Factor Mitigation Resolution Logic
Minimum Minimal Even List (N = 2)
e.g., [1, 100]		 Slow/fast pointers or reversal logic throwing null pointer exceptions. Handled natively: slow moves to Node(100), fast to NULL. Reversing Node(100) yields Node(100). Step 3 calculates 1 + 100 = 101 properly.
Identical Node Values
e.g., [4, 4, 4, 4]		 Potential edge cases in value comparisons. Twin sums remain constant (4 + 4 = 8). Max tracker evaluates 8 consistently across all iterations.
Strictly Decreasing / Increasing Values
e.g., [1, 2, 3, 1000] vs [1000, 3, 2, 1]		 Misidentifying maximum sum depending on positioning. Twin pairs compare index 0 with N-1, index 1 with N-2. Correctly matches 1 + 1000 = 1001 and 2 + 3 = 5 regardless of ordering direction.

Complexity Analysis Performance Metrics

Approach Category Time Complexity Space Complexity Performance Evaluation Rating
Approach 1: Auxiliary Array Buffer O(N) O(N) Space Memory Sub-Optimal. Converts linked list to array requiring O(N) extra memory.
Approach 2: In-Place Half Reversal O(N) O(1) Space Absolute Production Standard. Finds midpoint, reverses second half in-place, and evaluates twin sums using O(1) auxiliary space.

LeetCode 682 Easy Master Edition

An engineering deep dive into stateful score tracking, Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) stack evaluation, and sequential array simulation.

Problem Statement

You are keeping the scores for a baseball game with strange rules. At the beginning of the game, you start with an empty record.

You are given a list of strings operations, where operations[i] is the i-th operation you must apply to the record and is one of the following:

  • An integer x: Record a new score of x.
  • "+": Record a new score that is the sum of the previous two scores.
  • "D": Record a new score that is the double of the previous score.
  • "C": Invalidate the previous score, removing it from the record.

Return the sum of all the scores on the record after applying all the operations.

The test cases are generated such that the answer and all intermediate calculations fit in a 32-bit integer and that all operations are valid.

Constraints

  • 1 <= operations.length <= 1000
  • operations[i] is "C", "D", "+", or a string representing an integer in the range [-30000, 30000].
  • For operation "+", there will always be at least two previous scores on the record.
  • For operations "C" and "D", there will always be at least one previous score on the record.

Visualizing the Intent

Let's process operations sequentially and observe how scores accumulate:

Operations Stream: ["5", "2", "C", "D", "+"] 1. Op "5" : Add 5 to score record. -> Record: [5] 2. Op "2" : Add 2 to score record. -> Record: [5, 2] 3. Op "C" : Invalidate last score (remove 2)-> Record: [5] 4. Op "D" : Double last score (5 * 2 = 10) -> Record: [5, 10] 5. Op "+" : Sum last two scores (5 + 10 = 15)-> Record: [5, 10, 15] Total Sum of Scores = 5 + 10 + 15 = 30

Core Realization: The operations strictly depend on the most recently recorded scores. A Stack data structure is perfect here because adding a score corresponds to push, invalidating a score corresponds to pop, and accessing recent scores corresponds to inspecting top elements!

Solutions Breakdown

Optimal Approach - LIFO Stack Simulation

🧭 Intuition Breakdown (Stack State Machine)

1. Why a Stack Data Structure?
Look closely at the nature of the operations:

  • "C" (Cancel): Needs to delete the most recently added score. This matches the LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) pop() operation.
  • "D" (Double): Needs to inspect the most recent score (top of the stack stack[-1]), double it, and add the result to the record.
  • "+" (Sum): Needs to inspect the two most recent scores (stack[-1] and stack[-2]), add them together, and push the sum.
  • Integer x: Directly push the integer onto the record.

2. Algorithmic Execution Steps:
1. Initialize an empty stack (e.g. dynamic array/list) record.
2. Iterate through each string op in operations.
3. Apply the corresponding condition using simple branch checks (if-else).
4. Sum all elements remaining in record at the end and return the result.

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition: Har operation pichle scores par depend karti hai. Kyuki hume hamesha sabse latest score ki zaroorat hoti hai, isliye **Stack** sabse perfect tool hai!

  • Jab koi **Number** aaye: Use stack me push kar do.
  • Jab "C" aaye: Aakhri score ko galat maanke stack se hata do (pop()).
  • Jab "D" aaye: Stack ke sabse upar wale score ko 2 se multiply karke naya score push kar do.
  • Jab "+" aaye: Stack ke top do scores (stack[-1] aur stack[-2]) ko add karke naya score push kar do.

Aakhir me stack ke saare elements ka total sum return kar do. Single pass O(N) time lagta hai aur O(N) space.

📋 Full Line-by-Line Trace Dry Run 1: Standard Operations Sequence

Input: operations = ["5", "2", "C", "D", "+"]

Initialize: stack = [] ================================================================================= STEP 1: Process op = "5" ================================================================================= • Condition Check: "5" is an integer value. • Convert to integer: int("5") = 5 • Stack Action: stack.push(5) • Stack State: [5] ================================================================================= STEP 2: Process op = "2" ================================================================================= • Condition Check: "2" is an integer value. • Convert to integer: int("2") = 2 • Stack Action: stack.push(2) • Stack State: [5, 2] ================================================================================= STEP 3: Process op = "C" ================================================================================= • Condition Check: op == "C" (Cancel/Invalidate) • Stack Action: stack.pop() -> Removes 2 from top of stack • Stack State: [5] ================================================================================= STEP 4: Process op = "D" ================================================================================= • Condition Check: op == "D" (Double last score) • Top element: stack[-1] = 5 • New Score: 5 * 2 = 10 • Stack Action: stack.push(10) • Stack State: [5, 10] ================================================================================= STEP 5: Process op = "+" ================================================================================= • Condition Check: op == "+" (Sum last two scores) • Last two elements: stack[-1] = 10, stack[-2] = 5 • New Score: 10 + 5 = 15 • Stack Action: stack.push(15) • Stack State: [5, 10, 15] ================================================================================= FINAL SUMMATION ================================================================================= • Sum of stack elements = 5 + 10 + 15 = 30 Final Answer Returned: 30
📋 Full Line-by-Line Trace Dry Run 2: Negative Numbers & Consecutive Sums

Input: operations = ["5", "-2", "4", "C", "D", "9", "+", "+"]

Initialize: stack = [] • Process "5" -> Integer -> stack = [5] • Process "-2" -> Integer -> stack = [5, -2] • Process "4" -> Integer -> stack = [5, -2, 4] • Process "C" -> Invalidate top (4) -> stack.pop() -> stack = [5, -2] • Process "D" -> Double top (-2 * 2 = -4) -> stack.push(-4) -> stack = [5, -2, -4] • Process "9" -> Integer -> stack = [5, -2, -4, 9] • Process "+" -> Sum top two (-4 + 9 = 5) -> stack.push(5) -> stack = [5, -2, -4, 9, 5] • Process "+" -> Sum top two (9 + 5 = 14) -> stack.push(14) -> stack = [5, -2, -4, 9, 5, 14] Final Sum Calculation: 5 + (-2) + (-4) + 9 + 5 + 14 = 27 Final Answer Returned: 27

a) Source Code Implementation

class Solution:
    def calPoints(self, operations: list[str]) -> int:
        stack = []  # Stack to maintain active game score record

        for op in operations:  # Iterate sequentially through each operation token
            if op == "+":
                # HIGHLIGHT: Push sum of top two elements
                stack.append(stack[-1] + stack[-2])
            elif op == "D":
                # HIGHLIGHT: Push double of top element
                stack.append(2 * stack[-1])
            elif op == "C":
                # HIGHLIGHT: Remove previous score from record
                stack.pop()
            else:
                # Convert string token to integer and append to stack
                stack.append(int(op))

        return sum(stack)  # Return grand total sum of recorded scores
class Solution {
public:
    int calPoints(vector<string>& operations) {
        vector<int> record;  // Dynamic vector used as LIFO stack

        for (const string& op : operations) {  // Process operation string
            if (op == "+") {
                int n = record.size();
                // HIGHLIGHT: Sum last two scores
                record.push_back(record[n - 1] + record[n - 2]);
            } else if (op == "D") {
                // HIGHLIGHT: Double last score
                record.push_back(2 * record.back());
            } else if (op == "C") {
                // HIGHLIGHT: Pop last score
                record.pop_back();
            } else {
                record.push_back(stoi(op));  // Convert string to int
            }
        }

        int totalSum = 0;
        for (int score : record) {  // Accumulate scores
            totalSum += score;
        }
        return totalSum;  // Return final result
    }
};
class Solution {
    public int calPoints(String[] operations) {
        List<Integer> record = new ArrayList<>();  // ArrayList for dynamic stack behavior

        for (String op : operations) {  // Iterate through operation tokens
            if (op.equals("+")) {
                int size = record.size();
                // HIGHLIGHT: Sum last two entries
                record.add(record.get(size - 1) + record.get(size - 2));
            } else if (op.equals("D")) {
                // HIGHLIGHT: Double top entry
                record.add(2 * record.get(record.size() - 1));
            } else if (op.equals("C")) {
                // HIGHLIGHT: Remove top entry
                record.remove(record.size() - 1);
            } else {
                record.add(Integer.parseInt(op));  // Parse string integer
            }
        }

        int sum = 0;
        for (int score : record) {  // Calculate total score
            sum += score;
        }
        return sum;  // Return total score
    }
}
var calPoints = function(operations) {
    const stack = [];  // Array representing score stack

    for (let op of operations) {  // Process tokens
        if (op === "+") {
            // HIGHLIGHT: Push sum of last two values
            stack.push(stack[stack.length - 1] + stack[stack.length - 2]);
        } else if (op === "D") {
            // HIGHLIGHT: Push double of last value
            stack.push(2 * stack[stack.length - 1]);
        } else if (op === "C") {
            // HIGHLIGHT: Pop last value
            stack.pop();
        } else {
            stack.push(Number(op));  // Cast string to Number
        }
    }

    // Accumulate total score using reduce
    return stack.reduce((acc, val) => acc + val, 0);
};

Negative Integers
e.g., ["-10", "-20", "+"]		 String parsing issues with negative signs or wrong addition. Standard library integer parsers (int(), stoi, Integer.parseInt) handle negative strings natively. -10 + -20 = -30 works properly.
Multiple Consecutive Cancellations ("C")
e.g., ["5", "10", "C", "C"]		 Stack underflow error when popping from an empty stack. Problem constraints guarantee that for every "C" operation, there is always at least one valid score on the record.
Consecutive Additions ("+")
e.g., ["1", "2", "+", "+"]		 Index out of bounds when looking up stack[-2]. Problem constraints guarantee that for every "+" operation, there are at least two scores on the record.

Aggressive Cows

An exhaustive engineering manual analyzing search-space monotonicity, greedy placement feasibility, and binary search on answer paradigms.

Problem Statement

You are given an array stalls of positions where stalls are located on a 1D line, and an integer k representing the number of aggressive cows.

You need to assign k cows to the stalls such that the minimum distance between any two cows is as large as possible.

Return the maximum possible minimum distance between any two cows.

Constraints

  • 2 <= stalls.length <= 10^5
  • 0 <= stalls[i] <= 10^9
  • 2 <= k <= stalls.length

Visualizing the Intent

Let's map out how stall positions and cow placements affect distances:

Stalls: [1, 2, 8, 4, 9], Cows (k) = 3 Sorted Stalls: [1, 2, 4, 8, 9] Testing a Minimum Distance (dist = 3): - Place Cow 1 at stall 1. - Next valid stall must be >= 1 + 3 = 4. Place Cow 2 at stall 4. - Next valid stall must be >= 4 + 3 = 7. Place Cow 3 at stall 8. Result: Placed all 3 cows successfully! (Feasible) Testing a Minimum Distance (dist = 4): - Place Cow 1 at stall 1. - Next valid stall must be >= 1 + 4 = 5. Place Cow 2 at stall 8. - Next valid stall must be >= 8 + 4 = 12. No stall available! Result: Failed to place 3 cows! (Infeasible) Maximum Possible Minimum Distance = 3

Core Realization: This is a classic Binary Search on Answer problem. Instead of searching for indices in an array, we define a search range of possible distances [1, max_stall - min_stall] and test whether a target distance is feasible using a greedy placement helper function.

Solutions Breakdown

Approach 1 - Brute Force (Linear Search on Answer Space)

🧭 Intuition Breakdown (Linear Distance Search)

1. The Concept: Sort the stalls array. The smallest possible distance between two cows is 1, and the maximum possible distance is stalls[n-1] - stalls[0]. We can linearly test every integer distance dist starting from 1 upward. For each dist, we run a greedy check to see if all k cows can be placed with at least dist gap between them.

2. Why it Fails Constraints: The maximum possible distance can be as large as 10^9. Testing every distance linearly takes O((max_distance) * N) operations, which will cause a Time Limit Exceeded (TLE) error.

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition: Stalls ko sort kar lo. Distance ki minimum value 1 ho sakti hai aur maximum stalls[n-1] - stalls[0]. Hum distance = 1, 2, 3, 4... karke ek-ek check karte hain. Jaise hi koi distance dist aisa milta hai jisme k cows fit nahi ho sakti, toh usse piche wala distance dist - 1 humara maximum minimum distance hota hai. Lekin distance 10^9 tak ja sakta hai, isliye linear search se TLE aayega.

📋 Approach 1 Line-by-Line Trace Profile

Input: stalls = [1, 2, 4, 8, 9], k = 3

Sorted Stalls: [1, 2, 4, 8, 9] • dist = 1: Place at 1, 2, 4 -> 3 cows placed -> FEASIBLE • dist = 2: Place at 1, 4, 8 -> 3 cows placed -> FEASIBLE • dist = 3: Place at 1, 4, 8 -> 3 cows placed -> FEASIBLE • dist = 4: Place at 1, 8 (only 2 cows placed) -> INFEASIBLE! Loop stops at dist = 4. Last valid feasible distance = dist - 1 = 3.

a) Source Code Implementation

class BruteForceSolution:
    def canPlaceCows(self, stalls: list[int], k: int, dist: int) -> bool:
        cows_placed = 1  # Place first cow at first stall
        last_pos = stalls[0]  # Track position of last placed cow
        
        for i in range(1, len(stalls)):
            if stalls[i] - last_pos >= dist:  # Check if distance requirement is satisfied
                cows_placed += 1  # Place cow
                last_pos = stalls[i]  # Update last placed position
                if cows_placed == k:  # All k cows placed successfully
                    return True
        return False

    def solve(self, stalls: list[int], k: int) -> int:
        stalls.sort()  # Sort stall positions
        max_dist = stalls[-1] - stalls[0]  # Upper bound of distance search space
        
        for dist in range(1, max_dist + 1):  # Linear search across possible distances
            if not self.canPlaceCows(stalls, k, dist):
                return dist - 1  # Return last valid distance
        return max_dist
class BruteForceSolution {
private:
    bool canPlaceCows(const vector<int>& stalls, int k, int dist) {
        int cows_placed = 1;
        int last_pos = stalls[0];
        
        for (size_t i = 1; i < stalls.size(); ++i) {
            if (stalls[i] - last_pos >= dist) {
                cows_placed++;
                last_pos = stalls[i];
                if (cows_placed == k) return true;
            }
        }
        return false;
    }

public:
    int solve(vector<int>& stalls, int k) {
        sort(stalls.begin(), stalls.end());
        int max_dist = stalls.back() - stalls[0];
        
        for (int dist = 1; dist <= max_dist; ++dist) {
            if (!canPlaceCows(stalls, k, dist)) {
                return dist - 1;
            }
        }
        return max_dist;
    }
};

        int cowsPlaced = 1;

        for (int i = 1; i < stalls.length; i++) {
            if (stalls[i] - lastPos >= dist) {
                cowsPlaced++;

                if (cowsPlaced == k) return true;
            }
        }
        return false;
    }

    public int solve(int[] stalls, int k) {
        Arrays.sort(stalls);
        int maxDist = stalls[stalls.length - 1] - stalls[0];

                return dist - 1;
            }
        }
        return maxDist;
    }
}
class BruteForceSolution {
    canPlaceCows(stalls, k, dist) {
        let cowsPlaced = 1;
        let lastPos = stalls[0];
        
        for (let i = 1; i < stalls.length; i++) {
            if (stalls[i] - lastPos >= dist) {
                cowsPlaced++;
                lastPos = stalls[i];
                if (cowsPlaced === k) return true;
            }
        }
        return false;
    }

    solve(stalls, k) {
        stalls.sort((a, b) => a - b);
        const maxDist = stalls[stalls.length - 1] - stalls[0];
        
        for (let dist = 1; dist <= maxDist; dist++) {
            if (!this.canPlaceCows(stalls, k, dist)) {
                return dist - 1;
            }
        }
        return maxDist;
    }
}

Approach 2 - Optimal Solution: Binary Search on Answer Space

🧭 Deep Intuition Breakdown (Monotonic Feasibility Concept)

1. Monotonicity Property: Notice the behavior of the feasibility function canPlaceCows(dist):

Distance: 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 Feasible?: YES YES YES NO NO NO NO ^ (Largest Feasible Value!)

If distance D is feasible, then any distance < D is ALSO guaranteed to be feasible! Conversely, if distance D is impossible, then any distance > D is ALSO impossible. This monotonic transition from TRUE -> FALSE enables Binary Search!

2. Search Range & Decision Rules:
• low = 1 (minimum possible stall gap)
• high = stalls[n-1] - stalls[0] (maximum possible distance)
• Calculate mid = low + (high - low) // 2
• If canPlaceCows(mid) is TRUE: mid is a valid candidate! Record ans = mid, and try to find a larger minimum distance by setting low = mid + 1.
• If canPlaceCows(mid) is FALSE: mid is too large. Reduce distance by setting high = mid - 1.

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition behind Binary Search on Answer: Dhyan se dekho, agar dist = 3 par k cows fit ho sakti hain, toh dist = 2 aur dist = 1 par toh 100% fit ho jayengi! Aur agar dist = 4 par fit nahi ho sakti, toh 5, 6, 7 par bhi kabhi nahi hongi.

Yeh Monotonic Property (TRUE...TRUE -> FALSE...FALSE) hume Binary Search lagane ki permission deti hai! Linear loop ki jagah hum range [1, max_dist] par binary search chalate hain. Mid check karte hain: agar TRUE hua toh candidate answer save karke aur bade distance ke liye right jao (low = mid + 1), agar FALSE hua toh chote distance ke liye left aao (high = mid - 1).

📋 Full Line-by-Line Trace Dry Run 1: Standard Input

Input: stalls = [1, 2, 8, 4, 9], k = 3

Step 0: Sort stalls array -> stalls = [1, 2, 4, 8, 9] Initial range: low = 1, high = (9 - 1) = 8, ans = 0 ================================================================================= ITERATION 1: (low = 1, high = 8) ================================================================================= • mid = 1 + (8 - 1) // 2 = 4 • Test distance mid = 4 using greedy placement: - Place Cow 1 at stalls[0] = 1. - Next cow needs pos >= 1 + 4 = 5 -> Place Cow 2 at stalls[3] = 8. - Next cow needs pos >= 8 + 4 = 12 -> No stalls left! - Total cows placed = 2 < k (3). - canPlaceCows(stalls, 3, 4) -> FALSE! • Action: Distance 4 is too large. Shrink upper bound: high = mid - 1 = 4 - 1 = 3. Range becomes: [low = 1, high = 3]. ================================================================================= ITERATION 2: (low = 1, high = 3) ================================================================================= • mid = 1 + (3 - 1) // 2 = 2 • Test distance mid = 2 using greedy placement: - Place Cow 1 at stalls[0] = 1. - Next cow needs pos >= 1 + 2 = 3 -> Place Cow 2 at stalls[2] = 4. - Next cow needs pos >= 4 + 2 = 6 -> Place Cow 3 at stalls[3] = 8. - Total cows placed = 3 == k (3). - canPlaceCows(stalls, 3, 2) -> TRUE! • Action: Distance 2 is feasible! Record ans = 2. Try for a larger distance: low = mid + 1 = 2 + 1 = 3. Range becomes: [low = 3, high = 3]. ================================================================================= ITERATION 3: (low = 3, high = 3) ================================================================================= • mid = 3 + (3 - 3) // 2 = 3 • Test distance mid = 3 using greedy placement: - Place Cow 1 at stalls[0] = 1. - Next cow needs pos >= 1 + 3 = 4 -> Place Cow 2 at stalls[2] = 4. - Next cow needs pos >= 4 + 3 = 7 -> Place Cow 3 at stalls[3] = 8. - Total cows placed = 3 == k (3). - canPlaceCows(stalls, 3, 3) -> TRUE! • Action: Distance 3 is feasible! Update ans = 3. Try for a larger distance: low = mid + 1 = 3 + 1 = 4. Range becomes: [low = 4, high = 3]. ================================================================================= LOOP TERMINATION ================================================================================= • low <= high (4 <= 3) is FALSE! Loop terminates. • Return ans = 3. Final Answer Returned: 3
📋 Full Line-by-Line Trace Dry Run 2: Wide Gap Stalls

Input: stalls = [0, 3, 4, 7, 10, 9], k = 4

Step 0: Sort stalls array -> stalls = [0, 3, 4, 7, 9, 10] Initial range: low = 1, high = (10 - 0) = 10, ans = 0 • Iteration 1: low = 1, high = 10 -> mid = 5 - Greedy Check for dist 5: * Cow 1 at 0 * Cow 2 needs >= 5 -> at 7 * Cow 3 needs >= 12 -> Fails! Only 2 cows placed. - canPlaceCows(5) -> FALSE -> high = 4 • Iteration 2: low = 1, high = 4 -> mid = 2 - Greedy Check for dist 2: * Cow 1 at 0 * Cow 2 at 3 * Cow 3 at 7 * Cow 4 at 9 - canPlaceCows(2) -> TRUE -> ans = 2, low = 3 • Iteration 3: low = 3, high = 4 -> mid = 3 - Greedy Check for dist 3: * Cow 1 at 0 * Cow 2 at 3 * Cow 3 at 7 * Cow 4 at 10 - canPlaceCows(3) -> TRUE -> ans = 3, low = 4 • Iteration 4: low = 4, high = 4 -> mid = 4 - Greedy Check for dist 4: * Cow 1 at 0 * Cow 2 at 4 * Cow 3 at 9 (only 3 cows) - canPlaceCows(4) -> FALSE -> high = 3 Loop ends (low = 4, high = 3). Final Answer Returned: 3
📋 Full Line-by-Line Trace Dry Run 3 (Edge Case): Minimal 2 Cows & Equal Distances

Input: stalls = [1, 10, 20], k = 2

Sorted Stalls: [1, 10, 20] Initial range: low = 1, high = 19, ans = 0 • Iteration 1: low = 1, high = 19 -> mid = 10 - Check dist = 10: * Cow 1 at 1 * Cow 2 needs >= 11 -> placed at 20. - canPlaceCows(10) -> TRUE -> ans = 10, low = 11 • Iteration 2: low = 11, high = 19 -> mid = 15 - Check dist = 15: * Cow 1 at 1 * Cow 2 needs >= 16 -> placed at 20. - canPlaceCows(15) -> TRUE -> ans = 15, low = 16 • Iteration 3: low = 16, high = 19 -> mid = 17 - Check dist = 17: * Cow 1 at 1 * Cow 2 needs >= 18 -> placed at 20. - canPlaceCows(17) -> TRUE -> ans = 17, low = 18 • Iteration 4: low = 18, high = 19 -> mid = 18 - Check dist = 18: * Cow 1 at 1 * Cow 2 needs >= 19 -> placed at 20. - canPlaceCows(18) -> TRUE -> ans = 18, low = 19 • Iteration 5: low = 19, high = 19 -> mid = 19 - Check dist = 19: * Cow 1 at 1 * Cow 2 needs >= 20 -> placed at 20. - canPlaceCows(19) -> TRUE -> ans = 19, low = 20 Loop ends (low = 20, high = 19). Final Answer Returned: 19 (Max distance = stalls[last] - stalls[0])

a) Source Code Implementation

class Solution:
    def canPlaceCows(self, stalls: list[int], k: int, dist: int) -> bool:
        cows_placed = 1  # Always place first cow at first stall
        last_pos = stalls[0]  # Position of previously placed cow

        for i in range(1, len(stalls)):
            # If current stall is at least `dist` away from last cow position
            if stalls[i] - last_pos >= dist:
                cows_placed += 1  # Place next cow
                last_pos = stalls[i]  # Update position
                if cows_placed == k:
                    return True  # Successfully placed all k cows

        return False  # Couldn't place all k cows with this distance

    def solve(self, stalls: list[int], k: int) -> int:
        stalls.sort()  # Sort stalls in ascending order

        low = 1  # Minimum possible distance between two stalls
        high = stalls[-1] - stalls[0]  # Maximum possible distance
        ans = 0  # Variable to track maximum minimum distance found

        # Binary search over distance answer space
        while low <= high:
            mid = low + (high - low) // 2  # Candidate minimum distance

            # HIGHLIGHT: Check feasibility of distance mid using greedy helper
            if self.canPlaceCows(stalls, k, mid):
                ans = mid  # mid is feasible, save as candidate answer
                low = mid + 1  # Try searching for a larger minimum distance
            else:
                high = mid - 1  # mid is infeasible, reduce search distance

        return ans  # Return maximum feasible minimum distance
class Solution {
private:
    bool canPlaceCows(const vector<int>& stalls, int k, int dist) {
        int cows_placed = 1;
        int last_pos = stalls[0];

            }
        }
        return false;
    }

        sort(stalls.begin(), stalls.end());

            int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;

            // HIGHLIGHT: Feasibility check
            if (canPlaceCows(stalls, k, mid)) {
                ans = mid;
                low = mid + 1;  // Try larger distance
            } else {
                high = mid - 1;  // Try smaller distance
            }
        }
        return ans;
    }
};

            }

}

Strategic Edge Cases Tracking Matrix

To ensure maximum robustness, solutions are validated against critical boundary edge cases:

Edge Case Profile Algorithmic Risk Factor Mitigation Resolution Logic
k = 2 (Minimum Number of Cows)
e.g., stalls = [1, 2, 8, 4, 9], k = 2		 Incomplete placement logic or suboptimal distance choices. With 2 cows, placing one at stalls[0] and the second at stalls[N-1] gives the theoretical maximum possible distance stalls[N-1] - stalls[0]. The binary search cleanly converges on high = max_dist.

Backspace String Compare

An engineering manual analyzing stack-based string building vs. backward two-pointer space-optimized stream evaluation.

Problem Statement

Given two strings s and t, return true if they are equal when both are typed into empty text editors. '#' means a backspace character.

Note that after backspacing an empty text, the text will continue being empty.

Constraints

  • 1 <= s.length, t.length <= 200
  • s and t only contain lowercase letters and '#' characters.

Visualizing the Intent

Let's observe how backspaces cancel out preceding characters during keystroke simulation:

Example 1: s = "ab#c", t = "ad#c" - Processing s: 'a' -> 'b' -> '#' (deletes 'b') -> 'c' => Final s = "ac" - Processing t: 'a' -> 'd' -> '#' (deletes 'd') -> 'c' => Final t = "ac" Result: TRUE ("ac" == "ac") Example 2: s = "a#c", t = "b" - Processing s: 'a' -> '#' (deletes 'a') -> 'c' => Final s = "c" - Processing t: 'b' => Final t = "b" Result: FALSE ("c" != "b") Example 3: s = "a##c", t = "#a#c" - Processing s: 'a' -> '#' (deletes 'a') -> '#' (nothing left to delete) -> 'c' => Final s = "c" - Processing t: '#' (empty, stays empty) -> 'a' -> '#' (deletes 'a') -> 'c' => Final t = "c" Result: TRUE ("c" == "c")

Core Realization: The backspace character '#' operates strictly on the most recently typed valid character. This means processing forward requires maintaining a history buffer (Stack), whereas scanning backward allows us to skip valid characters dynamically as backspaces are encountered.

Solutions Breakdown

Approach 1 - Stack Simulation (Build String Representation)

🧭 Intuition Breakdown (Forward Character Buffering)

1. The Concept: Simulate the exact text-editor typing experience using a LIFO Stack buffer for each string. Process characters left-to-right:

  • If the character is a regular letter, push it onto the stack.
  • If the character is '#', pop the top element from the stack if the stack is not empty.

2. Verification: Convert both stacks back to strings (or compare stack contents directly) and return whether they are identical.

3. Complexity Tradeoff: This takes linear time O(N + M), where N and M are string lengths, but requires auxiliary memory space of O(N + M) for storing the final string outputs.

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition: Text editor ki tarah simulate karo. Ek **Stack** banao. Jab letter mile, stack me push kar do. Jab '#' (backspace) mile, toh stack se aakhri element pop kar do (agar stack empty na ho). Dono strings ke liye final stacks bana kar compare kar lo. Yeh O(N + M) time aur O(N + M) extra memory leta hai.

📋 Approach 1 Full Trace Dry Run 1: Cancelled Keystrokes

Input: s = "ab#c", t = "ad#c"

Processing String s = "ab#c": • char = 'a': stack_s = ['a'] • char = 'b': stack_s = ['a', 'b'] • char = '#': backspace! stack_s.pop() -> stack_s = ['a'] • char = 'c': stack_s = ['a', 'c'] Final stack_s = ['a', 'c'] Processing String t = "ad#c": • char = 'a': stack_t = ['a'] • char = 'd': stack_t = ['a', 'd'] • char = '#': backspace! stack_t.pop() -> stack_t = ['a'] • char = 'c': stack_t = ['a', 'c'] Final stack_t = ['a', 'c'] Compare stack_s == stack_t: ['a', 'c'] == ['a', 'c'] -> TRUE
📋 Approach 1 Full Trace Dry Run 2: Empty Backspacing & Mismatch

Input: s = "a##c", t = "b"

Processing String s = "a##c": • char = 'a': stack_s = ['a'] • char = '#': stack_s.pop() -> stack_s = [] • char = '#': stack_s is empty, ignore backspace -> stack_s = [] • char = 'c': stack_s = ['c'] Final stack_s = ['c'] Processing String t = "b": • char = 'b': stack_t = ['b'] Final stack_t = ['b'] Compare stack_s == stack_t: ['c'] == ['b'] -> FALSE

a) Source Code Implementation

class Solution:
    def backspaceCompare(self, s: str, t: str) -> bool:
        # Helper function to construct final string using a stack
        def build_string(string: str) -> list[str]:
            stack = []  # Stack buffer for keystrokes
            for char in string:
                if char != '#':
                    stack.append(char)  # Push letter
                elif stack:
                    stack.pop()  # Backspace deletes top character if stack non-empty
            return stack

        return build_string(s) == build_string(t)  # Compare generated stack representations
class Solution {
private:
    string buildString(const string& str) {
        string res = "";  // Using string as stack
        for (char c : str) {
            if (c != '#') {
                res.push_back(c);  // Append character
            } else if (!res.empty()) {
                res.pop_back();  // Backspace
            }
        }
        return res;
    }

public:
    bool backspaceCompare(string s, string t) {
        return buildString(s) == buildString(t);  // Compare evaluated strings
    }
};
class Solution {
    private String buildString(String str) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();  // Buffer for building output string
        for (char c : str.toCharArray()) {
            if (c != '#') {
                sb.append(c);  // Append letter
            } else if (sb.length() > 0) {
                sb.deleteCharAt(sb.length() - 1);  // Remove top character
            }
        }
        return sb.toString();
    }

    public boolean backspaceCompare(String s, String t) {
        return buildString(s).equals(buildString(t));  // Equality comparison
    }
}
var backspaceCompare = function(s, t) {
    const buildString = (str) => {
        const stack = [];
        for (let char of str) {
            if (char !== '#') {
                stack.push(char);  // Push letter
            } else {
                stack.pop();  // Pop last character
            }
        }
        return stack.join('');
    };

    return buildString(s) === buildString(t);  // Strict equality check
};

Approach 2 - Optimal Solution: Backward Two Pointers (O(1) Space)

🧭 Deep Intuition Breakdown (Reverse Skip Logic)

1. Why Traverse Backward?
When scanning from left to right, seeing a character 'a' doesn't inform us whether it will survive, because a backspace '#' might appear later! We are forced to buffer it.
However, when scanning from right to left, as soon as we see '#', we know immediately that the next valid letter to its left MUST be deleted! We can simply keep a skip counter (skip_s and skip_t) tracking how many upcoming letters need to be erased.

2. The Reverse Trajectory Algorithm:

  • Set pointers i = len(s) - 1 and j = len(t) - 1.
  • Move pointer i backward to find the next surviving valid character in s:
    • If s[i] == '#', increment skip_s += 1 and decrement i -= 1.
    • If skip_s > 0 and s[i] != '#', this character is deleted! Decrement skip_s -= 1 and i -= 1.
    • If skip_s == 0 and s[i] != '#', s[i] is a surviving valid character! Stop pointer i.
  • Repeat the exact same skip logic for pointer j in string t.
  • Compare s[i] and t[j]:
    • If both pointers point to valid characters, check if s[i] == t[j]. If not, return false!
    • If one pointer is exhausted (< 0) while the other still points to a valid character (>= 0), the strings have different active lengths, so return false!
  • Decrement i -= 1 and j -= 1 to inspect the next valid pair.

Reverse Skip Tracing Mechanics: s = "a b # c" t = "a d # c" ^ ^ ^ ^ i start j start 1. Rightmost chars: s[3] = 'c', t[3] = 'c'. Both non-'#'. Compare s[3] == t[3] -> 'c' == 'c' -> MATCH! Decrement: i = 2, j = 2 2. Next chars: s[2] = '#', t[2] = '#' - String s: see '#', set skip_s = 1, move i to 1 (s[1] = 'b'). skip_s > 0 so skip 'b', decrement skip_s = 0, move i to 0 (s[0] = 'a'). Next surviving char in s is 'a' at i = 0! - String t: see '#', set skip_t = 1, move j to 1 (t[1] = 'd'). skip_t > 0 so skip 'd', decrement skip_t = 0, move j to 0 (t[0] = 'a'). Next surviving char in t is 'a' at j = 0! 3. Compare surviving chars: s[0] == t[0] -> 'a' == 'a' -> MATCH! 4. Both strings exhausted -> Return TRUE! Space used = O(1)!
Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition behind Backward Two Pointers: Aage se chalne par hume pata nahi hota ki kaunsa letter delete hone wala hai. Lekin **peechhe se aage (right to left)** chalne par, jaise hi '#' milta hai, hume turant pata chal jata hai ki iske piche wale letter ko skip (delete) karna hai!

Hum do counters skip_s aur skip_t rakhte hain. Right se left jaate waqt jab bhi '#' mile, skip counter ko +1 badha do. Jab koi regular letter mile aur skip > 0 ho, toh us letter ko skip karke skip counter ko -1 kar do.

Dono strings ke **agle real surviving characters** ko aamne-samne compare karo. Agar match hon toh aage badho, nahi toh False return kar do. Isse space O(1) ho jati hai!

(i = -1, j = -1) • Both strings exhausted cleanly together. Final Answer Returned: TRUE
📋 Full Line-by-Line Trace Dry Run 2: Unbalanced Active Lengths

Input: s = "a#c", t = "b"

================================================================================= INITIALIZATION: i = 2 (s[2]='c'), j = 0 (t[0]='b') ================================================================================= ITERATION 1: • Find valid char for s starting at i = 2: - s[2] = 'c' -> Valid char found: s[2] = 'c' • Find valid char for t starting at j = 0: - t[0] = 'b' -> Valid char found: t[0] = 'b' • Compare valid characters: - Is s[2] ('c') == t[0] ('b')? -> 'c' != 'b' -> MISMATCH DETECTED! - Return FALSE immediately! Final Answer Returned: FALSE

Trace reverse evaluation: • Both strings end in "tw" -> 'w' matches 'w', 't' matches 't'. • s prefix remains: "bxj##" -> '#' erases 'j', '#' erases 'x'. Surviving char: 'b' at index 0. • t prefix remains: "bxo#j##" -> '#' erases 'j', '#' erases 'o', '#' erases 'x'. Surviving char: 'b' at index 0. • 'b' matches 'b'. Both exhausted -> Returns TRUE

a) Source Code Implementation

class Solution:
    def backspaceCompare(self, s: str, t: str) -> bool:
        i, j = len(s) - 1, len(t) - 1  # Initialize two pointers at string ends
        skip_s, skip_t = 0, 0  # Counters tracking active backspaces

        while i >= 0 or j >= 0:
            # Step 1: Find next valid surviving character in s
            while i >= 0:
                if s[i] == '#':
                    skip_s += 1
                    i -= 1
                elif skip_s > 0:
                    skip_s -= 1
                    i -= 1
                else:
                    break  # Valid surviving character found at s[i]

            # Step 2: Find next valid surviving character in t
            while j >= 0:
                if t[j] == '#':
                    skip_t += 1
                    j -= 1
                elif skip_t > 0:
                    skip_t -= 1
                    j -= 1
                else:
                    break  # Valid surviving character found at t[j]

            # Step 3: Compare surviving characters
            if i >= 0 and j >= 0:
                if s[i] != t[j]:
                    return False  # Character mismatch
            elif (i >= 0) != (j >= 0):
                return False  # One string has valid character remaining, the other is exhausted

            i -= 1
            j -= 1

        return True  # Both strings matched completely
class Solution {
public:
    bool backspaceCompare(string s, string t) {
        int i = s.length() - 1;
        int j = t.length() - 1;
        int skip_s = 0, skip_t = 0;

        while (i >= 0 || j >= 0) {
            // Find next valid character in s
            while (i >= 0) {
                if (s[i] == '#') { skip_s++; i--; }
                else if (skip_s > 0) { skip_s--; i--; }
                else break;
            }

            // Find next valid character in t
            while (j >= 0) {
                if (t[j] == '#') { skip_t++; j--; }
                else if (skip_t > 0) { skip_t--; j--; }
                else break;
            }

            // Compare characters
            if (i >= 0 && j >= 0) {
                if (s[i] != t[j]) return false;
            } else if ((i >= 0) != (j >= 0)) {
                return false;
            }

            i--;
            j--;
        }

        return true;
    }
};
class Solution {
    public boolean backspaceCompare(String s, String t) {
        int i = s.length() - 1;
        int j = t.length() - 1;

            while (i >= 0) {
                if (s.charAt(i) == '#') { skipS++; i--; }
                else if (skipS > 0) { skipS--; i--; }
                else break;
            }

            // Locate next valid character in t
            while (j >= 0) {
                if (t.charAt(j) == '#') { skipT++; j--; }
                else if (skipT > 0) { skipT--; j--; }
                else break;
            }

            // Check matching conditions
            if (i >= 0 && j >= 0) {
                if (s.charAt(i) != t.charAt(j)) return false;
            } else if ((i >= 0) != (j >= 0)) {
                return false;
            }

            i--;
            j--;
        }

        return true;
    }
}
var backspaceCompare = function(s, t) {
    let i = s.length - 1;
    let j = t.length - 1;

        // Backward scan for t

        } else if ((i >= 0) !== (j >= 0)) {

Strategic Edge Cases Tracking Matrix

To ensure total reliability in technical interviews, solutions must handle extreme backspace sequence patterns seamlessly:

Edge Case Profile Algorithmic Risk Factor Mitigation Resolution Logic
More Backspaces Than Letters
e.g., s = "a###", t = ""		 Attempting to pop from an empty stack or decrement pointer below zero safely. Stack approach checks if stack before popping. Two-pointer approach increments skip count and stops pointer decrement at index -1.
Strings Consisting Purely of Backspaces
e.g., s = "###", t = "#####"		 Both strings evaluate to empty strings "" == "". Skip counters consume all characters. Both pointers exhaust to -1 simultaneously. Condition (i >= 0) != (j >= 0) remains False and function returns True.
Different Length Strings Evaluating Same
e.g., s = "bxj##tw", t = "bxo#j##tw"		 Multiple nested backspaces skipping varied letter sequences. The while skip > 0 loop cleanly accumulates and consumes multiple backspaces sequentially, isolating the true surviving characters.

e.g., s = "ab#", t = "a"		 One pointer reaches -1 while the other pointer points to a valid letter index >= 0. Explicit boundary check (i >= 0) != (j >= 0) detects active length mismatch instantly and returns False.

Complexity Analysis Performance Metrics

LeetCode 155 Medium Master Edition

Min Stack

An engineering manual analyzing constant time O(1) stateful retrieval, auxiliary tracking stacks, and O(1) space mathematical encoding algorithms.

Problem Statement

Design a stack that supports push, pop, top, and retrieving the minimum element in constant time.

Implement the MinStack class:

  • MinStack() initializes the stack object.
  • void push(int val) pushes the element val onto the stack.
  • void pop() removes the element on the top of the stack.
  • int top() gets the top element of the stack.
  • int getMin() retrieves the minimum element in the stack.

You must implement a solution with O(1) time complexity for each function.

Constraints

  • -2^31 <= val <= 2^31 - 1
  • Methods pop, top and getMin will always be called on non-empty stacks.
  • At most 3 * 10^4 calls will be made to push, pop, top, and getMin.

Visualizing the Intent

Let's map out a sequence of operations and track how the minimum updates statefully:

Operation Sequence: 1. MinStack minStack = new MinStack(); 2. minStack.push(-2); --> Stack: [-2], Current Min: -2 3. minStack.push(0); --> Stack: [-2, 0], Current Min: -2 4. minStack.push(-3); --> Stack: [-2, 0, -3], Current Min: -3 5. minStack.getMin(); --> Returns -3 6. minStack.pop(); --> Stack: [-2, 0], Current Min reverts to -2! 7. minStack.top(); --> Returns 0 8. minStack.getMin(); --> Returns -2

Core Realization: A standard variable storing min_val works when elements are added, but breaks when the current minimum element is popped. We must preserve a historical record of what the minimum was at every state level of the stack so it can be restored seamlessly upon popping.

Solutions Breakdown

Approach 1 - Auxiliary Tracking (Two Stacks / Pair Storage)

🧭 Intuition Breakdown (State History Preservation)

1. The Core Idea: Every time a new element is pushed onto the main stack, the minimum value of the stack might change. If we snapshot the running minimum alongside the value at that exact stack height, popping an element automatically reveals the previous minimum without scanning!

2. Implementation Variants:

  • Variant A (Two Stacks): Maintain a main_stack for values and a parallel min_stack where min_stack.top() always stores the current global minimum up to that depth.
  • Variant B (Stack of Pairs): Store tuples or pairs directly inside a single stack: (value, min_so_far).

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition behind Auxiliary Tracking: Agar hum sirf ek single variable min_val rakhein, toh top element ko pop() karne par puraana minimum bhool jayenge. Iska solution yeh hai ki hum har node ke saath us waqt ka minimum bhi yaad rakhein.

Hum do stacks use kar sakte hain: ek normal numbers ke liye (main_stack) aur doosra minimum numbers ka record rakhne ke liye (min_stack). Jab bhi naya number aaye, min_stack.top() aur naye number me se jo chhota ho use min_stack me push kar do. Isse getMin(), push(), pop() sab O(1) me ho jayenge.

📋 Full Line-by-Line Trace Dry Run 1: Two-Stack Execution

Operations: push(5), push(3), push(7), push(2), pop(), getMin()

Initialize: main_stack = [], min_stack = [] ================================================================================= 1. push(5): ================================================================================= • main_stack.push(5) • min_stack is empty -> current minimum is 5. • min_stack.push(5) State: main_stack: [5] min_stack: [5] ================================================================================= 2. push(3): ================================================================================= • main_stack.push(3) • Compare val (3) with min_stack.top() (5) -> min(3, 5) = 3. • min_stack.push(3) State: main_stack: [5, 3] min_stack: [5, 3] ================================================================================= 3. push(7): ================================================================================= • main_stack.push(7) • Compare val (7) with min_stack.top() (3) -> min(7, 3) = 3. • min_stack.push(3) State: main_stack: [5, 3, 7] min_stack: [5, 3, 3] ================================================================================= 4. push(2): ================================================================================= • main_stack.push(2) • Compare val (2) with min_stack.top() (3) -> min(2, 3) = 2. • min_stack.push(2) State: main_stack: [5, 3, 7, 2] min_stack: [5, 3, 3, 2] • getMin() returns min_stack.top() -> 2 ================================================================================= 5. pop(): ================================================================================= • main_stack.pop() -> Removes 2 • min_stack.pop() -> Removes 2 State: main_stack: [5, 3, 7] min_stack: [5, 3, 3] ================================================================================= 6. getMin(): ================================================================================= • Returns min_stack.top() -> 3 (Reverted to previous minimum seamlessly!)
📋 Full Line-by-Line Trace Dry Run 2: Duplicate Minimum Values

Operations: push(2), push(2), pop(), getMin()

Initialize: main_stack = [], min_stack = [] • push(2): main_stack: [2], min_stack: [2] • push(2): main_stack: [2, 2], min_stack: [2, 2] (Pushes duplicate 2 to min_stack!) • pop(): main_stack.pop(), min_stack.pop() -> main_stack: [2], min_stack: [2] • getMin(): returns min_stack.top() = 2 (Correctly avoids premature loss of minimum!)

a) Source Code Implementation

class MinStack:
    def __init__(self):
        self.stack = []     # Primary stack for elements
        self.min_stack = [] # Auxiliary stack tracking minimums

    def push(self, val: int) -> None:
        self.stack.append(val)  # Push to main stack
        # Calculate current minimum and push to auxiliary stack
        current_min = min(val, self.min_stack[-1] if self.min_stack else val)
        self.min_stack.append(current_min)

    def pop(self) -> None:
        self.stack.pop()      # Remove top element from main stack
        self.min_stack.pop()  # Remove top element from auxiliary stack

    def top(self) -> int:
        return self.stack[-1]  # Return top value of main stack

    def getMin(self) -> int:
        return self.min_stack[-1]  # Return current minimum in O(1)
class MinStack {
private:
    stack<int> st;      // Main element stack
    stack<int> minSt;   // Auxiliary minimum stack

public:
    MinStack() {}

    void push(int val) {
        st.push(val);
        if (minSt.empty()) {
            minSt.push(val);
        } else {
            minSt.push(min(val, minSt.top()));
        }
    }

    void pop() {
        st.pop();
        minSt.pop();
    }

    int top() {
        return st.top();
    }

    int getMin() {
        return minSt.top();
    }
};
class MinStack {
    private Stack<Integer> st;
    private Stack<Integer> minSt;

    public MinStack() {
        st = new Stack<>();
        minSt = new Stack<>();
    }

    public void push(int val) {
        st.push(val);
        if (minSt.isEmpty()) {
            minSt.push(val);
        } else {
            minSt.push(Math.min(val, minSt.peek()));
        }
    }

    public void pop() {
        st.pop();
        minSt.pop();
    }

    public int top() {
        return st.peek();
    }

    public int getMin() {
        return minSt.peek();
    }
}
var MinStack = function() {
    this.stack = [];     // Main array
    this.minStack = [];  // Min tracking array
};

MinStack.prototype.push = function(val) {
    this.stack.push(val);
    if (this.minStack.length === 0) {
        this.minStack.push(val);
    } else {
        const currentMin = Math.min(val, this.minStack[this.minStack.length - 1]);
        this.minStack.push(currentMin);
    }
};

MinStack.prototype.pop = function() {
    this.stack.pop();
    this.minStack.pop();
};

MinStack.prototype.top = function() {
    return this.stack[this.stack.length - 1];
};

MinStack.prototype.getMin = function() {
    return this.minStack[this.minStack.length - 1];
};

Approach 2 - Optimal Solution: Mathematical Offset Encoding (O(1) Auxiliary Space)

🧭 Deep Intuition Breakdown (Single-Variable Encoding Magic)

1. The Question: Can we implement MinStack using only ONE stack and NO extra auxiliary memory arrays?

2. The Mathematical Encoding Trick:
Instead of pushing the actual value val directly when val < min_val, we push a specially modified modified value (flag) onto the stack that encodes BOTH the new value AND a trigger indicating that min_val has changed!

Encoding Formula (When pushing val < current_min): modified_val = 2 * val - current_min Notice the mathematical property: Since val < current_min: val - current_min < 0 val + (val - current_min) < val ==> 2 * val - current_min < val !! Key Insight: The encoded value pushed onto the stack is GUARANTEED to be strictly LESS than `val`! This acts as a sentinel flag telling us: "Hey! The real value pushed here was `val`, and the previous minimum before this operation can be recovered using math!"

3. Decoding Formulas:

  • During top(): If stack.top() < current_min, it means a flag was stored! The actual top value is current_min itself! Otherwise, the top value is simply stack.top().
  • During pop(): If stack.top() < current_min, we are popping the flag node where min_val updated! To restore the previous minimum before this node was pushed:
    previous_min = 2 * current_min - modified_val
    Proof: Substitute modified_val = 2 * val - current_min (where val is current_min): previous_min = 2 * val - (2 * val - prev_min) = prev_min !!

4. Integer Overflow Precaution:
Because 2 * val can overflow a standard 32-bit signed integer, calculations must be cast to 64-bit integers (e.g. long long in C++, long in Java) during encoding.

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition behind Mathematical Encoding: Bina kisi doosre stack ke O(1) space me kaam karne ke liye hum ek maths trick lagate hain.

Jab bhi koi naya number val aaye jo current min_val se chhota ho, hum stack me val daalne ki bajaye ek encoded formula wala Number daalte hain: 2 * val - min_val. Is encoded number ki khas baat yeh hai ki yeh hamesha val se chhota hota hai, jo hume ek signal (flag) deta hai.

• top() poochne par: Agar stack ka top element min_val se chhota hai, toh actual original number min_val hi hota hai.
• pop() karne par: Agar stack ka top element min_val se chhota hai, toh purana minimum wapas laane ke liye hum formula use karte hain: min_val = 2 * min_val - stack.top().

📋 Full Line-by-Line Trace Dry Run: Mathematical Encoding

Operations: push(5), push(3), push(2), pop(), top(), getMin()

Initialize: stack = [], min_val = Infinity ================================================================================= 1. push(5): ================================================================================= • Stack is empty. • Set min_val = 5. • Push raw value 5 directly. • Stack State: [5], min_val = 5 ================================================================================= 2. push(3): ================================================================================= • Compare 3 < min_val (5) -> TRUE! (New minimum detected!) • Encode value: modified = 2 * 3 - 5 = 6 - 5 = 1 • Push modified value (1) to stack. • Update min_val = 3. • Stack State: [5, 1], min_val = 3 (Notice stack.top() = 1 < min_val (3). Flag set!) ================================================================================= 3. push(2): ================================================================================= • Compare 2 < min_val (3) -> TRUE! (New minimum detected!) • Encode value: modified = 2 * 2 - 3 = 4 - 3 = 1 • Push modified value (1) to stack. • Update min_val = 2. • Stack State: [5, 1, 1], min_val = 2 ================================================================================= 4. getMin(): ================================================================================= • Return min_val -> 2 ================================================================================= 5. top(): ================================================================================= • Look at stack.top() = 1. • Is stack.top() (1) < min_val (2)? YES! • This means actual value pushed was min_val (2). • Return 2. ================================================================================= 6. pop(): ================================================================================= • Look at stack.top() = 1. • Is stack.top() (1) < min_val (2)? YES! (Flag node popped!) • Restore previous minimum: prev_min = 2 * min_val - stack.top() = 2 * 2 - 1 = 4 - 1 = 3! • Update min_val = 3. • Remove top element from stack. • Stack State: [5, 1], min_val = 3 ================================================================================= 7. getMin(): ================================================================================= • Return min_val -> 3 (Previous minimum successfully restored without extra stack!)

a) Source Code Implementation (Mathematical Encoding)

class MinStack:
    def __init__(self):
        self.stack = []  # Single stack storing values or encoded flags
        self.min_val = None  # Variable tracking global minimum

    def push(self, val: int) -> None:
        if not self.stack:
            self.stack.append(val)
            self.min_val = val
        elif val < self.min_val:
            # HIGHLIGHT: Push encoded value (2*val - min_val) and update min_val
            self.stack.append(2 * val - self.min_val)
            self.min_val = val
        else:
            self.stack.append(val)

    def pop(self) -> None:
        top_val = self.stack.pop()
        # If popped value is less than current min, it's a flag node
        if top_val < self.min_val:
            # HIGHLIGHT: Restore previous minimum using formula
            self.min_val = 2 * self.min_val - top_val

    def top(self) -> int:
        top_val = self.stack[-1]
        # If top is encoded flag, return min_val directly
        if top_val < self.min_val:
            return self.min_val
        return top_val

    def getMin(self) -> int:
        return self.min_val
class MinStack {
private:
    stack<long long> st;  // Use long long to prevent 32-bit integer overflow
    long long minVal;

public:
    MinStack() {}

    void push(int val) {
        long long v = val;
        if (st.empty()) {
            st.push(v);
            minVal = v;
        } else if (v < minVal) {
            // HIGHLIGHT: Push encoded value
            st.push(2 * v - minVal);
            minVal = v;
        } else {
            st.push(v);
        }
    }

    void pop() {
        long long topVal = st.top();
        st.pop();
        // If popped value is encoded flag, restore previous minimum
        if (topVal < minVal) {
            minVal = 2 * minVal - topVal;
        }
    }

    int top() {
        long long topVal = st.top();
        if (topVal < minVal) {
            return minVal;
        }
        return topVal;
    }

    int getMin() {
        return minVal;
    }
};
class MinStack {
    private Stack<Long> st;  // Stack holding Long values
    private Long minVal;

    public MinStack() {
        st = new Stack<>();
    }

    public void push(int val) {
        Long v = (long) val;
        if (st.isEmpty()) {
            st.push(v);
            minVal = v;
        } else if (v < minVal) {
            // HIGHLIGHT: Push encoded value
            st.push(2 * v - minVal);
            minVal = v;
        } else {
            st.push(v);
        }
    }

    public void pop() {
        Long topVal = st.pop();
        // Restore previous minimum on flag node
        if (topVal < minVal) {
            minVal = 2 * minVal - topVal;
        }
    }

    public int top() {
        Long topVal = st.peek();
        if (topVal < minVal) {
            return minVal.intValue();
        }
        return topVal.intValue();
    }

    public int getMin() {
        return minVal.intValue();
    }
}
var MinStack = function() {
    this.stack = [];
    this.minVal = null;
};

MinStack.prototype.push = function(val) {
    if (this.stack.length === 0) {
        this.stack.push(val);
        this.minVal = val;
    } else if (val < this.minVal) {
        // HIGHLIGHT: Push encoded value using formula
        this.stack.push(2 * val - this.minVal);
        this.minVal = val;
    } else {
        this.stack.push(val);
    }
};

MinStack.prototype.pop = function() {
    const topVal = this.stack.pop();
    if (topVal < this.minVal) {
        // HIGHLIGHT: Restore previous minimum
        this.minVal = 2 * this.minVal - topVal;
    }
};

MinStack.prototype.top = function() {
    const topVal = this.stack[this.stack.length - 1];
    if (topVal < this.minVal) {
        return this.minVal;
    }
    return topVal;
};

MinStack.prototype.getMin = function() {
    return this.minVal;
};

Strategic Edge Cases Tracking Matrix

Edge Case Profile Algorithmic Risk Factor Mitigation Resolution Logic
Duplicate Minimum Values
e.g., push(2), push(2), pop()		 In Approach 1, premature removal of min element. In Approach 2, equal values do not trigger encoding (val < min_val is False). In Approach 1, duplicate values are pushed to min_stack. In Approach 2, equal values are pushed raw without encoding because val < min_val evaluates to False.
Negative Integer Overflow
e.g., val = -2^31		 In Approach 2, computing 2 * val - min_val overflows signed 32-bit integer limits. Casting stack entries and minimum variables to 64-bit integer types (e.g. long long in C++, Long in Java).
Popping down to empty stack
e.g., push(5), pop()		 Dangling min_val reference or empty stack top access. When stack becomes empty, reset min_val = None / null. Problem statement guarantees top, pop, and getMin are only called on non-empty stacks.

Complexity Analysis Performance Metrics

Approach Category Time Complexity (All Ops) Space Complexity Performance Evaluation Rating
Approach 1: Auxiliary Min Stack / Pairs O(1) O(N) Space Standard Production Choice. Highly readable and robust. Allocates an extra stack or pairs storing up to N minimum snapshots.
Approach 2: Mathematical Offset Encoding O(1) O(1) Auxiliary Space Optimal Space Standard. Eliminates auxiliary min stack memory completely. Uses single-variable math offset tracking.
