Data Structure Design Fundamental Master Edition

Implement Stack Data Structure

An exhaustive engineering manual analyzing LIFO state management through Array buffers, Linked Lists, and Queue conversion primitives.

Problem Statement

Design and implement a custom Stack data structure that operates under the LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) discipline.

Your implementation must support the following standard operations, each executing in O(1) time complexity:

  • push(x): Inserts element x onto the top of the stack.
  • pop(): Removes and returns the element at the top of the stack.
  • top() / peek(): Returns the element at the top of the stack without removing it.
  • isEmpty(): Returns true if the stack contains no elements, otherwise false.
  • size(): Returns the total number of elements currently stored in the stack.

Visualizing the Intent

A stack behaves like a vertical tower of plates:

Operation Sequence: 1. push(10) -> Stack: [10] (Top is 10) 2. push(20) -> Stack: [10, 20] (Top is 20) 3. push(30) -> Stack: [10, 20, 30] (Top is 30) 4. top() -> Returns 30 5. pop() -> Removes 30, Stack: [10, 20] 6. top() -> Returns 20 7. isEmpty() -> Returns false

Core Realization: The last element inserted is ALWAYS the first element removed. We must maintain an explicit entry point pointer (the top index or head node reference) to perform all additions and removals strictly at one end in constant O(1) time.

Solutions Breakdown

Approach 1 - Array / Dynamic Array Implementation

🧭 Intuition Breakdown (Contiguous Memory Buffer)

1. The Concept: Use a linear array or dynamic list as an internal buffer. Maintain an integer pointer top_idx = -1 representing the index of the top element.

2. Mechanics:

  • push(x): Increment top_idx by 1 and place x at array[top_idx].
  • pop(): Read value at array[top_idx], decrement top_idx by 1.
  • top(): Return array[top_idx] directly.

3. Advantages & Tradeoffs: Contiguous memory provides optimal CPU cache locality and O(1) time complexity. However, static arrays require a fixed capacity limit (Overflow risk), whereas dynamic arrays occasionally incur O(N) reallocation cost during capacity doubling (amortized O(1)).

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition: Array base implementation me hum ek variable top_idx rakhte hain jo sabse aakhri element ke index ko point karta hai.

• Naya element push karne par: top_idx ko 1 se badhao aur number add kar do.
• Pop karne par: Top wale element ko nikalo aur top_idx ko 1 se kam kar do.
Yeh sabse fast hota hai kyuki memory ek saath continuous blocks me milti hai (Cache Friendly).

📋 Approach 1 Trace Dry Run 1: Standard Push & Pop Sequence

Operations: push(10), push(20), top(), pop(), isEmpty()

Initialize: arr = [], top_idx = -1 ================================================================================= 1. Execute push(10): ================================================================================= • Increment pointer: top_idx = -1 + 1 = 0 • Insert element: arr[0] = 10 • State: arr = [10], top_idx = 0 ================================================================================= 2. Execute push(20): ================================================================================= • Increment pointer: top_idx = 0 + 1 = 1 • Insert element: arr[1] = 20 • State: arr = [10, 20], top_idx = 1 ================================================================================= 3. Execute top(): ================================================================================= • Read arr[top_idx] -> arr[1] = 20 • Returns: 20 ================================================================================= 4. Execute pop(): ================================================================================= • Read arr[top_idx] -> arr[1] = 20 • Decrement pointer: top_idx = 1 - 1 = 0 • State: arr = [10], top_idx = 0 • Returns: 20 ================================================================================= 5. Execute isEmpty(): ================================================================================= • Check condition: top_idx == -1 -> 0 == -1 is FALSE. • Returns: false
📋 Approach 1 Trace Dry Run 2: Emptying the Stack completely

Operations: push(5), pop(), pop() [Underflow Check]

Initialize: arr = [], top_idx = -1 • push(5): top_idx = 0, arr = [5] • pop(): reads arr[0] = 5, top_idx = -1, arr = []. Returns 5. • pop(): check top_idx == -1 -> TRUE! Stack Underflow Error/Exception raised!

a) Source Code Implementation

class ArrayStack:
    def __init__(self):
        self.arr = []  # Internal dynamic array buffer

    def push(self, x: int) -> None:
        self.arr.append(x)  # Append element at end of dynamic array

    def pop(self) -> int:
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("Stack Underflow: Cannot pop from an empty stack")
        return self.arr.pop()  # Pop last inserted element

    def top(self) -> int:
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("Stack Empty: No top element exists")
        return self.arr[-1]  # Inspect last element

    def is_empty(self) -> bool:
        return len(self.arr) == 0  # Check if size is 0

    def size(self) -> int:
        return len(self.arr)  # Return total elements count
class ArrayStack {
private:
    vector<int> arr;  // Dynamic vector buffer

public:
    ArrayStack() {}

    void push(int x) {
        arr.push_back(x);  // Insert at back in O(1) amortized
    }

    int pop() {
        if (isEmpty()) {
            throw out_of_range("Stack Underflow");
        }
        int val = arr.back();
        arr.pop_back();  // Remove back element
        return val;
    }

    int top() {
        if (isEmpty()) {
            throw out_of_range("Stack is Empty");
        }
        return arr.back();  // Return back element
    }

    bool isEmpty() {
        return arr.empty();
    }

    int size() {
        return arr.size();
    }
};
class ArrayStack {
    private List<Integer> arr;

    public ArrayStack() {
        arr = new ArrayList<>();
    }

    public void push(int x) {
        arr.add(x);  // Add x to end of ArrayList
    }

    public int pop() {
        if (isEmpty()) {
            throw new EmptyStackException();
        }
        return arr.remove(arr.size() - 1);  // Remove and return last item
    }

    public int top() {
        if (isEmpty()) {
            throw new EmptyStackException();
        }
        return arr.get(arr.size() - 1);  // Peek last element
    }

    public boolean isEmpty() {
        return arr.isEmpty();
    }

    public int size() {
        return arr.size();
    }
}
class ArrayStack {
    constructor() {
        this.arr = [];  // Internal array buffer
    }

    push(x) {
        this.arr.push(x);  // Push to end
    }

    pop() {
        if (this.isEmpty()) throw new Error("Stack Underflow");
        return this.arr.pop();  // Pop last element
    }

    top() {
        if (this.isEmpty()) throw new Error("Stack is Empty");
        return this.arr[this.arr.length - 1];  // Inspect last element
    }

    isEmpty() {
        return this.arr.length === 0;
    }

    size() {
        return this.arr.length;
    }
}

Approach 2 - Singly Linked List Implementation (Dynamic Memory Allocation)

🧭 Intuition Breakdown (Head-Node Inversion)

1. The Concept: Represent the stack as a Singly Linked List. To ensure O(1) time complexity for all operations, we must perform insertion (push) and deletion (pop) strictly at the HEAD of the linked list!

2. Why Insert/Delete at Head?
• Adding a node at the head takes O(1) time: new_node.next = head; head = new_node.
• Removing a node from the head takes O(1) time: head = head.next.
• (Note: If we inserted/deleted at the tail, deleting would require traversing to the second-to-last node, taking O(N) time unless using a doubly linked list!).

Linked List Stack Representation: push(10) -> head -> [10] -> NULL push(20) -> head -> [20] -> [10] -> NULL push(30) -> head -> [30] -> [20] -> [10] -> NULL pop() -> head = head.next head -> [20] -> [10] -> NULL (Node 30 successfully removed in O(1)!)
Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition behind Linked List Stack: Linked list se stack banane ke liye saare operations **HEAD (Shuruat)** par hi hone chahiye.

• Push karne par: Naya node banao, uske next me current head ko jodo, aur naye node ko naya head bana do.
• Pop karne par: Direct head = head.next kar do.
Head par operations karne se time complexity bina kisi array reallocation ke hamesha 100% Guaranteed O(1) rehti hai!

📋 Approach 2 Trace Dry Run: Node Wire & Pointer Shifts

Operations: push(10), push(20), pop(), top()

Initialize: head = NULL, stack_size = 0 ================================================================================= 1. Execute push(10): ================================================================================= • Create node: Node(10) • Node(10).next = head (NULL) • head = Node(10) • stack_size = 1 State: head -> [10] -> NULL ================================================================================= 2. Execute push(20): ================================================================================= • Create node: Node(20) • Node(20).next = head (Node(10)) • head = Node(20) • stack_size = 2 State: head -> [20] -> [10] -> NULL ================================================================================= 3. Execute pop(): ================================================================================= • Read value at head: head.val = 20 • Advance head pointer: head = head.next -> Node(10) • stack_size = 1 State: head -> [10] -> NULL Returns: 20 ================================================================================= 4. Execute top(): ================================================================================= • Read head.val = 10 Returns: 10

a) Source Code Implementation

class Node:
    def __init__(self, val: int):
        self.val = val
        self.next = None

class LinkedListStack:
    def __init__(self):
        self.head = None  # Pointer to top node
        self.count = 0    # Track number of nodes

    def push(self, x: int) -> None:
        new_node = Node(x)
        new_node.next = self.head  # Wire new node to current head
        self.head = new_node       # Shift head pointer
        self.count += 1

    def pop(self) -> int:
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("Stack Underflow")
        popped_val = self.head.val
        self.head = self.head.next  # Advance head pointer to next node
        self.count -= 1
        return popped_val

    def top(self) -> int:
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("Stack is Empty")
        return self.head.val  # Head value represents top

    def is_empty(self) -> bool:
        return self.head is None

    def size(self) -> int:
        return self.count
class LinkedListStack {
private:
    struct Node {
        int val;
        Node* next;
        Node(int v) : val(v), next(nullptr) {}
    };

    Node* head;
    int count;

public:
    LinkedListStack() : head(nullptr), count(0) {}

    void push(int x) {
        Node* newNode = new Node(x);
        newNode->next = head;
        head = newNode;
        count++;
    }

    int pop() {
        if (isEmpty()) throw out_of_range("Stack Underflow");
        Node* temp = head;
        int val = temp->val;
        head = head->next;
        delete temp;  // Free memory
        count--;
        return val;
    }

    int top() {
        if (isEmpty()) throw out_of_range("Stack Empty");
        return head->val;
    }

    bool isEmpty() {
        return head == nullptr;
    }

    int size() {
        return count;
    }
};
class LinkedListStack {
    private static class Node {
        int val;
        Node next;
        Node(int val) { this.val = val; }
    }

    private Node head;
    private int count;

    public LinkedListStack() {
        head = null;
        count = 0;
    }

    public void push(int x) {
        Node newNode = new Node(x);
        newNode.next = head;
        head = newNode;
        count++;
    }

    public int pop() {
        if (isEmpty()) throw new EmptyStackException();
        int val = head.val;
        head = head.next;
        count--;
        return val;
    }

    public int top() {
        if (isEmpty()) throw new EmptyStackException();
        return head.val;
    }

    public boolean isEmpty() {
        return head == null;
    }

    public int size() {
        return count;
    }
}
class Node {
    constructor(val) {
        this.val = val;
        this.next = null;
    }
}

class LinkedListStack {
    constructor() {
        this.head = null;
        this.count = 0;
    }

    push(x) {
        const newNode = new Node(x);
        newNode.next = this.head;
        this.head = newNode;
        this.count++;
    }

    pop() {
        if (this.isEmpty()) throw new Error("Stack Underflow");
        const val = this.head.val;
        this.head = this.head.next;
        this.count--;
        return val;
    }

    top() {
        if (this.isEmpty()) throw new Error("Stack Empty");
        return this.head.val;
    }

    isEmpty() {
        return this.head === null;
    }

    size() {
        return this.count;
    }
}

Approach 3 - Implementing Stack using Queues (LeetCode 225 Pattern)

🧭 Deep Intuition Breakdown (Single Queue Rotation Paradigm)

1. The Challenge: A Queue operates under FIFO (First-In, First-Out) discipline. How do we make FIFO behave like LIFO (Last-In, First-Out)?

2. The Single Queue Rotation Strategy:
Whenever a new element x is pushed into the queue:

  1. Enqueue x into the queue.
  2. For all existing size - 1 elements, dequeue them from the front and immediately re-enqueue them back into the rear!
This circular rotation physically places the newly inserted element at the VERY FRONT of the queue!

Queue Rotation Mechanics (Push 30 into Queue [10, 20]): Step 1: Enqueue 30 at rear -> Queue: [10, 20, 30] (Front is 10) Step 2: Rotate size - 1 = 2 times: - Dequeue 10 -> Enqueue 10 -> Queue: [20, 30, 10] - Dequeue 20 -> Enqueue 20 -> Queue: [30, 10, 20] (Front is now 30!) Result: The most recently added element (30) is at the FRONT of the queue! A simple queue.pop() now mimics stack.pop() in O(1) time!
Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition: Queue (FIFO) ko Stack (LIFO) banane ke liye hum **Rotation Trick** use karte hain.

Jab bhi koi naya number push(x) ho, use queue me daalo. Phir baaki saare purane elements ko queue ke aage se nikal kar piche wapas daalte jao (rotate karo). Isse jo number abhi-abhi Aaya tha, wo Queue ke sabse front me aa jata hai! Ab Queue ka pop() direct Stack ka pop() ban jata hai.

📋 Approach 3 Trace Dry Run: Queue Inversion Rotation

Operations: push(10), push(20), pop()

Initialize: q = [] 1. push(10): • q.enqueue(10) -> q = [10] • Rotate size - 1 = 0 times -> q = [10] 2. push(20): • q.enqueue(20) -> q = [10, 20] (size = 2) • Rotate (size - 1) = 1 time: - Dequeue 10, Enqueue 10 -> q = [20, 10] (Front is 20) 3. pop(): • q.dequeue() -> Removes 20 from front. • q = [10] Returns: 20

a) Source Code Implementation

from collections import deque

class QueueStack:
    def __init__(self):
        self.q = deque()  # Double-ended queue acting as FIFO queue

    def push(self, x: int) -> None:
        self.q.append(x)  # Enqueue element at rear
        # Rotate all previous elements to move newly added element to front
        for _ in range(len(self.q) - 1):
            self.q.append(self.q.popleft())

    def pop(self) -> int:
        return self.q.popleft()  # Front element is top of stack

    def top(self) -> int:
        return self.q[0]  # Peek front element

    def is_empty(self) -> bool:
        return len(self.q) == 0

    def size(self) -> int:
        return len(self.q)
class QueueStack {
private:
    queue<int> q;

public:
    QueueStack() {}

    void push(int x) {
        q.push(x);
        int sz = q.size();
        // Rotate previous elements
        for (int i = 0; i < sz - 1; ++i) {
            q.push(q.front());
            q.pop();
        }
    }

    int pop() {
        int val = q.front();
        q.pop();
        return val;
    }

    int top() {
        return q.front();
    }

    bool isEmpty() {
        return q.empty();
    }

    int size() {
        return q.size();
    }
};
class QueueStack {
    private Queue<Integer> q;

    public QueueStack() {
        q = new LinkedList<>();
    }

    public void push(int x) {
        q.add(x);
        int sz = q.size();
        // Rotate elements
        for (int i = 0; i < sz - 1; i++) {
            q.add(q.remove());
        }
    }

    public int pop() {
        return q.remove();
    }

    public int top() {
        return q.peek();
    }

    public boolean isEmpty() {
        return q.isEmpty();
    }

    public int size() {
        return q.size();
    }
}
class QueueStack {
    constructor() {
        this.q = [];  // Simulating Queue using array
    }

    push(x) {
        this.q.push(x);
        const sz = this.q.length;
        for (let i = 0; i < sz - 1; i++) {
            this.q.push(this.q.shift());
        }
    }

    pop() {
        return this.q.shift();
    }

    top() {
        return this.q[0];
    }

    isEmpty() {
        return this.q.length === 0;
    }

    size() {
        return this.q.length;
    }
}

Strategic Edge Cases Tracking Matrix

Edge Case Profile Algorithmic Risk Factor Mitigation Resolution Logic
Stack Underflow
e.g., Calling pop() or top() on an empty stack.		 Undefined behavior, Segmentation fault, or NullPointerException. Guarded with initial checks: if (isEmpty()) throw Error/Exception.
Repeated Duplicate Values
e.g., push(5), push(5), push(5)		 Loss of duplicate nodes during deletion. Each push instantiates an independent memory node (Linked List) or array position, preserving exact duplicate counts.
Dynamic Memory Leak (C++)
Popping nodes in C++ without freeing heap memory.		 Memory leak accumulation in system RAM. Explicitly save node reference temp = head, advance head = head->next, and execute delete temp.

Complexity Analysis Performance Metrics

Approach Category Push Time Pop / Top Time Space Complexity Performance Evaluation Rating
Approach 1: Dynamic Array Stack O(1) Amortized O(1) O(N) Production Standard (Default). Optimal memory locality, standard language implementation.
Approach 2: Linked List Stack O(1) Guaranteed O(1) O(N) Strict Real-Time Choice. Guaranteed O(1) worst-case (no dynamic array doubling lag), slightly more memory per node (pointers).
Approach 3: Queue-Based Stack O(N) O(1) O(N) Theoretical / Interview Focus. Tradeoff: Push is O(N) due to rotation loop, making Pop O(1).

LeetCode 445 Medium Master Edition

Add Two Numbers II

An exhaustive engineering manual analyzing LIFO stack buffers, list reversal, head-insertion result building, and carry propagation.

Problem Statement

You are given two non-empty linked lists representing two non-negative integers. The most significant digit comes first and each of their nodes contains a single digit. Add the two numbers and return the sum as a linked list.

You may assume the two numbers do not contain any leading zero, except the number 0 itself.

Follow-up Requirement

Could you solve it without modifying the input lists (i.e. without reversing the input linked lists)?

Constraints

  • The number of nodes in each linked list is in the range [1, 100].
  • 0 <= Node.val <= 9
  • It is guaranteed that the list represents a number that does not have leading zeros.

Visualizing the Intent

Input: l1 = [7] -> [2] -> [4] -> [3] (represents 7243) l2 = [5] -> [6] -> [4] (represents 564) Math Addition (Right-to-Left): 7 2 4 3 + 5 6 4 --------- 7 8 0 7 Output: [7] -> [8] -> [0] -> [7]

Core Realization: Standard numerical addition starts from the least significant digit (least significant unit/rightmost digit) toward the most significant digit (leftmost digit). However, singly linked lists are traversed forward from head (MSD) to tail (LSD). To add right-to-left without reversing lists, we must process nodes in reverse order using a Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) order structure (Stack) or reverse the lists first.

Solutions Breakdown

Approach 1 - Reversing Input Linked Lists (In-Place Mutation)

🧭 Intuition Breakdown (Converting to Add Two Numbers I)

1. The Concept: If we reverse both input linked lists l1 and l2, the least significant digits align at the new heads. The problem transforms directly into the classic Add Two Numbers I (LeetCode 2).

2. Execution Steps:

  1. Reverse l1 and l2 in-place using the iterative 3-pointer technique.
  2. Perform standard right-to-left digit addition with carry tracking.
  3. Construct the resulting sum list.
  4. Reverse the result list to restore Most Significant Digit (MSD) first order.

3. Limitation: This approach mutates the input structure, which violates the strict interview follow-up condition ("Do not modify input lists").

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition: Sabse pehle dono input linked lists ko reverse kar do. Reverse karne se humare least significant digits (unit digits) aage aa jate hain. Uske baad simple carry addition karo, aur jo naya addition result mile use dobara reverse karke return kar do. Lekin yeh tarika original input lists ko modify kar deta hai.

📋 Approach 1 Line-by-Line Trace Profile

Input: l1 = [7, 2, 4, 3], l2 = [5, 6, 4]

Step 1: Reverse Input Lists • rev_l1 = [3] -> [4] -> [2] -> [7] • rev_l2 = [4] -> [6] -> [5] Step 2: Add Digits with Carry • Digit 1: 3 + 4 + 0(carry) = 7 -> digit = 7, carry = 0. Result: [7] • Digit 2: 4 + 6 + 0(carry) = 10 -> digit = 0, carry = 1. Result: [7] -> [0] • Digit 3: 2 + 5 + 1(carry) = 8 -> digit = 8, carry = 0. Result: [7] -> [0] -> [8] • Digit 4: 7 + 0 + 0(carry) = 7 -> digit = 7, carry = 0. Result: [7] -> [0] -> [8] -> [7] Step 3: Reverse Sum Result • Final Output: [7] -> [8] -> [0] -> [7]

a) Source Code Implementation

class Solution:
    def addTwoNumbers(self, l1: Optional[ListNode], l2: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        # Helper to reverse linked list in-place
        def reverse_list(head):
            prev, curr = None, head
            while curr:
                nxt = curr.next
                curr.next = prev
                prev = curr
                curr = nxt
            return prev

        r1 = reverse_list(l1)  # Reverse l1
        r2 = reverse_list(l2)  # Reverse l2

        dummy = ListNode(0)
        curr = dummy
        carry = 0

        # Standard addition pass
        while r1 or r2 or carry:
            v1 = r1.val if r1 else 0
            v2 = r2.val if r2 else 0

            val_sum = v1 + v2 + carry
            carry = val_sum // 10
            curr.next = ListNode(val_sum % 10)
            curr = curr.next

            if r1: r1 = r1.next
            if r2: r2 = r2.next

        return reverse_list(dummy.next)  # Reverse answer list to restore MSD order
class Solution {
private:
    ListNode* reverseList(ListNode* head) {
        ListNode* prev = nullptr;
        ListNode* curr = head;
        while (curr != nullptr) {
            ListNode* nxt = curr->next;
            curr->next = prev;
            prev = curr;
            curr = nxt;
        }
        return prev;
    }

public:
    ListNode* addTwoNumbers(ListNode* l1, ListNode* l2) {
        ListNode* r1 = reverseList(l1);
        ListNode* r2 = reverseList(l2);

        ListNode* dummy = new ListNode(0);
        ListNode* curr = dummy;
        int carry = 0;

        while (r1 != nullptr || r2 != nullptr || carry != 0) {
            int v1 = (r1 != nullptr) ? r1->val : 0;
            int v2 = (r2 != nullptr) ? r2->val : 0;

            int sum = v1 + v2 + carry;
            carry = sum / 10;
            curr->next = new ListNode(sum % 10);
            curr = curr->next;

            if (r1) r1 = r1->next;
            if (r2) r2 = r2->next;
        }

        return reverseList(dummy->next);
    }
};
class Solution {

Approach 2 - Optimal Solution: LIFO Stacks with Head Insertion (Without Input Mutation)

🧭 Deep Intuition Breakdown (LIFO Character Reversal & Head Insertion)

1. Satisfying the Follow-up: To add from right to left without modifying the original linked list pointers, we use two Stacks (LIFO buffers) to push all node values from l1 and l2.

2. How Stack popping aligns Least Significant Digits:
When traversing forward, the last element pushed onto stack1 and stack2 is the unit (least significant) digit. Popping from both stacks automatically processes values from right to left!

3. The Head-Insertion Construction Technique:
Because we calculate the sum from least significant to most significant digit, the digits are computed in reverse order of the final desired list.
Instead of creating nodes and appending to the tail (which would require reversing at the end), we use Head Insertion:

Head-Insertion Building Logic: Suppose calculated digits in order are: 7 (units), 0 (tens), 8 (hundreds), 7 (thousands) 1. Compute digit 7: node = new ListNode(7) head = node -> List: [7] -> NULL 2. Intuition behind Stacks + Head Insertion: Follow-up condition ke mutabiq hum input lists ko reverse nahi kar sakte. Iska sabse best tareeka hai Stacks (LIFO) use karna.

• Ab jab hum dono stacks se pop() karenge, toh unit digits sabse pehle bahar aayenge!

FINAL RETURNED LIST: 7 -> 8 -> 0 -> 7

LeetCode 2816 Medium Master Edition

Double a Number Represented as a Linked List

An engineering manual analyzing stack-based backward processing, two-pointer forward carry lookahead, and in-place list reversals.

Problem Statement

You are given the head of a non-empty linked list representing a non-negative integer without leading zeros.

Return the head of the linked list after doubling the number it represents.

Constraints

  • The number of nodes in the list is in the range [1, 10^5].
  • 0 <= Node.val <= 9
  • The input list represents a number that does not have leading zeros, except the number 0 itself.

Visualizing the Intent

Let's observe how doubling a number affects the digits and carry propagation:

Example 1: Input: head = [1, 8, 9] (represents 189) Calculation: 189 * 2 = 378 Output: [3, 7, 8] Example 2: Input: head = [9, 9, 9] (represents 999) Calculation: 999 * 2 = 1998 Output: [1, 9, 9, 8] (New head node created due to overflow carry at MSD!)

Core Realization: Standard multiplication proceeds from right to left (Least Significant Digit to Most Significant Digit). Because singly linked lists only traverse forward from head (MSD) to tail (LSD), we either need a structure to process nodes backward (Stack or List Reversal) or a lookahead technique that predicts carry during forward traversal.

Solutions Breakdown

Approach 1 - Reversing the Linked List (Two-Pass In-Place)

🧭 Intuition Breakdown (Inverting Traversal Direction)

1. The Concept: Reversing the linked list puts the least significant digit at the head. We can then perform standard scalar multiplication (doubling each node's value and tracking carry) moving forward.

2. Execution Steps:

  1. Reverse the input linked list in-place.
  2. Traverse the reversed list, calculating new_val = val * 2 + carry for each node. Update node.val = new_val % 10 and carry = new_val // 10.
  3. If a carry remains after the loop, append a new node with value carry to the tail.
  4. Reverse the list once more to restore the original most-significant-digit order and return the new head.

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition: Linked List ko double karne ke liye sabse pehle usko reverse kar do. Isse unit digit aage aa jata hai. Phir normal 2 se multiply karo aur carry aage pass karte jao. Phir se list ko reverse kardo taaki digits original order me aa jayein. Isme Space O(1) lagta hai par list ko 2-3 baar scan karna padta hai.

📋 Approach 1 Trace Profile

Input: [1, 8, 9]

Step 1: Reverse List • Reversed List: [9] -> [8] -> [1] Step 2: Double Values and Propagate Carry (carry = 0) • Node 9: val = 9 * 2 + 0 = 18 -> node.val = 8, carry = 1 • Node 8: val = 8 * 2 + 1 = 17 -> node.val = 7, carry = 1 • Node 1: val = 1 * 2 + 1 = 3 -> node.val = 3, carry = 0 • List state: [8] -> [7] -> [3] Step 3: Reverse List Back • Final Output: [3] -> [7] -> [8]

a) Source Code Implementation

class Solution:
    def doubleIt(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        def reverse(node):
            prev, curr = None, node
            while curr:
                nxt = curr.next
                curr.next = prev
                prev = curr
                curr = nxt
            return prev

        # Step 1: Reverse the list
        head = reverse(head)
        curr = head
        carry = 0
        prev = None

        # Step 2: Double values and manage carry
        while curr:
            total = curr.val * 2 + carry
            curr.val = total % 10
            carry = total // 10
            prev = curr
            curr = curr.next

        # Append new node if overflow carry remains
        if carry:
            prev.next = ListNode(carry)

        # Step 3: Reverse back
        return reverse(head)

Approach 2 - Stack Buffer Processing (Without Modifying Pointer Order)

🧭 Intuition Breakdown (LIFO Processing)

1. The Concept: Push all node references onto a Stack during a forward scan. Popping nodes off the stack processes them in reverse (least significant digit first) without mutating the linked list pointers.

2. Execution: Pop nodes one by one, calculate val = node.val * 2 + carry, update node.val = val % 10, and update carry = val // 10. If carry > 0 after popping all nodes, prepending a new head node with value 1 handles the overflow.

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition: Stack ek Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) structure hai. Saare nodes ko stack me push kar do. Phir pop() karke jab bahar nikalenge, toh unit digit sabse pehle milega. Direct multiply aur carry update karte jao. Agar aakhir me carry bache, toh aage naya node jod do.

a) Source Code Implementation

class Solution:
    def doubleIt(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:

        while curr:

            curr = curr.next

        carry = 0
        # Process nodes right-to-left via popping
        while stack:
            node = stack.pop()
            total = node.val * 2 + carry
            node.val = total % 10
            carry = total // 10

        # If carry remains, prepend a new head node
        if carry:
            new_head = ListNode(carry)
            new_head.next = head
            return new_head

        return head

Approach 3 - Optimal Solution: Single-Pass Forward Lookahead (O(1) Auxiliary Space)

🧭 Deep Intuition Breakdown (Forward Carry Prediction)

1. The Mathematical Property of Doubling:
When multiplying any single digit d ∈ [0, 9] by 2:

  • If d ∈ [0, 4], d * 2 ∈ [0, 8]. It produces NO CARRY (carry = 0).
  • If d ∈ [5, 9], d * 2 ∈ [10, 18]. It ALWAYS produces a carry of 1 to its left neighbor!
Because scalar doubling can ONLY ever generate a carry of 0 or 1, a node's incoming carry is entirely determined by whether its immediate successor (node.next) is >= 5!

2. The One-Pass Lookahead Strategy:

  1. Check the head node value. If head.val >= 5, doubling the entire number will overflow and create a new most significant digit 1 at the front. Prepend a new head node new_head = ListNode(0) pointing to head.
  2. Traverse forward node by node. For each curr node:
    • Double its value: curr.val = (curr.val * 2) % 10.
    • Look at curr.next: If curr.next exists and curr.next.val >= 5, add 1 to curr.val!
This allows us to complete the doubling operation in a single forward pass in O(N) time and O(1) auxiliary space without list reversals or stacks!

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition behind Forward Lookahead: 2 se multiplication ka ek simple rule hai: Kisi digit ko 2 se multiply karne par carry **tabhi aayega agar wo number 5 ya usse bada ho**! (kyuki 5*2 = 10, 6*2 = 12, etc.).

Iska matlab, hum aage se traversal karte waqt hi apne **agle node (curr.next)** ko dekh kar bata sakte hain ki piche carry 1 aayega ya nahi!

• Agar head.val >= 5 hai, toh shuruat me ek naya node 0 aage jod do.
• Har node par: curr.val = (curr.val * 2) % 10 karo. Aur agar agla node curr.next.val >= 5 hai, toh curr.val += 1 kar do. Bas ek single pass me kaam khatam!

📋 Full Trace Dry Run 1: Head >= 5 (Overflow New Head)

Input: head = [9, 9, 9]

================================================================================= STEP 1: CHECK HEAD OVERFLOW ================================================================================= • head.val = 9 >= 5 -> TRUE! • Prepend dummy node 0 at front: head = [0] -> [9] -> [9] -> [9] ================================================================================= STEP 2: SINGLE-PASS FORWARD TRAVERSAL ================================================================================= • Node 1 (val = 0, next = Node(9)): - Double val: (0 * 2) % 10 = 0 - Check next.val (9 >= 5) -> True! Add 1 to val. - Node 1 updated val = 1. - State: [1] -> [9] -> [9] -> [9] • Node 2 (val = 9, next = Node(9)): - Double val: (9 * 2) % 10 = 8 - Check next.val (9 >= 5) -> True! Add 1 to val (8 + 1 = 9). - Node 2 updated val = 9. - State: [1] -> [9] -> [9] -> [9] • Node 3 (val = 9, next = Node(9)): - Double val: (9 * 2) % 10 = 8 - Check next.val (9 >= 5) -> True! Add 1 to val (8 + 1 = 9). - Node 3 updated val = 9. - State: [1] -> [9] -> [9] -> [9] • Node 4 (val = 9, next = NULL): - Double val: (9 * 2) % 10 = 8 - Check next -> NULL (No carry). - Node 4 updated val = 8. - State: [1] -> [9] -> [9] -> [8] FINAL RETURNED LIST: [1, 9, 9, 8]
📋 Full Trace Dry Run 2: Intermittent Carries

Input: head = [1, 8, 9]

================================================================================= STEP 1: CHECK HEAD OVERFLOW ================================================================================= • head.val = 1 < 5 -> FALSE. No dummy node needed. ================================================================================= STEP 2: FORWARD TRAVERSAL ================================================================================= • Node 1 (val = 1, next = Node(8)): - Double val: (1 * 2) % 10 = 2 - Check next.val (8 >= 5) -> True! Add 1 (2 + 1 = 3). - Node 1 updated val = 3. • Node 2 (val = 8, next = Node(9)): - Double val: (8 * 2) % 10 = 6 - Check next.val (9 >= 5) -> True! Add 1 (6 + 1 = 7). - Node 2 updated val = 7. • Node 3 (val = 9, next = NULL): - Double val: (9 * 2) % 10 = 8 - Check next -> NULL. - Node 3 updated val = 8. FINAL RETURNED LIST: [3, 7, 8]

a) Source Code Implementation

class Solution:
    def doubleIt(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:

            curr.val = (curr.val * 2) % 10

            if curr.next and curr.next.val >= 5:

            curr = curr.next

        return head

        let newHead = new ListNode(0);
        newHead.next = head;
        head = newHead;
    }

    let curr = head;
    while (curr !== null) {
        curr.val = (curr.val * 2) % 10;

        // HIGHLIGHT: Lookahead for carry
        if (curr.next !== null && curr.next.val >= 5) {
            curr.val += 1;
        }

        curr = curr.next;
    }

    return head;
};

Strategic Edge Cases Tracking Matrix

To ensure high production robustness, algorithms are tested against critical edge cases:

Edge Case Profile Algorithmic Risk Factor Mitigation Resolution Logic
Single Zero Node
e.g., head = [0]		 Creating unnecessary extra leading nodes or wrong calculations. 0 < 5 so no new head is added. (0 * 2) % 10 = 0. Correctly returns [0].
Most Significant Digit >= 5
e.g., head = [5] or [9, 9]		 Overflow carry creating an extra digit at front. Check head.val >= 5 prepends ListNode(0) before iteration, allowing node 0 to absorb the carry and become 1.
Alternating High/Low Digits
e.g., head = [1, 5, 2, 9]		 Incorrect carry propagation across non-consecutive carries. Lookahead curr.next.val >= 5 evaluates independently per node, accurately adding 1 only when the immediate successor generates a carry.

Complexity Analysis Performance Metrics

Approach Category Time Complexity Space Complexity Performance Evaluation Rating
Approach 1: In-Place List Reversals O(N) O(1) Space Space Optimal / Multi-Pass. Scans the list 3 times (reverse, multiply, reverse back).
Approach 2: Stack Buffer Processing O(N) O(N) Space Sub-optimal Memory. Requires an extra stack array to hold all node references.
Approach 3: Single-Pass Forward Lookahead O(N) O(1) Space Absolute Production Standard. Single pass traversal, zero list reversals, zero extra stack memory. Maximum execution efficiency.

Plus One Linked List

An engineering manual analyzing backward carry propagation, double list reversal, recursive call stack unwinding, and single-pass non-nine pointer tracking.

Problem Statement

Given a non-empty linked list representing a non-negative integer, increment the integer by 1.

The digits are stored such that the most significant digit is at the head of the list, and each of their nodes contains a single digit.

You may assume the integer does not contain any leading zero, except the number 0 itself.

Constraints

  • The number of nodes in the list is in the range [1, 100].
  • 0 <= Node.val <= 9
  • The integer represented by the linked list does not contain leading zeros except for the number 0 itself.

Visualizing the Intent

Let's map out how incrementing by 1 impacts digits across a linked chain:

Example 1 (No Ripple Carry): Input: [1] -> [2] -> [3] (represents 123) Math: 123 + 1 = 124 Output: [1] -> [2] -> [4] Example 2 (Cascading Carry): Input: [1] -> [2] -> [9] (represents 129) Math: 129 + 1 = 130 Output: [1] -> [3] -> [0] Example 3 (Full Overflow Carry): Input: [9] -> [9] -> [9] (represents 999) Math: 999 + 1 = 1000 Output: [1] -> [0] -> [0] -> [0] (A new head node is prepended!)

Core Realization: Standard mathematical addition adds 1 to the least significant digit (LSD) at the tail. Because singly linked lists only allow forward traversal from head (MSD) to tail (LSD), we must resolve the direction mismatch between forward list traversal and backward carry ripple propagation.

Solutions Breakdown

Approach 1 - Double List Reversal (Two-Pass In-Place)

🧭 Intuition Breakdown (Inverting Direction)

1. The Concept: Reversing the linked list brings the least significant digit (LSD) to the head. We can then add 1 directly to the new head node, process any cascading carry of 1 through adjacent nodes, and reverse the list once more to restore the original most-significant-digit order.

2. Execution Steps:

  1. Reverse the linked list in-place.
  2. Initialize carry = 1. Traverse the list, setting new_sum = curr.val + carry, updating curr.val = new_sum % 10, and updating carry = new_sum // 10.
  3. If carry > 0 after reaching the tail, append a new node ListNode(carry) at the end.
  4. Reverse the modified list back and return the new head.

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition: Addition hamesha last digit (rightmost) se hoti hai. Isliye pehle poori list ko reverse kar do taaki unit digit aage aa jaye. Head me 1 add karo, aur jab tak digit 9 bane tab tak carry aage bhejte raho (jo 10 hone par 0 ban jaye). Aakhir me list ko waapas reverse kar do. Isme O(1) space lagti hai par list ko 2 baar scan karna padta hai.

📋 Approach 1 Trace Profile

Input: [1, 2, 9]

Step 1: Reverse List • Reversed List: [9] -> [2] -> [1] Step 2: Add 1 & Propagate Carry (carry = 1) • Node 9: sum = 9 + 1 = 10 -> node.val = 0, carry = 1 • Node 2: sum = 2 + 1 = 3 -> node.val = 3, carry = 0 • Node 1: sum = 1 + 0 = 1 -> node.val = 1, carry = 0 • Modified State: [0] -> [3] -> [1] Step 3: Reverse List Back • Final Output: [1] -> [3] -> [0]

a) Source Code Implementation

class Solution:
    def plusOne(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        # Helper to reverse linked list in-place
        def reverse(node):
            prev, curr = None, node
            while curr:
                nxt = curr.next
                curr.next = prev
                prev = curr
                curr = nxt
            return prev

        head = reverse(head)
        curr = head
        carry = 1
        prev = None

        # Add 1 and process carry forward
        while curr:
            total = curr.val + carry
            curr.val = total % 10
            carry = total // 10
            prev = curr
            curr = curr.next

        # If carry remains at the end, append new node
        if carry:
            prev.next = ListNode(carry)

        return reverse(head)
class Solution {
private:
    ListNode* reverse(ListNode* head) {
        ListNode* prev = nullptr;
        ListNode* curr = head;
        while (curr != nullptr) {
            ListNode* nxt = curr->next;
            curr->next = prev;
            prev = curr;
            curr = nxt;
        }
        return prev;
    }

public:
    ListNode* plusOne(ListNode* head) {
        head = reverse(head);
        ListNode* curr = head;
        ListNode* prev = nullptr;
        int carry = 1;

        while (curr != nullptr) {
            int total = curr->val + carry;
            curr->val = total % 10;
            carry = total / 10;
            prev = curr;
            curr = curr->next;
        }

        if (carry > 0) {
            prev->next = new ListNode(carry);
        }

        return reverse(head);
    }
};
class Solution {
    private ListNode reverse(ListNode head) {
        ListNode prev = null;
        ListNode curr = head;
        while (curr != null) {
            ListNode nxt = curr.next;
            curr.next = prev;
            prev = curr;
            curr = nxt;
        }
        return prev;
    }

    public ListNode plusOne(ListNode head) {
        head = reverse(head);
        ListNode curr = head;
        ListNode prev = null;
        int carry = 1;

        while (curr != null) {
            int total = curr.val + carry;
            curr.val = total % 10;
            carry = total / 10;
            prev = curr;
            curr = curr.next;
        }

        if (carry > 0) {
            prev.next = new ListNode(carry);
        }

        return reverse(head);
    }
}
var plusOne = function(head) {
    const reverse = (node) => {
        let prev = null, curr = node;
        while (curr !== null) {
            let nxt = curr.next;
            curr.next = prev;
            prev = curr;
            curr = nxt;
        }
        return prev;
    };

    head = reverse(head);
    let curr = head, prev = null, carry = 1;

    while (curr !== null) {
        let total = curr.val + carry;
        curr.val = total % 10;
        carry = Math.floor(total / 10);
        prev = curr;
        curr = curr.next;
    }

    if (carry > 0) {
        prev.next = new ListNode(carry);
    }

    return reverse(head);
};

Approach 2 - Recursive Unwinding (Implicit Call Stack)

🧭 Intuition Breakdown (Bottom-Up Return Propagation)

1. The Concept: Recursion naturally traverses to the end of the list first (base case at NULL) and then evaluates return statements in reverse order as call stack frames collapse.

2. How It Works:

  1. Recurse down to the terminal NULL pointer. The base case returns carry = 1 (representing the addition of 1 to the LSD).
  2. As recursion unwinds back up to each node:
    • Compute sum = curr.val + carry.
    • Update curr.val = sum % 10.
    • Return new_carry = sum // 10 back up to the parent frame.
  3. At the top caller frame (original head): If carry == 1, prepend a new dummy head ListNode(1).

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition: Recursion list ke end (tail) tak deep jao. Base case me carry 1 return karo. Jab call stack piche aayega (unwind hoga), har node apna val update karega aur carry aage parent node ko pass kar dega. Agar bilkul top head par abhi bhi carry 1 bach jaye, toh aage ek naya node 1 jod do.

📋 Approach 2 Trace Dry Run: Call Stack Unwinding

Input: [9, 9]

Winding Stack: • helper([9] -> [9]) -> helper([9]) -> helper(NULL) Unwinding Stack (Bottom-Up): • helper(NULL): Base case reached. Return carry = 1 • Frame for second Node(9): - carry received = 1 - sum = 9 + 1 = 10 -> node.val = 0 - return carry = 1 to parent frame • Frame for first Node(9): - carry received = 1 - sum = 9 + 1 = 10 -> node.val = 0 - return carry = 1 to main function Top Level: • carry = 1 remaining at head! Prepend new Node(1). • Result: [1] -> [0] -> [0]

a) Source Code Implementation

class Solution:
    def plusOne(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        # Recursive helper returning carry to parent node
        def add_carry(node) -> int:
            if not node:
                return 1  # Base case: add 1 at tail

            carry = add_carry(node.next)  # Recurse down to tail
            total = node.val + carry
            node.val = total % 10
            return total // 10

        carry = add_carry(head)
        # If head overflows, create new MSD head
        if carry:
            new_head = ListNode(carry)
            new_head.next = head
            return new_head

        return head
class Solution {
private:
    int addCarry(ListNode* node) {
        if (node == nullptr) return 1;  // Base case at end

        int carry = addCarry(node->next);
        int sum = node->val + carry;
        node->val = sum % 10;
        return sum / 10;
    }

public:
    ListNode* plusOne(ListNode* head) {
        int carry = addCarry(head);
        if (carry > 0) {
            ListNode* newHead = new ListNode(carry);
            newHead->next = head;
            return newHead;
        }
        return head;
    }
};
class Solution {
    private int addCarry(ListNode node) {
        if (node == null) return 1;  // Base case

        int carry = addCarry(node.next);
        int sum = node.val + carry;
        node.val = sum % 10;
        return sum / 10;
    }

    public ListNode plusOne(ListNode head) {
        int carry = addCarry(head);
        if (carry > 0) {
            ListNode newHead = new ListNode(carry);
            newHead.next = head;
            return newHead;
        }
        return head;
    }
}
var plusOne = function(head) {
    const addCarry = (node) => {
        if (!node) return 1;  // Base case

        let carry = addCarry(node.next);
        let sum = node.val + carry;
        node.val = sum % 10;
        return Math.floor(sum / 10);
    };

    let carry = addCarry(head);
    if (carry > 0) {
        let newHead = new ListNode(carry);
        newHead.next = head;
        return newHead;
    }
    return head;
};

Approach 3 - Optimal Solution: Single-Pass Two-Pointer (Last Non-Nine Tracking)

🧭 Deep Intuition Breakdown (Cascading Nine Isolation)

1. Mathematical Observation of Addition:
When adding 1 to a number, notice what happens to trailing digits:

  • If the last digit is < 9 (e.g. 123), adding 1 changes 3 -> 4. All preceding digits remain unchanged.
  • If trailing digits end in 9s (e.g. 1299), adding 1 converts ALL trailing 9s into 0s, and increments the rightmost non-nine digit by 1 (1299 + 1 = 1300)!
  • If ALL digits are 9s (e.g. 999), every digit turns to 0, and a new leading 1 is added at the front (999 + 1 = 1000).

2. The Single-Pass Two-Pointer Strategy:

  1. Create a dummy node dummy = ListNode(0) and point dummy.next = head.
  2. Maintain a pointer not_nine starting at dummy.
  3. Traverse the list with pointer curr:
    • Whenever curr.val != 9, update not_nine = curr!
  4. After the loop finishes, not_nine points to the last node in the list whose value is NOT 9!
  5. Increment not_nine.val += 1.
  6. Set all nodes following not_nine (which are guaranteed to be 9s) to 0!
  7. If dummy.val == 1 (occurs when all original nodes were 9), return dummy; otherwise return dummy.next.
This achieves maximum optimization: O(N) time in a single pass with O(1) auxiliary space!

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition behind Non-Nine Pointer: Jab bhi hum 1 add karte hain, saare trailing 9s badal kar 0 ho jaate hain, aur unse thik pehle jo **Aakhri Non-Nine Number** hota hai wo +1 ho jata hai!

• Example: 1 -> 2 -> 9 -> 9. Aakhri non-nine digit 2 hai.
• Hum ek pointer not_nine ko 2 par hold kar lete hain.
• Traversal khatam hote hi: not_nine.val += 1 (yani 2 -> 3) kar do, aur uske aage ke saare 9s ko 0 bana do -> 1 -> 3 -> 0 -> 0!
• Agar saare digits 9 hue (jaise 999), toh dummy head 0 (jo aage lagaya tha) wo 1 ban jata hai -> 1000! Single pass me bina list reverse kiye kam ho jata hai.

📋 Full Trace Dry Run 1: Trailing Nines Sequence

Input: [1, 2, 9, 9]

================================================================================= STEP 1: INITIALIZATION ================================================================================= • dummy = [0] -> [1] -> [2] -> [9] -> [9] • not_nine = dummy (val = 0) • curr = head (val = 1) ================================================================================= STEP 2: FIND LAST NON-NINE NODE ================================================================================= • curr = Node(1): val != 9 -> not_nine = Node(1) • curr = Node(2): val != 9 -> not_nine = Node(2) • curr = Node(9): val == 9 -> not_nine remains Node(2) • curr = Node(9): val == 9 -> not_nine remains Node(2) End of Traversal: not_nine points to Node(2). ================================================================================= STEP 3: INCREMENT & ZERO OUT TRAILING NINES ================================================================================= • Increment last non-nine: not_nine.val += 1 => Node(2).val becomes 3. • Set runner pointer: runner = not_nine.next (Node(9)) • Loop through trailing nodes: - runner = Node(9) -> runner.val = 0, runner = runner.next - runner = Node(9) -> runner.val = 0, runner = runner.next Current List State: dummy[0] -> [1] -> [3] -> [0] -> [0] ================================================================================= STEP 4: RETURN HEAD ================================================================================= • dummy.val == 0 -> return dummy.next -> Node(1) FINAL RETURNED LIST: [1, 3, 0, 0]
📋 Full Trace Dry Run 2: All Nines Overflow

Input: [9, 9, 9]

================================================================================= STEP 1: INITIALIZATION ================================================================================= • dummy = [0] -> [9] -> [9] -> [9] • not_nine = dummy (val = 0) • curr = head (val = 9) ================================================================================= STEP 2: FIND LAST NON-NINE NODE ================================================================================= • curr = Node(9) [idx 0]: val == 9 -> not_nine stays dummy • curr = Node(9) [idx 1]: val == 9 -> not_nine stays dummy • curr = Node(9) [idx 2]: val == 9 -> not_nine stays dummy End of Traversal: not_nine is still dummy (val = 0)! ================================================================================= STEP 3: INCREMENT & ZERO OUT TRAILING NINES ================================================================================= • Increment not_nine.val += 1 => dummy.val becomes 1. • Set trailing 9s to 0: - Node(9) -> 0 - Node(9) -> 0 - Node(9) -> 0 Current List State: dummy[1] -> [0] -> [0] -> [0] ================================================================================= STEP 4: RETURN HEAD ================================================================================= • dummy.val == 1 -> return dummy directly! FINAL RETURNED LIST: [1, 0, 0, 0]

a) Source Code Implementation

class Solution:
    def plusOne(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        dummy = ListNode(0)
        dummy.next = head

        not_nine = dummy  # Pointer to rightmost node whose value is not 9
        curr = head

        # Single pass: identify the last non-nine node
        while curr:
            if curr.val != 9:
                not_nine = curr
            curr = curr.next

        # Increment the last non-nine node
        not_nine.val += 1

        # Set all subsequent 9s to 0
        curr = not_nine.next
        while curr:
            curr.val = 0
            curr = curr.next

        # Return dummy if dummy expanded to 1, else original head
        return dummy if dummy.val == 1 else dummy.next
class Solution {
public:
    ListNode* plusOne(ListNode* head) {
        ListNode* dummy = new ListNode(0);
        dummy->next = head;

        ListNode* notNine = dummy;
        ListNode* curr = head;

        // Find last non-nine node
        while (curr != nullptr) {
            if (curr->val != 9) {
                notNine = curr;
            }
            curr = curr->next;
        }

        // HIGHLIGHT: Increment non-nine and zero out succeeding nodes
        notNine->val += 1;
        curr = notNine->next;
        while (curr != nullptr) {
            curr->val = 0;
            curr = curr->next;
        }

        return (dummy->val == 1) ? dummy : dummy->next;
    }
};
class Solution {
    public ListNode plusOne(ListNode head) {
        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0);
        dummy.next = head;

        ListNode notNine = dummy;
        ListNode curr = head;

        // Locate last non-nine element
        while (curr != null) {
            if (curr.val != 9) {
                notNine = curr;
            }
            curr = curr.next;
        }

        // HIGHLIGHT: Increment non-nine and convert remaining 9s to 0s
        notNine.val += 1;
        curr = notNine.next;
        while (curr != null) {
            curr.val = 0;
            curr = curr.next;
        }

        return (dummy.val == 1) ? dummy : dummy.next;
    }
}
var plusOne = function(head) {
    const dummy = new ListNode(0);
    dummy.next = head;

    let notNine = dummy;
    let curr = head;

    // Find last non-nine node
    while (curr !== null) {
        if (curr.val !== 9) {
            notNine = curr;
        }
        curr = curr.next;
    }

    // HIGHLIGHT: Update values
    notNine.val += 1;
    curr = notNine.next;
    while (curr !== null) {
        curr.val = 0;
        curr = curr.next;
    }

    return dummy.val === 1 ? dummy : dummy.next;
};

Strategic Edge Cases Tracking Matrix

To deliver robust engineering systems, algorithms are tested against critical numeric boundary cases:

Edge Case Profile Algorithmic Risk Factor Mitigation Resolution Logic
Single Zero Node
e.g., head = [0]		 Incorrect dummy head node insertion or modulo division error. 0 != 9, so not_nine updates to Node(0). 0 + 1 = 1. dummy.val == 0, so returns [1] cleanly.
Single Nine Node
e.g., head = [9]		 Carry overflow failing to allocate new leading digit. not_nine remains on dummy = [0]. dummy.val increments to 1, Node(9) turns to 0. Returns dummy = [1, 0].
All Nine Digits
e.g., head = [9, 9, 9, 9]		 Multiple cascading carries turning list into [1, 0, 0, 0, 0]. not_nine stays on dummy. dummy.val becomes 1, and all subsequent nodes turn to 0. Returns [1, 0, 0, 0, 0].
No Nines Present
e.g., head = [1, 2, 3]		 Unnecessary traversal or zero-out loop. not_nine lands on the tail Node(3). Node(3) increments to 4. not_nine.next is NULL, so zero-out loop executes 0 times. Returns [1, 2, 4].

Complexity Analysis Performance Metrics

Approach Category Time Complexity Space Complexity Performance Evaluation Rating
Approach 1: Double List Reversal O(N) O(1) Space Multi-Pass / Mutates List. Requires 3 full traversals (reverse, add, reverse back). Modifies structure multiple times.
Approach 2: Recursive Unwinding O(N) O(N) Stack Call-Stack Overhead. Elegant recursive logic, but consumes O(N) implicit call stack memory for recursion frames.
Approach 3: Single-Pass Two-Pointer O(N) O(1) Space Absolute Production Standard. Single forward traversal, zero list reversals, zero recursion stack memory. Maximum performance.

Valid Parentheses

An exhaustive engineering manual analyzing LIFO sequence matching, string replacement reduction, and hash-mapped stack boundary verification.

Problem Statement

Given a string s containing just the characters '(', ')', '{', '}', '[' and ']', determine if the input string is valid.

An input string is valid if:

  1. Open brackets must be closed by the same type of brackets.
  2. Open brackets must be closed in the correct order.
  3. Every close bracket has a corresponding open bracket of the same type.

Constraints

  • 1 <= s.length <= 10^4
  • s consists of parentheses only '()[]{}'.

Visualizing the Intent

Let's map out how nested and sequential parentheses match in a Last-In, First-Out manner:

Valid Example 1: s = "()[]{}" - Matches in pairs sequentially: () -> match, [] -> match, {} -> match. Output: true Valid Example 2: s = "{[]}" - Nested brackets: Inner pair [] matches first, leaving {}, which matches next. Output: true Invalid Example 1: s = "(]" - Opening '(' expects closing ')', but received ']'. Mismatch! Output: false Invalid Example 2: s = "([)]" - Interleaved brackets: Outer '(' closed before inner '[' is closed. Violation of closing order! Output: false

Core Realization: The most recently opened bracket MUST be the very first bracket to be closed. This strict temporal order ("last opened = first closed") corresponds exactly to the Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) property of a Stack.

Solutions Breakdown

Approach 1 - Brute Force (Sub-string Replacement Simulation)

🧭 Intuition Breakdown (Iterative Pair Elimination)

1. The Concept: If a string contains valid nested or adjacent parentheses, there must exist at least one innermost adjacent pair: "()", "{}", or "[]". Removing this inner pair preserves the validity of the surrounding brackets. We can repeatedly scan the string and replace any occurrence of "()", "{}", or "[]" with an empty string "" until no further replacements can be made.

2. Verification: If the string reduces to an empty string "", all brackets were matched correctly. If the string non-empty stabilizes with remaining unhandled brackets, the input is invalid.

3. Why it Fails Efficiency Constraints: String replacement scans the string up to N / 2 times, creating new string copies on each pass. This yields a time complexity of O(N^2) and space complexity of O(N^2) or O(N), making it unsuitably slow for large inputs.

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition: Har valid string ke andar kahin na kahin ek innermost pair jaise "()", "{}", ya "[]" zaroor hoga. Hum ek loop chalate hain aur jab tak string me "()", "{}", ya "[]" milta rahe, use mitaate (delete karte) jaate hain. Agar aakhir me string poori tarah khaali "" ho gayi, toh True, nahi toh False. Isme har step par nayi string banti hai jisse Time Complexity O(N^2) ho jaati hai.

📋 Approach 1 Line-by-Line Trace Profile

Input: s = "{[()]}"

Initial String: "{[()]}" • Pass 1: Scan for "()", "{}", "[]" - Found "()" inside "{[()]}". Replace with "" - String becomes: "{[]}" • Pass 2: Scan for "()", "{}", "[]" - Found "[]" inside "{[]}". Replace with "" - String becomes: "{}" • Pass 3: Scan for "()", "{}", "[]" - Found "{}" inside "{}". Replace with "" - String becomes: "" String is now empty! Result: TRUE

a) Source Code Implementation

class BruteForceSolution:
    def isValid(self, s: str) -> bool:
        # If length is odd, it can never be fully matched
        if len(s) % 2 != 0:
            return False

        # Continually replace valid adjacent pairs
        while "()" in s or "{}" in s or "[]" in s:
            s = s.replace("()", "")
            s = s.replace("{}", "")
            s = s.replace("[]", "")

        return s == ""  # Valid if string is completely consumed
class BruteForceSolution {
public:
    bool isValid(string s) {
        if (s.length() % 2 != 0) return false;

        size_t pos;
        while ((pos = s.find("()")) != string::npos ||
               (pos = s.find("{}")) != string::npos ||
               (pos = s.find("[]")) != string::npos) {
            s.erase(pos, 2);  // Erase matched pair
        }

        return s.empty();
    }
};
class BruteForceSolution {
    public boolean isValid(String s) {
        if (s.length() % 2 != 0) return false;

        while (s.contains("()") || s.contains("{}") || s.contains("[]")) {
            s = s.replace("()", "");
            s = s.replace("{}", "");
            s = s.replace("[]", "");
        }

        return s.isEmpty();
    }
}
var isValid = function(s) {
    if (s.length % 2 !== 0) return false;

    while (s.includes("()") || s.includes("{}") || s.includes("[]")) {
        s = s.replace("()", "").replace("{}", "").replace("[]", "");
    }

    return s === "";
};

Approach 2 - Optimal Solution: LIFO Stack with Hash Map Lookup

🧭 Deep Intuition Breakdown (Single-Pass Stack Matching)

1. The Core Mechanical Discovery: As we iterate left-to-right through string s, every opening bracket '(', '{', or '[' represents an incomplete scope that MUST be closed later. We push all opening brackets onto a Stack.

2. Resolving Closing Brackets:
When we encounter a closing bracket ')', '}', or ']', it MUST match the most recent opening bracket (the top of our stack):

  • Rule A (Empty Stack Underflow): If the stack is empty when a closing bracket arrives, there is no corresponding open bracket! Return false.
  • Rule B (Type Mismatch): Pop the top element from the stack. If the popped open bracket does not match the current closing bracket type, return false.
  • Rule C (Valid Match): If the popped open bracket matches the closing bracket, pop it successfully and continue to the next character.

3. Clean Hash Map Design:
Map each closing bracket as a key to its corresponding opening bracket value: {')': '(', '}': '{', ']': '['}. This simplifies type-checking to an O(1) hash table lookup.

4. Final Boundary Check:
After processing the entire string, the stack MUST be completely empty. If opening brackets remain on the stack (e.g. s = "(("), return false.

Hinglish Explanation (Main Ideas)

Intuition behind LIFO Stack: Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) property ka use karke hum brackets match karte hain.

• Jab bhi **Opening Bracket** ('(', '{', '[') mile: Usse Stack me push kar do.
• Jab **Closing Bracket** (')', '}', ']') mile: 1. Agar Stack pehle se khali hai -> Extra closing bracket! Return False.
2. Stack ke top element ko pop() karo. Agar top element current closing bracket se match nahi karta -> Mismatch! Return False.
• Loop khatam hone ke baad agar Stack bilkul khali hai (isEmpty() == True), toh iska matlab saare brackets perfectly closed hain! Time O(N) aur Space O(N) hai.

📋 Full Line-by-Line Trace Dry Run 1: Nested Valid Parentheses

Input: s = "{[()]}" (N = 6)

Initialize: stack = [], matching_map = {')': '(', '}': '{', ']': '['} ================================================================================= ITERATION 1: char = '{' (index 0) ================================================================================= • Is '{' in matching_map keys? No (it is an opening bracket). • Stack Action: push('{') • Stack State: ['{'] ================================================================================= ITERATION 2: char = '[' (index 1) ================================================================================= • Is '[' in matching_map keys? No (opening bracket). • Stack Action: push('[') • Stack State: ['{', '['] ================================================================================= ITERATION 3: char = '(' (index 2) ================================================================================= • Is '(' in matching_map keys? No (opening bracket). • Stack Action: push('(') • Stack State: ['{', '[', '('] ================================================================================= ITERATION 4: char = ')' (index 3) ================================================================================= • Is ')' in matching_map keys? YES (closing bracket!). • Target required opening bracket = matching_map[')'] = '(' • Is stack empty? No. • Pop top of stack -> top_char = '(' • Check: Does top_char ('(') == expected ('(')? YES! Match confirmed! • Stack State: ['{', '['] ================================================================================= ITERATION 5: char = ']' (index 4) ================================================================================= • Is ']' in matching_map keys? YES (closing bracket!). • Target required opening bracket = matching_map[']'] = '[' • Pop top of stack -> top_char = '[' • Check: Does top_char ('[') == expected ('[')? YES! Match confirmed! • Stack State: ['{'] ================================================================================= ITERATION 6: char = '}' (index 5) ================================================================================= • Is '}' in matching_map keys? YES (closing bracket!). • Target required opening bracket = matching_map['}'] = '{' • Pop top of stack -> top_char = '{' • Check: Does top_char ('{') == expected ('{')? YES! Match confirmed! • Stack State: [] ================================================================================= TERMINATION ================================================================================= • String fully processed. • Check: Is stack empty? YES! • Return TRUE! Final Answer Returned: TRUE
📋 Full Line-by-Line Trace Dry Run 2: Interleaved Invalid Sequence

Input: s = "([)]" (N = 4)

Initialize: stack = [] • i = 0, char = '(': push('(') -> stack = ['('] • i = 1, char = '[': push('[') -> stack = ['(', '['] • i = 2, char = ')': - Closing bracket detected! Requires matching '('. - Pop stack top -> top_char = '[' - Compare top_char ('[') against required ('(') -> MISMATCH! - Return FALSE immediately! Final Answer Returned: FALSE

a) Source Code Implementation

class Solution:
    def isValid(self, s: str) -> bool:
        # Odd length strings can never be fully balanced
        if len(s) % 2 != 0:
            return False

        stack = []  # Stack buffer for opening brackets
        # Map closing brackets to corresponding required opening brackets
        bracket_map = {')': '(', '}': '{', ']': '['}

        for char in s:
            if char in bracket_map:  # If character is a closing bracket
                # HIGHLIGHT: Check stack underflow or mismatched top bracket
                if not stack or stack[-1] != bracket_map[char]:
                    return False
                stack.pop()  # Pop matched opening bracket
            else:
                stack.append(char)  # Push opening bracket onto stack

        return len(stack) == 0  # Return True if all brackets resolved
class Solution {
public:
    bool isValid(string s) {
        if (s.length() % 2 != 0) return false;

        stack<char> st;
        unordered_map<char, char> bracket_map = {
            {')', '('},
            {'}', '{'},
            {']', '['}
        };

        for (char c : s) {
            if (bracket_map.count(c)) {  // Closing bracket found
                // HIGHLIGHT: Validate stack non-empty and top match
                if (st.empty() || st.top() != bracket_map[c]) {
                    return false;
                }
                st.pop();  // Pop matched bracket
            } else {
                st.push(c);  // Push opening bracket
            }
        }

        return st.empty();  // Return true if stack is clear
    }
};
class Solution {
    public boolean isValid(String s) {
        if (s.length() % 2 != 0) return false;

        Stack<Character> st = new Stack<>();
        Map<Character, Character> map = Map.of(
            ')', '(',
            '}', '{',
            ']', '['
        );

        for (char c : s.toCharArray()) {
            if (map.containsKey(c)) {
                // HIGHLIGHT: Stack check and character mismatch
                if (st.isEmpty() || st.peek() != map.get(c)) {
                    return false;
                }
                st.pop();
            } else {
                st.push(c);
            }
        }

        return st.isEmpty();
    }
}
var isValid = function(s) {
    if (s.length % 2 !== 0) return false;

    const stack = [];
    const bracketMap = {
        ')': '(',
        '}': '{',
        ']': '['
    };

    for (let char of s) {
        if (char in bracketMap) {
            // HIGHLIGHT: Stack top validation
            if (stack.length === 0 || stack[stack.length - 1] !== bracketMap[char]) {
                return false;
            }
            stack.pop();
        } else {
            stack.push(char);
        }
    }

    return stack.length === 0;
};

Strategic Edge Cases Tracking Matrix

To ensure system robustness, solutions are validated against critical boundary edge cases:

Edge Case Profile Algorithmic Risk Factor Mitigation Resolution Logic
Odd Length String
e.g., s = "(((" or "()"{"		 Impossible to form complete pairs; wasting traversal iterations. Guarded at function start: if len(s) % 2 != 0: return False. Exits immediately in O(1) time.
Starts with Closing Bracket
e.g., s = ")]}"		 Stack underflow error when popping from an empty stack. Condition if not stack checked prior to stack.pop() returning false safely.
Unclosed Opening Brackets
e.g., s = "((" or "{[]}" with trailing "("		 Traversal finishes successfully, but opening brackets remain unmatched. Final check return len(stack) == 0 ensures remaining unclosed brackets evaluate to false.
Type Mismatch in Nested Bracket
e.g., s = "(]" or "{[()]}" with wrong closing bracket		 Mismatched pairs passing undetected. Hash map comparison stack[-1] != map[char] guarantees strict matching across all 3 bracket types.

Complexity Analysis Performance Metrics

Approach Category Time Complexity Space Complexity Performance Evaluation Rating
Approach 1: String Replacement Simulation O(N^2) O(N^2) / O(N) Space Sub-optimal / Slow. Creates new string copies on every replacement step. Fails efficiency benchmarks for large strings.
Approach 2: LIFO Stack with Hash Map O(N) O(N) Space Absolute Production Standard. Single pass traversal over N characters. Pushing and popping takes O(1) time per element. Stack stores up to N elements in worst case.
