Find K Closest Elements

Complete technical guide: From full sorting to Max-Heap priority filtering, two-pointer window shrinking, and O(log(N - K)) binary search for the left boundary.

1. Problem Statement & Core Concept

Given a sorted integer array arr, two integers k and x, return the k closest integers to x in the array. The result should also be sorted in ascending order.

An integer a is closer to x than an integer b if:

  • |a - x| < |b - x|, or
  • |a - x| == |b - x| and a < b (Tie-breaker rule: smaller value wins).
Distance & Tie-Breaker Mechanics: Example 1: arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], k = 4, x = 3 - Distances to x=3: 1: |1 - 3| = 2 2: |2 - 3| = 1 3: |3 - 3| = 0 4: |4 - 3| = 1 5: |5 - 3| = 2 - Sorted by closeness: 3 (dist 0), 2 (dist 1), 4 (dist 1), 1 (dist 2) - Top 4 closest: [1, 2, 3, 4] Output: [1, 2, 3, 4] Example 2: arr = [1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3], k = 3, x = -1 - x = -1 is smaller than all elements. - The 3 closest elements are the first 3 smallest numbers in arr. Output: [1, 1, 2]

Constraints

  • 1 <= k <= arr.length
  • 1 <= arr.length <= 10^4
  • arr is sorted in ascending order.
  • -10^4 <= arr[i], x <= 10^4

2. Brute Force Approach & Implementation

🧭 Concept: Custom Distance Sorting

The simplest approach ignores that the input array is already sorted and sorts a copy of arr using a custom comparator:

Algorithm steps:

  • Sort the elements based on distance |val - x|.
  • In case of a tie |val1 - x| == |val2 - x|, preserve ascending order by comparing val1 < val2.
  • Take the first k elements from the sorted list.
  • Sort those k elements in ascending order to return the final answer.
Hinglish Explanation

Brute force tarika yeh hai ki hum array ke saare elements ko |num - x| distance ke basis par sort kar dein. Agar distance same ho, toh chote element ko pehle rakhein. Top k elements nikal kar unhe firse ascending order me sort kar dein.

Brute Force Implementation

class BruteForceSolution:
    def findClosestElements(self, arr: list[int], k: int, x: int) -> list[int]:
        # Sort by absolute distance |val - x|
        sorted_arr = sorted(arr, key=lambda val: abs(val - x))
        
        # Slice first k elements and sort ascending for output requirement
        res = sorted_arr[:k]
        res.sort()
        return res
class BruteForceSolution {
public:
    vector<int> findClosestElements(vector<int>& arr, int k, int x) {
        vector<int> sortedArr = arr;
        // Sort using custom lambda comparator
        sort(sortedArr.begin(), sortedArr.end(), [x](int a, int b) {
            if (abs(a - x) == abs(b - x)) return a < b;
            return abs(a - x) < abs(b - x);
        });

        vector<int> res(sortedArr.begin(), sortedArr.begin() + k);
        sort(res.begin(), res.end());
        return res;
    }
};
class BruteForceSolution {
    public List<Integer> findClosestElements(int[] arr, int k, int x) {
        List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int num : arr) list.add(num);

        list.sort((a, b) -> {
            int distA = Math.abs(a - x);
            int distB = Math.abs(b - x);
            if (distA == distB) return Integer.compare(a, b);
            return Integer.compare(distA, distB);
        });

        List<Integer> res = list.subList(0, k);
        Collections.sort(res);
        return res;
    }
}
var findClosestElements = function(arr, k, x) {
    let sorted = [...arr].sort((a, b) => {
        let distA = Math.abs(a - x);
        let distB = Math.abs(b - x);
        if (distA === distB) return a - b;
        return distA - distB;
    });

    let res = sorted.slice(0, k);
    return res.sort((a, b) => a - b);
};

3. Max-Heap Bounded Priority Queue Approach (O(N log K) Time)

🧭 Concept: Bounded Size-K Max-Heap Filtering

Instead of sorting all N elements, we can maintain a Max-Heap bounded to size k. The heap stores elements ordered primarily by distance |num - x| (larger distance at the top to be evicted first), and secondarily by value num (larger value evicted first when distances tie).

Algorithm steps:

  • Iterate through arr. For each element num, calculate distance = |num - x|.
  • Push (-distance, -num) into Python's min-heap (simulating Max-Heap behavior).
  • If the heap size exceeds k, pop the heap's top element. This automatically evicts the element that is furthest from x!
  • After processing all elements, extract the remaining k numbers, restore their sign, and return them sorted in ascending order.
Hinglish Explanation

Max-Heap tarika yeh hai ki hum k size ka heap banayein. Jab bhi heap me k se zyada elements hone lagein, hum sabse door waale (worst distance) element ko pop kar dein. Python me Max-Heap dikhane ke liye negative distance aur negative number use hota hai. Baad me final k elements ko ascending order me return kar dein.

Max-Heap Implementation

import heapq

class Solution:
    def findClosestElements(self, arr: list[int], k: int, x: int) -> list[int]:
        max_heap = []
        result = []

        for num in arr:
            distance = abs(num - x)
            # Store (-distance, -num) to maintain a Max-Heap in Python
            heapq.heappush(max_heap, (-distance, -num))

            # Keep heap bounded to size k
            while len(max_heap) > k:
                heapq.heappop(max_heap)
        
        # Extract numbers from heap
        for _, num in max_heap:
            result.append(-num)

        # Return sorted in ascending order
        return sorted(result)
class Solution {
public:
    vector<int> findClosestElements(vector<int>& arr, int k, int x) {
        // Max-Heap storing pair<distance, value>
        priority_queue<pair<int, int>> maxHeap;

        for (int num : arr) {
            int distance = abs(num - x);
            maxHeap.push({distance, num});

            if (maxHeap.size() > k) {
                maxHeap.pop();
            }
        }

        vector<int> result;
        while (!maxHeap.empty()) {
            result.push_back(maxHeap.top().second);
            maxHeap.pop();
        }

        sort(result.begin(), result.end());
        return result;
    }
};
class Solution {
    public List<Integer> findClosestElements(int[] arr, int k, int x) {
        // Max-Heap comparator: larger distance first, then larger value first
        PriorityQueue<int[]> maxHeap = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> {
            if (b[0] != a[0]) return Integer.compare(b[0], a[0]);
            return Integer.compare(b[1], a[1]);
        });

        for (int num : arr) {
            int distance = Math.abs(num - x);
            maxHeap.offer(new int[]{distance, num});

            if (maxHeap.size() > k) {
                maxHeap.poll();
            }
        }

        List<Integer> result = new ArrayList<>();
        while (!maxHeap.isEmpty()) {
            result.add(maxHeap.poll()[1]);
        }

        Collections.sort(result);
        return result;
    }
}
var findClosestElements = function(arr, k, x) {
    // Max-Heap implemented with array operations
    let maxHeap = [];

    for (let num of arr) {
        let distance = Math.abs(num - x);
        maxHeap.push([distance, num]);
        
        // Keep sorted by distance desc, value desc
        maxHeap.sort((a, b) => {
            if (b[0] !== a[0]) return b[0] - a[0];
            return b[1] - a[1];
        });

        if (maxHeap.length > k) {
            maxHeap.shift(); // Remove element with largest distance
        }
    }

    let result = maxHeap.map(item => item[1]);
    return result.sort((a, b) => a - b);
};

4. Two-Pointer Window Shrinking Approach (O(N) Time, O(1) Space)

🧭 Concept: Shrinking from Opposite Ends

Since the array is already sorted, the k closest elements must form a contiguous subarray of size k!

  • Place left = 0 and right = N - 1.
  • While the window size (right - left + 1) > k:
    • Compare distances of boundary elements: |arr[left] - x| vs |arr[right] - x|.
    • If |arr[left] - x| > |arr[right] - x|, arr[left] is further away -> Increment left++.
    • Else (if arr[left] is closer or equal in distance due to tie-breaker rule), arr[right] is further away -> Decrement right--.
  • Return arr[left..right].
Hinglish Explanation

Kyonki array pehle se sorted hai, k closest elements humesha ek contiguous sub-window banayenge. Pura array cover karke left=0 aur right=N-1 rakhein. Dono end ke elements ki distance x se check karke jo door hai us pointer ko hataate jayein jab tak window size k na ho jaye.

class TwoPointerSolution:
    def findClosestElements(self, arr: list[int], k: int, x: int) -> list[int]:
        left = 0
        right = len(arr) - 1

        while right - left + 1 > k:
            if abs(arr[left] - x) > abs(arr[right] - x):
                left += 1
            else:
                right -= 1

        return arr[left:right + 1]
class TwoPointerSolution {
public:
    vector<int> findClosestElements(vector<int>& arr, int k, int x) {
        int left = 0;
        int right = arr.size() - 1;

        while (right - left + 1 > k) {
            if (abs(arr[left] - x) > abs(arr[right] - x)) {
                left++;
            } else {
                right--;
            }
        }

        return vector<int>(arr.begin() + left, arr.begin() + right + 1);
    }
};
class TwoPointerSolution {
    public List<Integer> findClosestElements(int[] arr, int k, int x) {
        int left = 0;
        int right = arr.length - 1;

        while (right - left + 1 > k) {
            if (Math.abs(arr[left] - x) > Math.abs(arr[right] - x)) {
                left++;
            } else {
                right--;
            }
        }

        List<Integer> res = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = left; i <= right; i++) {
            res.add(arr[i]);
        }
        return res;
    }
}
var findClosestElements = function(arr, k, x) {
    let left = 0;
    let right = arr.length - 1;

    while (right - left + 1 > k) {
        if (Math.abs(arr[left] - x) > Math.abs(arr[right] - x)) {
            left++;
        } else {
            right--;
        }
    }

    return arr.slice(left, right + 1);
};

5. Optimal Binary Search for Left Boundary (O(log(N - K) + K))

💡 The Optimal Insight

Since the result is a contiguous subarray of size k, the problem reduces to: Where does the window of size k start?

The starting index left can range from index 0 to N - k.

For any candidate starting index mid, we compare two potential windows:

  • Window starting at mid (includes arr[mid]).
  • Window starting at mid + 1 (includes arr[mid + k]).

Comparison Rule:

If (x - arr[mid]) > (arr[mid + k] - x): The element arr[mid + k] is closer to x than arr[mid]. Therefore, the optimal left boundary MUST be to the right of mid! Set: left = mid + 1 Else: arr[mid] is closer to (or equidistant with tie-breaker advantage) x than arr[mid + k]. The optimal left boundary lies at mid or to its left! Set: right = mid
Binary Search State Trace: Array: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], k = 4, x = 3 Candidate Left range: [0, N - k] = [0, 5 - 4] = [0, 1] 1. mid = 0: - Compare arr[mid] (1) vs arr[mid + k] (5) - Distance check: (x - arr[0]) vs (arr[4] - x) => (3 - 1 = 2) vs (5 - 3 = 2) - Is (x - arr[mid]) > (arr[mid + k] - x)? Is 2 > 2? FALSE! - Condition False -> right = mid = 0. Binary Search Ends with left = 0! Result = arr[0 .. 0+4-1] = arr[0 .. 3] = [1, 2, 3, 4]

6. Boundary Traps & Edge Case Resolution

⚠️ Common Traps & Edge Cases

1. x is Out-of-Bounds (x < arr[0] or x > arr[N - 1]):
If x is smaller than all elements, the k closest elements are the first k elements. If x is larger, the k closest are the last k elements. Binary search handles both extreme bounds naturally without separate conditional checks.

2. Tie-Breakers (Equidistant Elements):
When x - arr[mid] == arr[mid + k] - x, using strictly > ensures that right = mid is chosen, preferring the smaller left element as required by the tie-breaker rule.

3. k == N:
The search space for left is [0, N - N] = [0, 0]. The binary search loop terminates immediately and returns the full array.

7. Optimal Source Code (O(log(N - K) + K))

class Solution:
    def findClosestElements(self, arr: list[int], k: int, x: int) -> list[int]:
        # Binary search range for the starting index 'left'
        left = 0
        right = len(arr) - k

        while left < right:
            mid = (left + right) // 2
            
            # HIGHLIGHT: Compare distance between arr[mid] and arr[mid + k] relative to x
            if x - arr[mid] > arr[mid + k] - x:
                left = mid + 1
            else:
                right = mid

        # Return subarray of length k starting at 'left'
        return arr[left:left + k]
class Solution {
public:
    vector<int> findClosestElements(vector<int>& arr, int k, int x) {
        int left = 0;
        int right = arr.size() - k;

        while (left < right) {
            int mid = left + (right - left) / 2;

            // HIGHLIGHT: Distance comparison between boundary elements
            if (x - arr[mid] > arr[mid + k] - x) {
                left = mid + 1;
            } else {
                right = mid;
            }
        }

        return vector<int>(arr.begin() + left, arr.begin() + left + k);
    }
};
class Solution {
    public List<Integer> findClosestElements(int[] arr, int k, int x) {
        int left = 0;
        int right = arr.length - k;

        while (left < right) {
            int mid = left + (right - left) / 2;

            // HIGHLIGHT: Compare distance to x
            if (x - arr[mid] > arr[mid + k] - x) {
                left = mid + 1;
            } else {
                right = mid;
            }
        }

        List<Integer> res = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = left; i < left + k; i++) {
            res.add(arr[i]);
        }
        return res;
    }
}
var findClosestElements = function(arr, k, x) {
    let left = 0;
    let right = arr.length - k;

    while (left < right) {
        let mid = Math.floor((left + right) / 2);

        // HIGHLIGHT: Distance check
        if (x - arr[mid] > arr[mid + k] - x) {
            left = mid + 1;
        } else {
            right = mid;
        }
    }

    return arr.slice(left, left + k);
};

8. Detailed Test Cases & Walkthroughs (N ≥ 10)

📋 1. Normal Test Case: arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], k = 4, x = 3
Binary Search for Left Boundary: Range: left = 0, right = 5 - 4 = 1 • Pass 1: mid = 0 - Compare x - arr[0] (3 - 1 = 2) vs arr[0 + 4] - x (5 - 3 = 2) - Is 2 > 2? False. - right = mid = 0 Loop ends! left = 0. Slice arr[0..3] -> [1, 2, 3, 4]
📋 2. Max-Heap Execution Walkthrough: arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], k = 4, x = 3
Processing with Size-4 Max-Heap (Heap stores (-distance, -num)): 1. num = 1 -> dist = |1 - 3| = 2 -> Push (-2, -1) -> Heap: [(-2, -1)] 2. num = 2 -> dist = |2 - 3| = 1 -> Push (-1, -2) -> Heap: [(-2, -1), (-1, -2)] 3. num = 3 -> dist = |3 - 3| = 0 -> Push (0, -3) -> Heap: [(-2, -1), (-1, -2), (0, -3)] 4. num = 4 -> dist = |4 - 3| = 1 -> Push (-1, -4) -> Heap: [(-2, -1), (-1, -2), (0, -3), (-1, -4)] (size = 4) 5. num = 5 -> dist = |5 - 3| = 2 -> Push (-2, -5) -> Heap size = 5 > 4! - Heap top is (-2, -1) [element 1 has distance 2]. - Pop top (-2, -1) or (-2, -5) based on priority -> Worst distance element 5 is evicted! - Heap maintains best 4 elements: {1, 2, 3, 4} Extract & Sort -> [1, 2, 3, 4]
📋 3. Large Execution Case (N = 10): arr = [1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11], k = 3, x = 6
Search Range for Left Boundary: left = 0, right = 10 - 3 = 7 • Step 1: mid = 3 (arr[3] = 5) - Compare x - arr[3] (6 - 5 = 1) vs arr[3 + 3] - x (arr[6] - 6 = 8 - 6 = 2) - Is 1 > 2? False. - right = 3 • Step 2: mid = 1 (arr[1] = 2) - Compare x - arr[1] (6 - 2 = 4) vs arr[1 + 3] - x (arr[4] - 6 = 6 - 6 = 0) - Is 4 > 0? True. - left = mid + 1 = 2 • Step 3: mid = 2 (arr[2] = 4) - Compare x - arr[2] (6 - 4 = 2) vs arr[2 + 3] - x (arr[5] - 6 = 7 - 6 = 1) - Is 2 > 1? True. - left = mid + 1 = 3 Loop ends! left = 3. Slice arr[3 .. 3+3-1] = arr[3 .. 5] -> [5, 6, 7]
📋 4. Edge Case: x Smaller than All Elements (arr = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50], k = 2, x = 1)
Search Range: left = 0, right = 3 • Step 1: mid = 1 (arr[1] = 20) - Compare 1 - 20 (-19) vs arr[3] - 1 (40 - 1 = 39) - Is -19 > 39? False. - right = 1 • Step 2: mid = 0 (arr[0] = 10) - Compare 1 - 10 (-9) vs arr[2] - 1 (30 - 1 = 29) - Is -9 > 29? False. - right = 0 Loop ends! left = 0. Slice arr[0..1] -> [10, 20]

9. Complexity Analysis Performance Metrics

Approach Category Time Complexity Space Complexity Performance Evaluation Rating
Approach 1: Custom Distance Sorting O(N log N) O(N) Auxiliary Sub-optimal. Fails to exploit that input array is already sorted.
Approach 2: Bounded Max-Heap O(N log K + K log K) O(K) Auxiliary Good. Uses a Max-Heap of size K to continuously filter worst-distance candidates.
Approach 3: Two-Pointer Window Shrinking O(N) O(1) Auxiliary Better. Linear time traversal shrinking window from N to K elements.
Approach 4: Binary Search Left Boundary O(log(N - K) + K) O(1) Auxiliary Absolute Production Standard. Finds starting index in O(log(N - K)) time and extracts K elements. Optimal execution.

Contains Duplicate II

Deep Engineering Guide: Deconstructing sliding window constraints, hash map index tracking, fixed-size hash sets, and O(N) linear time optimizations.

1. Problem Statement & Core Concept

Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return true if there are two distinct indices i and j in the array such that nums[i] == nums[j] and abs(i - j) <= k. Otherwise, return false.

Deconstructing the Math Behind the Problem

  • Equal Values Constraint: nums[i] == nums[j] (We need a duplicate value).
  • Index Distance Constraint: abs(i - j) <= k (The duplicate occurrences must be within k steps of each other).
  • Sliding Window Equivalence: Asking if two identical elements are within k distance is equivalent to asking: "Is there any duplicate value inside a sliding window of size at most k + 1?"
Problem Examples: Example 1: nums = [1, 2, 3, 1], k = 3 - Value '1' appears at index 0 and index 3. - Distance = |0 - 3| = 3. - Is 3 <= k (3)? TRUE! Output: true --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Example 2: nums = [1, 0, 1, 1], k = 1 - Value '1' appears at index 2 and index 3. - Distance = |2 - 3| = 1. - Is 1 <= k (1)? TRUE! Output: true --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Example 3: nums = [1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3], k = 2 - '1' at index 0 and 3 -> distance = 3 > 2 (Invalid) - '2' at index 1 and 4 -> distance = 3 > 2 (Invalid) - '3' at index 2 and 5 -> distance = 3 > 2 (Invalid) Output: false

Constraints

  • 1 <= nums.length <= 10^5
  • -10^9 <= nums[i] <= 10^9
  • 0 <= k <= 10^5

2. Brute Force Approach & Implementation

🧭 Concept: Double Loop Nested Subarray Scan

The naive approach tests all pairs of indices (i, j) directly:

Algorithm steps:

  • Outer loop selects index i from 0 to N - 1.
  • Inner loop selects index j from i + 1 up to min(i + k, N - 1).
  • If nums[i] == nums[j], return true immediately.
  • If no such pair is found after scanning all valid windows, return false.
Hinglish Explanation

Brute force tarika yeh hai ki hum har index i ke liye uske aage ke k elements ko inner loop se check karein. Agar koi duplicate mil jaye, toh turant true return kar dein.

Brute Force Implementation

class BruteForceSolution:
    def containsNearbyDuplicate(self, nums: list[int], k: int) -> bool:
        n = len(nums)
        # Check every element against next k elements
        for i in range(n):
            for j in range(i + 1, min(i + k + 1, n)):
                if nums[i] == nums[j]:
                    return True
        return False
class BruteForceSolution {
public:
    bool containsNearbyDuplicate(vector<int>& nums, int k) {
        int n = nums.size();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
            for (int j = i + 1; j <= i + k && j < n; ++j) {
                if (nums[i] == nums[j]) {
                    return true;
                }
            }
        }
        return false;
    }
};
class BruteForceSolution {
    public boolean containsNearbyDuplicate(int[] nums, int k) {
        int n = nums.length;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            for (int j = i + 1; j <= i + k && j < n; j++) {
                if (nums[i] == nums[j]) {
                    return true;
                }
            }
        }
        return false;
    }
}
var containsNearbyDuplicate = function(nums, k) {
    const n = nums.length;
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        for (let j = i + 1; j <= i + k && j < n; j++) {
            if (nums[i] === nums[j]) {
                return true;
            }
        }
    }
    return false;
};

3. Deep Intuition: Transitioning to Optimal Solutions

⚠️ Why Brute Force Fails

Time Complexity Failure: For each element, scanning up to k neighbors takes O(N * min(N, k)) Time Complexity. When k ≈ N and N = 100,000, operations scale to 10^10 steps, causing a severe Time Limit Exceeded (TLE) error.

We need an algorithm that inspects each element in O(1) time.

Optimal Strategy 1: Hash Map (Last Seen Index Tracking)

Instead of looking forward into future indices, we look backward in time! As we scan the array left-to-right, we maintain a Hash Map storing { number : last_seen_index }.

Hash Map Intuition Step-by-Step: 1. As we arrive at index `i` with value `num = nums[i]`: - Ask the Hash Map: "Have I seen `num` before?" - If YES, fetch its previous index `prev_index`. - Calculate distance: `i - prev_index`. - Is `i - prev_index <= k`? * If TRUE -> We found a valid nearby duplicate! Return true immediately! * If FALSE -> The previous occurrence is too far away. But this current index `i` is CLOSER to any potential future duplicate of `num`! - Update Hash Map: `seen[num] = i` (Store the latest index!). Why updating `seen[num] = i` is crucial: If we see the number again later, the distance to the LATEST occurrence will be SMALLER than the distance to older occurrences. Thus, always keeping the most recent index maximizes our chance of satisfying `abs(i - j) <= k`.

Optimal Strategy 2: Sliding Window Hash Set (Fixed Size k)

Instead of storing all indices in a Hash Map, maintain a Hash Set representing a sliding window of size at most k.

Sliding Window Hash Set Intuition Step-by-Step: Window Invariant: The Hash Set contains ONLY the elements present in the range `nums[i - k ... i - 1]`. Algorithm Flow: 1. For each index `i` and element `num = nums[i]`: - If `num` is already in Hash Set -> Duplicate exists within k distance! Return true! - Add `num` to Hash Set. - If `HashSet.size() > k` -> The window grew too large! Remove the oldest element `nums[i - k]` from Hash Set. Memory Advantage: The Hash Set NEVER holds more than `k` elements at any point! Space Complexity: O(min(N, k))!

4. Line-by-Line Technical Breakdown

🧭 Line-by-Line Logic: Approach A (Hash Map Index Tracking)
  1. seen = {}: Initialize an empty Hash Map to record the most recent index of each value.
  2. for i, num in enumerate(nums):: Loop through every element along with its current index i.
  3. if num in seen and i - seen[num] <= k:: Check if the number was previously encountered AND if the gap between current index i and seen[num] is less than or equal to k.
  4. return True: If both conditions hold, a valid pair exists. Return True immediately.
  5. seen[num] = i: Overwrite or set the latest index for num to i.
  6. return False: If the loop finishes without returning True, no valid duplicate pair exists in the entire array.
🧭 Line-by-Line Logic: Approach B (Sliding Window Hash Set)
  1. window = set(): Initialize an empty Hash Set that will hold at most k elements.
  2. for i, num in enumerate(nums):: Iterate through array index i and value num.
  3. if num in window: return True: If num is already in our size-k window, we found a duplicate within distance k!
  4. window.add(num): Insert num into the active window set.
  5. if len(window) > k: window.remove(nums[i - k]): Maintain the fixed window size constraint. If size exceeds k, drop the element that fell out of range on the left (i.e. nums[i - k]).

5. Boundary Traps & Edge Case Analysis

⚠️ Critical Edge Cases

1. k = 0:
Distinct indices require i != j. If k = 0, abs(i - j) <= 0 implies i == j, which violates distinct indices. The algorithm must return false. In Hash Set approach, window size k = 0 immediately evicts elements before matching, correctly returning false.

2. Multiple Duplicate Occurrences (e.g. nums = [1, 1, 1, 1], k = 2):
Updating seen[num] = i ensures that distance is always measured against the MOST RECENT instance, preventing false negatives from older out-of-range indices.

3. k Greater Than Array Length (k >= N):
The condition simply relaxes to checking if ANY duplicate exists anywhere in the array.

Edge Case Scenario Potential System Failure Resolution Logic
k = 0 False positives by comparing element with itself. i - seen[num] <= 0 is impossible for distinct indices. Automatically returns false.
k >= N Index out of bounds when accessing nums[i - k] in sliding window. Window size check len(window) > k never triggers if k >= N, safely retaining all elements.
Negative Values in Array Hash Map key indexing errors. Hash Maps / Hash Sets support negative integer keys naturally.

6. Optimal Source Code (Hash Map & Sliding Window Set)

Approach A: Hash Map (Last Seen Index Tracking) — Production Standard

class Solution:
    def containsNearbyDuplicate(self, nums: list[int], k: int) -> bool:
        seen = {}  # Map: value -> last seen index

        for i, num in enumerate(nums):
            # HIGHLIGHT: Check if number exists and is within distance k
            if num in seen and i - seen[num] <= k:
                return True
            
            # Update last seen index to current position
            seen[num] = i

        return False
class Solution {
public:
    bool containsNearbyDuplicate(vector<int>& nums, int k) {
        unordered_map<int, int> seen; // Map: value -> last seen index

        for (int i = 0; i < nums.size(); ++i) {
            int num = nums[i];
            
            // HIGHLIGHT: Distance check against last seen index
            if (seen.count(num) && i - seen[num] <= k) {
                return true;
            }
            seen[num] = i;
        }

        return false;
    }
};
class Solution {
    public boolean containsNearbyDuplicate(int[] nums, int k) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();

        for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
            int num = nums[i];

            // HIGHLIGHT: Index gap evaluation
            if (seen.containsKey(num) && i - seen.get(num) <= k) {
                return true;
            }
            seen.put(num, i);
        }

        return false;
    }
}
var containsNearbyDuplicate = function(nums, k) {
    const seen = new Map();

    for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        let num = nums[i];

        // HIGHLIGHT: Check gap
        if (seen.has(num) && i - seen.get(num) <= k) {
            return true;
        }
        seen.set(num, i);
    }

    return false;
};

Approach B: Fixed-Size Hash Set (Sliding Window O(min(N, k)) Memory)

class SolutionSet:
    def containsNearbyDuplicate(self, nums: list[int], k: int) -> bool:
        window = set()

        for i, num in enumerate(nums):
            # Duplicate found in active window of size k
            if num in window:
                return True
            
            window.add(num)

            # Maintain window size at most k
            if len(window) > k:
                window.remove(nums[i - k])

        return False
class SolutionSet {
public:
    bool containsNearbyDuplicate(vector<int>& nums, int k) {
        unordered_set<int> window;

        for (int i = 0; i < nums.size(); ++i) {
            if (window.count(nums[i])) {
                return true;
            }
            window.insert(nums[i]);

            if (window.size() > k) {
                window.erase(nums[i - k]);
            }
        }

        return false;
    }
};
class SolutionSet {
    public boolean containsNearbyDuplicate(int[] nums, int k) {
        Set<Integer> window = new HashSet<>();

        for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
            if (window.contains(nums[i])) {
                return true;
            }
            window.add(nums[i]);

            if (window.size() > k) {
                window.remove(nums[i - k]);
            }
        }

        return false;
    }
}
var containsNearbyDuplicateSet = function(nums, k) {
    const window = new Set();

    for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        if (window.has(nums[i])) {
            return true;
        }
        window.add(nums[i]);

        if (window.size > k) {
            window.delete(nums[i - k]);
        }
    }

    return false;
};

7. Detailed Dry Run Walkthroughs

📋 1. Detailed Walkthrough (Sliding Window Set): nums = [1, 2, 3, 0, 2, 2], k = 2

Goal: Find if there are two duplicate elements whose indices differ by at most k = 2.

Processing nums = [1, 2, 3, 0, 2, 2], k = 2 (Window Hash Set Approach): Initial State: window = Set() --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Step 1: i = 0, num = 1 - Is 1 in window? -> False. - Add 1 to window -> window = {1} - Check size: len(window) = 1 <= k (2) -> No removal needed. - Window State: {1} --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Step 2: i = 1, num = 2 - Is 2 in window? -> False. - Add 2 to window -> window = {1, 2} - Check size: len(window) = 2 <= k (2) -> No removal needed. - Window State: {1, 2} --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Step 3: i = 2, num = 3 - Is 3 in window? -> False. - Add 3 to window -> window = {1, 2, 3} - Check size: len(window) = 3 > k (2)! -> Evict oldest element falling out of range: nums[i - k] = nums[2 - 2] = nums[0] = 1! -> Remove 1 from window -> window = {2, 3} - Window State: {2, 3} --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Step 4: i = 3, num = 0 - Is 0 in window? -> False. - Add 0 to window -> window = {2, 3, 0} - Check size: len(window) = 3 > k (2)! -> Evict oldest element: nums[i - k] = nums[3 - 2] = nums[1] = 2! -> Remove 2 from window -> window = {3, 0} - Window State: {3, 0} *IMPORTANT NOTE HERE*: Notice that '2' was just removed! The earlier '2' at index 1 is now at distance |3 - 1| = 2, but moving to index 4 makes the distance |4 - 1| = 3 > 2 (Too far!). Evicting '2' at step 4 was CORRECT because index 1 is too far from any future index >= 4! --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Step 5: i = 4, num = 2 - Is 2 in window {3, 0}? -> False! - Add 2 to window -> window = {3, 0, 2} - Check size: len(window) = 3 > k (2)! -> Evict oldest element: nums[i - k] = nums[4 - 2] = nums[2] = 3! -> Remove 3 from window -> window = {0, 2} - Window State: {0, 2} --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Step 6: i = 5, num = 2 - Is 2 in window {0, 2}? -> TRUE! -> Value '2' is found in our active sliding window of size k = 2! -> Index 5 and Index 4 both have value 2. -> Distance = |5 - 4| = 1 <= k (2). Valid nearby duplicate found! --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- RESULT: Returns TRUE immediately at i = 5!
📋 2. Dry Run (Hash Map Approach): nums = [1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3], k = 2
Processing nums = [1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3], k = 2: • i = 0 (num = 1): - '1' not in seen. - Update seen = { 1: 0 } • i = 1 (num = 2): - '2' not in seen. - Update seen = { 1: 0, 2: 1 } • i = 2 (num = 3): - '3' not in seen. - Update seen = { 1: 0, 2: 1, 3: 2 } • i = 3 (num = 1): - '1' is in seen! Previous index = 0. - Calculate gap: i - seen[1] = 3 - 0 = 3. - Is 3 <= k (2)? FALSE! (Gap too large). - Update seen[1] = 3 -> seen = { 1: 3, 2: 1, 3: 2 } • i = 4 (num = 2): - '2' is in seen! Previous index = 1. - Calculate gap: i - seen[2] = 4 - 1 = 3. - Is 3 <= k (2)? FALSE! - Update seen[2] = 4 -> seen = { 1: 3, 2: 4, 3: 2 } • i = 5 (num = 3): - '3' is in seen! Previous index = 2. - Calculate gap: i - seen[3] = 5 - 2 = 3. - Is 3 <= k (2)? FALSE! - Update seen[3] = 5 Loop finishes -> Returns false.
📋 3. Dry Run (Sliding Window Set Approach): nums = [1, 2, 3, 1], k = 3
Processing nums = [1, 2, 3, 1], k = 3: • i = 0 (num = 1): - 1 in window? False. - window.add(1) -> window = {1} - len(window) (1) <= k (3) -> Keep window. • i = 1 (num = 2): - 2 in window? False. - window.add(2) -> window = {1, 2} - len(window) (2) <= k (3) -> Keep window. • i = 2 (num = 3): - 3 in window? False. - window.add(3) -> window = {1, 2, 3} - len(window) (3) <= k (3) -> Keep window. • i = 3 (num = 1): - 1 in window? TRUE! (Found duplicate within window size 3!) - Returns true immediately! Final Output = true

8. Complexity Analysis Performance Metrics

Approach Category Time Complexity Space Complexity Performance Evaluation Rating
Approach 1: Brute Force Nested Scan O(N * min(N, k)) O(1) Sub-optimal / TLE. Scans up to k elements for each position. Exceeds limits for large N and k.
Approach 2: Hash Map Index Tracking O(N) O(N) Auxiliary Absolute Production Standard. Single pass over N elements with O(1) average hash map lookup and insertion.
Approach 3: Sliding Window Hash Set O(N) O(min(N, k)) Auxiliary Absolute Production Standard (Memory Optimal). Maintains at most k elements in Hash Set. Optimal memory footprint when k << N.

Move Zeroes

Complete technical guide: From auxiliary array allocation to two-pointer overwriting, optimal in-place swapping, and handling sparse vs dense zero distributions.

1. Problem Statement & Core Concept

Given an integer array nums, move all 0's to the end of it while maintaining the relative order of the non-zero elements.

Strict Constraint: You must do this in-place without making a copy of the array.

Core Technical Requirements

  • In-Place Space Complexity: Space complexity must be O(1) auxiliary memory.
  • Order Preservation: Relative order of non-zero elements must remain intact (e.g. [0, 1, 0, 3, 12] -> [1, 3, 12, 0, 0]).
  • Operation Minimization: Minimize total array write operations (crucial when zero density is very high or very low).
Move Zeroes Operations Mechanics: Example 1: nums = [0, 1, 0, 3, 12] - Non-zero values in relative order: 1, 3, 12 - Shift all 0s to the right: [1, 3, 12, 0, 0] Output: [1, 3, 12, 0, 0] --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Example 2: nums = [0] - Single element 0, no shift needed. Output: [0] --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Example 3: nums = [1, 2, 3, 4] - No zeroes present, array remains unchanged. Output: [1, 2, 3, 4]

Constraints

  • 1 <= nums.length <= 10^4
  • -2^31 <= nums[i] <= 2^31 - 1

2. Naive / Auxiliary Array Approach & Implementation

🧭 Concept: Extra Array Memory Copy (Violates In-Place Requirement)

The naive approach allocates an extra array of the same size N:

Algorithm steps:

  • Create a temporary array temp of size N initialized with 0s.
  • Iterate through nums. Copy every non-zero element into temp sequentially.
  • Copy all elements from temp back into nums.
Hinglish Explanation

Naive tarika yeh hai ki hum ek N size ka naya temp array banayein. Pehle original array ke saare non-zero elements ko sequence me temp me daalein, aur baaki spaces ko 0 rehne dein. Phir us temp array ko wapas original nums me copy kar dein. Yeh O(N) Space leta hai jo constraint ko violate karta hai.

Naive Implementation

class NaiveSolution:
    def moveZeroes(self, nums: list[int]) -> None:
        n = len(nums)
        temp = [0] * n
        insert_idx = 0

        # Copy non-zero elements to temp array
        for num in nums:
            if num != 0:
                temp[insert_idx] = num
                insert_idx += 1

        # Copy temp array back into original array
        for i in range(n):
            nums[i] = temp[i]
class NaiveSolution {
public:
    void moveZeroes(vector<int>& nums) {
        int n = nums.size();
        vector<int> temp(n, 0);
        int insertIdx = 0;

        for (int num : nums) {
            if (num != 0) {
                temp[insertIdx++] = num;
            }
        }

        for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
            nums[i] = temp[i];
        }
    }
};
class NaiveSolution {
    public void moveZeroes(int[] nums) {
        int n = nums.length;
        int[] temp = new int[n];
        int insertIdx = 0;

        for (int num : nums) {
            if (num != 0) {
                temp[insertIdx++] = num;
            }
        }

        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            nums[i] = temp[i];
        }
    }
}
var moveZeroesNaive = function(nums) {
    const n = nums.length;
    const temp = new Array(n).fill(0);
    let insertIdx = 0;

    for (let num of nums) {
        if (num !== 0) {
            temp[insertIdx++] = num;
        }
    }

    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        nums[i] = temp[i];
    }
};

3. Intermediate Approach: Two-Pass Overwrite (O(N) Time, O(1) Space)

🧭 Concept: Compress Non-Zeroes then Zero-Fill Trailing Elements

To eliminate extra space, we can transform the operation into two linear passes over the same array:

  • Pass 1: Maintain a write pointer insert_idx. Iterate through nums with pointer i. Whenever nums[i] != 0, overwrite nums[insert_idx] = nums[i] and increment insert_idx++.
  • Pass 2: Fill all remaining indices from insert_idx to N - 1 with 0.
Hinglish Explanation

Intermediate tarika yeh hai ki hum 2-pass me kaam karein. Pehle pass me saare non-zero elements ko aage Shift/Overwrite kar dein index insert_idx par. Doosre pass me insert_idx se lekar array ke end tak ke bache hue positions ko 0 se bhar dein.

class TwoPassSolution:
    def moveZeroes(self, nums: list[int]) -> None:
        insert_idx = 0

        # Pass 1: Shift non-zero elements forward
        for i in range(len(nums)):
            if nums[i] != 0:
                nums[insert_idx] = nums[i]
                insert_idx += 1

        # Pass 2: Fill remaining indices with 0
        while insert_idx < len(nums):
            nums[insert_idx] = 0
            insert_idx += 1
class TwoPassSolution {
public:
    void moveZeroes(vector<int>& nums) {
        int insertIdx = 0;

        // Pass 1
        for (int i = 0; i < nums.size(); ++i) {
            if (nums[i] != 0) {
                nums[insertIdx++] = nums[i];
            }
        }

        // Pass 2
        while (insertIdx < nums.size()) {
            nums[insertIdx++] = 0;
        }
    }
};
class TwoPassSolution {
    public void moveZeroes(int[] nums) {
        int insertIdx = 0;

        // Pass 1
        for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
            if (nums[i] != 0) {
                nums[insertIdx++] = nums[i];
            }
        }

        // Pass 2
        while (insertIdx < nums.length) {
            nums[insertIdx++] = 0;
        }
    }
}
var moveZeroesTwoPass = function(nums) {
    let insertIdx = 0;

    // Pass 1
    for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        if (nums[i] !== 0) {
            nums[insertIdx++] = nums[i];
        }
    }

    // Pass 2
    while (insertIdx < nums.length) {
        nums[insertIdx++] = 0;
    }
};

4. Optimal Approach: One-Pass Two-Pointer Partitioning (O(N) Time, O(1) Space, Minimal Writes)

💡 The Optimal Insight

Can we accomplish everything in a single pass while minimizing array write operations?

Maintain a write pointer slow that tracks the boundary where the next non-zero element should go.

Iterate through the array with pointer fast:

  • When nums[fast] != 0: Swap nums[slow] and nums[fast], then increment slow++.

Invariant Maintained by Pointers:

1. All elements strictly before index `slow` are non-zeroes in their original relative order. 2. All elements between `slow` and `fast - 1` are zeroes. 3. All elements from `fast` to `N - 1` are unexamined elements.
One-Pass Swap Trace: Array: [0, 1, 0, 3, 12] slow = 0, fast = 0 • fast = 0 (val 0): Nothing done. • fast = 1 (val 1): Non-zero! Swap nums[0] (0) & nums[1] (1) -> [1, 0, 0, 3, 12]. slow = 1. • fast = 2 (val 0): Nothing done. • fast = 3 (val 3): Non-zero! Swap nums[1] (0) & nums[3] (3) -> [1, 3, 0, 0, 12]. slow = 2. • fast = 4 (val 12): Non-zero! Swap nums[2] (0) & nums[4] (12) -> [1, 3, 12, 0, 0]. slow = 3. Result = [1, 3, 12, 0, 0] in a single pass!

5. Boundary Traps & Performance Optimizations

⚠️ Common Traps & Edge Case Scenarios

1. Array with No Zeroes (e.g. [1, 2, 3]):
When no zeroes exist, slow and fast move together in lockstep (slow == fast). Self-swapping (swap(nums[i], nums[i])) is a safe no-op.

2. Array with All Zeroes (e.g. [0, 0, 0]):
slow remains at index 0 throughout the entire pass while fast iterates to the end. No swaps occur, preserving the array in O(N) time.

3. Minimizing Unnecessary Self-Swaps:
To avoid redundant self-swaps when slow == fast, add an optional check: if (slow != fast) swap(...).

6. Optimal Source Code (One-Pass Two-Pointer Partitioning)

class Solution:
    def moveZeroes(self, nums: list[int]) -> None:
        slow = 0  # Points to the boundary for next non-zero placement

        for fast in range(len(nums)):
            # HIGHLIGHT: Swap non-zero element to the slow boundary
            if nums[fast] != 0:
                if slow != fast:
                    nums[slow], nums[fast] = nums[fast], nums[slow]
                slow += 1
class Solution {
public:
    void moveZeroes(vector<int>& nums) {
        int slow = 0;

        for (int fast = 0; fast < nums.size(); ++fast) {
            // HIGHLIGHT: Swap non-zero value forward
            if (nums[fast] != 0) {
                if (slow != fast) {
                    swap(nums[slow], nums[fast]);
                }
                slow++;
            }
        }
    }
};
class Solution {
    public void moveZeroes(int[] nums) {
        int slow = 0;

        for (int fast = 0; fast < nums.length; fast++) {
            // HIGHLIGHT: Swap non-zero element with slow pointer
            if (nums[fast] != 0) {
                if (slow != fast) {
                    int temp = nums[slow];
                    nums[slow] = nums[fast];
                    nums[fast] = temp;
                }
                slow++;
            }
        }
    }
}
var moveZeroes = function(nums) {
    let slow = 0;

    for (let fast = 0; fast < nums.length; fast++) {
        // HIGHLIGHT: Swap non-zero forward
        if (nums[fast] !== 0) {
            if (slow !== fast) {
                [nums[slow], nums[fast]] = [nums[fast], nums[slow]];
            }
            slow++;
        }
    }
};

7. Detailed Dry Run Walkthroughs

📋 1. Standard Case: nums = [0, 1, 0, 3, 12]
Processing nums = [0, 1, 0, 3, 12] (One-Pass Two-Pointer Swap): Initial State: slow = 0 • fast = 0 (nums[0] = 0): - Is nums[0] != 0? False. - slow remains 0. Array: [0, 1, 0, 3, 12] • fast = 1 (nums[1] = 1): - Is nums[1] != 0? True. - slow (0) != fast (1) -> Swap nums[0] and nums[1] - Array becomes: [1, 0, 0, 3, 12] - slow becomes 1. • fast = 2 (nums[2] = 0): - Is nums[2] != 0? False. - slow remains 1. Array: [1, 0, 0, 3, 12] • fast = 3 (nums[3] = 3): - Is nums[3] != 0? True. - slow (1) != fast (3) -> Swap nums[1] and nums[3] - Array becomes: [1, 3, 0, 0, 12] - slow becomes 2. • fast = 4 (nums[4] = 12): - Is nums[4] != 0? True. - slow (2) != fast (4) -> Swap nums[2] and nums[4] - Array becomes: [1, 3, 12, 0, 0] - slow becomes 3. Loop Ends! Final Output Array = [1, 3, 12, 0, 0]
📋 2. Complex Case (Sparse Zeroes): nums = [4, 0, 0, 2, 0, 1, 0, 5] (N = 8)
Processing nums = [4, 0, 0, 2, 0, 1, 0, 5]: fast num slow Action Array State --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 0 4 0 slow == fast (No-op) [4, 0, 0, 2, 0, 1, 0, 5] (slow becomes 1) 1 0 1 Zero (Skip) [4, 0, 0, 2, 0, 1, 0, 5] 2 0 1 Zero (Skip) [4, 0, 0, 2, 0, 1, 0, 5] 3 2 1 Swap nums[1], nums[3] [4, 2, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 5] (slow becomes 2) 4 0 2 Zero (Skip) [4, 2, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 5] 5 1 2 Swap nums[2], nums[5] [4, 2, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 5] (slow becomes 3) 6 0 3 Zero (Skip) [4, 2, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 5] 7 5 3 Swap nums[3], nums[7] [4, 2, 1, 5, 0, 0, 0, 0] (slow becomes 4) Final Output = [4, 2, 1, 5, 0, 0, 0, 0]
📋 3. Edge Case: All Zeroes (nums = [0, 0, 0])
Processing nums = [0, 0, 0]: Initial State: slow = 0 • fast = 0 (nums[0] = 0): Skip • fast = 1 (nums[1] = 0): Skip • fast = 2 (nums[2] = 0): Skip Loop Ends! slow remains 0. Final Output Array = [0, 0, 0] (Zero unnecessary writes performed!)

8. Complexity Analysis Performance Metrics

Approach Category Time Complexity Space Complexity Array Write Operations Performance Evaluation Rating
Approach 1: Auxiliary Array Copy O(N) O(N) Auxiliary 2 * N writes Violates Constraints. Allocates O(N) extra memory, breaking in-place requirement.
Approach 2: Two-Pass Overwrite O(N) O(1) Auxiliary N writes Good. Operates in-place, but writes N times regardless of zero density.
Approach 3: One-Pass Two-Pointer Swap O(N) O(1) Auxiliary 2 * (count of non-zeroes) writes Absolute Production Standard. Solves in a single linear pass with optimal write efficiency (fewer writes when array is mostly zeroes).

LeetCode 933 Easy Master Edition

Number of Recent Calls

Complete technical guide: Rate-limiting sliding window design using Dynamic Arrays with Binary Search vs FIFO Queue eviction.

1. Problem Statement & Core Concept

You have a RecentCounter class which counts the number of recent requests within a certain time frame.

Implement the RecentCounter class:

  • RecentCounter() Initializes the counter with zero recent requests.
  • int ping(int t) Adds a new request at time t, where t represents some time in milliseconds, and returns the number of requests that has happened in the past 3000 milliseconds (inclusive). Specifically, return the number of requests that have happened in the inclusive range [t - 3000, t].

It is guaranteed that every call to ping uses a strictly larger value of t than the previous call (strictly increasing timestamps).

Recent Calls Mechanics Visualization: Window Range formula for call at time t: [t - 3000, t] 1. ping(1) - Range: [1 - 3000, 1] -> [-2999, 1] - Timestamps in range: [1] - Output: 1 2. ping(100) - Range: [100 - 3000, 100] -> [-2900, 100] - Timestamps in range: [1, 100] - Output: 2 3. ping(3001) - Range: [3001 - 3000, 3001] -> [1, 3001] - Timestamps in range: [1, 100, 3001] - Output: 3 4. ping(3002) - Range: [3002 - 3000, 3002] -> [2, 3002] - Timestamp 1 is now EXPIRED (1 < 2)! - Timestamps in range: [100, 3001, 3002] - Output: 3

Constraints

  • 1 <= t <= 10^9
  • Each test case will call ping with strictly increasing values of t.
  • At most 10^4 calls will be made to ping.

2. Dynamic Array + Binary Search Approach (Brute Force / Alternative)

🧭 Concept: Append All Requests & Binary Search Left Boundary

Since the input timestamps t are strictly increasing, appending every t to a dynamic array produces a naturally sorted list. We can find the number of valid requests in the range [t - 3000, t] using Binary Search:

Algorithm steps:

  • Maintain a dynamic array records storing every ping timestamp.
  • When ping(t) is called, append t to records.
  • Use Binary Search (lower_bound) to find the first index idx where records[idx] >= t - 3000.
  • The number of requests in the range [t - 3000, t] is simply len(records) - idx.
Hinglish Explanation

Is tarike me hum saare timestamps ko ek array me append karte jate hain. Kyonki timestamps strictly increasing hain, array pehle se sorted rahega. Jab bhi ping(t) aayega, hum Binary Search (bisect_left) se pehla aisa index dhoondenge jo t - 3000 se bada ya barabar ho. Valid calls ki ginti total_elements - low_index ho jayegi.

Dynamic Array + Binary Search Implementation

import bisect

class RecentCounterBS:
    def __init__(self):
        self.records = []

    def ping(self, t: int) -> int:
        self.records.append(t)
        # Binary search for lower bound of (t - 3000)
        min_time = t - 3000
        idx = bisect.bisect_left(self.records, min_time)
        return len(self.records) - idx
class RecentCounterBS {
private:
    vector<int> records;

public:
    RecentCounterBS() {}

    int ping(int t) {
        records.push_back(t);
        int minTime = t - 3000;
        auto it = lower_bound(records.begin(), records.end(), minTime);
        return records.end() - it;
    }
};
class RecentCounterBS {
    private List<Integer> records;

    public RecentCounterBS() {
        records = new ArrayList<>();
    }

    public int ping(int t) {
        records.add(t);
        int minTime = t - 3000;
        int idx = binarySearch(minTime);
        return records.size() - idx;
    }

    private int binarySearch(int target) {
        int left = 0, right = records.size() - 1;
        while (left <= right) {
            int mid = left + (right - left) / 2;
            if (records.get(mid) >= target) {
                right = mid - 1;
            } else {
                left = mid + 1;
            }
        }
        return left;
    }
}
var RecentCounterBS = function() {
    this.records = [];
};

RecentCounterBS.prototype.ping = function(t) {
    this.records.push(t);
    let minTime = t - 3000;
    
    // Binary Search for lower bound
    let left = 0, right = this.records.length - 1;
    while (left <= right) {
        let mid = Math.floor((left + right) / 2);
        if (this.records[mid] >= minTime) {
            right = mid - 1;
        } else {
            left = mid + 1;
        }
    }
    return this.records.length - left;
};

3. Why Binary Search Uses Unnecessary Memory & Shift to FIFO Queue

⚠️ Space Overhead of Storing All Historical Pings

Space Complexity: Appending every single timestamp without deleting old ones uses O(N) Space Complexity where N is the total number of pings called throughout the program's lifecycle.

Time Complexity: Each ping requires binary search across an ever-growing array, taking O(log N) Time Complexity per call.

In production systems handling millions of API calls, storing outdated timestamps older than 3000ms is wasteful. Can we achieve Amortized O(1) Time and O(W) Space (where W <= 3001 is the maximum requests inside the window)?

Reframing the Problem (FIFO Queue Window Architecture)

Notice that timestamps arrive in strict chronological order and expire in the exact same chronological order (First-In, First-Out).

Key Shift in Perspective (FIFO Queue / Sliding Window): 1. Storing All History (Array + Binary Search): Keep N elements forever -> Binary Search for boundary -> O(N) Space, O(log N) Time per ping. 2. FIFO Queue Window (Optimal): Maintain a Queue storing ONLY the timestamps within [t - 3000, t]. When ping(t) arrives: 1. Enqueue `t` into the back of the Queue. 2. While Queue is not empty and Queue.front() < (t - 3000): - Dequeue/Evict the expired element from the front! 3. Return Queue.size()! Amortized Time Complexity: O(1) per ping! Space Complexity: Bounded by maximum requests in a 3000ms interval (O(W) <= 3001).

Let's visualize the Queue operations for a stream of calls:

Calls Trace: ping(1), ping(100), ping(3001), ping(3002) 1. ping(1): - Enqueue 1 -> Queue = [1] - Front 1 >= (1 - 3000) -> No eviction. - Queue size = 1 2. ping(100): - Enqueue 100 -> Queue = [1, 100] - Front 1 >= (100 - 3000 = -2900) -> No eviction. - Queue size = 2 3. ping(3001): - Enqueue 3001 -> Queue = [1, 100, 3001] - Front 1 >= (3001 - 3000 = 1) -> Valid! No eviction. - Queue size = 3 4. ping(3002): - Enqueue 3002 -> Queue = [1, 100, 3001, 3002] - Front 1 < (3002 - 3000 = 2) -> EXPIRED! Dequeue 1. - New Front 100 >= 2 -> Stop eviction. - Queue = [100, 3001, 3002] - Queue size = 3

4. Core Mechanics: Queue Eviction Invariants

🧭 Defining the Active Window Invariant

The queue state maintains a strict invariant at the end of every ping(t) call:

Invariant: Every element x in Queue satisfies (t - 3000 <= x <= t)

Because input t is strictly monotonically increasing, timestamps in the queue are strictly sorted from head to tail. Therefore, checking Queue.front() < t - 3000 is sufficient to evict all expired elements!

Standalone Code: Helper Logic for Queue Eviction

def evict_expired_pings(queue: collections.deque, current_time: int) -> None:
    min_allowed = current_time - 3000
    # Evict expired timestamps from the front of the queue
    while queue and queue[0] < min_allowed:
        queue.popleft()

5. Boundary Traps & Edge Case Resolution

⚠️ Common Traps & Edge Case Scenarios

1. Inclusive Boundary Enforcement:
The range [t - 3000, t] is inclusive at both ends. An element with timestamp exactly equal to t - 3000 is STILL VALID. Only elements with timestamp < t - 3000 must be evicted!

2. Large Time Gaps Between Calls (e.g. ping(1) followed by ping(10000)):
When a large jump in time occurs, the while loop may evict all existing elements in the queue before adding the new timestamp. The queue size correctly resets to 1.

3. Choice of Data Structure Language Traps:
In JavaScript, using a standard array with Array.shift() takes O(N) time for pops! For O(1) performance in JS, maintain a head index pointer or use a custom linked-list queue.

6. Optimal Source Code with Line-by-Line Annotations (FIFO Queue)

from collections import deque

class RecentCounter:
    def __init__(self):
        # Initialize a double-ended queue for O(1) pops from head
        self.queue = deque()

    def ping(self, t: int) -> int:
        # Step 1: Add new request timestamp to queue
        self.queue.append(t)

        # HIGHLIGHT: Evict all expired timestamps older than (t - 3000)
        while self.queue[0] < t - 3000:
            self.queue.popleft()

        # Step 3: Queue length equals number of valid recent calls
        return len(self.queue)
class RecentCounter {
private:
    queue<int> q;

public:
    RecentCounter() {}

    int ping(int t) {
        q.push(t);

        // HIGHLIGHT: Pop expired timestamps from queue front
        while (!q.empty() && q.front() < t - 3000) {
            q.pop();
        }

        return q.size();
    }
};
class RecentCounter {
    private Queue<Integer> q;

    public RecentCounter() {
        q = new LinkedList<>();
    }

    public int ping(int t) {
        q.add(t);

        // HIGHLIGHT: Poll elements out of 3000ms window
        while (!q.isEmpty() && q.peek() < t - 3000) {
            q.poll();
        }

        return q.size();
    }
}
var RecentCounter = function() {
    this.stream = [];
    this.head = 0; // Pointer to simulate O(1) queue dequeue
};

RecentCounter.prototype.ping = function(t) {
    this.stream.push(t);

    // HIGHLIGHT: Advance head pointer to skip expired timestamps
    while (this.stream[this.head] < t - 3000) {
        this.head++;
    }

    return this.stream.length - this.head;
};

7. Detailed Test Cases & Walkthroughs

📋 1. Standard Case: ping(1), ping(100), ping(3001), ping(3002)
Step-by-step Queue Trace: Initial State: q = [] • ping(1): - Push 1 -> q = [1] - Window = [1 - 3000, 1] = [-2999, 1] - Front 1 >= -2999 -> No pop. - Return size = 1 • ping(100): - Push 100 -> q = [1, 100] - Window = [-2900, 100] - Front 1 >= -2900 -> No pop. - Return size = 2 • ping(3001): - Push 3001 -> q = [1, 100, 3001] - Window = [1, 3001] - Front 1 >= 1 -> No pop. (1 is INCLUSIVE!) - Return size = 3 • ping(3002): - Push 3002 -> q = [1, 100, 3001, 3002] - Window = [2, 3002] - Front 1 < 2 -> EXPIRED! Pop 1 -> q = [100, 3001, 3002] - Next Front 100 >= 2 -> Stop popping. - Return size = 3
📋 2. Large Time Gap Case: ping(1), ping(2), ping(10000)
Step-by-step Queue Trace: • ping(1): q = [1], return 1 • ping(2): q = [1, 2], return 2 • ping(10000): - Push 10000 -> q = [1, 2, 10000] - Window = [7000, 10000] - Front 1 < 7000 -> Pop 1 -> q = [2, 10000] - Front 2 < 7000 -> Pop 2 -> q = [10000] - Front 10000 >= 7000 -> Stop popping. - Return size = 1
📋 3. Dense Cluster Case: 5 calls in same millisecond ping(500)
Call 5 calls at t = 500: q state builds as: [500, 500, 500, 500, 500] All 5 elements have timestamp 500 >= (500 - 3000 = -2500). No elements evicted. Return size = 5

8. Complexity Analysis Performance Metrics

Approach Category Time Complexity per ping() Space Complexity Performance Evaluation Rating
Approach 1: Array + Binary Search O(log N) O(N) Total History Sub-optimal Space. Keeps every historical request forever, accumulating unbounded space memory over time.
Approach 2: FIFO Queue Sliding Window (Optimal) O(1) Amortized O(W) Bounded Absolute Production Standard. Each request is pushed and popped at most once. Space is bounded by max requests within 3000ms window (W <= 3001).

Senior Staff Mentorship Series

LLD Deep-Dive: Encapsulation & Data Hiding

Goal: Pass Low-Level Design (LLD) interviews at Tier-1 Tech companies by understanding state invariants, thread-safety boundaries, and anti-patterns from absolute first principles.

1. Why This Concept Exists

Imagine a massive software system built by 50 engineers. If every single variable inside every class is made public, any engineer can modify any variable from anywhere in the codebase.

Eventually, someone will write code that puts an object into a broken state—like setting a bank account balance to -$500 or setting an age variable to -25. Finding which line of code caused this bug in a codebase of 100,000 lines is almost impossible.

Encapsulation exists to create safety boundaries. It forces all state changes to pass through a single, controlled door (a class method) where rules can be strictly enforced before data is mutated.

2. The Real-World Problem It Solves

Imagine building a high-throughput Payment Wallet Engine for an e-commerce platform like Amazon.

The Disaster Without Encapsulation:

  • If wallet.balance is a raw public variable, any developer anywhere in the system can write wallet.balance = -500; or wallet.balance -= 100; directly.
  • No Validation: Negative balances or invalid transactions are allowed because no validation function intercepts the assignment.
  • No Audit Trail: Your financial system fails security compliance because you cannot track who modified the balance, when it happened, or why it was changed.

3. The Intuition First

Think of an ATM Machine.

The bank vault doesn't expose cash drawers directly to the sidewalk for anyone to grab (Public Data). If it did, anyone could walk up and take money without verification.

Instead, the bank puts the cash inside a locked vault (Private Data) and gives you a keypad and screen on the outside (Public Interface / Methods).

When you want $100:

  1. You press the button requesting $100.
  2. The ATM checks your PIN.
  3. The ATM checks if your account balance is ≥ $100.
  4. The ATM checks if the machine itself has physical cash notes left.
  5. The ATM logs the transaction in the bank server.
  6. Finally, the ATM dispenses $100 cash.

You never touched the cash vault directly. The machine guarded the money and executed all rules safely. That is Encapsulation and Data Hiding.

4. Formal Definition

Encapsulation

The practice of bundling data (attributes) and the functions (methods) that operate on that data into a single, cohesive structural container (a Class).

Data Hiding

The practice of restricting external access to an object's internal variables using visibility modifiers (private, protected), forcing all external code to interact via explicit methods.

The Key Difference Interviewers Test:

Encapsulation is about bundling things together into a container. Data Hiding is about putting a lock on that container to protect invariants. You can encapsulate without hiding data (e.g., a C-style struct with all public fields), but true Object-Oriented Design requires both.

5. Running Example: Digital Wallet System

Throughout this guide, we use an enterprise Digital Wallet to illustrate invariants, thread safety, and defensive copies.

Class Invariant Rule: "A class invariant is a rule that must ALWAYS remain true for an object to be valid. For our Wallet, the balance can NEVER be negative, and every balance change MUST create an audit log entry."

6. Where This Concept Appears in Low-Level Design (LLD)

Interviewers check if you know how encapsulation interacts with core system design concepts. Here are the three primary places it appears, with full beginner breakdowns:

A. Thread Synchronization Boundaries

Before understanding why encapsulation matters here, let's break down the basic concurrency concepts:

1. What is Thread Synchronization?

A Thread is a single worker executing code instructions inside a processor. In high-performance systems, multiple threads run at the same time (concurrently). Thread Synchronization means coordinating these parallel workers so they don't overwrite shared data simultaneously and corrupt memory.

2. What is a Mutex?

Mutex stands for Mutual Exclusion. Think of a Mutex as a physical key to a single-person bathroom lock. Only the person holding the key can enter the bathroom. If another person wants to use the bathroom, they must wait outside until the first person comes out and hands over the key.

3. What is a Lock?

A Lock is the action of grabbing the Mutex key, locking the door while you work on shared variables, and unlocking it when you finish so other threads can proceed safely.

4. What is a Deadlock?

A Deadlock occurs when Thread A is holding Key 1 and waiting for Key 2, while Thread B is holding Key 2 and waiting for Key 1. Both workers are stuck waiting forever, causing the software to freeze completely.

How Encapsulation Solves This in LLD:

If you make a Mutex variable public, external developers can manually call wallet.mutex.lock() from anywhere in the codebase. If they forget to unlock it or lock multiple mutexes in the wrong order, they cause system-wide Deadlocks.

By making the Mutex private inside the class, the class handles locking and unlocking internally within its own methods (withdraw(), deposit()). External callers don't even know a Mutex exists; they just call wallet.withdraw(50) safely!

B. The State Pattern & Valid Transitions

In an e-commerce platform, an order moves through states: CREATED → PAID → SHIPPED → DELIVERED.

If the orderState variable is public, code elsewhere can write order.state = "DELIVERED" on an unpaid order! Encapsulation ensures that the Order class hides the state variable and only allows state progression through validation methods like pay() or ship().

C. Domain-Driven Aggregates

An Order object contains a list of OrderItem objects inside it. If external code can grab the raw list and modify items directly, the Order cannot recalculate its total price, tax, or discounts correctly. Encapsulating the list ensures all additions go through order.addItem().

7. Where Interviewers Expect You to Use It in Coding Rounds

During a 45-minute LLD interview, the interviewer won't ask you "What is Encapsulation?". Instead, they watch your code to see if you naturally apply these three patterns:

1. Defensive Copying in Getters (Crucial Interview Trap!)

The Mistake: You make a list private (private List<String> logs;), but write a getter like this:

public List<String> getLogs() { return this.logs; } // LEAK!

Why Interviewers Reject This: Even though the variable logs is marked private, returning the raw list hands the caller a direct pointer/reference to internal memory. The caller can run wallet.getLogs().clear(); and delete your audit trail!

What They Expect: You must return a Defensive Copy (a brand new copy of the list) or a Read-Only view wrapper so external changes don't affect your class memory.

2. Eliminating Naked Setters

The Mistake: Automatically generating getters and setters for every variable without thinking.

What They Expect: Replacing naked setters like setBalance(double b) with business-meaningful domain methods like deposit(double amount) or withdraw(double amount) that validate input before modifying state.

3. Hiding Constructors (Factory & Singleton Patterns)

What They Expect: Marking constructors private or protected so client code cannot randomly run new Object(), forcing instantiation through controlled factory methods (WalletFactory.createWallet()).

8. Common Mistakes and Misconceptions Broken Down

1. The "Anemic Domain Model" Anti-Pattern

Let's break down what this fancy term means step-by-step:

What is an "Anemic" Model?

In medical terms, "anemic" means weak or lacking substance. In software, an Anemic Domain Model is a class that has data fields, but zero business logic or rules inside it. It's just a dummy bucket of variables.

Line-by-Line Example of the Mistake:

// ANEMIC CLASS (BAD DESIGN)
class UserAccount {
    private double balance; // Marked private... BUT:

    public double getBalance() { return balance; }
    public void setBalance(double b) { this.balance = b; } // Naked Setter!
}

Why This Fails Encapsulation Completely:

Even though balance is marked private, the public setter setBalance() allows external code to write account.setBalance(-999). The class performs zero validation. Business logic gets pushed out into external service classes, forcing external code to manually calculate new balances. Data and logic are separated, ruining encapsulation.

2. Misunderstanding Encapsulation vs. Security

Data hiding is an architectural boundary to prevent developer programming errors—it is NOT cryptographic security. A reverse engineer with a debugger can always inspect RAM memory. Data hiding is for code quality and bug prevention, not data encryption.

9. Best Practices Used in Production

  • Tell, Don't Ask Principle: Don't ask an object for its data, do calculations outside, and push data back. Command the object to perform the task directly (wallet.withdraw(100);).
  • Immutable Fields by Default: Mark fields const (C++), final (Java), or readonly whenever they shouldn't change after construction.
  • Wrap Collection Outputs: Use read-only wrappers like Collections.unmodifiableList() in Java or return by value copies in C++.

10. Implementation Code Walkthrough

❌ BAD Implementation (Leaky Invariants & Anemic Model)

// BAD DESIGN: Zero state protection, reference leaks, anemic domain model
class DigitalWallet {
public:
    double balance; // DANGEROUS: Public data member allows setting negative balance!
    std::vector<std::string> logs;

    // DANGEROUS: Returns direct mutable reference to internal collection!
    std::vector<std::string>& getLogs() { 
        return logs; 
    }
};

// How external code breaks this bad class:
DigitalWallet wallet;
wallet.balance = -99999.0; // INVARIANT BROKEN: Balance is negative!
wallet.getLogs().clear();   // AUDIT BROKEN: External code wiped all system logs!

✅ GOOD Production Implementation (Encapsulated, Thread-Safe & Leak-Proof)

Toggle language tabs to see production-grade encapsulation across C++, Python, Java, and JavaScript:

#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <string>
#include <mutex>

class DigitalWallet {
private:
    double balance;
    std::vector<std::string> logs;
    mutable std::mutex mtx; // Private Mutex: Thread-safety locked inside class!

    void addLog(const std::string& msg) {
        logs.push_back(msg);
    }

public:
    explicit DigitalWallet(double initialBalance) {
        balance = (initialBalance >= 0.0) ? initialBalance : 0.0;
        addLog("Wallet created with initial balance: $" + std::to_string(balance));
    }

    // Domain Method enforcing invariants and locking internally
    bool withdraw(double amount) {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mtx); // Safely lock mutex
        if (amount <= 0.0 || amount > balance) {
            addLog("Withdrawal failed for amount: $" + std::to_string(amount));
            return false;
        }
        balance -= amount;
        addLog("Successfully withdrew: $" + std::to_string(amount));
        return true;
    }

    double getBalance() const {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mtx);
        return balance;
    }

    // Defensive Copying: Returns a NEW COPY of vector, preventing external tampering!
    std::vector<std::string> getLogs() const {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mtx);
        return logs; 
    }
};
from typing import List
import threading

class DigitalWallet:
    def __init__(self, initial_balance: float):
        self.__balance = initial_balance if initial_balance >= 0.0 else 0.0
        self.__logs: List[str] = [f"Created with: ${self.__balance}"]
        self.__lock = threading.Lock() # Private thread lock

    def withdraw(self, amount: float) -> bool:
        with self.__lock:
            if amount <= 0.0 or amount > self.__balance:
                self.__logs.append(f"Withdrawal failed: ${amount}")
                return False
            self.__balance -= amount
            self.__logs.append(f"Withdrew: ${amount}")
            return True

    @property
    def balance(self) -> float:
        with self.__lock:
            return self.__balance

    def get_logs(self) -> List[str]:
        with self.__lock:
            # Defensive Copy via list constructor
            return list(self.__logs)
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.List;

public class DigitalWallet {
    private double balance;
    private final List<String> logs;

    public DigitalWallet(double initialBalance) {
        this.balance = Math.max(0.0, initialBalance);
        this.logs = new ArrayList<>();
        this.logs.add("Created with: $" + this.balance);
    }

    public synchronized boolean withdraw(double amount) {
        if (amount <= 0.0 || amount > balance) {
            logs.add("Withdrawal failed: $" + amount);
            return false;
        }
        balance -= amount;
        logs.add("Withdrew: $" + amount);
        return true;
    }

    public synchronized double getBalance() { return balance; }

    // Unmodifiable wrapper prevents external collection tampering!
    public synchronized List<String> getLogs() {
        return Collections.unmodifiableList(new ArrayList<>(logs));
    }
}
class DigitalWallet {
    #balance = 0;
    #logs = [];

    constructor(initialBalance) {
        this.#balance = initialBalance >= 0 ? initialBalance : 0;
        this.#logs.push(`Created with: $${this.#balance}`);
    }

    withdraw(amount) {
        if (amount <= 0 || amount > this.#balance) {
            this.#logs.push(`Withdrawal failed: $${amount}`);
            return false;
        }
        this.#balance -= amount;
        this.#logs.push(`Withdrew: $${amount}`);
        return true;
    }

    get balance() { return this.#balance; }

    getLogs() {
        // Return shallow copy using spread operator
        return [...this.#logs];
    }
}
11. Your 30-Second Interview Answer (Easy & To-The-Point)

"Encapsulation is bundling data and methods inside a class, while Data Hiding restricts direct access to internal variables. We use them in Low-Level Design to protect class invariants—ensuring external code can never corrupt object state. In production, I implement this by making fields private, using domain methods like withdraw() instead of naked setters, returning defensive copies of internal lists, and encapsulating synchronization locks inside the class."

12. LLD Revision Cheat Sheet
  • Core Goal: Prevent state corruption and enforce Class Invariants.
  • Encapsulation vs Data Hiding:
    • Encapsulation → Bundle data + methods together.
    • Data Hiding → Hide internal data and expose only controlled operations.
  • Red Flag to Avoid: Creating naked setters for all fields (Anemic Domain Model).
  • Red Flag to Avoid: Returning direct memory references to internal collections/lists.
  • Green Flag to Show: Using domain methods (withdraw() instead of setBalance()).
  • Green Flag to Show: Returning defensive copies or read-only wrappers for lists.
  • System Design Tip: Keep Mutexes and Locks private inside the class to prevent deadlocks.
title: Encapsulation & Data Hiding (Beginner friendly)
