Find K Pairs with Smallest Sums

Complete Technical & Mentorship Guide: Deep intuition, line-by-line breakdowns for all approaches, mathematical explanations of Max-Heap mechanics, and detailed dry runs.

1. Problem Statement & Core Concept

You are given two integer arrays nums1 and nums2 sorted in non-decreasing order and an integer k.

Define a pair (u, v) which consists of one element u from nums1 and one element v from nums2.

Return the k pairs (u1, v1), (u2, v2), ..., (uk, vk) with the smallest sums.

Pair Sum Mechanics Visualization: Example 1: nums1 = [1, 7, 11], nums2 = [2, 4, 6], k = 3 - All possible pairs and their sums: (1, 2) -> 3 (1, 4) -> 5 (1, 6) -> 7 (7, 2) -> 9 (7, 4) -> 11 ... - The 3 smallest sum pairs are: [1, 2], [1, 4], [1, 6] Output: [[1, 2], [1, 4], [1, 6]] --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Example 2: nums1 = [1, 1, 2], nums2 = [1, 2, 3], k = 2 - Pair sums: (1, 1) -> 2 (1, 1) -> 2 (1, 2) -> 3 ... - The 2 smallest sum pairs are: [1, 1], [1, 1] Output: [[1, 1], [1, 1]]

Constraints

  • 1 <= nums1.length, nums2.length <= 10^5
  • -10^9 <= nums1[i], nums2[j] <= 10^9
  • nums1 and nums2 are sorted in non-decreasing order.
  • 1 <= k <= 10^4
  • k <= nums1.length * nums2.length

2. Approach 1: Naive Cartesian Product + Full Sort

🧭 Senior Mentor Explanation: The Brute Force Idea

Hey junior, whenever you see a problem asking for pairs between two arrays, the most straightforward thing that comes to mind is: "Why not build every single pair, calculate their sums, and then sort them?"

Think of it as creating a full grid (Cartesian Product) of size N1 x N2:

  • Outer loop picks an element u from nums1.
  • Inner loop picks an element v from nums2.
  • We record [u, v] along with its sum u + v into a big list.
  • Sort the entire list based on the sum and take the first k items.
Hinglish Explanation

Dekho, sabse simple Soch yeh hai ki hum saare combinations bana lein. Pehle array se u aur doosre se v leke har pair ka sum nikalein, poori list ko sort karein, aur pehle k pairs return kar dein. Problem yeh hai ki jab arrays bade honge (10^5 length), toh 10^10 pairs banenge, jisse memory crash ho jayegi aur code TLE (Time Limit Exceeded) dega.

Line-by-Line Code Breakdown (Approach 1)

  1. all_pairs = []: We create an array to store every possible pair along with its sum.
  2. for x in nums1: for y in nums2:: Two nested loops that iterate through every possible combination of elements from both arrays.
  3. all_pairs.append(([x, y], x + y)): We store a tuple containing the pair [x, y] and its calculated sum x + y.
  4. all_pairs.sort(key=lambda item: item[1]): We sort the list based on the sum (located at index 1 of the tuple) in ascending order.
  5. return [item[0] for item in all_pairs[:k]]: We slice the top k smallest pairs and extract just the pair values [x, y] to return.

Naive Full-Sort Implementation

class NaiveSolution:
    def kSmallestPairs(self, nums1: list[int], nums2: list[int], k: int) -> list[list[int]]:
        all_pairs = []
        # Generate all N * M pairs
        for x in nums1:
            for y in nums2:
                all_pairs.append(([x, y], x + y))

        # Sort by pair sum O(NM log(NM))
        all_pairs.sort(key=lambda item: item[1])
        
        # Extract top k pairs
        return [item[0] for item in all_pairs[:k]]
class NaiveSolution {
public:
    vector<vector<int>> kSmallestPairs(vector<int>& nums1, vector<int>& nums2, int k) {
        vector<pair<int, vector<int>>> allPairs;

        for (int x : nums1) {
            for (int y : nums2) {
                allPairs.push_back({x + y, {x, y}});
            }
        }

        sort(allPairs.begin(), allPairs.end());

        vector<vector<int>> result;
        for (int i = 0; i < min((int)allPairs.size(), k); ++i) {
            result.push_back(allPairs[i].second);
        }
        return result;
    }
};
class NaiveSolution {
    public List<List<Integer>> kSmallestPairs(int[] nums1, int[] nums2, int k) {
        List<int[]> allPairs = new ArrayList<>();

        for (int x : nums1) {
            for (int y : nums2) {
                allPairs.add(new int[]{x, y, x + y});
            }
        }

        allPairs.sort((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[2], b[2]));

        List<List<Integer>> result = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < Math.min(allPairs.size(), k); i++) {
            result.add(Arrays.asList(allPairs.get(i)[0], allPairs.get(i)[1]));
        }
        return result;
    }
}
var kSmallestPairsNaive = function(nums1, nums2, k) {
    let allPairs = [];

    for (let x of nums1) {
        for (let y of nums2) {
            allPairs.push([[x, y], x + y]);
        }
    }

    allPairs.sort((a, b) => a[1] - b[1]);

    return allPairs.slice(0, k).map(item => item[0]);
};

3. Approach 2: Max-Heap Bounded Priority Queue with Pruning

🧭 Senior Mentor Explanation: Improving Space to O(K)

Now, junior, let's ask ourselves: "Do we really need to store ALL pairs if we only want the K smallest ones?"

No! We can maintain a Bouncer at a Club analogy:

  • We build a Max-Heap bounded to size k.
  • The Max-Heap holds our current "VIP Candidate List" of smallest pairs.
  • Because it's a Max-Heap, the pair with the largest sum among the VIP candidates sits right at the top (the root).
  • When a new pair comes along:
    • If the heap has fewer than k items, let the new pair in!
    • If the heap is full (size k) and the new pair has a sum smaller than the heap's top (largest VIP sum), we kick out the top item and let the new smaller pair in!
Hinglish Explanation

Max-Heap ka matlab hai ek aisi bucket jo sirf k items rakhti hai. Bucket me sabse BADA sum hamesha sabse OOPAR (top) par hota hai. Jab bhi koi naya pair aata hai, hum use top wale se compare karte hain. Agar naya pair top wale se CHOTA hai, toh hum top wale ko nikal phenkte hain (evict) aur naye pair ko daal dete hain. Isse humari memory kabhi bhi k se badi nahi hoti!

Deep Line-by-Line Breakdown & Mathematical Explanation

🔍 Deep Explanation of the Heap Operations Line 
elif pair_sum < -max_heap[0][0]:
    heapq.heappushpop(max_heap, (-pair_sum, u, v))

Let's dissect every single token in this condition so you understand it completely:

1. Why the Negative Sign -max_heap[0][0]?

Python's heapq module only implements a Min-Heap (where heap[0] is always the SMALLEST value). But we need a Max-Heap to keep track of the largest element in our current top-k set so we can evict it when a smaller sum arrives.

To turn a Min-Heap into a Max-Heap, we negate the numbers before pushing them into the heap!

  • Suppose our pair sums are 5, 7, and 9.
  • We push -5, -7, and -9 into Python's Min-Heap.
  • Python sees -9 as the smallest number, so max_heap[0] becomes -9.
  • To get the actual positive sum 9 back, we apply a negative sign: -(-9) = 9!
  • Therefore, -max_heap[0][0] extracts the actual positive maximum sum currently inside the heap.

2. What does pair_sum < -max_heap[0][0] check?

It checks: "Is the current candidate pair_sum strictly smaller than the WORST (largest) sum currently in our top-k heap?"

If YES, the current candidate pair is better (smaller sum) than the worst pair in our heap. Therefore, the worst pair MUST be evicted and replaced by this new pair!

3. Why heapq.heappushpop?

heapq.heappushpop(heap, item) pushes item onto the heap and then pops and returns the smallest item from the heap in a single atomic operation.

Because we push negated values, the largest original sum (which is the most negative number) gets popped off! This combines eviction and insertion in O(log K) time, which is faster than doing a separate pop() followed by a push().

4. Why the else: break Pruning Line?

else:
    # Pruning: nums2 is sorted, so subsequent v values will yield even larger sums
    break

Since nums2 is sorted in non-decreasing order (e.g. [2, 4, 6, 8]), if u + nums2[j] is ALREADY greater than or equal to the maximum sum in our heap, then for the next element nums2[j+1], u + nums2[j+1] will be EVEN LARGER!

None of the remaining elements in nums2 for this fixed u can possibly qualify for our top-k list. We can safely break the inner loop early, skipping millions of useless iterations!

Full Code Line-by-Line Breakdown (Approach 2)

  1. max_heap = []: Initializes the list used by heapq as a priority queue.
  2. for u in nums1: for v in nums2:: Iterates through elements, attempting pairs (u, v).
  3. pair_sum = u + v: Computes the sum for the current pair.
  4. if len(max_heap) < k: heapq.heappush(max_heap, (-pair_sum, u, v)): If the heap has fewer than k elements, we unconditionally accept the pair by pushing its negated sum onto the heap.
  5. elif pair_sum < -max_heap[0][0]: heapq.heappushpop(...): If the heap is full and current pair_sum is smaller than the maximum sum in the heap (-max_heap[0][0]), replace the maximum sum with this new smaller pair.
  6. else: break: If pair_sum is not smaller than the maximum sum in the heap, all remaining elements in nums2 for this u will be even larger. Break the inner loop early.
  7. return [[u, v] for _, u, v in max_heap]: Extracts and returns the pairs stored in the heap.

Max-Heap Implementation

import heapq

class MaxHeapSolution:
    def kSmallestPairs(self, nums1: list[int], nums2: list[int], k: int) -> list[list[int]]:
        max_heap = []  # Max-Heap storing (-sum, u, v)

        for u in nums1:
            for v in nums2:
                pair_sum = u + v
                if len(max_heap) < k:
                    heapq.heappush(max_heap, (-pair_sum, u, v))
                elif pair_sum < -max_heap[0][0]:
                    heapq.heappushpop(max_heap, (-pair_sum, u, v))
                else:
                    # Pruning: nums2 is sorted, so subsequent v values will yield even larger sums
                    break

        return [[u, v] for _, u, v in max_heap]
class MaxHeapSolution {
public:
    vector<vector<int>> kSmallestPairs(vector<int>& nums1, vector<int>& nums2, int k) {
        // Max-Heap storing tuple<sum, u, v>
        priority_queue<tuple<int, int, int>> maxHeap;

        for (int u : nums1) {
            for (int v : nums2) {
                int sum = u + v;
                if (maxHeap.size() < k) {
                    maxHeap.push({sum, u, v});
                } else if (sum < get<0>(maxHeap.top())) {
                    maxHeap.pop();
                    maxHeap.push({sum, u, v});
                } else {
                    break;
                }
            }
        }

        vector<vector<int>> result;
        while (!maxHeap.empty()) {
            auto [sum, u, v] = maxHeap.top();
            maxHeap.pop();
            result.push_back({u, v});
        }
        return result;
    }
};
class MaxHeapSolution {
    public List<List<Integer>> kSmallestPairs(int[] nums1, int[] nums2, int k) {
        // Max-Heap ordered by pair sum descending
        PriorityQueue<int[]> maxHeap = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Integer.compare(b[0], a[0]));

        for (int u : nums1) {
            for (int v : nums2) {
                int sum = u + v;
                if (maxHeap.size() < k) {
                    maxHeap.offer(new int[]{sum, u, v});
                } else if (sum < maxHeap.peek()[0]) {
                    maxHeap.poll();
                    maxHeap.offer(new int[]{sum, u, v});
                } else {
                    break;
                }
            }
        }

        List<List<Integer>> result = new ArrayList<>();
        while (!maxHeap.isEmpty()) {
            int[] top = maxHeap.poll();
            result.add(Arrays.asList(top[1], top[2]));
        }
        return result;
    }
}
var kSmallestPairsMaxHeap = function(nums1, nums2, k) {
    let maxHeap = [];

    for (let u of nums1) {
        for (let v of nums2) {
            let sum = u + v;
            if (maxHeap.length < k) {
                maxHeap.push([sum, u, v]);
                maxHeap.sort((a, b) => b[0] - a[0]);
            } else if (sum < maxHeap[0][0]) {
                maxHeap.shift();
                maxHeap.push([sum, u, v]);
                maxHeap.sort((a, b) => b[0] - a[0]);
            } else {
                break;
            }
        }
    }

    return maxHeap.map(item => [item[1], item[2]]);
};

4. Approach 3: Optimal Min-Heap Multi-Way Pointer Merge

💡 Senior Mentor Explanation: Merging Sorted Streams (K Sorted Lists)

Now, junior, let's look at the master-level solution that top tech companies expect.

Notice the problem statement says: Both arrays are sorted in non-decreasing order! We haven't fully used this superpower yet.

Imagine writing down the pair sums in a 2D matrix where row i uses nums1[i] and columns use nums2[j]:



Row 0 (nums1[0]): (nums1[0]+nums2[0]), (nums1[0]+nums2[1]), (nums1[0]+nums2[2]), ... Row 1 (nums1[1]): (nums1[1]+nums2[0]), (nums1[1]+nums2[1]), (nums1[1]+nums2[2]), ... Row 2 (nums1[2]): (nums1[2]+nums2[0]), (nums1[2]+nums2[1]), (nums1[2]+nums2[2]), ...

Look closely at each row individually! Since nums2 is sorted, EVERY ROW IS ALREADY SORTED FROM LEFT TO RIGHT!

This problem is identical to: "Merge K Sorted Lists and find the first K elements!"

How the Algorithm Works:

  1. We put the first element of each row into a Min-Heap. That's (nums1[i] + nums2[0], i, 0) for each row i up to min(N1, k).
  2. The Min-Heap gives us the absolute smallest pair currently available across all rows in O(1) time.
  3. We pop that smallest pair (i, j) and add [nums1[i], nums2[j]] to our result.
  4. Now, since we just consumed column j of row i, who is the NEXT candidate from row i? Column j + 1! So we push (nums1[i] + nums2[j + 1], i, j + 1) into the Min-Heap.
  5. Repeat this k times. Done!
Hinglish Explanation

Samjho ki hamare paas N1 alag-alag sorted queues hain. Har queue nums1[i] se shuru hoti hai. Sabhi queues ka pehla element sabse chota hota hai. Hum har queue ka pehla element Min-Heap me daal dete hain. Jo sabse chota nikalta hai, use answer me add karte hain aur USI queue ke agle element (j + 1) ko heap me daal dete hain. Isse hume pure N1 * N2 pairs explore karne hi nahi padte!

Full Code Line-by-Line Breakdown (Approach 3)

  1. res = []: Array to collect our final k smallest pairs.
  2. if not nums1 or not nums2 or k == 0: return res: Guard clause against empty arrays or requesting 0 pairs.
  3. min_heap = []: Min-Heap storing tuples (pair_sum, i, j) where i is index in nums1 and j is index in nums2.
  4. for i in range(min(len(nums1), k)):: We only need to initialize at most k rows because we will never pick pairs beyond the Kth row for the smallest k sums.
  5. heapq.heappush(min_heap, (nums1[i] + nums2[0], i, 0)): Push the first pair of row i (which is nums1[i] + nums2[0]) along with row index i and column index 0.
  6. while min_heap and len(res) < k:: Main loop runs until we collect k pairs or run out of candidate pairs in the heap.
  7. pair_sum, i, j = heapq.heappop(min_heap): Pop the absolute smallest pair sum currently in the heap.
  8. res.append([nums1[i], nums2[j]]): Add the pair values corresponding to indices i and j to our answer list.
  9. if j + 1 < len(nums2): heapq.heappush(min_heap, (nums1[i] + nums2[j + 1], i, j + 1)): If row i has a next element at column j + 1, push that next candidate into the Min-Heap!
  10. return res: Return the final list of k smallest pairs.

Min-Heap Multi-Way Pointer Implementation

import heapq

class Solution:
    def kSmallestPairs(self, nums1: list[int], nums2: list[int], k: int) -> list[list[int]]:
        res = []
        if not nums1 or not nums2 or k == 0:
            return res

        min_heap = []

        # Step 1: Push first element of each row (up to min(N1, k))
        for i in range(min(len(nums1), k)):
            # Heap element tuple: (sum, i, j)
            heapq.heappush(min_heap, (nums1[i] + nums2[0], i, 0))

        # Step 2: Extract top k smallest pairs
        while min_heap and len(res) < k:
            pair_sum, i, j = heapq.heappop(min_heap)
            res.append([nums1[i], nums2[j]])

            # Step 3: Advance row pointer j -> j + 1
            if j + 1 < len(nums2):
                heapq.heappush(min_heap, (nums1[i] + nums2[j + 1], i, j + 1))

        return res
class Solution {
public:
    vector<vector<int>> kSmallestPairs(vector<int>& nums1, vector<int>& nums2, int k) {
        vector<vector<int>> res;
        if (nums1.empty() || nums2.empty() || k == 0) return res;

        // Min-Heap storing tuple<sum, i, j>
        priority_queue<tuple<long long, int, int>, 
                       vector<tuple<long long, int, int>>, 
                       greater<tuple<long long, int, int>>> minHeap;

        int n1 = nums1.size();
        int n2 = nums2.size();

        for (int i = 0; i < min(n1, k); ++i) {
            minHeap.push({(long long)nums1[i] + nums2[0], i, 0});
        }

        while (!minHeap.empty() && res.size() < k) {
            auto [sum, i, j] = minHeap.top();
            minHeap.pop();

            res.push_back({nums1[i], nums2[j]});

            if (j + 1 < n2) {
                minHeap.push({(long long)nums1[i] + nums2[j + 1], i, j + 1});
            }
        }

        return res;
    }
};
class Solution {
    public List<List<Integer>> kSmallestPairs(int[] nums1, int[] nums2, int k) {
        List<List<Integer>> res = new ArrayList<>();
        if (nums1.length == 0 || nums2.length == 0 || k == 0) return res;

        // Min-Heap storing int[]{sum, i, j}
        PriorityQueue<int[]> minHeap = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]));

        for (int i = 0; i < Math.min(nums1.length, k); i++) {
            minHeap.offer(new int[]{nums1[i] + nums2[0], i, 0});
        }

        while (!minHeap.isEmpty() && res.size() < k) {
            int[] top = minHeap.poll();
            int i = top[1];
            int j = top[2];

            res.add(Arrays.asList(nums1[i], nums2[j]));

            if (j + 1 < nums2.length) {
                minHeap.offer(new int[]{nums1[i] + nums2[j + 1], i, j + 1});
            }
        }

        return res;
    }
}
var kSmallestPairs = function(nums1, nums2, k) {
    let res = [];
    if (!nums1.length || !nums2.length || k === 0) return res;

    // Min-Heap array simulator
    let minHeap = [];

    for (let i = 0; i < Math.min(nums1.length, k); i++) {
        minHeap.push([nums1[i] + nums2[0], i, 0]);
    }
    minHeap.sort((a, b) => a[0] - b[0]);

    while (minHeap.length > 0 && res.length < k) {
        let [sum, i, j] = minHeap.shift();
        res.push([nums1[i], nums2[j]]);

        if (j + 1 < nums2.length) {
            minHeap.push([nums1[i] + nums2[j + 1], i, j + 1]);
            minHeap.sort((a, b) => a[0] - b[0]);
        }
    }

    return res;
};

5. Boundary Traps & Edge Case Resolution

⚠️ Common Traps & Edge Cases

1. k Larger Than Total Possible Pairs (k > N1 * N2):
If k exceeds the total number of pair combinations, the Min-Heap will eventually become empty. Always guard heap pops with while min_heap and len(result) < k.

2. Memory Overflow on Initial Heap Load:
Pushing all N1 rows when N1 = 100,000 and k = 10 wastes memory. Cap the initial row loop to min(N1, k)!

3. Large Integer Overflows:
Element sums 10^9 + 10^9 = 2 * 10^9 fit comfortably inside standard 32-bit signed integers, but in languages like C++/Java using long long / long for sums avoids accidental sign overflow.

title: Find K Pairs with Smallest Sums

content:
LeetCode 347 Medium Master Edition

Top K Frequent Elements

Complete Technical & Mentorship Guide: Deep intuition, line-by-line breakdowns across all approaches, Min-Heap mechanics, Bucket Sort optimizations, and dry runs.

1. Problem Statement & Core Concept

Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k most frequent elements. You may return the answer in any order.

Top K Frequent Elements Visualization: Example 1: nums = [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3], k = 2 - Element Frequencies: 1 -> 3 times 2 -> 2 times 3 -> 1 time - Top 2 most frequent elements: 1 (count 3) and 2 (count 2) Output: [1, 2] --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Example 2: nums = [1], k = 1 - Element Frequencies: 1 -> 1 time - Top 1 most frequent element: 1 Output: [1]

Constraints & Requirements

  • 1 <= nums.length <= 10^5
  • -10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4
  • k is in the range [1, number of unique elements in the array].
  • It is guaranteed that the answer is unique.
  • Follow-up Challenge: Your algorithm's time complexity must be better than O(N log N), where N is the array size.

2. Approach 1: Frequency HashMap + Full Sorting (O(N log N))

🧭 Senior Mentor Explanation: The Brute Force Idea

Hey junior, the most straightforward approach to finding the most frequent items is a 2-step process:

  1. Count how many times each number appears using a Hash Map (Frequency Counter).
  2. Sort the unique elements based on their frequency count in descending order and slice the top k elements.
Hinglish Explanation

Sabse pehle hum Hash Map se har number ki frequency count kar lenge. Phir unique elements ko unke frequency count ke hisab se descending order me sort kar denge, aur pehle k numbers return kar denge. Isme sorting ka time O(U log U) lagega jahan U unique elements ka count hai.

Line-by-Line Code Breakdown (Approach 1)

  1. count = Counter(nums): Build a frequency map where keys are unique numbers and values are their frequencies.
  2. sorted_unique = sorted(count.keys(), key=lambda x: count[x], reverse=True): Sort unique keys based on their counts in descending order.
  3. return sorted_unique[:k]: Slice the first k elements from the sorted unique list.

Full-Sort Implementation

from collections import Counter

class NaiveSolution:
    def topKFrequent(self, nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
        count = Counter(nums)
        sorted_unique = sorted(count.keys(), key=lambda x: count[x], reverse=True)
        return sorted_unique[:k]
class NaiveSolution {
public:
    vector<int> topKFrequent(vector<int>& nums, int k) {
        unordered_map<int, int> counts;
        for (int num : nums) counts[num]++;

        vector<pair<int, int>> freqList;
        for (auto& [num, freq] : counts) {
            freqList.push_back({freq, num});
        }

        sort(freqList.rbegin(), freqList.rend());

        vector<int> result;
        for (int i = 0; i < k; ++i) {
            result.push_back(freqList[i].second);
        }
        return result;
    }
};
class NaiveSolution {
    public int[] topKFrequent(int[] nums, int k) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> counts = new HashMap<>();
        for (int num : nums) counts.put(num, counts.getOrDefault(num, 0) + 1);

        List<Integer> unique = new ArrayList<>(counts.keySet());
        unique.sort((a, b) -> Integer.compare(counts.get(b), counts.get(a)));

        int[] result = new int[k];
        for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) result[i] = unique.get(i);
        return result;
    }
}
var topKFrequentNaive = function(nums, k) {
    const counts = new Map();
    for (let num of nums) counts.set(num, (counts.get(num) || 0) + 1);

    const unique = Array.from(counts.keys());
    unique.sort((a, b) => counts.get(b) - counts.get(a));

    return unique.slice(0, k);
};

3. Approach 2: Min-Heap Bounded Priority Queue (O(N log K))

🧭 Senior Mentor Explanation: Maintaining a Bounded Size-K Heap

Junior, can we do better than sorting all unique items? Yes!

Think of a Min-Heap of fixed capacity k:

  • The Min-Heap stores pairs: (frequency, element).
  • The root of the heap (at index 0) holds the item with the smallest frequency currently in our top-k candidates.
  • We process unique elements one by one. Whenever the heap size exceeds k, we pop the root (evicting the element with the lowest frequency).
  • When all unique elements are processed, the heap retains only the k elements with the highest frequencies!
Hinglish Explanation

Size-K Min-Heap ka matlab hai ek aisi bucket jo sirf k items rakhti hai. Heap me sabse CHOTA frequency wala element hamesha top (root) par hota hai. Jab bhi size k + 1 hota hai, hum sabse choti frequency wale element ko evict (pop) kar dete hain. Processing ke baad heap me bas top-k sabse zyada frequency wale items bachte hain.

Line-by-Line Code Breakdown (Approach 2)

  1. count = Counter(nums): Compute frequencies for all elements in nums.
  2. min_heap = []: Initialize the Min-Heap array.
  3. for num, freq in count.items():: Loop over each unique number and its frequency.
  4. heapq.heappush(min_heap, (freq, num)): Push the tuple (freq, num) onto the heap. Python orders tuples by their first value (frequency).
  5. if len(min_heap) > k: heapq.heappop(min_heap): If size exceeds k, evict the candidate with the smallest frequency.
  6. return [num for freq, num in min_heap]: Unpack and return the remaining k elements from the heap.

Min-Heap Implementation

import heapq
from collections import Counter

class HeapSolution:
    def topKFrequent(self, nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
        count = Counter(nums)
        min_heap = []

        for num, freq in count.items():
            # Push (frequency, num) pair
            heapq.heappush(min_heap, (freq, num))
            # Maintain heap bounded to size k
            if len(min_heap) > k:
                heapq.heappop(min_heap)

        return [num for freq, num in min_heap]
class HeapSolution {
public:
    vector<int> topKFrequent(vector<int>& nums, int k) {
        unordered_map<int, int> counts;
        for (int num : nums) counts[num]++;

        // Min-Heap storing pair<freq, num>
        priority_queue<pair<int, int>, vector<pair<int, int>>, greater<pair<int, int>>> minHeap;

        for (auto& [num, freq] : counts) {
            minHeap.push({freq, num});
            if (minHeap.size() > k) {
                minHeap.pop();
            }
        }

        vector<int> result;
        while (!minHeap.empty()) {
            result.push_back(minHeap.top().second);
            minHeap.pop();
        }
        return result;
    }
};
class HeapSolution {
    public int[] topKFrequent(int[] nums, int k) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> counts = new HashMap<>();
        for (int num : nums) counts.put(num, counts.getOrDefault(num, 0) + 1);

        // Min-Heap ordering by frequency ascending
        PriorityQueue<Map.Entry<Integer, Integer>> minHeap = 
            new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a.getValue(), b.getValue()));

        for (Map.Entry<Integer, Integer> entry : counts.entrySet()) {
            minHeap.offer(entry);
            if (minHeap.size() > k) {
                minHeap.poll();
            }
        }

        int[] result = new int[k];
        for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) {
            result[i] = minHeap.poll().getKey();
        }
        return result;
    }
}
var topKFrequentHeap = function(nums, k) {
    const counts = new Map();
    for (let num of nums) counts.set(num, (counts.get(num) || 0) + 1);

    let minHeap = [];
    for (let [num, freq] of counts) {
        minHeap.push([freq, num]);
        minHeap.sort((a, b) => a[0] - b[0]);
        if (minHeap.length > k) {
            minHeap.shift();
        }
    }

    return minHeap.map(item => item[1]);
};

4. Approach 3: Optimal Bucket Sort / Frequency Array (O(N) Linear Time)

💡 The Bucket Sort Principle (Linear Time Transformation)

Junior, can we solve this in strict O(N) Linear Time without sorting or heapifying?

Observe this key bounded property:

Max Frequency Bound: An element in an array of size N can appear at most N times (frequency range = 0 to N).

We construct an array of buckets/lists of length N + 1, where Index = Frequency Count and Value = List of elements having that exact frequency!

Bucket Structure Architecture: nums = [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3], N = 6 1. Count Frequencies: {1: 3, 2: 2, 3: 1} 2. Initialize Buckets (indices 0 to N): buckets[0] = [] buckets[1] = [3] (3 appears 1 time) buckets[2] = [2] (2 appears 2 times) buckets[3] = [1] (1 appears 3 times) buckets[4] = [] buckets[5] = [] buckets[6] = [] 3. Iterate BACKWARD from index 6 down to 0: - Extract elements until result length reaches k! - Index 3 -> Add [1] (result = [1]) - Index 2 -> Add [2] (result = [1, 2]) - Result size = 2 == k -> STOP!
Hinglish Explanation

Kyonki N elements ke array me koi bhi number max N baar hi aa sakta hai, hum ek bucket array banate hain jahan Index hi Frequency hai. buckets[3] = [1] ka matlab hai number 1 exact 3 baar aaya hai. Phir hum bucket ko peeche se (highest frequency se) traverse karke top-k numbers pick kar lete hain. Isme koi comparison sort nahi hota, isliye time strictly O(N) lagta hai!



Line-by-Line Code Breakdown (Approach 3)

  1. count = Counter(nums): Map each unique element to its frequency count.
  2. buckets = [[] for _ in range(len(nums) + 1)]: Create N + 1 empty buckets.
  3. for num, freq in count.items(): buckets[freq].append(num): Place each number into its corresponding frequency bucket.
  4. res = []: Array to collect the top k frequent elements.
  5. for i in range(len(buckets) - 1, 0, -1):: Loop backward from the highest possible frequency (N) down to 1.
  6. for num in buckets[i]: res.append(num): Append all numbers possessing frequency i to the result list.
  7. if len(res) == k: return res: Once we collect k items, return immediately.

Bucket Sort Implementation

from collections import Counter

class Solution:
    def topKFrequent(self, nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
        count = Counter(nums)
        # Create N + 1 frequency buckets
        buckets = [[] for _ in range(len(nums) + 1)]

        # Populate buckets: index = frequency
        for num, freq in count.items():
            buckets[freq].append(num)

        res = []
        # Traverse buckets backward (highest frequency first)
        for i in range(len(buckets) - 1, 0, -1):
            for num in buckets[i]:
                res.append(num)
                if len(res) == k:
                    return res

        return res
class Solution {
public:
    vector<int> topKFrequent(vector<int>& nums, int k) {
        unordered_map<int, int> counts;
        for (int num : nums) counts[num]++;

        int n = nums.size();
        vector<vector<int>> buckets(n + 1);

        for (auto& [num, freq] : counts) {
            buckets[freq].push_back(num);
        }

        vector<int> result;
        for (int i = n; i >= 1; --i) {
            for (int num : buckets[i]) {
                result.push_back(num);
                if (result.size() == k) return result;
            }
        }
        return result;
    }
};
class Solution {
    public int[] topKFrequent(int[] nums, int k) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> counts = new HashMap<>();
        for (int num : nums) counts.put(num, counts.getOrDefault(num, 0) + 1);

        int n = nums.length;
        List<Integer>[] buckets = new List[n + 1];
        for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) buckets[i] = new ArrayList<>();

        for (Map.Entry<Integer, Integer> entry : counts.entrySet()) {
            buckets[entry.getValue()].add(entry.getKey());
        }

        int[] result = new int[k];
        int idx = 0;
        for (int i = n; i >= 1; i--) {
            for (int num : buckets[i]) {
                result[idx++] = num;
                if (idx == k) return result;
            }
        }
        return result;
    }
}
var topKFrequent = function(nums, k) {
    const counts = new Map();
    for (let num of nums) counts.set(num, (counts.get(num) || 0) + 1);

    const n = nums.length;
    const buckets = Array.from({ length: n + 1 }, () => []);

    for (let [num, freq] of counts) {
        buckets[freq].push(num);
    }

    const result = [];
    for (let i = n; i >= 1; i--) {
        for (let num of buckets[i]) {
            result.push(num);
            if (result.length === k) return result;
        }
    }
    return result;
};

5. Boundary Traps & Edge Case Analysis

⚠️ Common Traps & Edge Cases

1. k Equals Total Unique Elements (k == U):
All unique numbers must be returned. Bucket sort and Min-Heap collect all unique numbers smoothly without missing any bucket.

2. All Elements Are Identical (e.g. nums = [7, 7, 7, 7], k = 1):
Frequency map contains {7: 4}. Bucket index 4 contains [7]. Loop at i = 4 returns [7] instantly.

3. Negative Numbers in Input (e.g. nums = [-1, -1, -2], k = 1):
Hash Maps use values as keys, naturally supporting negative integers without array indexing offset problems.

6. Detailed Dry Run Walkthroughs

📋 Dry Run 1: Approach 2 (Min-Heap) — nums = [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3], k = 2
Goal: Maintain Min-Heap of size k = 2. Frequency Map: {1: 3, 2: 2, 3: 1} Iteration over Unique Elements: • Element 1 (freq 3): - Push (3, 1) -> Heap State: [(3, 1)] • Element 2 (freq 2): - Push (2, 2) -> Heap State: [(2, 2), (3, 1)] (Min-Heap root is freq 2) • Element 3 (freq 1): - Push (1, 3) -> Heap State: [(1, 3), (3, 1), (2, 2)] (Heap size 3 > k=2!) - Evict Root -> Pop (1, 3) - Heap State after Pop: [(2, 2), (3, 1)] Processing Finished! Extract elements from Heap -> [2, 1] Result = [2, 1] (Valid top 2 frequent elements)
📋 Dry Run 2: Approach 3 (Bucket Sort) — nums = [4, 1, -1, 2, -1, 2, 3], k = 2
Processing nums = [4, 1, -1, 2, -1, 2, 3], N = 7, k = 2 1. Frequency Counting: 4 -> 1 1 -> 1 -1 -> 2 2 -> 2 3 -> 1 Map: {4:1, 1:1, -1:2, 2:2, 3:1} 2. Bucket Setup (Array of size 8): buckets[0] = [] buckets[1] = [4, 1, 3] buckets[2] = [-1, 2] buckets[3..7] = [] 3. Backward Traversal (i = 7 down to 1): • i = 7, 6, 5, 4, 3: empty • i = 2: buckets[2] has [-1, 2] - Add -1 -> res = [-1] - Add 2 -> res = [-1, 2] - res.length == k (2) -> STOP! Result = [-1, 2]

7. Complexity Analysis Performance Metrics

Approach Category Time Complexity Space Complexity Performance Evaluation Rating
Approach 1: Full Sorting O(N log N) O(U) Auxiliary Sub-optimal. Sorts all U unique elements. Violates follow-up requirement when U is large.
Approach 2: Bounded Min-Heap O(N log K) O(U) Auxiliary Production Standard (Streaming/Online). Efficient memory footprint; ideal when K is small or data arrives continuously.
Approach 3: Bucket Sort (Optimal) O(N) Strict Linear O(N) Auxiliary Absolute Production Standard. Solves in pure linear time using frequency-bounded array buckets. Optimal execution speed.

LeetCode 151 Medium Master Edition

Reverse Words in a String

Complete Technical & Mentorship Guide: Deep intuition, line-by-line breakdowns across all approaches, Built-in Tokenization, LIFO Stack, Two-Pointer In-Place Reversals, and dry runs.

1. Problem Statement & Core Concept

Given an input string s, reverse the order of the words.

A word is defined as a sequence of non-space characters. The words in s will be separated by at least one space.

Return a string of the words in reverse order concatenated by a single space.

Note: s may contain leading or trailing spaces or multiple spaces between two words. The returned string should only have a single space separating the words. Do not include any extra spaces.

Reverse Words Mechanics Visualization: Example 1: s = "the sky is blue" - Words extracted: ["the", "sky", "is", "blue"] - Reversed order: ["blue", "is", "sky", "the"] - Joined with single space: "blue is sky the" Output: "blue is sky the" --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Example 2: s = " hello world " - Ignore leading and trailing spaces. - Words extracted: ["hello", "world"] - Reversed order: ["world", "hello"] Output: "world hello" --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Example 3: s = "a good example" - Multiple spaces between "good" and "example" should be reduced to a single space. - Words extracted: ["a", "good", "example"] - Reversed order: ["example", "good", "a"] Output: "example good a"

Constraints & Requirements

  • 1 <= s.length <= 10^4
  • s contains English letters (upper-case and lower-case), digits, and spaces ' '.
  • There is at least one word in s.
  • Follow-up Challenge: Could you solve it in-place with O(1) extra space (assuming mutable string types)?

2. Approach 1: Built-In Tokenization & Reversal (Language High-Level)

🧭 Senior Mentor Explanation: The High-Level Idea

Hey junior, in most production languages, string manipulation standard libraries provide built-in functions designed specifically for splitting, stripping whitespace, and reversing lists:

  1. Strip & Split: Trim leading/trailing whitespace and tokenise the string by spaces, automatically filtering out empty string tokens caused by multiple consecutive spaces.
  2. Reverse: Reverse the array/list of word tokens.
  3. Join: Concatenate the reversed word tokens back into a single string delimited by a single space ' '.
Hinglish Explanation

Sabse simple tarika yeh hai ki hum language ke built-in split() function ka use karein. Python me s.split() bina kisi argument ke run karne par saare extra spaces ko automatic ignore kar deta hai aur clean words ki list deta hai. Phir hum us list ko reverse() karke single space " " se join kar dete hain.

Line-by-Line Code Breakdown (Approach 1)

  1. words = s.split(): Splits string s by whitespace into a list of word strings. Multiple consecutive spaces are automatically handled as a single delimiter, and leading/trailing spaces are stripped.
  2. words.reverse(): Reverses the list of word tokens in-place.
  3. return " ".join(words): Combines the reversed words into a new string separated by exactly one space between adjacent words.

Built-In Implementation

class BuiltInSolution:
    def reverseWords(self, s: str) -> str:
        # s.split() automatically strips whitespace and handles multiple consecutive spaces
        words = s.split()
        # Reverse the list of word tokens
        words.reverse()
        # Join reversed words with a single space
        return " ".join(words)
class BuiltInSolution {
public:
    string reverseWords(string s) {
        stringstream ss(s);
        string word;
        vector<string> words;

        // Extract word tokens via stringstream
        while (ss >> word) {
            words.push_back(word);
        }

        // Reverse tokens
        reverse(words.begin(), words.end());

        // Reconstruct string
        string result = "";
        for (size_t i = 0; i < words.size(); ++i) {
            result += words[i];
            if (i != words.size() - 1) result += " ";
        }
        return result;
    }
};
class BuiltInSolution {
    public String reverseWords(String s) {
        // Trim spaces and split by regex \s+ (one or more whitespace characters)
        String[] words = s.trim().split("\\s+");
        
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (int i = words.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            sb.append(words[i]);
            if (i > 0) sb.append(" ");
        }
        return sb.toString();
    }
}
var reverseWordsBuiltIn = function(s) {
    // Trim spaces, split by regex for whitespace, reverse, and join
    return s.trim().split(/\s+/).reverse().join(' ');
};

3. Approach 2: Custom Two-Pointer / Deque Right-to-Left Manual Scan

🧭 Senior Mentor Explanation: Manual Parsing from Right to Left

Junior, what if an interviewer asks: "Solve this without using built-in split or regex libraries?"

We can parse the string directly from right to left:

  • Start a pointer i at the end of the string (len(s) - 1).
  • Skip all trailing or intermediate spaces by moving i backward until it hits a non-space character (marking the end of a word, end = i).
  • Move another pointer start backward through the characters of the word until hitting a space or index -1.
  • Extract the slice s[start + 1 : end + 1]—this is a complete word! Append it to our result list.
  • Set i = start and repeat until the beginning of the string is reached.
Hinglish Explanation

Agar interviewer keh de ki split() ya regex function use nahi karna hai, toh hum string ko aakhiri index se Right-to-Left manual scan kar sakte hain. Pehle saare extra spaces ko skip karo, phir word ki ending (end) aur starting (start) location identify karke word nikalo, aur result me append karte jao. Isse bina kisi built-in library ke words naturally reverse order me mil jate hain.

Line-by-Line Code Breakdown (Approach 2)

  1. words = []: Array to collect words extracted in reverse order.
  2. n = len(s) and i = n - 1: Start scanning from the last character index.
  3. while i >= 0:: Main loop traversing backward to index 0.
  4. while i >= 0 and s[i] == ' ': i -= 1: Skip any trailing or redundant intermediate spaces.
  5. if i < 0: break: If we have reached before the start of the string, break out of loop.
  6. end = i: Mark the boundary end of the current word.
  7. while i >= 0 and s[i] != ' ': i -= 1: Move i backward until reaching a space or index -1, finding the start of the word.
  8. words.append(s[i + 1 : end + 1]): Extract the substring slice for the current word and append to our list.
  9. return " ".join(words): Join extracted words with single space separator.

Right-to-Left Manual Scan Implementation

class ManualScanSolution:
    def reverseWords(self, s: str) -> str:
        words = []
        n = len(s)
        i = n - 1

        while i >= 0:
            # Step 1: Skip trailing or intermediate spaces
            while i >= 0 and s[i] == ' ':
                i -= 1
            
            if i < 0:
                break

            # Step 2: Mark end of word
            end = i

            # Step 3: Find start of word
            while i >= 0 and s[i] != ' ':
                i -= 1

            # Step 4: Extract word slice s[i + 1 : end + 1]
            words.append(s[i + 1 : end + 1])

        return " ".join(words)
class ManualScanSolution {
public:
    string reverseWords(string s) {
        string result = "";
        int n = s.length();
        int i = n - 1;

        while (i >= 0) {
            // Skip spaces
            while (i >= 0 && s[i] == ' ') i--;
            if (i < 0) break;

            int end = i;
            while (i >= 0 && s[i] != ' ') i--;

            string word = s.substr(i + 1, end - i);
            if (!result.empty()) result += " ";
            result += word;
        }

        return result;
    }
};
class ManualScanSolution {
    public String reverseWords(String s) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        int i = s.length() - 1;

        while (i >= 0) {
            while (i >= 0 && s.charAt(i) == ' ') i--;
            if (i < 0) break;

            int end = i;
            while (i >= 0 && s.charAt(i) != ' ') i--;

            if (sb.length() > 0) sb.append(" ");
            sb.append(s.substring(i + 1, end + 1));
        }

        return sb.toString();
    }
}
var reverseWordsScan = function(s) {
    let result = [];
    let i = s.length - 1;

    while (i >= 0) {
        while (i >= 0 && s[i] === ' ') i--;
        if (i < 0) break;

        let end = i;
        while (i >= 0 && s[i] !== ' ') i--;

        result.push(s.slice(i + 1, end + 1));
    }

    return result.join(' ');
};

4. Approach 3: Optimal In-Place Three-Step Reversal (O(1) Auxiliary Space)

💡 Senior Mentor Explanation: In-Place Modification Mechanics

Junior, what if the interviewer asks the C++/mutable-string follow-up question: "Can you do this in-place with O(1) auxiliary extra memory?"

We solve this using a classic 3-step geometric inversion technique:

  1. Step 1 — Clean Extra Spaces In-Place (Two Pointers): Use a write pointer slow and read pointer fast to trim leading/trailing spaces and condense multiple internal spaces to a single space. Resize string to length slow.
  2. Step 2 — Reverse the ENTIRE Cleaned String: Reversing the entire string flips the order of words into their correct positions, but ALSO reverses the individual characters inside every word (e.g. "blue is sky" -> "yks si eulb").
  3. Step 3 — Reverse Each Individual Word Back: Scan through the reversed string, find word boundaries [start, end], and reverse each word back locally (e.g. "yks" -> "sky", "eulb" -> "blue")!
Hinglish Explanation

In-Place O(1) Memory ka magical formula 3 steps me kaam karta hai:

  1. Step 1: Two pointers (slow aur fast) se saare faltu extra spaces mita kar clean single-space string banao in-place.
  2. Step 2: Poori clean string ko A to Z reverse kar do. Isse words ki position toh correct ho jati hai lekin words ke letters bhi ulte ho jate hain (e.g., "sky" ban jata hai "yks").
  3. Step 3: Har ek individual word ke start aur end ko pakad kar use wapas local reverse kar do (e.g., "yks" wapas ban jata hai "sky"). Result ready in O(1) memory!
In-Place Three-Step Reversal Mechanics: Initial Input: s = " the sky is blue " Step 1: Clean Extra Spaces In-Place (Two Pointers slow & fast): Resulting Cleaned String: "the sky is blue" Step 2: Reverse Entire String (Left = 0, Right = N - 1): "eulb si yks eht" Notice: Word order is correct ("blue" is at start, "the" is at end), but words are mirrored! Step 3: Reverse Each Word In-Place Locally: - Word 1: "eulb" -> Reverse -> "blue" - Word 2: "si" -> Reverse -> "is" - Word 3: "yks" -> Reverse -> "sky" - Word 4: "eht" -> Reverse -> "the" Final Result: "blue is sky the" Auxiliary Memory: O(1) Extra Space!

Line-by-Line Code Breakdown (Approach 3)

  1. reverse(s, left, right): Helper function that reverses characters between indices left and right using two-pointer swaps.
  2. clean_spaces(s):
    • Uses fast pointer to scan the string and slow pointer to write valid characters.
    • Skips leading spaces before writing.
    • Appends a single space ' ' before writing subsequent words.
    • Trims trailing unwritten characters at the end.
  3. reverse(s, 0, len(s) - 1): Reverses the full cleaned string.
  4. reverse_each_word(s): Iterates through the reversed string, finds word start/end indices, and calls reverse(s, start, end) for every word.

In-Place Three-Step Reversal Implementation

class Solution {
private:
    // Two-pointer reverse helper
    void reverse(string& s, int left, int right) {
        while (left < right) {
            swap(s[left++], s[right--]);
        }
    }

    // Step 1: Clean spaces in-place using slow/fast pointers
    void cleanSpaces(string& s) {
        int n = s.length();
        int slow = 0, fast = 0;

        while (fast < n) {
            // Skip spaces
            while (fast < n && s[fast] == ' ') fast++;
            // Write word characters
            if (fast < n) {
                if (slow != 0) s[slow++] = ' '; // Add single space separator
                while (fast < n && s[fast] != ' ') {
                    s[slow++] = s[fast++];
                }
            }
        }
        s.resize(slow); // Trim string to actual length
    }

public:
    string reverseWords(string s) {
        // 1. Clean extra spaces in-place
        cleanSpaces(s);

        // 2. Reverse entire string
        reverse(s, 0, s.length() - 1);

        // 3. Reverse each individual word back
        int start = 0, n = s.length();
        for (int end = 0; end <= n; ++end) {
            if (end == n || s[end] == ' ') {
                reverse(s, start, end - 1);
                start = end + 1;
            }
        }

        return s;
    }
};
class Solution:
    def reverseWords(self, s: str) -> str:
        # Convert immutable string to mutable list of characters
        l = list(s)

        def reverse(arr, left, right):
            while left < right:
                arr[left], arr[right] = arr[right], arr[left]
                left += 1
                right -= 1

        # Step 1: Clean spaces
        slow, fast, n = 0, 0, len(l)
        while fast < n:
            while fast < n and l[fast] == ' ':
                fast += 1
            if fast < n:
                if slow != 0:
                    l[slow] = ' '
                    slow += 1
                while fast < n and l[fast] != ' ':
                    l[slow] = l[fast]
                    slow += 1
                    fast += 1

        l = l[:slow]

        # Step 2: Reverse entire character list
        reverse(l, 0, len(l) - 1)

        # Step 3: Reverse each word back
        start = 0
        for end in range(len(l) + 1):
            if end == len(l) or l[end] == ' ':
                reverse(l, start, end - 1)
                start = end + 1

        return "".join(l)
class Solution {
    public String reverseWords(String s) {
        char[] a = s.toCharArray();
        int n = a.length;

        // Step 1: Clean spaces
        int slow = 0, fast = 0;
        while (fast < n) {
            while (fast < n && a[fast] == ' ') fast++;
            if (fast < n) {
                if (slow != 0) a[slow++] = ' ';
                while (fast < n && a[fast] != ' ') a[slow++] = a[fast++];
            }
        }

        // Step 2: Reverse full range up to slow
        reverse(a, 0, slow - 1);

        // Step 3: Reverse individual words
        int start = 0;
        for (int end = 0; end <= slow; end++) {
            if (end == slow || a[end] == ' ') {
                reverse(a, start, end - 1);
                start = end + 1;
            }
        }

        return new String(a, 0, slow);
    }

    private void reverse(char[] a, int left, int right) {
        while (left < right) {
            char temp = a[left];
            a[left++] = a[right];
            a[right--] = temp;
        }
    }
}
var reverseWordsInPlace = function(s) {
    let a = s.split('');
    let n = a.length;

    function reverse(left, right) {
        while (left < right) {
            [a[left], a[right]] = [a[right], a[left]];
            left++;
            right--;
        }
    }

    // Step 1: Clean spaces
    let slow = 0, fast = 0;
    while (fast < n) {
        while (fast < n && a[fast] === ' ') fast++;
        if (fast < n) {
            if (slow !== 0) a[slow++] = ' ';
            while (fast < n && a[fast] !== ' ') a[slow++] = a[fast++];
        }
    }
    a.length = slow;

    // Step 2: Reverse full array
    reverse(0, a.length - 1);

    // Step 3: Reverse individual words
    let start = 0;
    for (let end = 0; end <= a.length; end++) {
        if (end === a.length || a[end] === ' ') {
            reverse(start, end - 1);
            start = end + 1;
        }
    }

    return a.join('');
};

5. Boundary Traps & Edge Case Resolution

⚠️ Common Traps & Edge Cases

1. String Contains Only Spaces (e.g. s = " "):
The problem constraints guarantee at least one word exists. However, in general applications, space cleaning logic reduces empty strings down to length 0 safely.

2. Single Word with Padding (e.g. s = " hello "):
Step 1 cleans to "hello". Step 2 reverses to "olleh". Step 3 reverses back to "hello".

3. Off-by-One in Word End Condition:
When iterating to reverse individual words, the loop boundary must extend to end <= N (where N is the cleaned length) so that the final word reaching the end of the string triggers reverse(start, N - 1).

6. Detailed Dry Run Walkthroughs

📋 Dry Run 1: Approach 2 (Right-to-Left Scan) — s = " a good example "
Processing s = " a good example " (Length N = 20): Initial Pointer: i = 19 • Pass 1: Skip trailing spaces at indices 19, 18. - i stops at 17 (char 'e'). end = 17. - Scan word backward until space: i moves 17 -> 16 -> 15 -> ... -> 9 (space at 9). - Extract word: s[10..17] = "example". - words = ["example"]. i = 9. • Pass 2: Skip internal spaces at indices 9, 8, 7. - i stops at 6 (char 'd'). end = 6. - Scan word backward until space: i moves 6 -> 5 -> 4 -> 3 (space at 2). - Extract word: s[3..6] = "good". - words = ["example", "good"]. i = 2. • Pass 3: Skip internal space at index 2. - i stops at 1 (char 'a'). end = 1. - Scan word backward until space: i moves 1 -> 0 (space at -1). - Extract word: s[0..1] = "a". - words = ["example", "good", "a"]. i = -1. • Pass 4: i < 0 -> Loop terminates! Join with space: "example good a"
📋 Dry Run 2: Approach 3 (In-Place 3-Step) — s = " the sky "
Processing s = " the sky ": Step 1: Clean Spaces in-place (slow/fast pointers) - Fast skips initial 2 spaces -> fast = 2 ('t'). - Writes "the" -> slow = 3. - Fast skips 1 space -> writes ' ' -> slow = 4. - Fast reads "sky" -> writes "sky" -> slow = 7. - Fast skips trailing 2 spaces. - Resized string: "the sky" (length 7). Step 2: Reverse Full String - reverse(0, 6): "the sky" -> "yks eht" Step 3: Reverse Each Individual Word Back - Scan end = 0..7: - end = 3 (space at index 3): reverse(0, 2): "yks" -> "sky". String: "sky eht" - end = 7 (end of string): reverse(4, 6): "eht" -> "the". String: "sky the" Final Result = "sky the"

7. Complexity Analysis Performance Metrics

Approach Category Time Complexity Space Complexity Performance Evaluation Rating
Approach 1: Built-In Tokenization O(N) O(N) Auxiliary Good. High-level, concise, and clean for general software engineering.
Approach 2: Right-to-Left Manual Scan O(N) O(N) Auxiliary Production Standard (Immutable Strings). Single pass parsing without regex libraries.
Approach 3: In-Place Three-Step Reversal O(N) O(1) Auxiliary Absolute Production Standard (Mutable Strings). Operates in strictly linear O(N) time with zero extra auxiliary allocation. Answers the follow-up question.
title: Reverse Words in a String

C++ Inheritance & LLD Masterclass Notes

Implementation Details, Internal Mechanics, Low-Level Design Patterns, and Interview Blueprints

1. Basic Inheritance Implementation

Inheritance establishes a subtype relationship between a Base class and a Derived class. In C++, access specifiers control how inherited members are accessed outside and inside derived hierarchies.

Access Specifier Matrix

Base Member Specifier Public Inheritance Protected Inheritance Private Inheritance
public public in derived protected in derived private in derived
protected protected in derived protected in derived private in derived
private Inaccessible directly Inaccessible directly Inaccessible directly

Access Specifier Mechanics

#include 
#include 

class Base {
public:
    int publicVar = 1;
protected:
    int protectedVar = 2;
private:
    int privateVar = 3;
};

class PublicDerived : public Base {
public:
    void accessTest() {
        publicVar = 10;    // OK: Remains public
        protectedVar = 20; // OK: Remains protected
        // privateVar = 30; // ERROR: Private in Base is inaccessible
    }
};

class ProtectedDerived : protected Base {
public:
    void accessTest() {
        publicVar = 100;   // OK: Converted to protected inside ProtectedDerived
        protectedVar = 200;// OK: Remains protected
    }
};

class PrivateDerived : private Base {
public:
    void accessTest() {
        publicVar = 1000;  // OK: Converted to private inside PrivateDerived
        protectedVar = 2000;// OK: Converted to private inside PrivateDerived
    }
};

class GrandChild : public PrivateDerived {
public:
    void accessTest() {
        // publicVar = 5; // ERROR: Inaccessible! PrivateDerived turned it private
    }
};

int main() {
    PublicDerived pub;
    pub.publicVar = 42; // OK

    ProtectedDerived prot;
    // prot.publicVar = 42; // ERROR: publicVar is protected in ProtectedDerived

    PrivateDerived priv;
    // priv.publicVar = 42; // ERROR: publicVar is private in PrivateDerived

    return 0;
}
LLD Connection: Access Modes

Public inheritance represents a strict IS-A relationship (Liskov Substitution Principle). Private inheritance represents "Implemented-in-terms-of" and is usually an internal implementation detail, serving as a lower-level alternative to composition.

What Derived Classes Inherit vs What They Don't

  • Inherited: All data members, member functions (public/protected), friend declarations (to the base).
  • NOT Inherited: Constructors, Destructors, Copy/Move Assignment Operators (operator=), Friendships granted by the base class to third parties.

2. Constructor & Destructor Execution

During object instantiation, the compiler constructs base sub-objects prior to derived extensions. Destruction strictly mirrors this process in reverse order.

#include 
#include 

class Parent {
protected:
    std::string familyName;
public:
    Parent(const std::string& name) : familyName(name) {
        std::cout << "1. Parent Parameterized Constructor called for: " << familyName << "\n";
    }
    virtual ~Parent() {
        std::cout << "4. Parent Destructor called for: " << familyName << "\n";
    }
};

class Child : public Parent {
private:
    int age;
public:
    // Explicit initialization of Base class via member initializer list
    Child(const std::string& name, int age) : Parent(name), age(age) {
        std::cout << "2. Child Parameterized Constructor called. Age: " << age << "\n";
    }
    ~Child() override {
        std::cout << "3. Child Destructor called.\n";
    }
};

int main() {
    {
        Child c("Smith", 12);
    } // c goes out of scope here
    return 0;
}
Execution Order Rules

Construction Order: Base Class Constructors → Derived Class Member Initializers → Derived Class Constructor Body.

Destruction Order: Derived Class Destructor Body → Derived Class Member Destructors → Base Class Destructors.

3. Function Overriding Mechanics

Function overriding enables a derived class to provide a specific implementation of a method defined in a base class.

#include 
#include 

class BaseLogger {
public:
    virtual void log(const std::string& msg) {
        std::cout << "[BaseLogger]: " << msg << "\n";
    }
    void nonVirtualInfo() {
        std::cout << "Base non-virtual info\n";
    }
    virtual ~BaseLogger() = default;
};

class FileLogger : public BaseLogger {
public:
    // Explicit override specifier prevents signature mismatches
    void log(const std::string& msg) override {
        std::cout << "[FileLogger]: Writing to disk -> " << msg << "\n";
    }

    // Function Hiding (Not overriding! Missing 'virtual' in Base)
    void nonVirtualInfo() {
        std::cout << "FileLogger non-virtual info\n";
    }
};

int main() {
    FileLogger fl;
    BaseLogger* ptr = &fl;

    ptr->log("System Boot");            // Output: [FileLogger]: Writing to disk... (Runtime Dispatch)
    ptr->nonVirtualInfo();    // Output: Base non-virtual info (Compile-time Binding)

    return 0;
}
Common Mistake: Forgetting 'override'

If you change the parameter types in a derived function without using override, C++ silently performs Function Hiding rather than overriding. Always use override to enforce compile-time verification.

4. Runtime Polymorphism

Runtime polymorphism allows treating objects of different derived classes uniformly through a base pointer or reference.

#include 
#include 
#include 
#include 

// Abstract Base Class
class PaymentProcessor {
public:
    virtual bool pay(double amount) = 0; // Pure Virtual Function
    virtual ~PaymentProcessor() = default;
};

class CreditCardPayment : public PaymentProcessor {
private:
    std::string cardNumber;
public:
    CreditCardPayment(std::string card) : cardNumber(std::move(card)) {}
    bool pay(double amount) override {
        std::cout << "Processing Credit Card payment of $" << amount << " using card: " << cardNumber << "\n";
        return true;
    }
};

class UPIPayment : public PaymentProcessor {
private:
    std::string upiId;
public:
    UPIPayment(std::string id) : upiId(std::move(id)) {}
    bool pay(double amount) override {
        std::cout << "Processing UPI payment of $" << amount << " using VPA: " << upiId << "\n";
        return true;
    }
};

void executeCheckout(const std::vector<std::unique_ptr>& payments, double amount) {
    for (const auto& payment : payments) {
        payment->pay(amount); // Dynamic dispatch handles routing to the correct sub-type
    }
}

int main() {
    std::vector<std::unique_ptr> queue;
    queue.push_back(std::make_unique("4532-XXXX-XXXX-8901"));
    queue.push_back(std::make_unique("user@okaxis"));

    executeCheckout(queue, 150.75);
    return 0;
}

5. Virtual Functions & VTables

Virtual functions are resolved at runtime. When a class contains a virtual function, compilers insert a hidden pointer called vptr inside the object layout, pointing to a table of function pointers called the vtable.

#include 

class DynamicBase {
public:
    virtual void vfunc1() { std::cout << "DynamicBase::vfunc1\n"; }
    virtual void vfunc2() { std::cout << "DynamicBase::vfunc2\n"; }
    virtual ~DynamicBase() = default;
};

class DynamicDerived : public DynamicBase {
public:
    void vfunc1() override { std::cout << "DynamicDerived::vfunc1\n"; }
    // vfunc2 is inherited from DynamicBase
};

int main() {
    DynamicBase* obj = new DynamicDerived();
    
    /* Internal Dispatch Mechanism:
       1. Dereference obj to find hidden vptr
       2. Index vtable using vptr [Index 0 for vfunc1]
       3. Call pointer at vtable[0] -> resolves to DynamicDerived::vfunc1
    */
    obj->vfunc1(); 

    delete obj;
    return 0;
}
The Virtual Destructor Rule

If a class has any virtual functions, its destructor MUST be declared virtual. Deleting a derived instance via a base-class pointer without a virtual destructor results in undefined behavior (resource/memory leaks).

6. protected Members & Encapsulation

protected data members are accessible within the base class and any derived class, but inaccessible to outside code. While useful for framework development, overusing protected variables can create tight coupling across class hierarchies.

#include 
#include 

class AbstractAccount {
private:
    std::string accountId; // Fully encapsulated
protected:
    double balance;        // Derived classes can mutate directly

    // Recommended: Protected setter to maintain invariants
    void adjustBalance(double delta) {
        if (balance + delta < 0.0) {
            std::cout << "Error: Negative balance operation prohibited\n";
            return;
        }
        balance += delta;
    }

public:
    AbstractAccount(std::string id, double bal) : accountId(std::move(id)), balance(bal) {}
    virtual ~AbstractAccount() = default;
    double getBalance() const { return balance; }
};

class SavingsAccount : public AbstractAccount {
public:
    SavingsAccount(std::string id, double bal) : AbstractAccount(std::move(id), bal) {}
    
    void applyInterest(double rate) {
        // Direct protected variable access: balance += balance * rate;
        // Better practice via protected mutator:
        adjustBalance(balance * rate);
    }
};

7. Upcasting & Downcasting

Upcasting converts a derived reference/pointer to a base reference/pointer (always safe, implicit). Downcasting traverses down the hierarchy, requiring explicit runtime checks or static assertions.

#include 

class Device { public: virtual ~Device() = default; };
class SmartPhone : public Device {
public:
    void makeCall() { std::cout << "Calling...\n"; }
};
class SmartWatch : public Device {
public:
    void trackSteps() { std::cout << "Tracking...\n"; }
};

int main() {
    SmartPhone myPhone;
    
    // 1. Upcasting (Implicit, Safe)
    Device* devPtr = &myPhone; 

    // 2. Dynamic Downcasting (Safe Runtime Checked)
    SmartPhone* phonePtr = dynamic_cast(devPtr);
    if (phonePtr) {
        phonePtr->makeCall(); // Executed successfully
    }

    SmartWatch* watchPtr = dynamic_cast(devPtr);
    if (!watchPtr) {
        std::cout << "Downcast to SmartWatch failed! Pointer is nullptr.\n";
    }

    // 3. Static Downcasting (Fast, Unchecked, Dangerous if type wrong!)
    SmartPhone* uncheckedPhone = static_cast(devPtr);
    uncheckedPhone->makeCall();

    return 0;
}
LLD Principle: Avoid Downcasting

Frequent downcasting using dynamic_cast often indicates a violation of the Open/Closed Principle. If you constantly inspect concrete types to execute specific logic, consider moving that logic into a virtual method on the base class or using the Visitor Pattern.

8. Multiple Inheritance & Ambiguity

Multiple inheritance allows a derived class to inherit from more than one base class. This can introduce name ambiguity when multiple base classes share identical method names.

#include 

class Printer {
public:
    void start() { std::cout << "Printer initialized\n"; }
    void print() { std::cout << "Printing document...\n"; }
};

class Scanner {
public:
    void start() { std::cout << "Scanner initialized\n"; }
    void scan() { std::cout << "Scanning page...\n"; }
};

class MultiFunctionPrinter : public Printer, public Scanner {
public:
    // Disambiguating overridden method
    void start() {
        Printer::start();
        Scanner::start();
        std::cout << "All-in-One device fully ready.\n";
    }
};

int main() {
    MultiFunctionPrinter mfp;
    // mfp.start(); // AMBIGUOUS compile error if start() is not overridden in derived class
    mfp.start(); // Explicit resolution inside overridden method
    
    // Direct qualification access:
    mfp.Printer::start();
    return 0;
}

9. The Diamond Problem

The Diamond Problem arises when a derived class inherits from two classes that both inherit from a common base class. Without virtual inheritance, the derived class contains two separate instances of the original base class data.

#include 

class PoweredDevice {
public:
    int voltage;
    PoweredDevice(int v) : voltage(v) {
        std::cout << "PoweredDevice constructed with " << v << "V\n";
    }
};

// Virtual Inheritance solves duplicate instance generation
class ScannerV : virtual public PoweredDevice {
public:
    ScannerV(int v) : PoweredDevice(v) {}
};

class PrinterV : virtual public PoweredDevice {
public:
    PrinterV(int v) : PoweredDevice(v) {}
};

class Copier : public ScannerV, public PrinterV {
public:
    // CRITICAL: Most-derived class MUST explicitly construct virtual base!
    Copier(int v) : PoweredDevice(v), ScannerV(v), PrinterV(v) {}
};

int main() {
    Copier copier(220);
    std::cout << "Voltage: " << copier.voltage << "V\n"; // No ambiguity! Single instance.
    return 0;
}

10. Inheritance vs Composition

"Prefer composition over inheritance." Inheritance enforces an strict IS-A relationship and binds behaviors at compile-time. Composition establishes a HAS-A relationship, allowing behavior to be swapped dynamically at runtime.

Metric Inheritance (IS-A) Composition (HAS-A)
Coupling Tight (White-box reuse) Loose (Black-box reuse)
Flexibility Fixed at compile time Dynamic at runtime
Encapsulation Base internals exposed to derived Component internal state preserved 
#include 
#include 

// COMPOSITION EXAMPLE
class EngineInterface {
public:
    virtual void start() = 0;
    virtual ~EngineInterface() = default;
};

class V8Engine : public EngineInterface {
public:
    void start() override { std::cout << "V8 Engine roaring to life!\n"; }
};

class ElectricMotor : public EngineInterface {
public:
    void start() override { std::cout << "Silent electric motor active.\n"; }
};

class VehicleComposite {
private:
    std::unique_ptr engine; // HAS-A relation
public:
    VehicleComposite(std::unique_ptr eng) : engine(std::move(eng)) {}
    
    void setEngine(std::unique_ptr newEngine) {
        engine = std::move(newEngine); // Behavior swapped dynamically at runtime!
    }
    void drive() {
        engine->start();
    }
};

11. Comprehensive LLD Systems

System 1: E-Commerce Food Delivery Architecture

Requirements: Support multiple pricing engines, flexible payment processing, and dynamic push notifications for orders.

#include 
#include 
#include 
#include 

// 1. Notification Abstraction (Inheritance used for strategy variation)
class INotificationService {
public:
    virtual void notify(const std::string& userId, const std::string& msg) = 0;
    virtual ~INotificationService() = default;
};

class PushNotificationService : public INotificationService {
public:
    void notify(const std::string& userId, const std::string& msg) override {
        std::cout << "[PUSH] User " << userId << ": " << msg << "\n";
    }
};

// 2. Discount Strategy (Polymorphic behavior)
class DiscountStrategy {
public:
    virtual double applyDiscount(double total) = 0;
    virtual ~DiscountStrategy() = default;
};

class FestivalDiscount : public DiscountStrategy {
public:
    double applyDiscount(double total) override { return total * 0.80; } // 20% off
};

// 3. Core Order System using Composition
class FoodOrder {
private:
    std::string orderId;
    double basePrice;
    std::unique_ptr discount;
    std::shared_ptr notifier;
public:
    FoodOrder(std::string id, double price, 
              std::unique_ptr disc, 
              std::shared_ptr notif) 
        : orderId(std::move(id)), basePrice(price), discount(std::move(disc)), notifier(std::move(notif)) {}

    void processOrder() {
        double finalAmount = discount->applyDiscount(basePrice);
        std::cout << "Order " << orderId << " processed. Final Cost: $" << finalAmount << "\n";
        notifier->notify("USR-901", "Your food is on the way! Total: $" + std::to_string(finalAmount));
    }
};

int main() {
    auto notifier = std::make_shared();
    auto discount = std::make_unique();
    
    FoodOrder order("ORD-5541", 100.0, std::move(discount), notifier);
    order.processOrder();
    
    return 0;
}

12. Bad vs Good Inheritance

The Square-Rectangle Liskov Substitution Principle Violation

Inheriting Square from Rectangle seems intuitive geometrically, but breaks invariants programmatically.

// ❌ BAD INHERITANCE DESIGN
class BadRectangle {
protected:
    int width, height;
public:
    virtual void setWidth(int w) { width = w; }
    virtual void setHeight(int h) { height = h; }
    int getArea() const { return width * height; }
};

class BadSquare : public BadRectangle {
public:
    void setWidth(int w) override { width = height = w; }
    void setHeight(int h) override { width = height = h; }
};

void clientTest(BadRectangle& r) {
    r.setWidth(5);
    r.setHeight(4);
    // Expects area = 20. But if r is BadSquare, setHeight(4) made width=4, area = 16!
    // Destroys polymorphic substitutability!
}

// ✅ BETTER ALTERNATIVE: Shared Abstract Interface or Immutable Value Objects
class IShape {
public:
    virtual int calculateArea() const = 0;
    virtual ~IShape() = default;
};

class GoodSquare : public IShape {
private:
    int side;
public:
    GoodSquare(int s) : side(s) {}
    int calculateArea() const override { return side * side; }
};

13. Core Interview Deep-Dives

Q1: Can constructors or destructors be virtual?

Constructors: NO. Constructors cannot be virtual. When a constructor runs, the object is still being constructed, so the vptr is not yet fully initialized to point to the derived class's vtable.

Destructors: YES. Destructors must be virtual whenever polymorphic deletion through a base-class pointer is intended.

Q2: Can private methods be overridden in derived classes?

YES! C++ accessibility (public/private) is completely separate from dynamic dispatch (virtual). A derived class can override a private virtual method defined in a base class, which is the foundational mechanism behind the Template Method Pattern.

#include 
#include 

// Template Method Design Pattern utilizing Private Virtual Overriding
class AlgorithmPipeline {
public:
    void runPipeline() {
        stepOne();
        stepTwoCustom(); // Polymorphic dispatch call!
    }
    virtual ~AlgorithmPipeline() = default;
private:
    void stepOne() { std::cout << "Fixed Step 1 Executed\n"; }
    virtual void stepTwoCustom() = 0; // Private, yet overridable!
};

class CustomPipeline : public AlgorithmPipeline {
private:
    void stepTwoCustom() override {
        std::cout << "Customized Step 2 Executed\n";
    }
};

int main() {
    std::unique_ptr pipeline = std::make_unique();
    pipeline->runPipeline();
    return 0;
}

14. Object Slicing

Object Slicing occurs when an instance of a derived class is assigned or passed by value to a base class variable. The derived-specific attributes are "sliced off", leaving only the base sub-object behind.

#include 

class BaseData {
public:
    int x = 10;
    virtual void print() const { std::cout << "Base x: " << x << "\n"; }
};

class DerivedData : public BaseData {
public:
    int y = 20;
    void print() const override { std::cout << "Derived x: " << x << ", y: " << y << "\n"; }
};

void passByValue(BaseData obj) { // OBJECT SLICING OCCURS HERE!
    obj.print();
}

void passByReference(const BaseData& obj) { // PREVENTS SLICING
    obj.print();
}

int main() {
    DerivedData d;
    passByValue(d);     // Prints: "Base x: 10" (vptr reset to Base, y sliced out)
    passByReference(d); // Prints: "Derived x: 10, y: 20" (Polymorphism intact)
    return 0;
}

15. Function Hiding Mechanics

If a derived class declares a member function with the same name as a function in the base class, it hides all overloads of that function in the base class, regardless of parameter signatures, unless explicitly brought into scope using using.

#include 
#include 

class BaseOverload {
public:
    void display() { std::cout << "Base display no args\n"; }
    void display(int a) { std::cout << "Base display int: " << a << "\n"; }
};

class DerivedHider : public BaseOverload {
public:
    // Unhide Base methods:
    using BaseOverload::display;

    // Declaring a display function hides all BaseOverload::display overloads without the 'using' directive above
    void display(const std::string& s) {
        std::cout << "Derived display string: " << s << "\n";
    }
};

int main() {
    DerivedHider dh;
    dh.display("Hello"); // OK
    dh.display(100);     // OK because of 'using BaseOverload::display;'
    return 0;
}

16. final Specifier Usage

The final specifier prevents further inheritance of a class or overriding of a virtual method.

#include 

class BaseTerminal {
public:
    virtual void criticalStep() final {
        std::cout << "Core security operation, locked from overriding\n";
    }
    virtual ~BaseTerminal() = default;
};

class SecureSystem final : public BaseTerminal {
public:
    // void criticalStep() override; // ERROR: Cannot override final method
};

// class SubSystem : public SecureSystem {}; // ERROR: Cannot derive from final class

17. Quick Language Reference

Feature Syntax Key LLD & Technical Impact
Override Enforcement void func() override; Ensures matching signature with base virtual method at compile time.
Prevent Overriding/Derivation final keyword Locks virtual implementations or prevents a class from being inherited.
Dynamic Casting dynamic_cast(ptr) Safe downcasting using RTTI; returns nullptr on failure.
Static Casting static_cast(ptr) Fast downcasting without RTTI checks; unsafe if type mismatches.
Unhide Overloads using Base::func; Brings base class overloads into derived class scope.
