LeetCode 901 Medium Monotonic Stack / Online Streaming

Online Stock Span

Balanced DSA Master Notes: Real-time Streaming, Previous Greater Element, and Span Compression.

1. What is Being Asked?

Design an algorithm that collects daily price quotes for some stock and returns the span of that stock's price for the current day.

The span of the stock's price in one day is the maximum number of consecutive days (starting from today and going backward) for which the stock price was less than or equal to today's price.

Example Walkthrough:
• Day 1: next(100) → [100] → Span is 1 (only today).
• Day 2: next(80) → [100, 80] → 80 < 100 → Span is 1 (only today).
• Day 3: next(60) → [100, 80, 60] → Span is 1.
• Day 4: next(70) → [100, 80, 60, 70] → 70 ≥ 60 → Span is 2 (60 and 70).
• Day 5: next(60) → [100, 80, 60, 70, 60] → Span is 1.
• Day 6: next(75) → 75 ≥ 60, 70, 60 → Span is 4 (days 3, 4, 5, 6).
• Day 7: next(85) → 85 ≥ 75, 60, 70, 60, 80 → Span is 6.

2. 🧠 How Do I Recognize This Pattern?

We need the count of consecutive elements ≤ current price looking backward ↓ The span extends backward until we hit the Previous Greater Element ↓ Whenever smaller previous elements are seen, they will NEVER block any future day that is ≥ today ↓ We can compress past spans into a strictly decreasing stack: (price, span) ↓ Pattern: Monotonic Decreasing Stack (Online Stream)

3 Quick Clues in Future Problems:

  • Streaming / Online queries: Data arrives one element at a time via next(val) calls.
  • Looking back for a boundary: Finding the nearest element that breaks a monotonic property (Previous Greater/Smaller).
  • Consecutive range counting: Subsuming smaller intermediate elements into a cumulative weight or span.

3. Progressive Approaches (Brute → Optimal)

Approach 1 (Brute Force): Store All History & Linear Scan Backwards time: O(n) per call, O(n^2) total | space: O(n)

1. Core Idea & Intuition

Maintain an array of all historical prices. Every time next(price) is called, append price to the array and iterate backward from the end, incrementing span as long as previous prices are ≤ price. Stop when a strictly larger price is encountered or the beginning of the list is reached.

2. Multi-Language Code

class StockSpannerBruteForce:
    def __init__(self):
        self.prices = []

    def next(self, price: int) -> int:
        self.prices.append(price)
        span = 0
        # Scan backwards from today
        for p in reversed(self.prices):
            if p <= price:
                span += 1
            else:
                break
        return span
class StockSpannerBruteForce {
private:
    vector<int> prices;
public:
    StockSpannerBruteForce() {}

    int next(int price) {
        prices.push_back(price);
        int span = 0;
        for (int i = prices.size() - 1; i >= 0; --i) {
            if (prices[i] <= price) {
                span++;
            } else {
                break;
            }
        }
        return span;
    }
};
class StockSpannerBruteForce {
    private List<Integer> prices;

    public StockSpannerBruteForce() {
        prices = new ArrayList<>();
    }

    public int next(int price) {
        prices.add(price);
        int span = 0;
        for (int i = prices.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            if (prices.get(i) <= price) {
                span++;
            } else {
                break;
            }
        }
        return span;
    }
}
var StockSpannerBF = function() {
    this.prices = [];
};

StockSpannerBF.prototype.next = function(price) {
    this.prices.push(price);
    let span = 0;
    for (let i = this.prices.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        if (this.prices[i] <= price) {
            span++;
        } else {
            break;
        }
    }
    return span;
};

3. Complexity & Inefficiency

• Time Complexity: time: O(n) per call, O(n^2) total in the worst case (e.g. non-decreasing array like [10, 20, 30, 40, 50] where every call re-scans the full prefix).

• Space Complexity: space: O(n) to store all historical prices.

• Why we can do better: We repeatedly re-scan the exact same smaller numbers over and over again without remembering their aggregated spans.

Approach 2 (Optimal): Monotonic Decreasing Stack with Span Accumulation

time: O(1) amortized per call | space: O(n)

1. Core Idea & Intuition:
Instead of re-walking day by day, we maintain a stack of pairs: (price, span). The stack elements are kept strictly in decreasing order of price.

  • When a new price arrives, start with span = 1 (today itself).
  • While stack.top().price ≤ price: The current price is greater than or equal to the previous price peak. Pop it and absorb its span: span += popped_span!
  • Push (price, span) onto the stack and return span.

2. Multi-Language Code:

class StockSpanner:
    def __init__(self):
        # Monotonic stack storing pairs: (price, accumulated_span)
        self.stack = []

    def next(self, price: int) -> int:
        span = 1  # Today's day count

        # Pop all previous days with price <= current price and absorb their spans
        while self.stack and self.stack[-1][0] <= price:
            prev_price, prev_span = self.stack.pop()
            span += prev_span

        # Push the current price with its total compressed span
        self.stack.append((price, span))
        return span
class StockSpanner {
private:
    // Stack storing pairs: {price, accumulated_span}
    stack<pair<int, int>> st;
public:
    StockSpanner() {}

    int next(int price) {
        int span = 1;

        // Pop and absorb smaller/equal past spans
        while (!st.empty() && st.top().first <= price) {
            span += st.top().second;
            st.pop();
        }

        st.push({price, span});
        return span;
    }
};
class StockSpanner {
    // Stack stores int[] of size 2: [price, span]
    private Deque<int[]> stack;

    public StockSpanner() {
        stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    }

    public int next(int price) {
        int span = 1;

        while (!stack.isEmpty() && stack.peek()[0] <= price) {
            span += stack.pop()[1];
        }

        stack.push(new int[]{price, span});
        return span;
    }
}
var StockSpanner = function() {
    this.stack = []; // Array of [price, span]
};

StockSpanner.prototype.next = function(price) {
    let span = 1;

    while (this.stack.length > 0 && this.stack[this.stack.length - 1][0] <= price) {
        const [prevPrice, prevSpan] = this.stack.pop();
        span += prevSpan;
    }

    this.stack.push([price, span]);
    return span;
};

Important Line Explanations:

  • while stack and stack[-1][0] ≤ price: span += stack.pop()[1]: Since the current price dominates the top of the stack, any future day that exceeds price will automatically exceed the popped element as well. Thus, we safely discard the popped price and absorb its precomputed span into span in O(1) time.
  • stack.push((price, span)): We only keep strictly decreasing prices in the stack, ensuring the stack size remains minimal.

4. Detailed Step-by-Step Dry Runs

📋 Dry Run 1: Standard Stream of 7 Days ([100, 80, 60, 70, 60, 75, 85])
Call Price Initial Span Stack Before & Pop Actions Final Span Stack After [ (price, span) ]
1 100 1 Stack empty → No pops 1 [(100, 1)]
2 80 1 Top (100) > 80 → No pops 1 [(100, 1), (80, 1)]
3 60 1 Top (80) > 60 → No pops 1 [(100, 1), (80, 1), (60, 1)]
4 70 1 Top (60) ≤ 70 → Pop (60, 1), span = 1 + 1 = 2. Top (80) > 70 → Stop 2 [(100, 1), (80, 1), (70, 2)]
5 60 1 Top (70) > 60 → No pops 1 [(100, 1), (80, 1), (70, 2), (60, 1)]
6 75 1 Pop (60, 1) → span = 2.
Pop (70, 2) → span = 2 + 2 = 4.
Top (80) > 75 → Stop		 4 [(100, 1), (80, 1), (75, 4)]
7 85 1 Pop (75, 4) → span = 1 + 4 = 5.
Pop (80, 1) → span = 5 + 1 = 6.
Top (100) > 85 → Stop		 6 [(100, 1), (85, 6)]

Returned Spans: [1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 4, 6].

📋 Dry Run 2: Monotonically Increasing Prices ([10, 20, 30, 40, 50])

Demonstrating how each day collapses the entire previous stack in a single pop action:

Call Price Stack State Before Pop & Span Calculation Result Span Stack State After
1 10 [] Stack empty → span = 1 1 [(10, 1)]
2 20 [(10, 1)] Pop (10, 1) → span = 1 + 1 = 2 2 [(20, 2)]
3 30 [(20, 2)] Pop (20, 2) → span = 1 + 2 = 3 3 [(30, 3)]
4 40 [(30, 3)] Pop (30, 3) → span = 1 + 3 = 4 4 [(40, 4)]
5 50 [(40, 4)] Pop (40, 4) → span = 1 + 4 = 5 5 [(50, 5)]

Notice: The stack size never exceeds 1 element! Total pops across all 5 calls = 4. Amortized O(1) operations per call.

5. Complexity Derivation & Common Pitfalls

Metric Complexity Derivation
Time Complexity time: O(1) amortized Across n total calls to next(), each price is pushed onto the stack exactly once and popped at most once. Total operations across n calls is 2n, giving an amortized time of O(1) per query.
Space Complexity space: O(n) In the worst-case scenario (strictly decreasing stock prices like [100, 90, 80, 70]), no elements are popped, and the stack stores up to n pairs.
⚠️ Top 2 Mistakes to Avoid:
  1. Popping with < instead of ≤: The problem states that the span includes days where price was less than or equal to today's price. If you write stack[-1][0] < price, equal prices (e.g. [80, 80]) will not be absorbed, giving a span of 1 instead of 2.
  2. Storing only prices in the stack without cumulative spans: If you only store raw prices, when you pop a price, you lose count of all the earlier days that the popped price had previously absorbed! You MUST store the pair (price, span).

6. Practice Test Cases (Try Yourself!)

🎯 Practice Case 1: Strictly Decreasing Stream

Calls: [next(90), next(80), next(70), next(60)]

Expected Output: [1, 1, 1, 1]

What this tests: Every new price is strictly smaller than the previous, so no elements are ever popped. Stack grows to maximum size n.

🎯 Practice Case 2: Valley and Mountain Recovery with Duplicates

Calls: [next(30), next(30), next(20), next(20), next(35)]

Expected Output: [1, 2, 1, 2, 5]

What this tests: Tests equal-price absorption on consecutive days and verifying that a larger final price (35) collapses the entire valley into a total span of 5.

7. 🧠 Final Takeaway & 30-Second Recall

🧠 Quick Summary:
• Pattern: Monotonic Decreasing Stack with Span Accumulation.
• Key Invariant: Stack elements are stored as (price, span) in strictly descending order.
• Complexity: time: O(1) amortized per call, space: O(n).

⏱️ 30-Second Recall: For each incoming price, initialize span = 1. While the stack's top price is ≤ price, pop it and add its precomputed span to the current span. Push (price, span) onto the stack. Each element is pushed and popped at most once, achieving amortized O(1) time per query.

SQL Learning Series: Fundamentals to Interview Level

Filtering & Sorting

1. What is it?

📖 The Origin Story: Searching the Million-Row Warehouse Imagine running an e-commerce platform with 10 million products. When a user opens their phone and types "Red Nike Shoes under $100", sending all 10 million product files to the user's phone will freeze their app and crash your database server. We need a way to instruct the database storage layer to open disk files, evaluate conditions row-by-row, reject irrelevant data immediately, and send back only the matching 15 rows sorted by price. That is why SQL filtering (WHERE) and sorting (ORDER BY) are mandatory foundational building blocks of software engineering.

Simple Explanation

Filtering evaluates every single row in a table against boolean criteria and retains only the rows that evaluate to TRUE.

Sorting (ORDER BY) takes the filtered rows and arranges them in a specific logical sequence (e.g., lowest to highest price, latest to oldest date, or A to Z alphabetical order).

💡 Hinglish Summary: Core Idea Jab database me millions of rows hon, toh pure table ko fetch karna slow aur dangerous hota hai. Filtering (WHERE) ek chhalni (sieve) ki tarah kaam karta hai jo sirf zaroori rows ko pass hone deta hai. Sorting (ORDER BY) us filtered result ko ek proper order (jaise low-to-high price ya A-to-Z names) me arrange karta hai.

2. Syntax

SELECT column1, column2, column3
FROM table_name
WHERE condition1 AND/OR/NOT condition2
ORDER BY column1 [ASC|DESC], column2 [ASC|DESC];

Detailed Breakdown of Syntax Components

  • WHERE: Introduces row-level filtering logic. Evaluates *before* grouping or projections.
  • AND: Requires **both** surrounding conditions to evaluate to TRUE.
  • OR: Requires **at least one** surrounding condition to evaluate to TRUE.
  • NOT: Negates/flips a boolean condition.
  • BETWEEN low AND high: Inclusive range match check. Equivalent to val >= low AND val <= high.
  • IN (v1, v2, ...): Membership test against a discrete list of values.
  • LIKE 'pattern': Wildcard pattern matcher using % (multi-char) and _ (single-char).
  • IS NULL / IS NOT NULL: Special comparison checks reserved explicitly for unknown/missing states.
  • ORDER BY: Sorts output. Defaults to ASC (Ascending) if omitted.

3. Dataset for Examples

Table: employees

106AnneShirleyHR52000.00NULL2022-02-14
107RobertBruceSales82000.000.202017-07-04
108JaneDoeEngineering88000.000.052023-01-10

4. Individual Operator Examples (Exhaustive List)

1. Basic Filtering: WHERE

SELECT emp_id, first_name, last_name, department

emp_idfirst_namelast_namedepartment

5. Practice Problems (40 Questions)

Solve these questions on paper or in your SQL environment before checking the answers.

Level 1: Basic Filters (1–10)

  1. Retrieve all employees working in the 'Engineering' department.
  2. Find all employees earning a salary greater than or equal to $80,000.
  3. List all employees hired after January 1, 2020.
  4. Find all employees whose employee ID is equal to 105.
  5. List all employees whose salary is not equal to $62,000.
  6. Select all fields from `employees` sorted by `last_name` alphabetically.
  7. Find all employees whose salary is less than $60,000.
  8. List all employees hired before 2018-01-01.
  9. Find all employees whose employee ID is greater than 104.
  10. Select all employees ordered by `hire_date` from newest to oldest.

Level 2: Combining AND, OR, NOT (11–20)

  1. Find all employees in 'Sales' who earn less than $70,000.
  2. Find employees working in either 'HR' or 'Marketing'.
  3. Find employees in 'Engineering' OR 'Sales' who were hired before 2020-01-01.
  4. Find employees who do NOT work in 'HR' or 'Marketing'.
  5. Find employees whose first name is 'Sarah' AND last name is 'Connor'.
  6. Select all employees who are NOT in the 'Sales' department and have a salary above $80,000.
  7. Find employees who work in 'Engineering' AND earn more than $90,000.
  8. Find employees who work in 'Sales' OR have a salary under $60,000.
  9. Find employees who do NOT work in 'Sales' AND do NOT work in 'Engineering'.
  10. Find employees where department is 'Engineering' AND (salary > 100000 OR hire_date < '2016-01-01').

Level 3: BETWEEN, IN, LIKE (21–30)

  1. Find all employees with salaries between $60,000 and $90,000 (inclusive).
  2. Select all employees hired between '2018-01-01' and '2020-12-31'.
  3. Find all employees working in 'Sales', 'HR', or 'Marketing' using the `IN` operator.
  4. Retrieve all employees with IDs 101, 103, or 107.
  5. Find all employees whose last name starts with the letter 'S'.
  6. Select all employees whose first name ends with the letter 'a'.
  7. Find all employees whose first or last name contains the substring 'son'.
  8. Retrieve all employees whose first name is exactly 4 characters long using `LIKE` and `_`.
  9. List all employees whose department is NOT in 'Engineering' or 'HR'.
  10. Find all employees whose last name starts with 'B' or 'G'.

Level 4: NULL Handling & Advanced Sorting (31–40)

  1. Find all employees who receive a commission (`commission_pct` is not null).
  2. Retrieve all employees where the `commission_pct` is missing (`NULL`).
  3. List all employees who do NOT have a commission, sorted by `salary` descending.
  4. Select all employees sorted by `department` ascending, then by `hire_date` ascending.
  5. Retrieve the top 3 highest-paid employees (using `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT`).
  6. Find employees whose salary is between $50,000 and $100,000 AND whose commission percentage is `NULL`.
  7. Find employees whose last name starts with 'S' AND who either work in 'Sales' OR earn more than $90,000.
  8. Select employees ordered by `commission_pct` ascending with NULLs placed last.
  9. Find all employees whose first name contains 'e' as the second letter (e.g., 'Mercer').
  10. List all employees sorted by department ascending, and commission_pct descending.

6. What SQL Topic Should You Learn Next?

You should learn SQL Aggregations (GROUP BY, HAVING, COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) next.

Why?

Now that you know how to filter individual rows using WHERE, the natural next step in software architecture and data analysis is summarizing datasets. GROUP BY allows you to calculate metrics like "Total Revenue per Department" or "Average Salary per Role". Understanding how WHERE (row-level filtering) works before GROUP BY (group-level filtering with HAVING) is critical to mastering SQL query execution order!
title: Filtering & Sorting

content:
SQL Learning Series: Fundamentals to Interview Level

Aggregations & Grouping Masterclass

1. What is it?

📖 The Origin Story: The CEO's Executive Summary Imagine the CEO of an e-commerce platform walks into your engineering room and asks: "What was our total revenue last month, how many orders did we process, and what is the average order value per city?" If you send the CEO a raw dump of 500,000 individual transactional records, you will likely get reprimanded. Executives and analytical backends do not care about individual rows; they need summarized metrics. Aggregation functions condense hundreds of thousands of individual records into single scalar summary metrics, while GROUP BY categorizes data into buckets before summarizing.

Simple Explanation

An Aggregate Function takes multiple values from a column across many rows and computes a single summary result (such as counting total rows, calculating an average, or finding the maximum value).

GROUP BY splits a table into distinct buckets based on matching values in one or more specified columns, allowing aggregate functions to run independently on each bucket.

HAVING acts as a filter applied after aggregation occurs, allowing you to filter out entire groups based on summarized values (for example, keeping only departments whose average salary exceeds $80,000).

💡 Hinglish Summary: Core Idea Jab hume hazaron rows ka summary calculate karna ho (jaise total revenue, average salary, ya count of total students), tab hum Aggregate Functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN) use karte hain. **GROUP BY** data ko category-wise buckets me todta hai (jaise department-wise salary calculate karna). Aur **HAVING** grouped/aggregated summary result par filter lagane ke liye use hota hai (jaise un departments ko dikhao jinki avg salary > 80k hai).

2. Syntax & Logical Execution Order

SELECT column_name, COUNT(*), AVG(salary)
FROM employees
WHERE hire_date >= '2020-01-01'
GROUP BY column_name
HAVING AVG(salary) > 50000
ORDER BY AVG(salary) DESC;

Critical Software Engineering Concept: SQL Logical Processing Order

To avoid syntax errors, you must memorize how the SQL engine processes this query under the hood:

  1. FROM: Fetches the source table from disk.
  2. WHERE: Filters individual raw rows before grouping.
  3. GROUP BY: Groups the remaining rows into buckets based on unique values.
  4. HAVING: Filters out entire aggregated groups based on group calculations.
  5. SELECT: Projects the final output columns and executes remaining aggregations.
  6. DISTINCT: Eliminates duplicate rows from the final projection if specified.
  7. ORDER BY: Sorts the aggregated result set.
  8. LIMIT / OFFSET: Restricts output row count for pagination.

3. Datasets for Examples

Table 1: employees

emp_id first_name department salary commission_pct
101SarahEngineering95000.000.10
102JohnSales62000.000.25
103AlexEngineering110000.00NULL
104MariaMarketing58000.00NULL
105JamesSales75000.000.15
106AnneHR52000.00NULL
107RobertSales82000.000.20
108JaneEngineering88000.000.05

Table 2: orders

order_id customer_id status total_amount shipping_city
5001201COMPLETED250.00New York
5002202PENDING100.00Chicago
5003201COMPLETED1200.00New York
5004203CANCELLED50.00Los Angeles
5005204PROCESSING500.00Chicago
5006205COMPLETED300.00Houston
5007202CANCELLED150.00NULL

4. Individual Operator & Concept Examples (Exhaustive List)

1. Row Counting: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column)

Requirement: Count the total number of employees, and count how many employees earn a commission.

SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_employees, 
       COUNT(commission_pct) AS employees_with_commission
FROM employees;
total_employeesemployees_with_commission
85

Explanation: COUNT(*) counts all rows regardless of contents. COUNT(commission_pct) ignores the 3 NULL values in that column and returns 5.

2. Distinct Counting: COUNT(DISTINCT column)

Requirement: Count the total number of unique departments operating in the company.

SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT department) AS unique_dept_count 
FROM employees;
unique_dept_count
4

3. Summation: SUM(column)

Requirement: Calculate the total monthly payroll cost across all employees.

SELECT SUM(salary) AS total_payroll 
FROM employees;
total_payroll
622000.00

4. Average Calculation: AVG(column)

Requirement: Calculate the average salary of all employees.

SELECT AVG(salary) AS average_salary 
FROM employees;
average_salary
77750.00

5. Extremes Detection: MAX(column) and MIN(column)

Requirement: Find the highest and lowest salary paid by the company.

SELECT MAX(salary) AS highest_salary, 
       MIN(salary) AS lowest_salary 
FROM employees;
highest_salarylowest_salary
110000.0052000.00

6. Categorical Grouping: GROUP BY column

Requirement: Calculate the employee count and average salary for each department.

SELECT department, 
       COUNT(*) AS emp_count, 
       AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY department;
departmentemp_countavg_salary
Engineering397666.67
Sales373000.00
Marketing158000.00
HR152000.00

7. Multi-Column Grouping: GROUP BY col1, col2

Requirement: Find total revenue per shipping city and order status.

SELECT shipping_city, status, SUM(total_amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY shipping_city, status;
shipping_citystatusrevenue
New YorkCOMPLETED1450.00
ChicagoPENDING100.00
ChicagoPROCESSING500.00
Los AngelesCANCELLED50.00
HoustonCOMPLETED300.00
NULLCANCELLED150.00

8. Combining WHERE and GROUP BY

Requirement: Calculate total sales revenue per city, considering ONLY COMPLETED orders.

SELECT shipping_city, SUM(total_amount) AS completed_revenue
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'COMPLETED'
GROUP BY shipping_city;
shipping_citycompleted_revenue
New York1450.00
Houston300.00

9. Group Filtering: HAVING

Requirement: Find departments that have an average salary greater than $70,000.

SELECT department, AVG(salary) AS avg_dept_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
HAVING AVG(salary) > 70000;
departmentavg_dept_salary
Engineering97666.67
Sales73000.00

10. Full Stack Pipeline: WHERE + GROUP BY + HAVING + ORDER BY

Requirement: Find departments with more than 1 employee earning over $60,000, sorted by total payroll descending.

SELECT department, 
       COUNT(*) AS high_earner_count, 
       SUM(salary) AS total_dept_payroll
FROM employees
WHERE salary > 60000
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY total_dept_payroll DESC;
departmenthigh_earner_counttotal_dept_payroll
Engineering3293000.00
Sales3219000.00

5. Important Edge Cases & Common Mistakes

1. The Ultimate Interview Trap: WHERE vs HAVING

  • WHERE filters raw, individual rows before any grouping occurs. It cannot contain aggregate functions like AVG(salary).
  • HAVING filters summarized groups after GROUP BY completes. It requires aggregate expressions or columns present in the GROUP BY clause.

2. Non-Aggregated Columns in SELECT Clause Exception

In standard SQL (and strictly enforced in PostgreSQL), every column present in your SELECT clause MUST either be wrapped inside an Aggregate Function OR explicitly listed in the GROUP BY clause.

INCORRECT SQL (Fails with syntax error):

-- ERROR: column "first_name" must appear in the GROUP BY clause or be used in an aggregate function
SELECT department, first_name, AVG(salary)
FROM employees
GROUP BY department;

CORRECT SQL:

SELECT department, AVG(salary)
FROM employees
GROUP BY department;

3. Aggregate Functions and NULL Behavior

All aggregate functions except COUNT(*) automatically ignore NULL values during calculation!

  • If a column contains values (10, 20, NULL):
  • SUM = 30
  • AVG = 15 (calculates 30 / 2 valid rows, NOT 30 / 3)
  • If you want NULL treated as zero, wrap it in COALESCE: AVG(COALESCE(column, 0))

6. Practice Problems (30 Aggregate Queries)

Test your knowledge by attempting these queries. Answers are withheld so you can practice independently!

Level 1: Basic Aggregations (1–10)

  1. Write a query to calculate the total number of orders in the orders table.
  2. Find the total revenue generated from all orders combined.
  3. Calculate the average total amount spent per order.
  4. Find the maximum salary paid to any single employee.
  5. Find the minimum salary paid in the company.
  6. Count the total number of orders that have a status of 'COMPLETED'.
  7. Calculate the total salary spent specifically on the 'Sales' department.
  8. Count how many unique customers have placed at least one order.
  9. Find the average commission percentage among employees who earn a commission.
  10. Count the number of non-null entries in the shipping_city column of orders.

Level 2: Grouping with GROUP BY (11–20)

  1. Find the total number of employees working in each department.
  2. Calculate the average salary for each department.
  3. Find the maximum salary paid in each department.
  4. Calculate the total order revenue generated per shipping_city.
  5. Find the total count of orders grouped by their status.
  6. Calculate the average order value for each customer ID.
  7. Find the minimum and maximum order total per order status.
  8. Group employees by department and count how many earn a commission in each department.
  9. Calculate the total revenue per shipping city for COMPLETED orders only.
  10. Group orders by customer ID and calculate total spending per customer.

Level 3: Advanced Group Filtering with HAVING & Multi-Level Logic (21–30)

  1. Find departments that employ more than 2 people.
  2. Find departments where the average salary is greater than $80,000.
  3. List shipping cities that have generated more than $1,000 in total revenue.
  4. Find customers who have placed more than 1 order.
  5. Find departments where the minimum salary is above $55,000.
  6. List order statuses that have a total order count greater than 1, sorted by order count descending.
  7. Find departments whose total payroll expense exceeds $200,000.
  8. List shipping cities with an average order amount greater than $250, considering only COMPLETED orders.
  9. Find customers whose average order total is above $300, ordered by average order total descending.
  10. Find departments that have at least 2 employees earning over $70,000, and display their average salary.

7. Quick Revision Cheat Sheet

  • Execution Order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY.
  • COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col): COUNT(*) counts all rows; COUNT(col) ignores NULL values.
  • NULL Handling: SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX automatically ignore NULL values.
  • WHERE vs HAVING:
    • WHERE filters raw rows before grouping.
    • HAVING filters summarized groups after GROUP BY.
  • Grouping Rule: Any non-aggregated column in the SELECT clause MUST appear in the GROUP BY clause.

8. What SQL Topic Should You Learn Next?

You should learn SQL Joins (`INNER JOIN`, `LEFT JOIN`, `RIGHT JOIN`, `FULL OUTER JOIN`, `CROSS JOIN`, `SELF JOIN`) next.

Why?

Now that you can filter rows (`WHERE`) and summarize datasets (`GROUP BY`), real-world production databases rarely store all attributes in a single table. Data is normalized across multiple tables (e.g., `customers`, `orders`, `order_items`). Mastering Joins is essential for combining multiple relational tables together before running filtering and aggregations!

SQL Learning Series: Fundamentals to Interview Level

Data Insertion, Retrieval, Distinction, & Pagination

1. What is it?

📖 The Origin Story: Navigating Infinite Feeds Imagine opening an app like Instagram, Amazon, or Swiggy. Millions of items exist in their production database. If the mobile app requested all millions of records at once, the phone screen would freeze, consume hundreds of megabytes of mobile data, and crash the server thread. To build smooth digital experiences, applications load data in chunks (e.g., 10 items at a time as you scroll). In SQL, INSERT populates data, SELECT reads it, DISTINCT strips away duplicates, and LIMIT / OFFSET power backend API **pagination**.

Simple Explanation

INSERT adds new records (rows) into an existing table structure.

SELECT reads and retrieves specific columns or expressions from one or more tables.

DISTINCT filters out identical duplicate rows from the result set, returning unique values only.

LIMIT caps the maximum number of rows returned by a query.

OFFSET specifies how many initial rows to skip before starting to collect rows for output.

💡 Hinglish Summary: Core Idea INSERT se hum table me nayi rows daalte hain. **SELECT** se hum data ko fetch karte hain. **DISTINCT** duplicate rows ko hata kar sirf unique values dikhta hai. Aur jab table me hazaron records hon, toh UI par 10-10 records per page (pagination) dikhane ke liye hum **LIMIT** (kitne rows chahiye) aur **OFFSET** (kitne rows skip karne hain) ka combination use karte hain.

2. Syntax & Detailed Anatomy

1. Data Insertion (`INSERT INTO`)

INSERT INTO table_name (column1, column2, column3)
VALUES 
    (val1_a, val2_a, val3_a),
    (val1_b, val2_b, val3_b);

2. Data Retrieval & Pagination Pipeline

SELECT DISTINCT column1, column2
FROM table_name
ORDER BY column1 ASC
LIMIT page_size OFFSET skip_count;

Anatomy & Math of Offset Pagination

To implement Page $N$ pagination (where Page numbers start at 1, and size is $K$ items per page):

  • LIMIT = $K$
  • OFFSET = $(N - 1) \times K$
  • *Example (Page 1, 10 per page):* LIMIT 10 OFFSET 0 (Skips 0, gets rows 1–10)
  • *Example (Page 2, 10 per page):* LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10 (Skips first 10, gets rows 11–20)
  • *Example (Page 3, 10 per page):* LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20 (Skips first 20, gets rows 21–30)

3. Manual Dataset Setup (50 Sample Rows Insertion)

-- 1. Create Table Schema
CREATE TABLE students (

    full_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,

    city VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    marks INT CHECK (marks >= 0 AND marks <= 100),
    enrollment_year INT
);

-- 2. Insert 50 Rows Manually

6. Offset Pagination: LIMIT & OFFSET

-- Page 1 (Items 1-3): LIMIT 3 OFFSET 0

-- Page 2 (Items 4-6): LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3

student_idfull_name

7. Insert & Return Primary Key: INSERT INTO ... RETURNING

In backend engineering, when you insert a new record, you often need the generated auto-increment ID back immediately. PostgreSQL provides the RETURNING clause for this.

INSERT INTO students (student_id, full_name, course, city, marks, enrollment_year)
VALUES (53, 'Vijay Thalapathy', 'Cyber Security', 'Chennai', 89, 2023)
RETURNING student_id, full_name;

5. Edge Cases & Common Pitfalls

1. Unordered Pagination Bug (Intermittent Data Shift)

If you execute SELECT * FROM table LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10 without an explicit ORDER BY clause, the database does NOT guarantee row order. Between requests, physical page re-alignments can cause the API to return duplicate items across pages or miss items entirely!

Golden Rule: Always pair LIMIT and OFFSET with a deterministic ORDER BY clause (ideally sorting by Primary Key or Unique Column).

2. Performance Breakdown of High OFFSET Values

Executing OFFSET 1000000 LIMIT 10 forces the database server to read 1,000,010 records from disk, process them, discard the first 1,000,000, and return 10 rows. This can lead to significant query slowdowns on large tables.

Production Alternative: Use Cursor-based (Keyset) Pagination:

-- Fast Keyset Pagination using indexed Primary Key
SELECT * FROM students 
WHERE student_id > 1000000 
ORDER BY student_id ASC 
LIMIT 10;

3. DISTINCT Position Requirement

The DISTINCT keyword MUST immediately follow SELECT. You cannot place it inside individual column positions in standard SQL projections.

SELECT full_name, DISTINCT(city) FROM students; → ❌ Syntax Error

SELECT DISTINCT full_name, city FROM students; → ✅ Valid

6. Practice Questions (30 Queries)

Write out these queries based on the provided 50-row students dataset:

Level 1: Basic Retrieval & Distinction (1–10)

  1. Write a query to retrieve all records and columns from the students table.
  2. Select only the full_name and marks of all students.
  3. List all unique courses offered in the university without duplicates.
  4. Find all distinct cities where students reside.
  5. Fetch the top 5 students with the highest marks.
  6. Select the first 10 students enrolled in the database sorted by student_id ascending.
  7. Get a distinct list of enrollment years present in the system.
  8. Retrieve the names and cities of the 5 lowest-scoring students.
  9. Select distinct combinations of course and enrollment_year.
  10. Write a single INSERT statement to manually add 2 new student records.

Level 2: Filtering with Capping & Pagination (11–20)

  1. Find the top 3 scoring students from 'Delhi'.
  2. List the 5 newest students enrolled in 2023, ordered by student_id descending.
  3. Fetch Page 1 of students (5 records per page) sorted alphabetically by full_name.
  4. Fetch Page 2 of students (5 records per page) sorted alphabetically by full_name.
  5. Fetch Page 3 of students (10 records per page) sorted by student_id.
  6. Retrieve 5 students from 'Computer Science' skipping the first 2 highest scorers.
  7. List distinct cities for students who scored above 85 marks.
  8. Fetch the 4 highest scoring students enrolled in 2021.
  9. Retrieve 10 students starting from the 21st record in the table.
  10. Select distinct courses that have students from 'Mumbai'.

Level 3: Advanced Pagination & Application Scenarios (21–30)

  1. Write the exact query for Page 4 of a UI data table displaying 8 items per page, sorted by marks descending.
  2. Find the top 2 highest scoring students for each city (hint: use sorting, filtering, and limit per standalone query).
  3. Retrieve 5 students enrolled in 'Cyber Security' skipping the first 3 lowest scorers.
  4. Find all unique cities represented by students enrolled in 2022 or 2023.
  5. Calculate the SQL offset value required to display Page 7 when page size is set to 15 items per page.
  6. Fetch 3 students from 'Bangalore' with marks between 70 and 90, sorted by marks descending.
  7. Write an insert query using PostgreSQL's RETURNING clause to return the new student's ID and name.
  8. Select distinct enrollment years for students whose marks are greater than 90.
  9. Fetch the 5 most recently inserted students using student_id descending and LIMIT.
  10. Retrieve 10 items from students skipping 40 rows to inspect the tail end of the dataset.

7. Quick Revision Cheat Sheet

  • Execution Order: FROM → WHERE → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT / OFFSET.
  • Pagination Formula: OFFSET = (PageNumber - 1) * PageSize.
  • Multi-row Insert: Combine tuples using commas: INSERT INTO t VALUES (r1), (r2), (r3);
  • DISTINCT Scope: Evaluates across ALL selected projection columns combined.
  • Deterministic Rule: Never use LIMIT and OFFSET without an explicit ORDER BY clause.

8. What SQL Topic Should You Learn Next?

You should learn Data Mutation & Maintenance (`UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `TRUNCATE`, `DROP`) next.

Why?

Now that you know how to insert (`INSERT`) and retrieve (`SELECT`, `DISTINCT`, `LIMIT`) records, you must master how to safely modify existing rows (`UPDATE`) and remove obsolete data (`DELETE` vs `TRUNCATE` vs `DROP`) without corrupting production environments.

LeetCode 61 Medium Master Edition

Rotate List

Complete Technical & Mentorship Guide: Deep intuition, line-by-line breakdowns across all approaches, Circular Ring Ring-Linking, Modulo Optimization, and dry runs.

1. Problem Statement & Core Concept

Given the head of a linked list, rotate the list to the right by k places.

Rotate List Visualization: Example 1: head = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], k = 2 Original List: 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> NULL - Rotate 1 time right: 5 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> NULL - Rotate 2 times right: 4 -> 5 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> NULL Output: [4, 5, 1, 2, 3] --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Example 2: head = [0, 1, 2], k = 4 Length = 3. Notice that rotating 3 times returns the list to its ORIGINAL state! Therefore, k = 4 rotations is equivalent to k % length = 4 % 3 = 1 rotation. - Rotate 1 time right: 2 -> 0 -> 1 -> NULL Output: [2, 0, 1]

Constraints & Requirements

  • The number of nodes in the list is in the range [0, 500].
  • -100 <= Node.val <= 100
  • 0 <= k <= 2 * 10^9 (Notice k can be much larger than list length!).

2. Approach 1: Naive Step-by-Step Traversal (O(k * N) Time)

🧭 Senior Mentor Explanation: The Brute Force Idea

Hey junior, when someone says "rotate right by 1 position", what does that actually mean for a linked list?

It means taking the last node of the list, detaching it from its second-to-last neighbor, and placing it right in front of the current head!

So the brute force idea is: "Why not repeat this single-step rotation process k times?"

  1. Loop k times.
  2. In each iteration, traverse to the second-to-last node.
  3. Detach the last node and make it the new head.
Hinglish Explanation

Sabse naive tarika yeh hai ki hum 1-step rotation ko k baar repeat karein. Har ek step me, hum pure list par traverse karke second-last node tak jayenge, aakhiri node ko Tod kar aage head par laga denge. Par socho, agar k = 2 * 10^9 hua, toh code O(k * N) ki wajah se TLE (Time Limit Exceeded) de dega.

Line-by-Line Code Breakdown (Approach 1)

  1. if not head or not head.next or k == 0: return head: If the list is empty, has 1 node, or k = 0, no rotation is needed.
  2. for _ in range(k):: Repeat single-node rotation k times.
  3. prev, curr = None, head: Initialize pointers to find the second-to-last node.
  4. while curr.next: prev = curr; curr = curr.next: Traverse until curr sits on the last node and prev sits on second-to-last.
  5. prev.next = None: Cut off the last node from the list end.
  6. curr.next = head: Attach the old last node in front of the current head.
  7. head = curr: Update head pointer to the newly attached node.

Naive Simulation Implementation

class NaiveSolution:
    def rotateRight(self, head: Optional[ListNode], k: int) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        if not head or not head.next or k == 0:
            return head

        # Simulate 1-step rotation k times O(k * N)
        for _ in range(k):
            prev, curr = None, head
            while curr.next:
                prev = curr
                curr = curr.next

            prev.next = None
            curr.next = head
            head = curr

        return head
class NaiveSolution {
public:
    ListNode* rotateRight(ListNode* head, int k) {
        if (!head || !head->next || k == 0) return head;

        for (int i = 0; i < k; ++i) {
            ListNode* prev = nullptr;
            ListNode* curr = head;
            while (curr->next) {
                prev = curr;
                curr = curr->next;
            }
            prev->next = nullptr;
            curr->next = head;
            head = curr;
        }
        return head;
    }
};
class NaiveSolution {
    public ListNode rotateRight(ListNode head, int k) {
        if (head == null || head.next == null || k == 0) return head;

        for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) {
            ListNode prev = null;
            ListNode curr = head;
            while (curr.next != null) {
                prev = curr;
                curr = curr.next;
            }
            prev.next = null;
            curr.next = head;
            head = curr;
        }
        return head;
    }
}
var rotateRightNaive = function(head, k) {
    if (!head || !head.next || k === 0) return head;

    for (let i = 0; i < k; i++) {
        let prev = null;
        let curr = head;
        while (curr.next) {
            prev = curr;
            curr = curr.next;
        }
        prev.next = null;
        curr.next = head;
        head = curr;
    }
    return head;
};

3. Approach 2: Optimal Circular Ring-Linking Technique (O(N) Time, O(1) Space)

💡 Senior Mentor Explanation: Turning a Line into a Ring

Junior, can we do this in pure O(N) Linear Time regardless of how big k is?

Look at what rotation actually does mathematically:

  1. If a list has length L = 5, rotating it 5 times brings it back to its original state!
  2. Therefore, rotating k times is IDENTICAL to rotating k % L times! (e.g. k = 2,000,000,002 on size 5 becomes 2000000002 % 5 = 2 rotations!).

The Ring Technique Algorithm:

  1. Step 1 — Find Length & Tail: Traverse to the end of the list to count total length L and find the tail node.
  2. Step 2 — Modulo Reduction: Compute effective rotations k = k % L. If k == 0, return head immediately!
  3. Step 3 — Connect Tail to Head (Form a Ring!): Connect tail.next = head. Now the list is a circular ring!
  4. Step 4 — Find New Cut Point: The new head will be at index L - k. The new tail will be at index L - k - 1.
  5. Step 5 — Sever the Ring: Traverse L - k steps from the ring start, break the link (new_tail.next = None), and return new_head!
Hinglish Explanation

Subah ka bhula raat ko ghar aaye! Pehle list ki length L aur tail node dhoond lo. k = k % L karke extra rotations ko khatam kar do. Phir tail ko head se jod kar ek Circular Ring bana lo (tail.next = head). Ab bas hume ring ko sahi jagah par todna hai! Naya head L - k index par hoga. Naye tail ke next ko None set karke ring ko khol do. Ho gaya O(N) me solve!

Circular Ring Linking Mechanics: Input: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], k = 2 Step 1: Traverse to find length L = 5 and tail = Node(5). Step 2: Effective rotations k = 2 % 5 = 2. Step 3: Connect tail to head -> 5.next = 1 (Forms Circular Ring: 1->2->3->4->5->1...) Step 4: Find new cut point. - New Tail location = L - k - 1 = 5 - 2 - 1 = index 2 (Node 3). - New Head location = L - k = 5 - 2 = index 3 (Node 4). Step 5: Sever Ring at Node 3. - new_head = Node(4) - Node(3).next = NULL Result: 4 -> 5 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> NULL Auxiliary Memory: O(1) Extra Space!

Line-by-Line Code Breakdown (Approach 2)

  1. if not head or not head.next or k == 0: return head: Guard clause for edge cases (empty list, single node, or 0 rotations).
  2. length = 1, tail = head: Start counting length from 1, initializing tail pointer at head.
  3. while tail.next: length += 1; tail = tail.next: Traverse to the last node while counting total length.
  4. k = k % length: Reduce k using modulo. If k == 0, no shift occurs; return head.
  5. tail.next = head: FORM RING! Connect tail to head, creating a circular linked list.
  6. steps_to_new_tail = length - k: Calculate how many nodes from head to reach the new tail position.
  7. new_tail = tail: Start pointer for ring severance traversal.
  8. for _ in range(steps_to_new_tail): new_tail = new_tail.next: Advance pointer to the node that will become the new end of the list.
  9. new_head = new_tail.next: The node following new_tail becomes the new starting head.
  10. new_tail.next = None: SEVER RING! Break the circular link to form a valid linear linked list again.
  11. return new_head: Return the new rotated head.

Optimal Circular Ring Implementation

class Solution:
    def rotateRight(self, head: Optional[ListNode], k: int) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        if not head or not head.next or k == 0:
            return head

        # Step 1: Compute length and find tail
        length = 1
        tail = head
        while tail.next:
            length += 1
            tail = tail.next

        # Step 2: Modulo reduction
        k = k % length
        if k == 0:
            return head

        # HIGHLIGHT: Step 3 - Connect tail to head to form a circular ring
        tail.next = head

        # Step 4: Find new tail at position (length - k) from ring start
        steps_to_new_tail = length - k
        new_tail = tail
        for _ in range(steps_to_new_tail):
            new_tail = new_tail.next

        # HIGHLIGHT: Step 5 - Sever the ring to form new linear list
        new_head = new_tail.next
        new_tail.next = None

        return new_head
class Solution {
public:
    ListNode* rotateRight(ListNode* head, int k) {
        if (!head || !head->next || k == 0) return head;

        int length = 1;
        ListNode* tail = head;
        while (tail->next) {
            length++;
            tail = tail->next;
        }

        k = k % length;
        if (k == 0) return head;

        // Connect ring
        tail->next = head;

        int stepsToNewTail = length - k;
        ListNode* newTail = tail;
        for (int i = 0; i < stepsToNewTail; ++i) {
            newTail = newTail->next;
        }

        ListNode* newHead = newTail->next;
        newTail->next = nullptr;

        return newHead;
    }
};
class Solution {
    public ListNode rotateRight(ListNode head, int k) {
        if (head == null || head.next == null || k == 0) return head;

        int length = 1;
        ListNode tail = head;
        while (tail.next != null) {
            length++;
            tail = tail.next;
        }

        k = k % length;
        if (k == 0) return head;

        // Connect ring
        tail.next = head;

        int stepsToNewTail = length - k;
        ListNode newTail = tail;
        for (int i = 0; i < stepsToNewTail; i++) {
            newTail = newTail.next;
        }

        ListNode newHead = newTail.next;
        newTail.next = null;

        return newHead;
    }
}
var rotateRight = function(head, k) {
    if (!head || !head.next || k === 0) return head;

    let length = 1;
    let tail = head;
    while (tail.next) {
        length++;
        tail = tail.next;
    }

    k = k % length;
    if (k === 0) return head;

    // Connect ring
    tail.next = head;

    let stepsToNewTail = length - k;
    let newTail = tail;
    for (let i = 0; i < stepsToNewTail; i++) {
        newTail = newTail.next;
    }

    let newHead = newTail.next;
    newTail.next = null;

    return newHead;
};

4. Boundary Traps & Edge Case Analysis

⚠️ Common Traps & Edge Cases

1. k is a Multiple of Length (e.g. k = 10, length = 5):
k % length = 10 % 5 = 0. Rotating 5 or 10 times results in the exact original list. Modulo check if k == 0: return head prevents forming and breaking the ring unnecessarily.

2. Empty List or Single Node List (head == None or head.next == None):
Dividing by length 0 or attempting tail.next on null causes runtime crashes. Early guard check if not head or not head.next: return head safely short-circuits execution.

3. k Extremely Large (k = 2 * 10^9):
Without modulo reduction, looping 2 * 10^9 times causes Time Limit Exceeded. k % length reduces the iteration bound to at most length - 1 steps!

5. Detailed Dry Run Walkthroughs

📋 Dry Run 1: Standard Case — head = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], k = 2
Processing [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], k = 2: Step 1: Compute length & find tail: - tail starts at Node(1). - Loop advances tail to Node(5). - Total length = 5. Step 2: Modulo Reduction: - k = 2 % 5 = 2. Step 3: Connect Ring: - tail.next = head => Node(5).next = Node(1). - List is now circular: 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 1... Step 4: Find new tail: - steps_to_new_tail = length - k = 5 - 2 = 3. - new_tail starts at tail = Node(5). * Iteration 1: new_tail = Node(1) * Iteration 2: new_tail = Node(2) * Iteration 3: new_tail = Node(3) Step 5: Sever Ring: - new_head = new_tail.next = Node(4) - new_tail.next = None (Node(3).next = NULL) Final Output = [4, 5, 1, 2, 3]
📋 Dry Run 2: k Larger than Length — head = [0, 1, 2], k = 4
Processing [0, 1, 2], k = 4: Step 1: Compute length & find tail: - tail advances to Node(2). - Total length = 3. Step 2: Modulo Reduction: - k = 4 % 3 = 1. Step 3: Connect Ring: - tail.next = head => Node(2).next = Node(0). - Ring: 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 0... Step 4: Find new tail: - steps_to_new_tail = 3 - 1 = 2. - new_tail starts at Node(2). * Iteration 1: new_tail = Node(0) * Iteration 2: new_tail = Node(1) Step 5: Sever Ring: - new_head = Node(1).next = Node(2) - new_tail.next = None (Node(1).next = NULL) Final Output = [2, 0, 1]
📋 Dry Run 3: Multiple of Length — head = [1, 2], k = 2
Processing [1, 2], k = 2: - Length = 2, tail = Node(2). - k = 2 % 2 = 0. - Condition `if k == 0` triggers! Returns head [1, 2] immediately without modifying pointers.

6. Complexity Analysis Performance Metrics

Approach Category Time Complexity Space Complexity List Pass Count Performance Evaluation Rating
Approach 1: Naive Simulation O(k * N) O(1) Auxiliary k Passes Sub-optimal / TLE. Fails for large k (e.g. k = 2 * 10^9).
Approach 2: Circular Ring-Linking (Optimal) O(N) O(1) Auxiliary 1 Pass (N steps) Absolute Production Standard. Solves in single linear pass by forming a ring and severing at L - (k % L). Optimal execution time and space bounds.

LeetCode 875 Medium Master Edition

Koko Eating Bananas

Complete Technical & Mentorship Guide: Monotonic search spaces, ceiling integer math tricks, Linear Scanning vs Binary Search on Answer, overflow prevention, and detailed dry runs.

1. Problem Statement & Core Concept

Koko loves to eat bananas. There are n piles of bananas, the i-th pile has piles[i] bananas. The guards have gone and will come back in h hours.

Koko can decide her bananas-per-hour eating speed of k. Each hour, she chooses some pile of bananas and eats k bananas from that pile. If the pile has less than k bananas, she eats all of them instead and will not eat any more bananas during this hour.

Koko likes to eat slowly but still wants to finish eating all the bananas before the guards return.

Return the minimum integer k such that she can eat all the bananas within h hours.

Problem Examples: Example 1: piles = [3, 6, 7, 11], h = 8 - Test speed k = 4: Pile 3: ⌈3 / 4⌉ = 1 hour Pile 6: ⌈6 / 4⌉ = 2 hours Pile 7: ⌈7 / 4⌉ = 2 hours Pile 11: ⌈11 / 4⌉ = 3 hours Total hours = 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 8 <= 8 (Valid!) - Speeds < 4 require more than 8 hours. Output: 4 --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Example 2: piles = [30, 11, 23, 4, 20], h = 5 - h == len(piles) = 5. Koko has exactly 1 hour per pile! - She must finish each pile in a single hour -> k must be >= max(piles) = 30. Output: 30 --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Example 3: piles = [30, 11, 23, 4, 20], h = 6 - Speed k = 23: ⌈30/23⌉ = 2, ⌈11/23⌉ = 1, ⌈23/23⌉ = 1, ⌈4/23⌉ = 1, ⌈20/23⌉ = 1 Total hours = 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6 <= 6. Output: 23


Constraints & Mathematical Range Bounds

  • 1 <= piles.length <= 10^4
  • piles.length <= h <= 10^9
  • 1 <= piles[i] <= 10^9
  • Minimum Possible Speed: k_min = 1 (cannot eat 0 bananas per hour).
  • Maximum Possible Speed: k_max = max(piles) (eating faster than the biggest pile in 1 hour provides zero time advantage due to the 1-pile-per-hour restriction).

2. Approach 1: Linear Search Over Answer Space (Brute Force O(max(P) * N))

🧭 Senior Mentor Explanation: The Brute Force Idea

Hey junior, when a problem asks for the "minimum speed k that satisfies a condition", the most intuitive approach is:

"Why not start testing speed from k = 1 and increment by 1 until Koko finishes in <= h hours?"

For any speed k, the hours required to finish pile p is ceil(p / k).

Integer Ceiling Division Trick: In code without using floating-point math:
ceil(p / k) = (p + k - 1) // k.

Hinglish Explanation

Sabse pehle dimaag me yahi aata hai ki hum speed = 1 se shuru karein aur ek-ek karke speed badhayein jab tak total time h hours ke barabar ya usse kam na ho jaye. Lekin agar max pile 10^9 hai, toh loop 1 billion baar chalega, jisse code TLE (Time Limit Exceeded) de dega.

Line-by-Line Code Breakdown (Approach 1)

  1. speed = 1: Start checking from the slowest possible eating rate.
  2. while True:: Keep testing speeds until a valid one is found.
  3. hours = sum((p + speed - 1) // speed for p in piles): Calculate total hours taken to eat all piles at current speed using ceiling integer arithmetic.
  4. if hours <= h: return speed: The very first speed where total hours is at most h is guaranteed to be the minimum speed!
  5. speed += 1: Increment candidate speed by 1 and repeat.

Linear Search Implementation

class LinearSearchSolution:
    def minEatingSpeed(self, piles: list[int], h: int) -> int:
        speed = 1
        while True:
            # Calculate hours needed for current speed using integer ceiling
            hours = 0
            for p in piles:
                hours += (p + speed - 1) // speed

            if hours <= h:
                return speed
            speed += 1
class LinearSearchSolution {
public:
    int minEatingSpeed(vector<int>& piles, int h) {
        int speed = 1;
        while (true) {
            long long hours = 0;
            for (int p : piles) {
                hours += (p + speed - 1LL) / speed;
            }
            if (hours <= h) return speed;
            speed++;
        }
    }
};
class LinearSearchSolution {
    public int minEatingSpeed(int[] piles, int h) {
        int speed = 1;
        while (true) {
            long hours = 0;
            for (int p : piles) {
                hours += (p + speed - 1L) / speed;
            }
            if (hours <= h) return speed;
            speed++;
        }
    }
}
var minEatingSpeedLinear = function(piles, h) {
    let speed = 1;
    while (true) {
        let hours = 0;
        for (let p of piles) {
            hours += Math.ceil(p / speed);
        }
        if (hours <= h) return speed;
        speed++;
    }
};

3. Approach 2: Optimal Binary Search on Answer Space (O(N log(max(P))))

💡 Senior Mentor Explanation: The Monotonicity Discovery

Junior, look at how the total time required behaves as speed k increases:

Speed (k) vs Feasibility (hours <= h): k = 1 -> hours = 27 (> 8) -> FALSE (Too slow) k = 2 -> hours = 15 (> 8) -> FALSE (Too slow) k = 3 -> hours = 10 (> 8) -> FALSE (Too slow) k = 4 -> hours = 8 (<= 8) -> TRUE (Valid! -> FIRST TRUE) k = 5 -> hours = 8 (<= 8) -> TRUE (Valid) k = 6 -> hours = 6 (<= 8) -> TRUE (Valid) ... k = max -> hours = len(piles) -> TRUE (Valid) Feasibility Pattern: [ F, F, F, T, T, T, T, T ... ] ^ We want the FIRST True!

Because the hours function is monotonically non-increasing (higher speed always results in equal or fewer hours), the boolean predicate canFinish(k) produces a sorted boolean range: [False, False, ..., True, True, True].

Whenever you see a monotonic search space, you can immediately apply BINARY SEARCH on the answer!

  1. Set search bounds: left = 1, right = max(piles).
  2. Compute midpoint speed mid = left + (right - left) // 2.
  3. Evaluate if Koko can finish at speed mid in <= h hours:
    • If TRUE (Feasible): Speed mid works! But maybe a slower speed also works? Set right = mid (keep mid as a candidate answer in our search range).
    • If FALSE (Infeasible): Speed mid is too slow! Any speed <= mid will also be too slow. Set left = mid + 1.
  4. When left == right, the loop terminates at the exact minimum feasible speed!
Hinglish Explanation

Speed badhane par time humesha GHAT-TA hai. Isliye hamara answer space sorted hai (pehle saare False aayenge, fir saare True aayenge). Binary Search me agar mid speed par Koko finish kar leti hai, toh matlab mid valid hai, par hum aur choti speed check karne ke liye right = mid kar dete hain. Agar finish nahi kar paati, toh hum left = mid + 1 karte hain. Isse 10^9 ka search space sirf 30 steps me solve ho jata hai!



Line-by-Line Code Breakdown (Approach 2)

  1. left, right = 1, max(piles): The minimum possible eating speed is 1; the maximum useful speed is the size of the largest pile.
  2. while left < right:: Loop until the search interval narrows down to a single candidate.
  3. mid = (left + right) // 2: Candidate speed being tested.
  4. hours = sum((p + mid - 1) // mid for p in piles): Calculate the exact total hours consumed by all piles at speed mid.
  5. if hours <= h: right = mid: If feasible, search for an even smaller speed on the left half while retaining mid.
  6. else: left = mid + 1: If infeasible, discard mid and everything below it by shifting the left boundary.
  7. return left: When left == right, left is the minimum valid speed.

Optimal Binary Search Implementation

class Solution:
    def minEatingSpeed(self, piles: list[int], h: int) -> int:
        left = 1
        right = max(piles)

        while left < right:
            mid = (left + right) // 2
            
            # Calculate total hours at eating rate 'mid'
            hours = 0
            for p in piles:
                hours += (p + mid - 1) // mid

            # HIGHLIGHT: Binary search condition on feasibility
            if hours <= h:
                right = mid      # Mid is valid, look for smaller valid speed
            else:
                left = mid + 1   # Mid is too slow, speed must be higher

        return left
class Solution {
public:
    int minEatingSpeed(vector<int>& piles, int h) {
        int left = 1;
        int right = *max_element(piles.begin(), piles.end());

        while (left < right) {
            int mid = left + (right - left) / 2;

            long long hours = 0;
            for (int p : piles) {
                hours += (p + mid - 1LL) / mid;
            }

            if (hours <= h) {
                right = mid;
            } else {
                left = mid + 1;
            }
        }

        return left;
    }
};
class Solution {
    public int minEatingSpeed(int[] piles, int h) {
        int left = 1;
        int right = 1;
        for (int p : piles) {
            if (p > right) right = p;
        }

        while (left < right) {
            int mid = left + (right - left) / 2;

            long hours = 0;
            for (int p : piles) {
                hours += (p + mid - 1L) / mid;
            }

            if (hours <= h) {
                right = mid;
            } else {
                left = mid + 1;
            }
        }

        return left;
    }
}
var minEatingSpeed = function(piles, h) {
    let left = 1;
    let right = Math.max(...piles);

    while (left < right) {
        let mid = Math.floor((left + right) / 2);

        let hours = 0;
        for (let p of piles) {
            hours += Math.ceil(p / mid);
        }

        if (hours <= h) {
            right = mid;
        } else {
            left = mid + 1;
        }
    }

    return left;
};

4. Boundary Traps & Integer Overflow Prevention

⚠️ Common Traps & 64-Bit Overflows

1. 64-bit Integer Overflow in C++ and Java:
If piles[i] = 10^9 and piles.length = 10^4 with a slow speed like mid = 1, the accumulated hours will be 10^4 * 10^9 = 10^13! This exceeds the 32-bit signed integer limit (2 * 10^9). In C++ and Java, the hours accumulator MUST be long long / long.

2. Integer Ceiling Addition Overflow:
When doing (p + mid - 1) / mid, if p = 2 * 10^9 and mid = 2 * 10^9, the addition p + mid can overflow a 32-bit integer. Write it with 1LL in C++: (p + mid - 1LL) / mid.

3. Range Bounds Selection:
left must start at 1, NEVER 0 (to prevent division-by-zero crashes). right can safely be max(piles).

5. Detailed Dry Run Walkthroughs

📋 Dry Run 1: piles = [3, 6, 7, 11], h = 8
Search Range Setup: left = 1, right = max([3, 6, 7, 11]) = 11 • Pass 1: mid = (1 + 11) // 2 = 6 Calculate hours for speed 6: - ⌈3 / 6⌉ = 1 - ⌈6 / 6⌉ = 1 - ⌈7 / 6⌉ = 2 - ⌈11 / 6⌉ = 2 Total hours = 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 6 <= 8 (Feasible!) right = mid = 6 -> Search range: [1, 6] • Pass 2: mid = (1 + 6) // 2 = 3 Calculate hours for speed 3: - ⌈3 / 3⌉ = 1 - ⌈6 / 3⌉ = 2 - ⌈7 / 3⌉ = 3 - ⌈11 / 3⌉ = 4 Total hours = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 > 8 (Too slow!) left = mid + 1 = 4 -> Search range: [4, 6] • Pass 3: mid = (4 + 6) // 2 = 5 Calculate hours for speed 5: - ⌈3 / 5⌉ = 1 - ⌈6 / 5⌉ = 2 - ⌈7 / 5⌉ = 2 - ⌈11 / 5⌉ = 3 Total hours = 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 8 <= 8 (Feasible!) right = mid = 5 -> Search range: [4, 5] • Pass 4: mid = (4 + 5) // 2 = 4 Calculate hours for speed 4: - ⌈3 / 4⌉ = 1 - ⌈6 / 4⌉ = 2 - ⌈7 / 4⌉ = 2 - ⌈11 / 4⌉ = 3 Total hours = 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 8 <= 8 (Feasible!) right = mid = 4 -> Search range: [4, 4] • Loop Ends (left == right == 4) Final Result = 4
📋 Dry Run 2: piles = [30, 11, 23, 4, 20], h = 6
Search Range: left = 1, right = 30 • Pass 1: mid = 15 Hours = ⌈30/15⌉ + ⌈11/15⌉ + ⌈23/15⌉ + ⌈4/15⌉ + ⌈20/15⌉ = 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 8 > 6 (Too slow) left = 16 -> Range: [16, 30] • Pass 2: mid = 23 Hours = ⌈30/23⌉ + ⌈11/23⌉ + ⌈23/23⌉ + ⌈4/23⌉ + ⌈20/23⌉ = 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6 <= 6 (Feasible!) right = 23 -> Range: [16, 23] • Pass 3: mid = 19 Hours = ⌈30/19⌉ + ⌈11/19⌉ + ⌈23/19⌉ + ⌈4/19⌉ + ⌈20/19⌉ = 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 8 > 6 (Too slow) left = 20 -> Range: [20, 23] • Pass 4: mid = 21 Hours = 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 7 > 6 (Too slow) left = 22 -> Range: [22, 23] • Pass 5: mid = 22 Hours = 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 7 > 6 (Too slow) left = 23 -> Range: [23, 23] Final Result = 23

6. Complexity Analysis Performance Metrics

Approach Category Time Complexity Space Complexity Iteration Count Performance Evaluation Rating
Approach 1: Linear Search Over Speeds O(max(P) * N) O(1) Auxiliary Up to 10^9 loops Sub-optimal / TLE. Checks every integer speed sequentially. Exceeds time limit.
Approach 2: Binary Search on Answer (Optimal) O(N log(max(P))) O(1) Auxiliary log2(10^9) ≈ 30 loops Absolute Production Standard. Halves search space on every iteration. Solves within a few milliseconds.

LeetCode 205 Easy Master Edition

Isomorphic Strings

Complete Technical & Mentorship Guide: Bijection invariants, one-to-one & onto mapping rules, dual hash maps, first-occurrence transformation arrays, and dry runs.

1. Problem Statement & Core Concept

Given two strings s and t, determine if they are isomorphic.

Two strings s and t are isomorphic if the characters in s can be replaced to get t.

All occurrences of a character must be replaced with another character while preserving the order of characters. No two characters may map to the same character, but a character may map to itself.

Mathematical Definition (Bijection / Bijective Mapping): A valid mapping f: s -> t MUST satisfy two strict conditions: 1. Injective (One-to-One): If s[i] == s[j], then t[i] MUST equal t[j]. (No single character in 's' can map to two different characters in 't'). 2. Surjective / No Collisions (Onto): If s[i] != s[j], then t[i] MUST NOT equal t[j]. (No two different characters in 's' can map to the SAME character in 't'). --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Example 1: s = "egg", t = "add" Mapping: 'e' -> 'a', 'g' -> 'd' Both conditions satisfied! Output: true Example 2: s = "foo", t = "bar" Mapping: 'f' -> 'b', 'o' -> 'a', then 'o' tries to map to 'r'! 'o' cannot map to both 'a' and 'r' (Violates Rule 1). Output: false Example 3: s = "paper", t = "title" Mapping: 'p' -> 't', 'a' -> 'i', 'p' -> 't' (consistent), 'e' -> 'l', 'r' -> 'e' Output: true Example 4: s = "badc", t = "baba" Mapping: 'b' -> 'b', 'a' -> 'a', 'd' -> 'b' (COLLISION: 'b' and 'd' both map to 'b'!) Violates Rule 2. Output: false

Constraints & Requirements

  • 1 <= s.length <= 5 * 10^4
  • t.length == s.length
  • s and t consist of any valid ASCII characters.

2. Approach 1: Dual Hash Map / Two-Way Bijection Tracking (O(N) Time, O(1) Space)

🧭 Senior Mentor Explanation: Why One Hash Map is NOT Enough

Hey junior, the most common trap people fall into is using only ONE hash map map_s_to_t. Let's see why that fails:

Take s = "badc" and t = "baba":

  • 'b' -> 'b' (stored in map)
  • 'a' -> 'a' (stored in map)
  • 'd' is not in map, so we map 'd' -> 'b'.

A single map thinks this is fine! But notice: both 'b' and 'd' are now mapping to 'b'! That violates the rule that no two characters may map to the same character.

The Solution: Maintain TWO maps (or one map and one set):

  1. map_s_to_t: Maps character from s to character in t.
  2. map_t_to_s: Maps character from t to character in s (guarantees no collisions!).
Hinglish Explanation

Single map se sirf yeh check hota hai ki s ka letter do alag letters me na badle. Lekin yeh bhi check karna padta hai ki t ka same letter do alag s ke letters se na aaya ho (jaise 'b' aur 'd' dono 'b' me map ho gaye). Isliye hum Two-Way Map use karte hain: s -> t aur t -> s.

Line-by-Line Code Breakdown (Approach 1)

  1. map_st = {}, map_ts = {}: Initialize two hash maps for bi-directional character translation.
  2. for c1, c2 in zip(s, t):: Iterate simultaneously through paired characters from both strings.
  3. if (c1 in map_st and map_st[c1] != c2) or (c2 in map_ts and map_ts[c2] != c1): return False: If c1 was mapped to something other than c2, OR c2 was mapped from something other than c1, the bijection is broken! Return False immediately.
  4. map_st[c1] = c2; map_ts[c2] = c1: Record the two-way relationship.
  5. return True: If all character pairs satisfy the bijection, return True.

Dual Hash Map Implementation

class DualMapSolution:
    def isIsomorphic(self, s: str, t: str) -> bool:
        map_st = {}
        map_ts = {}

        for c1, c2 in zip(s, t):
            # HIGHLIGHT: Check both s -> t and t -> s consistency
            if (c1 in map_st and map_st[c1] != c2) or \
               (c2 in map_ts and map_ts[c2] != c1):
                return False

            map_st[c1] = c2
            map_ts[c2] = c1

        return True
class DualMapSolution {
public:
    bool isIsomorphic(string s, string t) {
        unordered_map<char, char> mapST;
        unordered_map<char, char> mapTS;

        for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); ++i) {
            char c1 = s[i], c2 = t[i];

            if ((mapST.count(c1) && mapST[c1] != c2) ||
                (mapTS.count(c2) && mapTS[c2] != c1)) {
                return false;
            }

            mapST[c1] = c2;
            mapTS[c2] = c1;
        }

        return true;
    }
};
class DualMapSolution {
    public boolean isIsomorphic(String s, String t) {
        Map<Character, Character> mapST = new HashMap<>();
        Map<Character, Character> mapTS = new HashMap<>();

        for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
            char c1 = s.charAt(i);
            char c2 = t.charAt(i);

            if ((mapST.containsKey(c1) && mapST.get(c1) != c2) ||
                (mapTS.containsKey(c2) && mapTS.get(c2) != c1)) {
                return false;
            }

            mapST.put(c1, c2);
            mapTS.put(c2, c1);
        }

        return true;
    }
}
var isIsomorphicDualMap = function(s, t) {
    const mapST = new Map();
    const mapTS = new Map();

    for (let i = 0; i < s.length; i++) {
        const c1 = s[i], c2 = t[i];

        if ((mapST.has(c1) && mapST.get(c1) !== c2) ||
            (mapTS.has(c2) && mapTS.get(c2) !== c1)) {
            return false;
        }

        mapST.set(c1, c2);
        mapTS.set(c2, c1);
    }

    return true;
};

3. Approach 2: Optimal Fixed-Size Index Tracking Arrays (O(N) Time, O(1) Fixed Memory)

💡 Senior Mentor Explanation: The Structural Pattern Matching Trick

Junior, is there an even cleaner way to check if two strings have the exact same structure without building explicit hash maps?

The Structural Invariant:

If two strings are isomorphic, the last seen position (or first seen position) of s[i] and t[i] must match at EVERY step!
Pattern Tracking Example: s = "e g g" t = "a d d" Step 0 (i = 0): - 'e' last seen at index 0. - 'a' last seen at index 0. - Both match! Update: last_seen['e'] = 1, last_seen['a'] = 1 Step 1 (i = 1): - 'g' last seen at index 0 (never seen before). - 'd' last seen at index 0 (never seen before). - Both match! Update: last_seen['g'] = 2, last_seen['d'] = 2 Step 2 (i = 2): - 'g' last seen at index 2 (from step 1). - 'd' last seen at index 2 (from step 1). - Both match! (Both repeat at the exact same relative time!) Result: True!
Hinglish Explanation

Dono strings me har character ka last seen index hamesha barabar hona chahiye. Agar s[i] pichli baar index 2 par dekha gaya tha, toh t[i] bhi pichli baar index 2 par hi dekha jana chahiye tha! Hum size-256 ke do fixed arrays use karte hain, jo pure O(1) space me bina kisi hash map overhead ke execute hota hai.

Line-by-Line Code Breakdown (Approach 2)

  1. index_s = [0] * 256, index_t = [0] * 256: Fixed-size arrays initialized to 0 to store the 1-based last seen positions for all 256 ASCII characters.
  2. for i in range(len(s)):: Single pass loop comparing character structural histories.
  3. if index_s[ord(s[i])] != index_t[ord(t[i])]: return False: If the previous occurrence position of s[i] does not match the previous occurrence position of t[i], the structural isomorphism is broken!
  4. index_s[ord(s[i])] = i + 1; index_t[ord(t[i])] = i + 1: Update the recorded position to i + 1 (1-based indexing so that 0 represents "never seen before").
  5. return True: If loop finishes, return True.

Optimal Fixed-Size Index Array Implementation

class Solution:
    def isIsomorphic(self, s: str, t: str) -> bool:
        # Store 1-based last seen positions for ASCII 256 characters
        last_s = [0] * 256
        last_t = [0] * 256

        for i in range(len(s)):
            c1 = ord(s[i])
            c2 = ord(t[i])

            # HIGHLIGHT: Compare previous occurrence positions
            if last_s[c1] != last_t[c2]:
                return False

            # Record current position (1-based to distinguish from default 0)
            last_s[c1] = i + 1
            last_t[c2] = i + 1

        return True
class Solution {
public:
    bool isIsomorphic(string s, string t) {
        int lastS[256] = {0};
        int lastT[256] = {0};

        for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); ++i) {
            unsigned char c1 = s[i];
            unsigned char c2 = t[i];

            if (lastS[c1] != lastT[c2]) {
                return false;
            }

            lastS[c1] = i + 1;
            lastT[c2] = i + 1;
        }

        return true;
    }
};
class Solution {
    public boolean isIsomorphic(String s, String t) {
        int[] lastS = new int[256];
        int[] lastT = new int[256];

        for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
            char c1 = s.charAt(i);
            char c2 = t.charAt(i);

            if (lastS[c1] != lastT[c2]) {
                return false;
            }

            lastS[c1] = i + 1;
            lastT[c2] = i + 1;
        }

        return true;
    }
}
var isIsomorphic = function(s, t) {
    const lastS = new Array(256).fill(0);
    const lastT = new Array(256).fill(0);

    for (let i = 0; i < s.length; i++) {
        const c1 = s.charCodeAt(i);
        const c2 = t.charCodeAt(i);

        if (lastS[c1] !== lastT[c2]) {
            return false;
        }

        lastS[c1] = i + 1;
        lastT[c2] = i + 1;
    }

    return true;
};

4. Boundary Traps & Edge Case Analysis

⚠️ Common Traps & Bijection Collisions

1. The Collision Trap (Two chars in 's' mapping to one in 't'):
Example: s = "badc", t = "baba".
At index 2, s[2] = 'd' (seen at pos 0) and t[2] = 'b' (seen at pos 1).
last_s['d'] (0) != last_t['b'] (1) catches the collision instantly!

2. Why 1-Based Indexing (i + 1) is Required in Array Approach:
If we use 0-based indexing last_s[c] = i, the very first index 0 cannot be distinguished from the default unvisited value 0! Storing i + 1 ensures unvisited remains 0 while visited positions are > 0.

3. Single Character String (s = "a", t = "a"):
Single loop iteration runs, last_s['a'] == last_t['a'] == 0 matches, returns True.

5. Detailed Dry Run Walkthroughs

📋 Dry Run 2: Collision Invalidation — s = "badc", t = "baba"
Processing s = "badc", t = "baba": • i = 0 ('b', 'b'): - last_s['b'] = 0, last_t['b'] = 0 (Match!) - Set last_s['b'] = 1, last_t['b'] = 1 • i = 1 ('a', 'a'): - last_s['a'] = 0, last_t['a'] = 0 (Match!) - Set last_s['a'] = 2, last_t['a'] = 2 • i = 2 ('d', 'b'): - Check: last_s['d'] = 0 (first time seen) - Check: last_t['b'] = 1 (seen previously at step 0!) - Is 0 == 1? FALSE! (Collision Detected: 'b' was already claimed by 'b') Returns False immediately!
📋 Dry Run 3: Inconsistent Target Mapping — s = "foo", t = "bar"
Processing s = "foo", t = "bar": • i = 0 ('f', 'b'): - last_s['f'] = 0, last_t['b'] = 0 (Match!) -> set to 1 • i = 1 ('o', 'a'): - last_s['o'] = 0, last_t['a'] = 0 (Match!) -> set to 2 • i = 2 ('o', 'r'): - last_s['o'] = 2 (seen at step 1) - last_t['r'] = 0 (first time seen) - Is 2 == 0? FALSE! ('o' cannot map to both 'a' and 'r') Returns False immediately!
