Merge Strings Alternately

Complete Technical & Mentorship Guide: Two-pointer zip merging, string builder memory optimizations, single-pointer index bounds, and detailed dry runs.

1. Problem Statement & Core Concept

You are given two strings word1 and word2. Merge the strings by adding letters in alternating order, starting with word1.

If a string is longer than the other, append the additional letters onto the end of the merged string.

Return the merged string.

Merging Mechanics Visualization: Example 1: word1 = "abc", word2 = "pqr" - Alternating order: 'a' -> 'p' -> 'b' -> 'q' -> 'c' -> 'r' - Output: "apbqcr" --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Example 2: word1 = "ab", word2 = "pqrs" - Alternating: 'a' -> 'p' -> 'b' -> 'q' - Remaining suffix from word2: "rs" - Merged Output: "apbq" + "rs" = "apbqrs" --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Example 3: word1 = "abcd", word2 = "pq" - Alternating: 'a' -> 'p' -> 'b' -> 'q' - Remaining suffix from word1: "cd" - Merged Output: "apbq" + "cd" = "apbqcd"

Constraints

  • 1 <= word1.length, word2.length <= 100
  • word1 and word2 consist of lowercase English letters.

2. Approach 1: Two Pointers with Suffix Appending (O(N + M) Time, O(1) Auxiliary Space)

🧭 Senior Mentor Explanation: The Independent Pointer Technique

Hey junior, the most intuitive way to interleave two sequences is using two distinct pointers i and j:

  1. Start i = 0 at word1 and j = 0 at word2.
  2. While both pointers are within bounds (i < len(word1) and j < len(word2)):
    • Append word1[i] and increment i += 1.
    • Append word2[j] and increment j += 1.
  3. Once one string is exhausted, directly append the leftover slice from the other string: word1[i:] or word2[j:].
Hinglish Explanation

Sabse clear tareeka do pointers i aur j maintain karna hai. Jab tak dono strings me characters bache hain, ek character word1 se lo aur ek word2 se. Jaise hi koi ek string khatam ho jaye, doosri string ke bache hue characters ko aakhir me seedha attach kar do.

Line-by-Line Code Breakdown (Approach 1)

  1. res = []: Array/StringBuilder to collect characters efficiently without immutable string concatenation overhead.
  2. i = 0, j = 0: Pointers tracking position in word1 and word2.
  3. n, m = len(word1), len(word2): String lengths.
  4. while i < n and j < m:: Interleave characters while both strings have elements remaining.
  5. res.append(word1[i]); res.append(word2[j]): Add alternating characters and advance both pointers.
  6. res.append(word1[i:] / word2[j:]): Append remaining trailing suffix if lengths differ.
  7. return "".join(res): Convert character buffer to final string.

Two-Pointer Implementation

class TwoPointerSolution:
    def mergeAlternately(self, word1: str, word2: str) -> str:
        res = []
        i, j = 0, 0
        n, m = len(word1), len(word2)

        # Step 1: Interleave while both have characters
        while i < n and j < m:
            res.append(word1[i])
            res.append(word2[j])
            i += 1
            j += 1

        # Step 2: Append remaining suffix
        if i < n:
            res.append(word1[i:])
        if j < m:
            res.append(word2[j:])

        return "".join(res)
class TwoPointerSolution {
public:
    string mergeAlternately(string word1, string word2) {
        string res = "";
        int i = 0, j = 0;
        int n = word1.length(), m = word2.length();

        while (i < n && j < m) {
            res += word1[i++];
            res += word2[j++];
        }

        if (i < n) res += word1.substr(i);
        if (j < m) res += word2.substr(j);

        return res;
    }
};
class TwoPointerSolution {
    public String mergeAlternately(String word1, String word2) {
        StringBuilder res = new StringBuilder();
        int i = 0, j = 0;
        int n = word1.length(), m = word2.length();

        while (i < n && j < m) {
            res.append(word1.charAt(i++));
            res.append(word2.charAt(j++));
        }

        if (i < n) res.append(word1.substring(i));
        if (j < m) res.append(word2.substring(j));

        return res.toString();
    }
}
var mergeAlternately = function(word1, word2) {
    const res = [];
    let i = 0, j = 0;
    const n = word1.length, m = word2.length;

    while (i < n && j < m) {
        res.push(word1[i++]);
        res.push(word2[j++]);
    }

    if (i < n) res.push(word1.slice(i));
    if (j < m) res.push(word2.slice(j));

    return res.join('');
};

3. Approach 2: Single-Pointer Max Loop (O(max(N, M)) Time, O(1) Auxiliary Space)

💡 Senior Mentor Explanation: Single Index Traversal

Can we write this even more concisely using a single loop variable?

Run a loop from index i = 0 up to max(len(word1), len(word2)) - 1:

  • If i < len(word1): Append word1[i].
  • If i < len(word2): Append word2[i].

This automatically handles both the alternating phase AND any trailing leftover characters without needing separate if (i < n) slice appends at the end!

Hinglish Explanation

Single pointer approach me hum loop ko 0 se lekar max(len(word1), len(word2)) tak chalate hain. Har iteration me agar index word1 ke range me hai toh uska character lo, aur agar word2 ke range me hai toh uska lo. Isse extra suffix check karne ki zaroorat nahi padti.

Single-Pointer Trace: word1 = "ab", word2 = "pqrs" n = 2, m = 4. max_len = 4 • i = 0: - i < 2 -> Append word1[0] = 'a' - i < 4 -> Append word2[0] = 'p' Buffer = "ap" • i = 1: - i < 2 -> Append word1[1] = 'b' - i < 4 -> Append word2[1] = 'q' Buffer = "apbq" • i = 2: - i >= 2 (word1 finished) -> Skip - i < 4 -> Append word2[2] = 'r' Buffer = "apbqr" • i = 3: - i >= 2 (word1 finished) -> Skip - i < 4 -> Append word2[3] = 's' Buffer = "apbqrs" Result = "apbqrs"

Line-by-Line Code Breakdown (Approach 2)

  1. res = []: Output buffer.
  2. for i in range(max(len(word1), len(word2))):: Loop bounded by the longer string.
  3. if i < len(word1): res.append(word1[i]): Safe bounds check for word1.
  4. if i < len(word2): res.append(word2[i]): Safe bounds check for word2.
  5. return "".join(res): Return combined string.

Single-Pointer Implementation

class SinglePointerSolution:
    def mergeAlternately(self, word1: str, word2: str) -> str:
        res = []
        n, m = len(word1), len(word2)

        for i in range(max(n, m)):
            if i < n:
                res.append(word1[i])
            if i < m:
                res.append(word2[i])

        return "".join(res)
class SinglePointerSolution {
public:
    string mergeAlternately(string word1, string word2) {
        string res = "";
        int n = word1.length(), m = word2.length();
        int maxLen = max(n, m);

        for (int i = 0; i < maxLen; ++i) {
            if (i < n) res += word1[i];
            if (i < m) res += word2[i];
        }

        return res;
    }
};
class SinglePointerSolution {
    public String mergeAlternately(String word1, String word2) {
        StringBuilder res = new StringBuilder();
        int n = word1.length(), m = word2.length();
        int maxLen = Math.max(n, m);

        for (int i = 0; i < maxLen; i++) {
            if (i < n) res.append(word1.charAt(i));
            if (i < m) res.append(word2.charAt(i));
        }

        return res.toString();
    }
}
var mergeAlternatelySinglePointer = function(word1, word2) {
    const res = [];
    const n = word1.length, m = word2.length;
    const maxLen = Math.max(n, m);

    for (let i = 0; i < maxLen; i++) {
        if (i < n) res.push(word1[i]);
        if (i < m) res.push(word2[i]);
    }

    return res.join('');
};

4. Boundary Traps & Performance Optimizations

⚠️ Common Traps & String Immutability Overhead

1. String Immutability Trap (in Java/Python):
In Java and Python, repeated string concatenation (s += char) inside a loop creates a brand-new string object on every step, leading to O((N + M)^2) time complexity! Always use a list array with "".join() in Python or StringBuilder in Java.

2. Differing Length Strings:
If word1 is shorter than word2, or vice versa, the solution must ensure no characters are dropped from the longer string.

3. Equal Length Strings:
Both loops terminate simultaneously with no trailing elements appended.

5. Detailed Dry Run Walkthroughs

📋 Dry Run 1: word1 = "abc", word2 = "pqr" (Equal Lengths)
Initial: i = 0, j = 0, n = 3, m = 3, res = [] • Step 1 (i=0, j=0): res.append('a'), res.append('p') -> res = ['a', 'p'], i=1, j=1 • Step 2 (i=1, j=1): res.append('b'), res.append('q') -> res = ['a', 'p', 'b', 'q'], i=2, j=2 • Step 3 (i=2, j=2): res.append('c'), res.append('r') -> res = ['a', 'p', 'b', 'q', 'c', 'r'], i=3, j=3 Loop ends (i == 3, j == 3). No remaining suffix. Final Output = "apbqcr"
📋 Dry Run 2: word1 = "abcd", word2 = "pq" (word1 Longer)
Initial: i = 0, j = 0, n = 4, m = 2, res = [] • Step 1 (i=0, j=0): append 'a', 'p' -> res = ['a', 'p'], i=1, j=1 • Step 2 (i=1, j=1): append 'b', 'q' -> res = ['a', 'p', 'b', 'q'], i=2, j=2 Loop ends because j = 2 == m. Suffix check: i = 2 < 4 -> Append word1[2:] = "cd" res becomes ['a', 'p', 'b', 'q', 'cd'] Final Output = "apbqcd"

6. Complexity Analysis Performance Metrics

Approach Category Time Complexity Space Complexity Loop Iterations Performance Evaluation Rating
Approach 1: Two Pointers (While Loop) O(N + M) O(1) Auxiliary min(N, M) + suffix slice Absolute Production Standard. Optimal time and memory; performs the minimal number of character checks.
Approach 2: Single-Pointer Max Loop O(max(N, M)) O(1) Auxiliary max(N, M) Clean & Concise. Slightly shorter code structure with bounds checks in loop.

4Sum

Complete Technical & Learning-First Notes: Pattern derivation from 2Sum & 3Sum, duplicate elimination mathematics, 32-bit integer overflow protection, general K-Sum recursion, and deep step-by-step state dry runs.

1. Problem Understanding & Core Constraints

Given an array nums of n integers and an integer target, return an array of all the unique quadruplets [nums[a], nums[b], nums[c], nums[d]] such that:

  • 0 <= a, b, c, d < n
  • a, b, c, and d are distinct indices (each element used at most once per quadruplet).
  • nums[a] + nums[b] + nums[c] + nums[d] == target
  • The solution set must not contain duplicate quadruplets.
Problem Examples: Example 1: Input: nums = [1, 0, -1, 0, -2, 2], target = 0 Sorted: [-2, -1, 0, 0, 1, 2] Quadruplets summing to 0: 1. [-2, -1, 1, 2] -> (-2) + (-1) + 1 + 2 = 0 2. [-2, 0, 0, 2] -> (-2) + 0 + 0 + 2 = 0 3. [-1, 0, 0, 1] -> (-1) + 0 + 0 + 1 = 0 Output: [[-2, -1, 1, 2], [-2, 0, 0, 2], [-1, 0, 0, 1]] --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Example 2 (Duplicates & Boundary Test): Input: nums = [2, 2, 2, 2, 2], target = 8 Sorted: [2, 2, 2, 2, 2] Output: [[2, 2, 2, 2]] (Even though 5 combinations exist, only 1 UNIQUE quadruplet is valid) --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Example 3 (Integer Overflow Trap in 32-bit typed languages): Input: nums = [1000000000, 1000000000, 1000000000, 1000000000], target = -294967296 Sum of four 10^9 numbers = 4 * 10^9 (Exceeds INT32_MAX = 2,147,483,647). Output: []

Critical Constraints & What Makes This Problem Difficult

  • 1 <= nums.length <= 200
  • -10^9 <= nums[i] <= 10^9
  • -10^9 <= target <= 10^9
  • Hardest Part 1 (Duplicate Prevention without Extra Space): You cannot simply generate all tuples and insert them into a Set without incurring substantial time and memory overhead. We must skip duplicates in O(1) memory.
  • Hardest Part 2 (32-Bit Integer Overflow): Summing four values up to 10^9 can reach 4 * 10^9, overflowing standard 32-bit signed integers in C++ and Java.

2. Pattern Recognition & First 60-Seconds Breakdown

🧭 How to Recognize This Pattern in 30–60 Seconds

Clues in the Problem Statement:

  • Fixed-Size Tuple Sum: We need a combination of k = 4 numbers summing to a fixed target.
  • Unique Result Constraint: Results cannot contain duplicate combinations.
  • Small Input Size (N <= 200): An O(N^3) solution will execute roughly 200^3 / 6 ≈ 1.33 * 10^6 operations, well within the standard 1-second (~10^8 operations) budget.

Questions to Ask Yourself:

  1. "Can I reduce 4Sum to 3Sum, and 3Sum to 2Sum?" Yes! By fixing 1 variable (nums[i]), we get 3Sum. By fixing a 2nd variable (nums[j]), we reduce the problem to 2Sum on a sorted subarray.
  2. "Does sorting ruin anything?" No, the problem asks for the elements themselves, not the original indices. Sorting takes O(N log N), which is completely dominated by the O(N^3) search loops.
  3. "Why does Sorting make duplicate removal trivial?" Because in a sorted array, all identical values cluster together adjacent to each other. Skipping duplicates is as simple as while nums[k] == nums[k-1]: skip.

3. Deep Intuition: Building the Mental Model Before Code

💡 The Reduction Hierarchy (K-Sum Framework)

To master all K-Sum problems forever, recognize the hierarchy:

  • 2Sum: Sort the array. Place pointer left at start, right at end.
    • If sum == target: Record pair, advance both pointers past duplicates.
    • If sum < target: Need a larger sum → left++.
    • If sum > target: Need a smaller sum → right--.
  • 3Sum: Run 1 outer loop i from 0 to N - 3. For each i, solve 2Sum on range [i + 1, N - 1] for target target - nums[i].
  • 4Sum: Run 2 outer loops i and j. For each fixed pair (i, j), solve 2Sum on range [j + 1, N - 1] for target target - nums[i] - nums[j].

Why Two Pointers Works Over Sorted Arrays:

When the array is sorted, nums[left] + nums[right] is strictly monotonic with respect to pointer movement. Incrementing left is guaranteed to never decrease the sum; decrementing right is guaranteed to never increase the sum. This allows us to eliminate an entire row/column of possibilities in O(1) time, converting an O(N^2) pair search into an O(N) two-pointer sweep.

Hinglish Explanation

4Sum ko yaad karne ke bajaye chain samjho: 4Sum = Loop 1 + 3Sum = Loop 1 + Loop 2 + 2Sum. Pehla loop nums[i] fix karta hai, doosra loop nums[j] fix karta hai. Ab bache hue array me hum 2-Pointer technique (left aur right) laga kar bache hue do numbers dhoondhte hain. Sorted array hone ki wajah se duplicates ko skip karna bohot easy ho jata hai: agar nums[i] == nums[i-1] hai, toh loop ko continue kar do.

4. How I Should Think in an Interview

Step 1 — Understand & State Constraints:
"We need 4 unique elements from distinct indices summing to target. The result cannot contain duplicate quadruplets. N <= 200."

Step 2 — Propose Brute Force & Explain Bottleneck:
"A naive approach uses 4 nested loops checking all combinations in O(N^4). To avoid duplicate quadruplets, we would have to sort each quadruplet and store them in a Hash Set, taking O(N^4) time and O(N) space."

Step 3 — Formulate the Optimization:
"We can sort the array upfront in O(N log N). With a sorted array, we fix the first two numbers nums[i] and nums[j] using two nested loops, and use two pointers (left and right) to find the remaining two numbers in O(N) time. This reduces the total complexity to O(N^3) with O(1) auxiliary space."

Step 4 — Proactively Mention Edge Cases & Traps:
"Because values can be up to 10^9, the sum of four integers can reach 4 * 10^9, which overflows a 32-bit signed integer. I will cast the sum calculation to 64-bit integer (long long in C++ / long in Java). I will also skip duplicate adjacent values at every level (loops i, j, and pointers left, right) to guarantee uniqueness without a hash set."

5. Approach 1: Brute Force with Set Deduplication (O(N^4))

🧭 Algorithm Description

Run 4 nested loops over indices i < j < k < l. Whenever nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] + nums[l] == target, sort the four numbers and insert the tuple into a Hash Set to filter duplicates.

Brute Force Implementation (Python)

class BruteForceSolution:
    def fourSum(self, nums: list[int], target: int) -> list[list[int]]:
        n = len(nums)
        res_set = set()
        
        # 4 nested loops explore all combinations O(N^4)
        for i in range(n):
            for j in range(i + 1, n):
                for k in range(j + 1, n):
                    for l in range(k + 1, n):
                        if nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] + nums[l] == target:
                            quad = tuple(sorted([nums[i], nums[j], nums[k], nums[l]]))
                            res_set.add(quad)
                            
        return [list(q) for q in res_set]

6. Approach 2: Hash Set Lookup (O(N^3) Time, O(N) Space)

🧭 Concept: 3 Loops + Hash Set Lookup

We can optimize the 4th loop by using a Hash Set for the inner search:

  • Sort the array first to make duplicate handling easier.
  • Use 3 nested loops: i, j, and k.
  • The required 4th value is needed = target - (nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k]).
  • Maintain a hash set of elements seen in the current j loop between index j + 1 and k - 1.

Drawback: Requires extra hash set allocations for every loop iteration, leading to higher constant factors and O(N) memory overhead.

7. Approach 3: Optimal Sorting + Two Pointers (O(N^3) Time, O(1) Space)

💡 The Optimal Blueprint
  1. Sort nums: Puts all duplicate elements side-by-side and enables monotonic two-pointer narrowing.
  2. Outer Loop i (from 0 to N - 4):
    • Duplicate Skip: If i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i - 1], continue.
    • Early Pruning (Branch & Bound Optimization):
      • If nums[i] + nums[i+1] + nums[i+2] + nums[i+3] > target: The smallest possible 4-sum from this point onwards exceeds target. We can break immediately!
      • If nums[i] + nums[N-3] + nums[N-2] + nums[N-1] < target: The largest possible 4-sum containing nums[i] is still smaller than target. We can continue to a larger nums[i]!
  3. Inner Loop j (from i + 1 to N - 3):
    • Duplicate Skip: If j > i + 1 and nums[j] == nums[j - 1], continue.
    • Early Pruning: Apply similar minimum and maximum 4-sum checks for nums[i] + nums[j].
  4. Two-Pointer Window (left = j + 1, right = N - 1):
    • Calculate curr_sum = nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[left] + nums[right] (using 64-bit precision).
    • If curr_sum == target: Record [nums[i], nums[j], nums[left], nums[right]].
      Advance left++ while nums[left] == nums[left - 1] to skip duplicate 3rd elements.
      Advance right-- while nums[right] == nums[right + 1] to skip duplicate 4th elements.
    • If curr_sum < target: Increment left++ to increase total sum.
    • If curr_sum > target: Decrement right-- to decrease total sum.
Two-Pointer Pointer Architecture: Sorted Array: [ -2, -1, 0, 0, 1, 2 ] ↑ ↑ ↑ ↑ i j left right 1. Fix i = 0 (val -2) 2. Fix j = 1 (val -1) 3. Target for (left + right) = target - nums[i] - nums[j] = 0 - (-2) - (-1) = 3 4. Check nums[left] + nums[right] = 0 + 2 = 2 < 3 -> left++

8. Approach Comparison & Decision Framework

Approach Category Time Complexity Space Complexity Handles Duplicates Interview Rating
1. Brute Force (4 Loops + Set) O(N^4) O(N) Via Hash Set tuple storage Sub-optimal / TLE. Demonstrates understanding, but fails time limits.
2. Hash Set 3-Loops O(N^3) O(N) Via Set deduplication Acceptable. Good stepping stone, but memory overhead is unnecessary.
3. Sorting + Two Pointers (Optimal) O(N^3) O(1) Auxiliary In-place pointer skipping Absolute Production Standard. Clean, optimal memory, handles 64-bit sums seamlessly.

9. Comprehensive Dry Run with State Transition Table & Test Cases for Practice

📋 Worked Dry Run: Trace on nums = [1, 0, -1, 0, -2, 2], target = 0

Initial State:
Sorted nums = [-2, -1, 0, 0, 1, 2], length n = 6, target = 0, result = []

i (val) j (val) left (val) right (val) Current Sum Condition Check Action Taken Result State
0 (-2) 1 (-1) 2 (0) 5 (2) -2 + -1 + 0 + 2 = -1 -1 < 0 left++ → 3 []
0 (-2) 1 (-1) 3 (0) 5 (2) -2 + -1 + 0 + 2 = -1 -1 < 0 left++ → 4 []
0 (-2) 1 (-1) 4 (1) 5 (2) -2 + -1 + 1 + 2 = 0 0 == 0 (MATCH!) Record, left++ → 5, right-- → 4 [[-2, -1, 1, 2]]
0 (-2) 1 (-1) left (5) >= right (4) → Exit inner while loop.
0 (-2) 2 (0) 3 (0) 5 (2) -2 + 0 + 0 + 2 = 0 0 == 0 (MATCH!) Record, left++ → 4, right-- → 4 [..., [-2, 0, 0, 2]]
0 (-2) 2 (0) left (4) >= right (4) → Exit inner while loop.
0 (-2) 3 (0) nums[3] == nums[2] (duplicate j) → continue.
1 (-1) 2 (0) 3 (0) 5 (2) -1 + 0 + 0 + 2 = 1 1 > 0 right-- → 4 [[-2,-1,1,2], [-2,0,0,2]]
1 (-1) 2 (0) 3 (0) 4 (1) -1 + 0 + 0 + 1 = 0 0 == 0 (MATCH!) Record, left++ → 4, right-- → 3 [..., [-1, 0, 0, 1]]

Final Merged Result: [[-2, -1, 1, 2], [-2, 0, 0, 2], [-1, 0, 0, 1]]

🎯 Challenge Test Case 1: Heavy Duplicates & Zero Target

Input: nums = [-3, -1, 0, 2, 4, -3, 2, -1, 0, 2], target = 0

Why this test case is powerful: It forces you to sort an array with multiple duplicate values ([-3, -3, -1, -1, 0, 0, 2, 2, 2, 4]) and tests whether your i, j, and two-pointer duplicate-skipping loops successfully avoid emitting repeated quadruplets.

Sorted Array: [-3, -3, -1, -1, 0, 0, 2, 2, 2, 4] Unique Quadruplets found: 1. [-3, -1, 0, 4] -> -3 + (-1) + 0 + 4 = 0 2. [-3, -1, 2, 2] -> -3 + (-1) + 2 + 2 = 0 3. [-3, 0, 1, 2] (invalid, 1 not in array) 4. [-3, 0, 0, ?] (no valid pair) 5. [-1, -1, 0, 2] -> -1 + (-1) + 0 + 2 = 0 Expected Output: [[-3, -1, 0, 4], [-3, -1, 2, 2], [-1, -1, 0, 2]]
🎯 Challenge Test Case 2: 32-bit Integer Overflow & Extreme Positives

Input: nums = [1000000000, 1000000000, 1000000000, 1000000000], target = 4000000000 (or 0)

Why this test case is powerful: Four values of 10^9 sum to 4 * 10^9, which exceeds INT32_MAX (2,147,483,647). If your code does not use 64-bit integer casting (long long in C++, long in Java), the sum rolls over to a negative number (-294967296) and produces a silent logical failure.

Input: nums = [1000000000, 1000000000, 1000000000, 1000000000], target = 0 Sum Calculation: 10^9 + 10^9 + 10^9 + 10^9 = 4,000,000,000 (4 * 10^9) Check: 4,000,000,000 == 0 -> False Expected Output: []

10. Edge Cases & Boundary Conditions

  • Input Length Less Than 4 (len(nums) < 4):
    Handled immediately by range(n - 3) which evaluates to an empty range when n < 4, returning [] safely without index errors.
  • All Elements Identical (e.g. [2, 2, 2, 2, 2], target = 8):
    At i = 0, j = 1, left = 2, right = 3, the sum is 8. After recording [2, 2, 2, 2], left skips past index 4 and right skips down, terminating the while loop. All subsequent i and j loop steps trigger duplicate skips (nums[i] == nums[i-1]). Exactly ONE quadruplet is returned!
  • 32-Bit Integer Overflow (e.g. four 10^9 values):
    In C++ and Java, nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[left] + nums[right] exceeds 2^31 - 1. Explicit casting to long long / long ensures the comparison against target is exact.
  • Negative Target (e.g. target = -10 with negative numbers):
    Two-pointer logic operates identically because the difference current_sum - target preserves directional monotonicity on sorted negative numbers.

11. Common Mistakes & Anti-Patterns

⚠️ 3 Common Implementation Bugs

Mistake 1: Incorrect Duplicate Skip Condition on j:
Writing if nums[j] == nums[j - 1]: continue without checking j > i + 1.
Why it's wrong: If nums = [2, 2, 2, 2], when i = 0 (val 2), j = 1 (val 2) would be skipped, completely missing the valid combination [2, 2, 2, 2]!
Fix: Always write: if j > i + 1 and nums[j] == nums[j - 1]: continue.

Mistake 2: Forgetting to skip duplicates on BOTH left and right after a match:
Only incrementing left += 1 without the inner while nums[left] == nums[left-1] loop.
Why it's wrong: Produces duplicate quadruplets in the output list.

Mistake 3: Missing 64-bit cast in C++/Java:
Writing int sum = nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[left] + nums[right].
Why it's wrong: Silent 32-bit integer overflow wraps around to negative values, causing wrong answers on LeetCode test cases.

12. Generalization to K-Sum (Recursive Backtracking + 2Sum Base Case)

🚀 The Generalized K-Sum Template

Any K-Sum problem can be solved recursively using the exact same template:

  • Base Case (k == 2): Run standard two-pointer 2Sum on sorted range.
  • Recursive Step (k > 2): Loop i from start to N - k, skip duplicates, and recursively call kSum(k - 1, i + 1, target - nums[i]).

Generalized K-Sum Implementation (Python)

class KSumSolution:
    def fourSum(self, nums: list[int], target: int) -> list[list[int]]:
        nums.sort()

        def kSum(nums: list[int], target: int, k: int) -> list[list[int]]:
            res = []
            if not nums:
                return res

            # Early Pruning: average value bounds
            avg = target // k
            if nums[0] > avg or avg > nums[-1]:
                return res

            # Base Case: 2Sum Two-Pointer Sweep
            if k == 2:
                l, r = 0, len(nums) - 1
                while l < r:
                    curr = nums[l] + nums[r]
                    if curr == target:
                        res.append([nums[l], nums[r]])
                        l += 1
                        while l < r and nums[l] == nums[l - 1]: l += 1
                        r -= 1
                        while l < r and nums[r] == nums[r + 1]: r -= 1
                    elif curr < target:
                        l += 1
                    else:
                        r -= 1
                return res

            # Recursive Step: Reduce (k) to (k - 1)
            for i in range(len(nums)):
                if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]:
                    continue
                for sub in kSum(nums[i + 1:], target - nums[i], k - 1):
                    res.append([nums[i]] + sub)

            return res

        return kSum(nums, target, 4)

13. Complexity Analysis & Proof of Optimality

Time Complexity: O(N^(K-1)) = O(N^3)

  • Sorting the array takes O(N log N).
  • Outer loop i runs O(N) times.
  • Inner loop j runs O(N) times.
  • Two-pointer sweep left/right traverses the remaining array in O(N) time.
  • Total time = O(N log N) + O(N * N * N) = O(N^3).

Space Complexity: O(1) Auxiliary Space

  • Only four pointer variables (i, j, left, right) are used.
  • Sorting in C++ (std::sort) takes O(log N) stack memory; in Python (Timsort) takes O(N) memory.
  • Output array storage is excluded from auxiliary space accounting.

Is this Asymptotically Optimal?
Yes. Without additional constraints (like 4Sum II with separate independent arrays), finding all unique quadruplets in a general 1D array has a known lower bound of O(N^3) using comparison-based two-pointer approaches.

14. Pattern Transfer: "If You See This, Think This"

Pattern Transfer Cheat Sheet: 1. Target sum of K elements in SINGLE array: ↳ Think: Sort + (K - 2) Nested Loops + 2-Pointer Base Case (O(N^(K-1))) 2. Target sum of 4 elements from 4 SEPARATE arrays (4Sum II): ↳ Think: Hash Map of Pair Sums (AB[a + b] = count) -> O(N^2) Time! 3. Number of valid triangles (nums[i] + nums[j] > nums[k]): ↳ Think: Sort + Fix largest side + 2-Pointer Count (3Sum variation) 4. Closest sum to target: ↳ Think: Sort + 2-Pointer tracking minimum absolute delta |sum - target|

Pattern Recognition Checklist

  1. Are we asked to find combinations of a fixed number of items (2, 3, 4, K)? → K-Sum Pattern.
  2. Does element order matter? → No → Sort the array immediately.
  3. Are duplicate answers forbidden? → Skip adjacent identical elements in-place.

15. Realistic Interview Script

"To solve 4Sum, I reduce it to the well-known 3Sum and 2Sum problems. First, I sort the array in O(N log N). Sorting gives us two huge advantages: it allows monotonic two-pointer searching, and it places identical numbers side-by-side so we can eliminate duplicates without a Hash Set."

"I will run two nested loops for the first two elements, nums[i] and nums[j]. Within each loop, I skip identical consecutive elements. Then, for the remaining two elements, I initialize two pointers, left and right, at the boundaries of the remaining subarray."

"To prevent 32-bit signed integer overflow, I cast the four-element sum to 64-bit integers. When a match is found, I record the quadruplet and advance both left and right past any duplicate values. This achieves optimal O(N^3) time complexity and O(1) auxiliary space."

16. Final Revision Sheet & 30-Second Recall

⚡ What to Remember
  • Pattern: Sorting + Multi-Loop Two Pointers (K-Sum).
  • Core Invariant: nums is sorted → nums[left] + nums[right] responds monotonically to pointer shifts.
  • Duplicate Rule: if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i-1]: continue and if j > i + 1 and nums[j] == nums[j-1]: continue.
  • Overflow Guard: Cast to long long in C++ / long in Java before summing.
  • Optimal Complexity: O(N^3) Time, O(1) Auxiliary Space.
⏱️ 30-Second Recall

Sort the array. Fix nums[i] in loop 1, fix nums[j] in loop 2. Use left and right pointers to find the remaining pair in O(N). Skip duplicates after processing each index and each match. Cast sums to 64-bit integers to prevent overflow.

17. Code Implementation & Deep Line-by-Line Breakdown

Full multi-language implementations with inline reasoning comments and detailed outside-code breakdowns.

class Solution:
    def fourSum(self, nums: list[int], target: int) -> list[list[int]]:
        # Step 1: Sort the array to enable two-pointer traversal and duplicate skipping
        nums.sort()
        n = len(nums)
        result = []

        # Outer loop 1: Fix the first element nums[i]
        for i in range(n - 3):
            # WHY: Skip duplicate values for the first element to prevent identical quadruplets
            if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]:
                continue

            # PRUNING 1: If smallest possible 4-sum with nums[i] exceeds target, no solution exists further
            if nums[i] + nums[i + 1] + nums[i + 2] + nums[i + 3] > target:
                break
            # PRUNING 2: If largest possible 4-sum with nums[i] is below target, increment i
            if nums[i] + nums[n - 3] + nums[n - 2] + nums[n - 1] < target:
                continue

            # Outer loop 2: Fix the second element nums[j]
            for j in range(i + 1, n - 2):
                # WHY: Skip duplicate values for the second element (ensure j is beyond i + 1)
                if j > i + 1 and nums[j] == nums[j - 1]:
                    continue

                # PRUNING 3 & 4 for j loop
                if nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[j + 1] + nums[j + 2] > target:
                    break
                if nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[n - 2] + nums[n - 1] < target:
                    continue

                # Step 3: Two-Pointer search for remaining 2 elements
                left = j + 1
                right = n - 1

                while left < right:
                    curr_sum = nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[left] + nums[right]

                    if curr_sum == target:
                        result.append([nums[i], nums[j], nums[left], nums[right]])
                        
                        # Advance left and skip all duplicates
                        left += 1
                        while left < right and nums[left] == nums[left - 1]:
                            left += 1
                        
                        # Decrement right and skip all duplicates
                        right -= 1
                        while left < right and nums[right] == nums[right + 1]:
                            right -= 1

                    elif curr_sum < target:
                        # Sum too small -> advance left to increase total
                        left += 1
                    else:
                        # Sum too large -> decrement right to decrease total
                        right -= 1

        return result
class Solution {
public:
    vector<vector<int>> fourSum(vector<int>& nums, int target) {
        int n = nums.size();
        vector<vector<int>> result;
        if (n < 4) return result;

        // Step 1: Sort array
        sort(nums.begin(), nums.end());

        for (int i = 0; i < n - 3; ++i) {
            // Duplicate skip for i
            if (i > 0 && nums[i] == nums[i - 1]) continue;

            // 64-bit overflow prevention during pruning
            if ((long long)nums[i] + nums[i+1] + nums[i+2] + nums[i+3] > target) break;
            if ((long long)nums[i] + nums[n-3] + nums[n-2] + nums[n-1] < target) continue;

            for (int j = i + 1; j < n - 2; ++j) {
                // Duplicate skip for j
                if (j > i + 1 && nums[j] == nums[j - 1]) continue;

                if ((long long)nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[j+1] + nums[j+2] > target) break;
                if ((long long)nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[n-2] + nums[n-1] < target) continue;

                int left = j + 1, right = n - 1;

                while (left < right) {
                    // Cast to long long to prevent 32-bit arithmetic overflow
                    long long sum = (long long)nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[left] + nums[right];

                    if (sum == target) {
                        result.push_back({nums[i], nums[j], nums[left], nums[right]});
                        left++;
                        while (left < right && nums[left] == nums[left - 1]) left++;
                        right--;
                        while (left < right && nums[right] == nums[right + 1]) right--;
                    } else if (sum < target) {
                        left++;
                    } else {
                        right--;
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        return result;
    }
};
class Solution {
    public List<List<Integer>> fourSum(int[] nums, int target) {
        int n = nums.length;
        List<List<Integer>> result = new ArrayList<>();
        if (n < 4) return result;

        Arrays.sort(nums);

        for (int i = 0; i < n - 3; i++) {
            if (i > 0 && nums[i] == nums[i - 1]) continue;

            // Cast to long to prevent integer overflow
            if ((long)nums[i] + nums[i+1] + nums[i+2] + nums[i+3] > target) break;
            if ((long)nums[i] + nums[n-3] + nums[n-2] + nums[n-1] < target) continue;

            for (int j = i + 1; j < n - 2; j++) {
                if (j > i + 1 && nums[j] == nums[j - 1]) continue;

                if ((long)nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[j+1] + nums[j+2] > target) break;
                if ((long)nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[n-2] + nums[n-1] < target) continue;

                int left = j + 1, right = n - 1;

                while (left < right) {
                    long sum = (long)nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[left] + nums[right];

                    if (sum == target) {
                        result.add(Arrays.asList(nums[i], nums[j], nums[left], nums[right]));
                        left++;
                        while (left < right && nums[left] == nums[left - 1]) left++;
                        right--;
                        while (left < right && nums[right] == nums[right + 1]) right--;
                    } else if (sum < target) {
                        left++;
                    } else {
                        right--;
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        return result;
    }
}
var fourSum = function(nums, target) {
    const n = nums.length;
    const result = [];
    if (n < 4) return result;

    nums.sort((a, b) => a - b);

    for (let i = 0; i < n - 3; i++) {
        if (i > 0 && nums[i] === nums[i - 1]) continue;

        for (let j = i + 1; j < n - 2; j++) {
            if (j > i + 1 && nums[j] === nums[j - 1]) continue;

            let left = j + 1;
            let right = n - 1;

            while (left < right) {
                const sum = nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[left] + nums[right];

                if (sum === target) {
                    result.push([nums[i], nums[j], nums[left], nums[right]]);
                    left++;
                    while (left < right && nums[left] === nums[left - 1]) left++;
                    right--;
                    while (left < right && nums[right] === nums[right + 1]) right--;
                } else if (sum < target) {
                    left++;
                } else {
                    right--;
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return result;
};

Outside-Code Line-by-Line Breakdown

  1. nums.sort(): Orders numbers ascendingly. This is the foundational prerequisite for monotonic two-pointer movement and adjacent duplicate detection.
  2. for i in range(n - 3):: Outer loop fixes the 1st number. It stops at n - 4 because at least 3 elements are needed after i.
  3. if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]: continue: If the current starting number is identical to the previous starting number, we skip it because all quadruplets beginning with this value were already generated in the previous iteration.
  4. for j in range(i + 1, n - 2):: Second loop fixes the 2nd number.
  5. if j > i + 1 and nums[j] == nums[j - 1]: continue: Skips duplicate 2nd numbers. Note the condition j > i + 1: we allow using duplicate numbers across different indices (e.g. nums[i] == nums[j] is valid), but reject duplicate choices for index j within the same i scope.
  6. while left < right:: Inner 2Sum two-pointer search.
  7. sum == target → left++; while nums[left] == nums[left - 1]: left++: Once a valid match is found, advance left and skip all identical adjacent numbers to avoid duplicate quadruplets.

LeetCode 202 Easy Fast & Slow Pointers

Happy Number

Balanced DSA Master Notes: Deep mental model, zero bloat, progressive understanding.

1. What is Being Asked?

Given: A positive integer n.

Operation: Replace n with the sum of the squares of its digits.

Goal: Return true if this process eventually reaches 1. Return false if it loops endlessly in a cycle without ever reaching 1.

Conceptual Walkthrough:
• n = 19: 1^2 + 9^2 = 82 → 8^2 + 2^2 = 68 → 6^2 + 8^2 = 100 → 1^2 + 0^2 + 0^2 = 1 (Happy!) → true
• n = 2: 2 → 4 → 16 → 37 → 58 → 89 → 145 → 42 → 20 → 4 (Caught in loop: 4 repeats!) → false

2. 🧠 How Do I Recognize This Pattern?

Each number produces exactly ONE deterministic next number: x → getNext(x) ↓ The search space is finite (numbers do not grow to infinity) ↓ A finite graph with 1 outgoing edge per node MUST end in a cycle ↓ Pattern: Implicit Linked List Cycle Detection → Floyd's Fast & Slow Pointers

3 Quick Clues in Future Problems:

  • Deterministic Single-Step Transition: State A always leads to State B.
  • Infinite Loop Warning: The problem mentions "repeats endlessly in a cycle".
  • Implicit Pointer Problem: You don't need a ListNode class to use linked list pointer algorithms.

3. Intuition: How We Discover the Solution

Step 1 — Why Numbers Can't Grow to Infinity:
Could a number keep getting bigger forever? Take the largest 3-digit number 999: its sum of squares is 81 + 81 + 81 = 243 (smaller than 999). Even for a 10-digit number like 1,999,999,999, the next value is at most 730. Numbers always collapse into a bounded range [1, 730].

Step 2 — The State Machine:
Because the values are trapped in a finite range [1, 730], following the transitions must eventually repeat a number we have seen before (Pigeonhole Principle). There are only two possible outcomes:

  1. We reach 1 (which loops to 1 forever: 1 → 1 → 1).
  2. We enter a closed cycle of other numbers (e.g., 4 → 16 → ... → 4).

Step 3 — Deriving Floyd's Algorithm (O(1) Space):
We can detect if a cycle contains 1 without storing past numbers in a Hash Set by using two runners:

  • slow advances 1 step at a time: slow = getNext(slow)
  • fast advances 2 steps at a time: fast = getNext(getNext(fast))
  • If there is a cycle, fast will lap slow and they will meet. If they meet at 1, it's happy; if they meet at any other number, it's an unhappy loop.

4. The Starting Approach: Hash Set Tracking

Idea: Store every generated number in a Hash Set. If n == 1, return true. If n is already in the set, we entered a loop → return false.

def isHappyHashSet(n: int) -> bool:
    seen = set()
    while n != 1 and n not in seen:
        seen.add(n)
        n = getNext(n)
    return n == 1

Complexity: Time: O(log N) | Space: O(log N) to store seen numbers.

Why We Can Do Better: We can eliminate the Hash Set memory completely by using two pointers.

5. Optimal Approach: Floyd's Fast & Slow Pointers

class Solution:
    def isHappy(self, n: int) -> bool:
        def getNext(num: int) -> int:
            total_sum = 0
            while num > 0:
                digit = num % 10
                total_sum += digit * digit
                num //= 10
            return total_sum

        # Fast starts 1 step ahead so the while condition (slow != fast) is initially true
        slow = n
        fast = getNext(n)

        while fast != 1 and slow != fast:
            slow = getNext(slow)              # Move 1 step
            fast = getNext(getNext(fast))   # Move 2 steps

        # If fast hit 1, it's happy; if slow == fast != 1, we caught an unhappy cycle
        return fast == 1
class Solution {
private:
    int getNext(int num) {
        int total = 0;
        while (num > 0) {
            int d = num % 10;
            total += d * d;
            num /= 10;
        }
        return total;
    }
public:
    bool isHappy(int n) {
        int slow = n, fast = getNext(n);
        while (fast != 1 && slow != fast) {
            slow = getNext(slow);
            fast = getNext(getNext(fast));
        }
        return fast == 1;
    }
};
class Solution {
    private int getNext(int num) {
        int total = 0;
        while (num > 0) {
            int d = num % 10;
            total += d * d;
            num /= 10;
        }
        return total;
    }
    public boolean isHappy(int n) {
        int slow = n, fast = getNext(n);
        while (fast != 1 && slow != fast) {
            slow = getNext(slow);
            fast = getNext(getNext(fast));
        }
        return fast == 1;
    }
}
var isHappy = function(n) {
    const getNext = (num) => {
        let total = 0;
        while (num > 0) {
            const d = num % 10;
            total += d * d;
            num = Math.floor(num / 10);
        }
        return total;
    };

    let slow = n, fast = getNext(n);
    while (fast !== 1 && slow !== fast) {
        slow = getNext(slow);
        fast = getNext(getNext(fast));
    }
    return fast === 1;
};

Key Line Explanation:

  • fast = getNext(n): fast is placed 1 step ahead so the loop condition slow != fast is true from the start.
  • fast != 1 and slow != fast: The loop stops when either fast hits 1 (Happy!) or fast collides with slow (Unhappy loop detected).

6. Detailed Step-by-Step Dry Runs

📋 Dry Run 1: Standard Happy Case (n = 19)
Iteration Slow Pointer (1 step) Fast Pointer (2 steps) Condition (fast != 1 && slow != fast) Decision / Meaning
Start 19 82 82 != 1 and 19 != 82 (True) Pointers not met, fast has not reached 1 → Advance
Step 1 82 100 (82 → 68 → 100) 100 != 1 and 82 != 100 (True) Advance again
Step 2 68 1 (100 → 1 → 1) fast == 1 → Loop Terminates! Fast reached 1 → Return true
📋 Dry Run 2: Multi-Digit Unhappy Number with Full Loop (n = 354)

Transition Chain for 354:
• 354 → 3^2 + 5^2 + 4^2 = 9 + 25 + 16 = 50
• 50 → 5^2 + 0^2 = 25 → 2^2 + 5^2 = 29 → 2^2 + 9^2 = 85 → 8^2 + 5^2 = 89
• 89 → 145 → 42 → 20 → 4 → 16 → 37 → 58 → 89 (Trapped in 8-node cycle!)

Step # Slow Value Fast Value Calculation for Fast (2 jumps) Check Condition
Init 354 50 getNext(354) = 50 50 != 1 && 354 != 50 (Continue)
1 50 29 50 → 25 → 29 29 != 1 && 50 != 29 (Continue)
2 25 89 29 → 85 → 89 89 != 1 && 25 != 89 (Continue)
3 29 42 89 → 145 → 42 42 != 1 && 29 != 42 (Continue)
4 85 4 42 → 20 → 4 4 != 1 && 85 != 4 (Continue)
5 89 37 4 → 16 → 37 37 != 1 && 89 != 37 (Continue)
6 145 89 37 → 58 → 89 89 != 1 && 145 != 89 (Continue)
7 42 42 89 → 145 → 42 slow == 42 && fast == 42 (COLLISION!)

Conclusion: slow and fast collide at node 42 without hitting 1. Loop exits → Returns false.

7. Complexity Derivation

Metric Complexity Derivation
Time Complexity O(log N) Processing digits takes time proportional to the number of digits in N, which is O(log10 N). After step 1, values drop to ≤ 730 where cycle detection completes in at most 20 constant steps. Total time = O(log N) + O(1) = O(log N).
Space Complexity O(1) Only two integer variables (slow and fast) are used. Zero memory allocated on the heap.

8. Edge Cases & Common Mistakes

Edge Case Why It Matters How Solution Handles It
n = 1 Smallest possible input; already happy. fast = getNext(1) = 1. While loop condition fast != 1 is false immediately → returns true.
n = 2^31 - 1 (Max Int) Largest possible 32-bit integer. Max digit square sum of 1,999,999,999 is 730. Instantly collapses into a small number without overflow.
⚠️ Top 2 Mistakes:
  1. Initializing slow = n, fast = n: The loop while slow != fast immediately aborts on line 1 before checking anything. fast must be initialized to getNext(n).
  2. String-based digit extraction: Doing str(n) and slicing creates unnecessary heap objects in every iteration. Use n % 10 and n //= 10.

9. Practice Test Cases (Try Yourself!)

🎯 Practice Case 1: Large Number with Expanding Step (n = 568)

Input: n = 568

Expected Output: false

What this tests: 568 → 25 + 36 + 64 = 125 → 1 + 4 + 25 = 30 → 9 → 81 → 65 → 61 → 37 → 58 ... Tests numbers that expand to multiple intermediate values before falling into the 4-cycle.

🎯 Practice Case 2: Smallest Single-Digit Happy Number > 1 (n = 7)

Input: n = 7

Expected Output: true

What this tests: 7 is the only single-digit number > 1 that is happy (7 → 49 → 97 → 130 → 10 → 1). It tests expanding from a single digit before collapsing to 1.

10. 🔄 If You See This → Think This

Deterministic state transition + Potential infinite loop ↓ Think: Floyd's Fast & Slow Pointers (O(1) Space)

Where else does this appear?

  • LeetCode 141 (Linked List Cycle): Standard loop detection in explicit node chains.
  • LeetCode 287 (Find the Duplicate Number): Array values acting as pointers in an implicit cycle graph.
🧠 Final Takeaway:
• Pattern: Implicit Cycle Detection (Two Pointers)
• Core Invariant: Digit square sums never exceed 730 for 32-bit ints; numbers must cycle or hit 1.
• Complexity: O(log N) Time, O(1) Space.

⏱️ 30-Second Recall: Treat getNext(n) as a linked list pointer. Advance slow by 1 step and fast by 2 steps. If fast == 1, return true. If slow == fast, a cycle occurred → return false.

11. Optional Deep Dives

🔍 Deep Dive 1: Mathematical Proof of Boundedness

For a number with d digits, the maximum possible sum of squared digits is d * 81.

  • 3 digits (up to 999): max sum is 3 * 81 = 243 < 999
  • 4 digits (up to 9999): max sum is 4 * 81 = 324 < 9999
  • 10 digits (up to 2 * 10^9): max sum is 1^2 + 9 * 81 = 730 << 2 * 10^9

For any number ≥ 1000, getNext(n) < n strictly decreases. The sequence is pulled into the finite range [1, 730]. In a finite set, an infinite sequence must repeat a state.

🔍 Deep Dive 2: The Magical Constant 4 (Number Theory Fact)

In base 10, mathematicians have proven that every single unhappy number eventually falls into the exact same 8-number cycle:

4 → 16 → 37 → 58 → 89 → 145 → 42 → 20 → 4

Hence, checking while n != 1 and n != 4: n = getNext(n) works, though Floyd's pointer algorithm is the universal pattern to demonstrate in interviews.

Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix

Complete Technical & Learning Notes: From Flatten Sorting to Min-Heap Multi-Way Merge and Binary Search on Value Domain.

1. What is Being Asked?

Given: An n x n matrix where each row and column is independently sorted in ascending order, and an integer k.

Goal: Return the k-th smallest element across the entire matrix (1-indexed sorted order).

Structural Invariants of the Matrix:
• Global Minimum: Strictly located at top-left: matrix[0][0]
• Global Maximum: Strictly located at bottom-right: matrix[n-1][n-1]
• Non-Sorted Diagonals: Diagonals are NOT sorted (e.g. matrix[1][0] can be larger than matrix[0][2]).

2. 🧠 How Do I Recognize This Pattern?

We need the K-th ranked element from a 2D sorted grid with O(1) space constraint ↓ The global search range is bounded: [low = matrix[0][0], high = matrix[n-1][n-1]] ↓ For any candidate 'mid', can we count elements ≤ mid efficiently? ↓ Because rows & cols are sorted, a Staircase Traversal counts ≤ mid in O(n) time! ↓ Pattern: Binary Search on Answer Range (Value Domain) + Staircase Counting

3 Clues That Point to This Pattern:

  • Sorted Rows and Columns: Matrix is sorted along both 1D axes, but flattening takes too much space.
  • Monotonic Rank Function: As candidate value mid increases, the count of elements ≤ mid increases monotonically.
  • Targeting the K-th element: Bounded numerical search space with efficient counting indicates Binary Search on Values.

3. Progressive Approaches (Brute → Better → Optimal)

Approach 1 (Brute Force): Flatten Matrix & Full Sort Time: O(n^2 log(n^2)) | Space: O(n^2)

1. Core Idea & Intuition

The most naive human approach ignores the 2D row/column sorting entirely. We extract all n x n numbers into a 1D array, sort the array, and return the item at index k - 1.

2. Multi-Language Code

class BruteForceSolution:
    def kthSmallest(self, matrix: list[list[int]], k: int) -> int:
        flat = []
        # Collect all n^2 elements
        for row in matrix:
            for val in row:
                flat.append(val)

        # Full sort over n^2 items
        flat.sort()
        return flat[k - 1]
class BruteForceSolution {
public:
    int kthSmallest(vector<vector<int>>& matrix, int k) {
        vector<int> flat;
        for (const auto& row : matrix) {
            for (int val : row) {
                flat.push_back(val);
            }
        }
        sort(flat.begin(), flat.end());
        return flat[k - 1];
    }
};
class BruteForceSolution {
    public int kthSmallest(int[][] matrix, int k) {
        int n = matrix.length;
        int[] flat = new int[n * n];
        int idx = 0;
        for (int r = 0; r < n; r++) {
            for (int c = 0; c < n; c++) {
                flat[idx++] = matrix[r][c];
            }
        }
        Arrays.sort(flat);
        return flat[k - 1];
    }
}
var kthSmallestBF = function(matrix, k) {
    const flat = [];
    for (const row of matrix) {
        for (const val of row) {
            flat.push(val);
        }
    }
    flat.sort((a, b) => a - b);
    return flat[k - 1];
};

3. Step-by-Step Dry Run (Matrix 3x3, k = 8)

matrix = [[1, 5, 9], [10, 11, 13], [12, 13, 15]], k = 8

  1. Flatten array: [1, 5, 9, 10, 11, 13, 12, 13, 15]
  2. Sort array: [1, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 13, 15]
  3. Index k - 1 = 7: flat[7] = 13. Output: 13.

4. Complexity & Inefficiency

• Time Complexity: O(n^2 log(n^2)) due to sorting n^2 numbers.

• Space Complexity: O(n^2) to hold the flattened array.

• Why we can do better: Completely ignores that rows and columns are already sorted, wasting massive time and memory.

Approach 2 (Better): Min-Heap Multi-Way Row Merge Time: O(k log min(k, n)) | Space: O(min(k, n))

1. Core Idea & Intuition

Notice that each row in the matrix is an already-sorted stream. This is identical to Merge K Sorted Lists:

  • Initialize a Min-Heap with the first element of each row: (matrix[r][0], r, 0) for r < min(n, k).
  • Pop the smallest element from the heap. This gives the globally next smallest element.
  • If the popped element has a right neighbor in the same row (col + 1 < n), push (matrix[r][col + 1], r, col + 1) into the heap.
  • Repeat k times. The k-th popped element is our answer!

2. Multi-Language Code

import heapq

class MinHeapSolution:
    def kthSmallest(self, matrix: list[list[int]], k: int) -> int:
        n = len(matrix)
        min_heap = []

        # Push first element of each row: (val, row, col)
        for r in range(min(n, k)):
            heapq.heappush(min_heap, (matrix[r][0], r, 0))

        # Pop smallest element k times
        for _ in range(k):
            val, r, c = heapq.heappop(min_heap)
            if c + 1 < n:
                heapq.heappush(min_heap, (matrix[r][c + 1], r, c + 1))

        return val
class MinHeapSolution {
public:
    int kthSmallest(vector<vector<int>>& matrix, int k) {
        int n = matrix.size();
        // Min-Heap storing tuple
        priority_queue<tuple<int, int, int>, 
                       vector<tuple<int, int, int>>, 
                       greater<tuple<int, int, int>>> minHeap;

        for (int r = 0; r < min(n, k); ++r) {
            minHeap.push({matrix[r][0], r, 0});
        }

        int val = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < k; ++i) {
            auto [v, r, c] = minHeap.top();
            minHeap.pop();
            val = v;

            if (c + 1 < n) {
                minHeap.push({matrix[r][c + 1], r, c + 1});
            }
        }
        return val;
    }
};
class MinHeapSolution {
    public int kthSmallest(int[][] matrix, int k) {
        int n = matrix.length;
        PriorityQueue<int[]> minHeap = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]));

        for (int r = 0; r < Math.min(n, k); r++) {
            minHeap.offer(new int[]{matrix[r][0], r, 0});
        }

        int val = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) {
            int[] top = minHeap.poll();
            val = top[0];
            int r = top[1], c = top[2];

            if (c + 1 < n) {
                minHeap.offer(new int[]{matrix[r][c + 1], r, c + 1});
            }
        }
        return val;
    }
}
var kthSmallestHeap = function(matrix, k) {
    const n = matrix.length;
    const minHeap = [];

    for (let r = 0; r < Math.min(n, k); r++) {
        minHeap.push([matrix[r][0], r, 0]);
    }
    minHeap.sort((a, b) => a[0] - b[0]);

    let val = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < k; i++) {
        const [v, r, c] = minHeap.shift();
        val = v;

        if (c + 1 < n) {
            minHeap.push([matrix[r][c + 1], r, c + 1]);
            minHeap.sort((a, b) => a[0] - b[0]);
        }
    }
    return val;
};

3. Step-by-Step Dry Run (Matrix 3x3, k = 3)

matrix = [[1, 5, 9], [10, 11, 13], [12, 13, 15]], k = 3

  1. Init Heap: [(1, r=0, c=0), (10, r=1, c=0), (12, r=2, c=0)]
  2. Pop 1 (val=1): Push next from row 0: (5, r=0, c=1). Heap: [(5, 0, 1), (10, 1, 0), (12, 2, 0)]
  3. Pop 2 (val=5): Push next from row 0: (9, r=0, c=2). Heap: [(9, 0, 2), (10, 1, 0), (12, 2, 0)]
  4. Pop 3 (val=9): 3rd pop reached → Return 9.

4. Complexity & Trade-offs

• Time Complexity: O(k log min(k, n)). Excellent when k is very small.

• Space Complexity: O(min(k, n)) to store heap elements.

• Why we can do better: If k ≈ n^2, time becomes O(n^2 log n) which is slower than binary search and uses extra heap memory.

Approach 3 (Optimal): Binary Search on Value Space with Staircase Counting

Time: O(n log(max - min)) | Space: O(1)

1. Core Idea & Intuition:
Instead of searching by matrix indices, we binary search over the numerical range between low = matrix[0][0] and high = matrix[n-1][n-1]. For each candidate mid, we count how many elements are ≤ mid in O(n) time by walking a staircase from the bottom-left corner.

2. Multi-Language Code:

class Solution:
    def kthSmallest(self, matrix: list[list[int]], k: int) -> int:
        n = len(matrix)
        low = matrix[0][0]
        high = matrix[n - 1][n - 1]

        # Helper: Counts elements <= mid in O(n) using staircase traversal
        def countLessEqual(mid: int) -> int:
            count = 0
            row, col = n - 1, 0  # Start at bottom-left corner
            
            while row >= 0 and col < n:
                if matrix[row][col] <= mid:
                    # If current <= mid, all cells above it in this column are also <= mid
                    count += row + 1
                    col += 1  # Advance to next column
                else:
                    row -= 1  # Move up to find smaller values
            return count

        # Binary search over the value domain [low, high]
        while low < high:
            mid = low + (high - low) // 2
            if countLessEqual(mid) < k:
                low = mid + 1   # Answer is strictly greater than mid
            else:
                high = mid      # mid could be our answer, keep it in range

        return low
class Solution {
private:
    int countLessEqual(const vector<vector<int>>& matrix, int mid, int n) {
        int count = 0;
        int row = n - 1, col = 0;
        while (row >= 0 && col < n) {
            if (matrix[row][col] <= mid) {
                count += row + 1;
                col++;
            } else {
                row--;
            }
        }
        return count;
    }
public:
    int kthSmallest(vector<vector<int>>& matrix, int k) {
        int n = matrix.size();
        int low = matrix[0][0], high = matrix[n - 1][n - 1];

        while (low < high) {
            int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
            if (countLessEqual(matrix, mid, n) < k) {
                low = mid + 1;
            } else {
                high = mid;
            }
        }
        return low;
    }
};
class Solution {
    private int countLessEqual(int[][] matrix, int mid, int n) {
        int count = 0;
        int row = n - 1, col = 0;
        while (row >= 0 && col < n) {
            if (matrix[row][col] <= mid) {
                count += row + 1;
                col++;
            } else {
                row--;
            }
        }
        return count;
    }

    public int kthSmallest(int[][] matrix, int k) {
        int n = matrix.length;
        int low = matrix[0][0], high = matrix[n - 1][n - 1];

        while (low < high) {
            int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
            if (countLessEqual(matrix, mid, n) < k) {
                low = mid + 1;
            } else {
                high = mid;
            }
        }
        return low;
    }
}
var kthSmallest = function(matrix, k) {
    const n = matrix.length;
    let low = matrix[0][0];
    let high = matrix[n - 1][n - 1];

    const countLessEqual = (mid) => {
        let count = 0;
        let row = n - 1, col = 0;
        while (row >= 0 && col < n) {
            if (matrix[row][col] <= mid) {
                count += row + 1;
                col++;
            } else {
                row--;
            }
        }
        return count;
    };

    while (low < high) {
        let mid = Math.floor(low + (high - low) / 2);
        if (countLessEqual(mid) < k) {
            low = mid + 1;
        } else {
            high = mid;
        }
    }
    return low;
};

4. Detailed Step-by-Step Dry Runs

📋 Dry Run 1: Standard Matrix (n = 3, k = 8)

  [10, 11, 13],
  [12, 13, 15] ]

4 13 14 13 count = 8 (all except 15) 8 < 8 (False) → high = mid [13, 13]

Termination: low == high == 13. Output = 13.

📋 Dry Run 2: Large 4x4 Matrix with Multiple Duplicate Values (n = 4, k = 11)

Matrix:

  [ 5,  8, 12, 16],
  [ 8, 12, 15, 20],
  [11, 15, 18, 25] ]

Sorted flat view of all 16 items: [2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 8, 10, 11, 12, 12, 15, 15, 16, 18, 20, 25].

Pass Low High Mid Staircase Count Steps Total ≤ mid Decision Next Bounds
1 2 25 13 Col 0 (r=3 → +4), Col 1 (r=2 → +3), Col 2 (r=1 → +2), Col 3 (r=0 → +1) 10 10 < 11 → low = mid + 1 [14, 25]
2 14 25 19 Col 0 (+4), Col 1 (+4), Col 2 (r=3 → +4), Col 3 (r=1 → +2) 14 14 ≥ 11 → high = mid [14, 19]
3 14 19 16 Col 0 (+4), Col 1 (+4), Col 2 (r=2 → +3), Col 3 (r=1 → +2) 13 13 ≥ 11 → high = mid [14, 16]
4 14 16 15 Col 0 (+4), Col 1 (+4), Col 2 (r=2 → +3), Col 3 (r=0 → +1) 12 12 ≥ 11 → high = mid [14, 15]

Termination: low == high == 15. Output = 15 (the 11th element).

5. Complexity Derivation & Common Pitfalls

Metric Complexity Derivation
Time Complexity O(n log(max - min)) Binary Search runs for log(max - min) iterations. In each iteration, countLessEqual() visits at most 2n cells (moving up/right). Total time = O(n log(max - min)).
Space Complexity O(1) Strictly constant memory: only scalar variables (low, high, mid, row, col) are used. Zero extra data structures created.
⚠️ Top 2 Mistakes to Avoid:
  1. Setting high = mid - 1 on count ≥ k: Unlike standard binary search looking for an exact integer target, mid might be the actual K-th smallest element. Setting high = mid - 1 would throw away the valid answer. Always use high = mid.
  2. Binary searching on row/column indices: Diagonal values are not sorted, making 2D coordinate binary search invalid. You must binary search across the value domain [matrix[0][0], matrix[n-1][n-1]].

6. Practice Test Cases (Try Yourself!)

🎯 Practice Case 1: Negative Numbers & Skewed Spread

Input: matrix = [[-10, -5, 0], [-4, -1, 3], [-2, 2, 7]], k = 4

Expected Output: -2

What this tests: Trace staircase traversal across negative value boundaries where low = -10 and high = 7.

🎯 Practice Case 2: Identical Grid Elements

Input: matrix = [[1, 1, 1], [1, 1, 1], [1, 1, 1]], k = 5

Expected Output: 1

What this tests: Range starts with low = 1, high = 1. Tests immediate loop termination when all elements are duplicates.

7. 🧠 Final Takeaway & 30-Second Recall

🧠 Quick Summary:
• Pattern: Binary Search on Value Domain + O(n) Staircase Counting.
• Key Invariant: countLessEqual(mid) is monotonic with respect to mid.
• Complexity: O(n log(max - min)) Time, O(1) Space.

⏱️ 30-Second Recall: Binary search on the value range between top-left and bottom-right. For each mid, count numbers ≤ mid in O(n) by starting at the bottom-left and moving up/right. If count < k, search higher (low = mid + 1); otherwise, narrow down (high = mid).

8. Optional Deep Dives

🔍 Deep Dive 1: Why is the final 'low' guaranteed to be a number IN the matrix?

A natural question: "We are binary searching continuous integers. What if low stops at a number that isn't actually in the matrix?"

Proof:

  1. If a candidate val is NOT in the matrix, countLessEqual(val) is identical to countLessEqual(val'), where val' is the closest smaller number that actually IS in the matrix.
  2. If countLessEqual(val) ≥ k, our code sets high = mid, shrinking the search range downwards toward val'.
  3. The algorithm narrows down to the smallest integer that satisfies count ≥ k. That boundary integer must be an actual number present in the matrix.

LeetCode 21 Easy Linked List / Two Pointers

Merge Two Sorted Lists

Balanced DSA Master Notes: In-place Pointer Relinking, Dummy Head Invariant, and Suffix Splice.

1. What is Being Asked?

Given: The heads of two sorted linked lists list1 and list2.

Goal: Merge the two lists into a single sorted linked list. The list should be made by splicing together the nodes of the first two lists.

Return: The head of the merged linked list.

Example Walkthrough:
• list1: 1 → 2 → 4
• list2: 1 → 3 → 4
• Merged Result: 1 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 4

Key Requirement: We do not create new nodes for existing numbers; we reuse existing list nodes by altering their next pointers in-place.

2. 🧠 How Do I Recognize This Pattern?

Two independent sorted streams that need to be unified into a single sorted stream ↓ At each step, the globally smallest remaining element is strictly at head(list1) or head(list2) ↓ Compare the two heads, attach the smaller one to our tail pointer, and advance that list ↓ Use a Dummy Node to eliminate edge-case checks for initializing the head ↓ Pattern: Two Pointers on Linked Lists (Dummy Head + In-Place Splicing)

3 Quick Clues in Future Problems:

  • Two or more sorted sequences: Merging sorted arrays, lists, or streams (Merge Sort core step).
  • Linked List construction: Whenever creating a new head from conditional choices, a dummy node avoids null pointer checks.
  • Unequal lengths: Once one list runs out, linked lists allow attaching the entire remaining chain in O(1) time via a single pointer assignment.

3. Progressive Approaches (Brute → Better → Optimal)

Approach 1 (Brute Force): Extract to Array, Sort, & Rebuild Nodes time: O((n + m) log(n + m)) | space: O(n + m)

1. Core Idea & Intuition

The most naive approach ignores that the lists are already sorted. We traverse both linked lists, dump all node values into an array, sort the array, and then allocate brand-new linked list nodes to form the merged result.

2. Multi-Language Code

class BruteForceSolution:
    def mergeTwoLists(self, list1: Optional[ListNode], list2: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        vals = []
        # Collect values from list1
        curr = list1
        while curr:
            vals.append(curr.val)
            curr = curr.next
            
        # Collect values from list2
        curr = list2
        while curr:
            vals.append(curr.val)
            curr = curr.next
            
        if not vals:
            return None
            
        vals.sort()
        
        # Rebuild brand new linked list
        head = ListNode(vals[0])
        tail = head
        for v in vals[1:]:
            tail.next = ListNode(v)
            tail = tail.next
            
        return head
class BruteForceSolution {
public:
    ListNode* mergeTwoLists(ListNode* list1, ListNode* list2) {
        vector<int> vals;
        while (list1) {
            vals.push_back(list1->val);
            list1 = list1->next;
        }
        while (list2) {
            vals.push_back(list2->val);
            list2 = list2->next;
        }
        if (vals.empty()) return nullptr;

        sort(vals.begin(), vals.end());
        ListNode* head = new ListNode(vals[0]);
        ListNode* tail = head;
        for (size_t i = 1; i < vals.size(); ++i) {
            tail->next = new ListNode(vals[i]);
            tail = tail->next;
        }
        return head;
    }
};
class BruteForceSolution {
    public ListNode mergeTwoLists(ListNode list1, ListNode list2) {
        List<Integer> vals = new ArrayList<>();
        while (list1 != null) {
            vals.add(list1.val);
            list1 = list1.next;
        }
        while (list2 != null) {
            vals.add(list2.val);
            list2 = list2.next;
        }
        if (vals.isEmpty()) return null;

        Collections.sort(vals);
        ListNode head = new ListNode(vals.get(0));
        ListNode tail = head;
        for (int i = 1; i < vals.size(); i++) {
            tail.next = new ListNode(vals.get(i));
            tail = tail.next;
        }
        return head;
    }
}
var mergeTwoListsBF = function(list1, list2) {
    const vals = [];
    while (list1) {
        vals.push(list1.val);
        list1 = list1.next;
    }
    while (list2) {
        vals.push(list2.val);
        list2 = list2.next;
    }
    if (vals.length === 0) return null;

    vals.sort((a, b) => a - b);
    const head = new ListNode(vals[0]);
    let tail = head;
    for (let i = 1; i < vals.length; i++) {
        tail.next = new ListNode(vals[i]);
        tail = tail.next;
    }
    return head;
};

3. Complexity & Inefficiency

• Time Complexity: time: O((n + m) log(n + m)) due to sorting.

• Space Complexity: space: O(n + m) to store array values and allocate brand-new nodes.

• Why we can do better: Both input lists are already sorted! Sorting from scratch throws away this structure and wastes memory on node re-allocation.

Approach 2 (Alternative): Elegant Recursion time: O(n + m) | space: O(n + m) stack

1. Core Idea & Intuition

Compare the heads of list1 and list2. Whichever head is smaller becomes the root of the merged list. Its next pointer is recursively set to the result of merging its remaining sublist with the other list.

2. Multi-Language Code

class RecursiveSolution:
    def mergeTwoLists(self, list1: Optional[ListNode], list2: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        # Base cases: if one list is empty, return the other
        if not list1:
            return list2
        if not list2:
            return list1

        if list1.val <= list2.val:
            list1.next = self.mergeTwoLists(list1.next, list2)
            return list1
        else:
            list2.next = self.mergeTwoLists(list1, list2.next)
            return list2
class RecursiveSolution {
public:
    ListNode* mergeTwoLists(ListNode* list1, ListNode* list2) {
        if (!list1) return list2;
        if (!list2) return list1;

        if (list1->val <= list2->val) {
            list1->next = mergeTwoLists(list1->next, list2);
            return list1;
        } else {
            list2->next = mergeTwoLists(list1, list2->next);
            return list2;
        }
    }
};
class RecursiveSolution {
    public ListNode mergeTwoLists(ListNode list1, ListNode list2) {
        if (list1 == null) return list2;
        if (list2 == null) return list1;

        if (list1.val <= list2.val) {
            list1.next = mergeTwoLists(list1.next, list2);
            return list1;
        } else {
            list2.next = mergeTwoLists(list1, list2.next);
            return list2;
        }
    }
}
var mergeTwoListsRecursive = function(list1, list2) {
    if (!list1) return list2;
    if (!list2) return list1;

    if (list1.val <= list2.val) {
        list1.next = mergeTwoListsRecursive(list1.next, list2);
        return list1;
    } else {
        list2.next = mergeTwoListsRecursive(list1, list2.next);
        return list2;
    }
};

3. Complexity & Trade-offs

• Time Complexity: time: O(n + m) as each node is visited once.

• Space Complexity: space: O(n + m) due to call stack frames.

• Trade-off: Extremely clean and concise, but risks Stack Overflow on very long lists ($N \ge 10^5$).

Approach 3 (Optimal): Iterative In-Place Splicing with Dummy Node

time: O(n + m) | space: O(1)

1. Core Idea & Intuition:
We maintain a dummy node to anchor the start of the merged list and a tail pointer pointing to the current end of the merged list. While both lists are non-empty, we compare list1.val and list2.val, attach the smaller node to tail.next, and advance that list's pointer. When one list is exhausted, we splice the entire remainder of the non-empty list in a single O(1) pointer link!

2. Multi-Language Code:

class Solution:
    def mergeTwoLists(self, list1: Optional[ListNode], list2: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        # Dummy node gives a stable reference to the head of the merged list
        dummy = ListNode(-1)
        tail = dummy

        # Compare and relink the smaller node
        while list1 and list2:
            if list1.val <= list2.val:
                tail.next = list1
                list1 = list1.next
            else:
                tail.next = list2
                list2 = list2.next
            tail = tail.next

        # HIGHLIGHT: Splice the remaining non-empty list in O(1) time
        tail.next = list1 if list1 else list2

        return dummy.next
class Solution {
public:
    ListNode* mergeTwoLists(ListNode* list1, ListNode* list2) {
        ListNode dummy(-1);
        ListNode* tail = &dummy;

        while (list1 && list2) {
            if (list1->val <= list2->val) {
                tail->next = list1;
                list1 = list1->next;
            } else {
                tail->next = list2;
                list2 = list2->next;
            }
            tail = tail->next;
        }

        tail->next = list1 ? list1 : list2;
        return dummy.next;
    }
};
class Solution {
    public ListNode mergeTwoLists(ListNode list1, ListNode list2) {
        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(-1);
        ListNode tail = dummy;

        while (list1 != null && list2 != null) {
            if (list1.val <= list2.val) {
                tail.next = list1;
                list1 = list1.next;
            } else {
                tail.next = list2;
                list2 = list2.next;
            }
            tail = tail.next;
        }

        tail.next = (list1 != null) ? list1 : list2;
        return dummy.next;
    }
}
var mergeTwoLists = function(list1, list2) {
    const dummy = new ListNode(-1);
    let tail = dummy;

    while (list1 && list2) {
        if (list1.val <= list2.val) {
            tail.next = list1;
            list1 = list1.next;
        } else {
            tail.next = list2;
            list2 = list2.next;
        }
        tail = tail.next;
    }

    tail.next = list1 || list2;
    return dummy.next;
};

Important Line Explanations:

  • dummy = ListNode(-1): Avoids writing separate logic for deciding which node becomes the real head. dummy.next will hold the final answer.
  • tail.next = list1 if list1 else list2: In an array, we must loop to copy leftover items. In a linked list, we simply point tail.next to the remaining chain in $O(1)$ operations.

4. Detailed Step-by-Step Dry Runs

📋 Dry Run 1: Interleaved List Nodes (list1 = [1, 2, 4], list2 = [1, 3, 4])
Step list1 Head list2 Head Comparison Action Taken Merged Chain Built
0 Node(1) Node(1) list1.val ≤ list2.val (1 ≤ 1) tail.next = list1; list1 = list1.next dummy → 1
1 Node(2) Node(1) list2.val < list1.val (1 < 2) tail.next = list2; list2 = list2.next dummy → 1 → 1
2 Node(2) Node(3) list1.val ≤ list2.val (2 ≤ 3) tail.next = list1; list1 = list1.next dummy → 1 → 1 → 2
3 Node(4) Node(3) list2.val < list1.val (3 < 4) tail.next = list2; list2 = list2.next dummy → 1 → 1 → 2 → 3
4 Node(4) Node(4) list1.val ≤ list2.val (4 ≤ 4) tail.next = list1; list1 = list1.next (None) dummy → 1 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4
5 None Node(4) list1 is exhausted! tail.next = list2 (Splice Node(4)) dummy → 1 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 4

Returned List: 1 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 4.

📋 Dry Run 2: Highly Unequal Lengths (list1 = [5, 10, 15, 20, 25], list2 = [2])
Step list1 Head list2 Head Action Merged Chain State
1 Node(5) Node(2) 2 < 5 → tail.next = list2; list2 = None dummy → 2
2 Node(5) None list2 is exhausted! → tail.next = list1 dummy → 2 → 5 → 10 → 15 → 20 → 25

Notice: The entire remaining chain [5, 10, 15, 20, 25] is linked in a single constant-time pointer step without looping through the remaining 5 nodes!

5. Complexity Derivation & Common Pitfalls

Metric Complexity Derivation
Time Complexity time: O(n + m) In each iteration of the while loop, exactly one node from either list1 or list2 is processed and appended. Total loop steps is at most $N + M$. The final remaining chain is spliced in $O(1)$. Total time is $O(n + m)$.
Space Complexity space: O(1) We only create a single dummy node and a tail pointer. Existing nodes are relinked in-place without allocating any extra memory.
⚠️ Top 2 Mistakes to Avoid:
  1. Forgetting to advance tail: Writing tail.next = list1; list1 = list1.next but forgetting tail = tail.next. This causes every new node to overwrite the same dummy.next slot.
  2. Allocating new ListNode instances unnecessarily: Creating new nodes inside the loop wastes memory and runtime. Always relink existing pointer references.

6. Practice Test Cases (Try Yourself!)

🎯 Practice Case 1: One List Completely Empty

Input: list1 = [], list2 = [0]

Expected Output: [0]

What this tests: Verifies that the while loop does not execute and the tail.next = list1 or list2 directly returns the non-empty list.

🎯 Practice Case 2: Completely Non-Overlapping Value Ranges

Input: list1 = [1, 2, 3], list2 = [7, 8, 9]

Expected Output: [1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 9]

What this tests: All elements of list1 are consumed first, followed by a single splice of list2 to the tail.

7. 🧠 Final Takeaway & 30-Second Recall

🧠 Quick Summary:
• Pattern: Two Pointers on Linked Lists (In-place Relinking).
• Key Invariant: dummy anchors the head; tail tracks the current end.
• Complexity: time: O(n + m), space: O(1).

⏱️ 30-Second Recall: Create a dummy node and a tail pointer. While both lists have nodes, attach the smaller node to tail.next and advance that list. When one list runs out, attach the remainder of the other list directly to tail.next in O(1) time. Return dummy.next.
